questions.stem: The germinal matrix of the nail bed is responsible for approximately what proportion of nail plate volume — a key point in nail bed reconstruction?

options.text: About 90%
About 10%
About 50%
0% (the sterile matrix produces all of it)

questions.explanation: The **germinal matrix produces ~90% of the nail plate volume**, so scarring/loss of the germinal matrix causes absence of nail growth. The **sterile matrix** adds only a thin layer to the undersurface of the nail, keeping it **adherent**; sterile matrix injury causes nail deformity/nonadherence rather than absence. This distinction drives whether a germinal or sterile matrix graft is needed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: The white arc (lunula) visible just distal to the eponychium represents:

options.text: The distal extent of the germinal matrix
The proximal border of the hyponychium
The nail vest (cuticle)
A subungual hematoma

questions.explanation: The **lunula** is the white arc distal to the eponychium and marks the **distal extent of the germinal matrix** (its opacity reflects the thicker, actively proliferating germinal cells). Distal to the lunula lies the sterile matrix. This landmark helps orient the surgeon to the germinal/sterile matrix boundary during nail bed surgery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: Which term refers to the skin distal to the nail bed (at the fingertip, sealing the space beneath the free nail edge)?

options.text: Hyponychium
Eponychium
Paronychium
Lunula

questions.explanation: The **hyponychium** is the skin/keratin junction **distal to the nail bed**, sealing beneath the free edge of the nail. The **eponychium** is the skin proximal to the nail (over the nail fold, producing the cuticle/nail vest), and the **paronychium** is the skin on each lateral side of the nail. The hyponychium has the **highest density of lymphatics of any dermal area in the body**, helping resist infection at this exposed site.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: What produces the 'shine' of the nail plate?

options.text: The dorsal roof of the nail fold
The sterile matrix
The hyponychium
The lunula

questions.explanation: The **dorsal roof of the nail fold produces the shine** on the dorsal surface of the nail. This is relevant to reconstruction (e.g., composite grafts must include the dorsal roof to restore a normal-appearing shiny nail). The germinal matrix (floor of the nail fold) makes most of the nail substance, while the sterile matrix keeps the nail adherent.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: Which dermal area of the body has the greatest density of lymphatics, aiding resistance to infection?

options.text: The hyponychium
The palmar skin
The dorsal hand skin
The eponychium

questions.explanation: The **hyponychium contains the greatest density of lymphatics of any dermal area in the body**, which helps deter infection at this frequently exposed and contaminated fingertip location. This robust lymphatic drainage is one reason distal fingertip/hyponychial injuries, despite exposure, resist deep infection relatively well.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: Nail bed lacerations are classified into four main patterns (in order of frequency). Which is correct?

options.text: Simple laceration, stellate laceration, severe crush, avulsion
Avulsion, crush, stellate, simple
Burn, laceration, tumor, congenital
Subungual hematoma only

questions.explanation: Nail bed trauma is classified as **simple laceration, stellate laceration, severe crush, and avulsion** — occurring in that order of frequency. A **subungual hematoma** is a fifth category. The crush component determines how much nail bed can be primarily repaired versus needs grafting, and the most distal nail bed (over the tuft) is the most commonly injured.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A patient has a painful subungual hematoma involving ~30% of the nail, an intact nail, and no displaced fracture. Appropriate management is:

options.text: Nail trephination (decompression) after surgical prep, leaving the nail in place
Immediate nail removal and formal nail bed exploration in all cases
No treatment — hematomas never need drainage
Amputation of the fingertip

questions.explanation: A symptomatic **subungual hematoma with an intact nail** is treated by **trephination (decompression)** for pain relief; the nail is left in place if largely adherent. Surgical prep before trephination reduces bacterial inoculation of the subungual space. Historically, hematomas involving >~25–50% of the nail prompted nail removal and repair, but current evidence supports simple trephination even for larger hematomas when the nail and its margins are intact.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: When repairing a nail bed laceration, which suture material is typically recommended?

options.text: Fine absorbable suture such as 7-0 chromic, placed under loupe magnification
4-0 nylon
2-0 silk
Steel wire

questions.explanation: Nail bed lacerations are repaired with **fine absorbable suture (e.g., 7-0 chromic) under loupe magnification** and tourniquet control, with conservative debridement. The absorbable suture avoids the need for removal from the delicate nail bed. **Tissue adhesive (2-octyl cyanoacrylate) is an alternative** for simple lacerations. Meticulous approximation minimizes scar and subsequent nail deformity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: After nail bed repair, replacing the native nail (or a substitute) under the nail fold serves what primary purpose?

options.text: It stents the nail fold open (preventing scar adhesion/synechiae between the dorsal roof and matrix) and molds the repaired bed
It provides the entire tensile strength of the repair
It permanently reattaches as the new nail
It is purely cosmetic with no functional benefit

questions.explanation: Replacing the nail (or silicone/nonadherent gauze) under the nail fold **stents the fold open, preventing scar formation/adhesion between the dorsal roof and the germinal matrix (which would cause pterygium/nail deformity), and molds the repaired nail bed**. A drainage hole is made in the replaced nail to prevent hematoma. The nail is secured with a suture through the nail fold or hyponychium.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A child presents with an apparent 'mallet-like' distal phalanx injury; the nail plate is displaced dorsally out of the proximal nail fold, and radiographs show a physeal fracture. This is a:

options.text: Seymour fracture — an open physeal fracture with interposed nail matrix requiring irrigation, matrix extraction, reduction, and nail-bed repair
A simple subungual hematoma
A benign nail avulsion needing no surgery
A glomus tumor

questions.explanation: A **Seymour fracture** is an open physeal (Salter-Harris) fracture of the distal phalanx in children, with the **nail plate lying superficial to (out of) the nail fold** and germinal matrix interposed in the fracture. It requires **irrigation/antibiotics, removal of the interposed matrix, fracture reduction, nail-bed repair, and nail replacement** as a stent. Missed injuries risk infection/osteomyelitis and growth disturbance — always rule it out when a nail bed injury has an underlying physeal fracture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: For a defect of the STERILE matrix that cannot be closed primarily, the preferred graft is:

options.text: A split-thickness sterile matrix graft (from adjacent uninjured nail bed or a toe), which causes no donor-site deformity
A full-thickness germinal matrix graft
A composite osteocutaneous graft
Leaving the defect to heal by secondary intention

questions.explanation: Sterile matrix defects are best resurfaced with a **split-thickness sterile matrix graft** — harvested from adjacent uninjured nail bed or a toe — because a thin split-thickness graft **leaves no donor-site nail deformity**. Small full-thickness losses left to secondary healing scar and deform the nail. Full-thickness grafts are reserved for when the surrounding perionychium is also missing.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: To reconstruct a defect of the GERMINAL matrix (which otherwise leaves a bald spot/absent nail), the graft must be:

options.text: A germinal matrix graft (commonly full-thickness, often from a toe), since split germinal grafts do not reliably produce nail
A split-thickness sterile matrix graft
A skin graft alone
Any dermal filler

questions.explanation: The germinal matrix generates nail substance, so replacing a germinal defect requires a **germinal matrix graft** — typically a full-thickness germinal matrix graft from a **toe** (commonly the second toe, which approximates fingernail width). Split-thickness or sterile grafts will not reliably regenerate nail. Patients are counseled about the expected donor toenail deformity and potentially imperfect fingernail result.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: If a nail bed avulsion involves more than ~50% of the nail bed (too large to harvest a split-thickness graft from the same finger), the graft should be harvested from:

options.text: An adjacent finger or a toe (patients often prefer a toe donor)
The palm
The forearm
The dorsal hand skin

questions.explanation: When the same finger lacks enough undamaged nail bed (defect >~50%), a split-thickness nail bed graft is taken from an **adjacent finger or a toe**. **Toe donors are often preferred** (and clinically better) to avoid risking a second fingernail deformity. The donor nail is removed, a thin (~0.010-inch) split-thickness sterile matrix graft is harvested, and the donor nail is replaced.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: After a nail is removed for nail bed repair, the NEW nail typically begins to grow again after a delay of about:

options.text: 3 to 4 weeks
3 to 4 days
6 months
1 year

questions.explanation: After nail removal, new nail growth resumes after a **delay of ~3–4 weeks** (a lag phase). Nail then grows at roughly **1 mm per week (≈0.1 mm/day)**, and the leading edge with its characteristic bulge reaches the fingertip at about **6–9 months** after injury. If the proximal nail was left in place, growth continues without delay. Toenails grow about **four times more slowly** than fingernails.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: The regenerating nail after a nail bed repair is expected to reach the fingertip approximately how long after injury?

options.text: 6 to 9 months
2 weeks
6 to 8 weeks
2 to 3 years

questions.explanation: The new nail's leading edge reaches the distal fingertip at about **6–9 months** after injury (after the ~3–4 week initial lag and ~1 mm/week growth). Patients should be counseled on this timeline and warned that some residual nail deformity can occur despite meticulous repair.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A 'hook nail' deformity after a fingertip amputation results from:

options.text: Loss of distal bony support with the nail bed curving palmarly over the shortened phalanx (often from closing the tip under tension over a nail bed left too long)
Scarring of the dorsal roof of the nail fold
A germinal matrix graft placed too proximally
Chronic Candida infection

questions.explanation: A **hook nail** develops when the distal phalanx bony support is lost and the **nail bed curves palmarly (volarly) over the end of the shortened bone** — often because a nail bed extending beyond the bone was pulled volarly during tip closure. Prevention: when bone is deficient, **shorten the nail bed to the end of the remaining bony support** rather than tension the pulp over an unsupported nail bed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A split nail with a pterygium (scar band bridging the nail fold) is most often caused by:

options.text: A longitudinal scar/ridge in the germinal (or sterile) matrix — scar produces no nail cells, so a split results
A subungual glomus tumor
Onychomycosis
A normal variant requiring no treatment

questions.explanation: A **split nail** arises from a **longitudinal scar/ridge in the germinal or sterile matrix**; because scar tissue produces no nail, the nail splits along the scar. A **pterygium** forms when scar bridges the dorsal roof to the matrix (adhesion). Reconstruction requires excising the scar and grafting matrix (germinal matrix graft from a toe for germinal defects), and stenting the nail fold open.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A patient develops a persistently NONADHERENT nail (onycholysis) after a sterile matrix injury. The best reconstructive option is:

options.text: Excise the scarred sterile matrix and place a split-thickness sterile matrix graft
Germinal matrix graft from a toe
Amputation of the fingertip
DIP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: Nonadherence results from **sterile matrix scarring** (the sterile matrix normally keeps the nail adherent). Reconstruction excises the scar and resurfaces with a **split-thickness sterile matrix graft** (from an adjacent nail bed or toe), which restores adherence without donor deformity. A germinal matrix graft is needed only for germinal (nail-production) defects, not adherence problems.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: The most common perionychial bacterial infection is acute paronychia. Which organism is most frequently isolated?

options.text: Staphylococcus aureus
Candida albicans
Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Eikenella corrodens

questions.explanation: **Acute paronychia** (infection of the paronychial fold, often after a hangnail or minor trauma) is most commonly caused by **Staphylococcus aureus**. Treatment is drainage — lifting the paronychium off the nail (± partial nail removal if pus tracks beneath the nail edge) and warm soaks; antibiotics are added for cellulitis. Incisions in the eponychium are avoided (they may not heal and cause notching).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: CHRONIC paronychia (e.g., in a dishwasher/diabetic with recurrent nail-fold inflammation) is most commonly caused by:

options.text: Candida (fungal) organisms, often with repeated moisture exposure
Staphylococcus aureus
Streptococcus pyogenes
Mycobacterium marinum

questions.explanation: **Chronic paronychia** is most often caused by **Candida (fungus)** (and sometimes gram-negative organisms), seen in people with **frequent water exposure, diabetes, or immunocompromise**. Management targets moisture avoidance, topical/oral antifungals, and avoiding cuticle trauma/irritants; refractory cases are treated with **eponychial marsupialization (Keyser-Eaton)** — excising a crescent of the proximal nail fold to heal secondarily.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: During drainage of an acute paronychia, incisions in the EPONYCHIUM should be avoided because:

options.text: They often fail to heal primarily in the presence of infection and can leave an eponychial notch/deformity
They injure the flexor tendon
They cause carpal tunnel syndrome
They are always unnecessary and paronychia never needs any drainage

questions.explanation: The chapter cautions that **incisions in the eponychium frequently fail to heal primarily with infection present and can leave a notch or square-corner deformity**. Adequate drainage of a paronychia is achieved by lifting the paronychium off the nail (± removing the undermined portion of nail), not by incising the eponychium — the author states none required an eponychial incision for drainage.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: The MOST COMMON perionychial infection overall is:

options.text: Fungal (onychomycosis / chronic fungal infection) of the subungual area
Acute bacterial paronychia
Felon
Herpetic whitlow

questions.explanation: Perionychial **subungual fungal infections (onychomycosis / chronic fungal infection) are the most common infections in the hand**. Treatment may include topical/oral antifungals, and for exposure/debulking of subungual fungus, nail removal (allowing the nail to regrow). Superimposed bacterial infection can occur. This contrasts with acute bacterial paronychia (Staph aureus), which is common but not the most frequent perionychial infection.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: The MOST COMMON tumor that deforms the nail bed is:

options.text: A DIP joint ganglion (often called a mucous cyst)
Glomus tumor
Subungual melanoma
Squamous cell carcinoma

questions.explanation: A **DIP joint ganglion ('mucous cyst')** is the **most common tumor deforming the nail bed**. It communicates with the DIP joint via an osteophyte (Kleinert). If it lies between the periosteum and nail floor, it pushes the nail up (ridged/ragged nail); if within the nail fold dorsally, it presses down (grooving/thinning). Treatment is **excision of the DIP osteophyte and cyst drainage** — osteophyte removal is key to preventing recurrence, and cyst-wall excision is unnecessary (and risks nail deformity).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A patient has exquisite point tenderness beneath the nail, a bluish subungual discoloration, and severe pain reproduced by cold. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.text: Glomus tumor
Subungual melanoma
Pyogenic granuloma
Onychomycosis

questions.explanation: A **glomus tumor** arises from the glomus body (thermoregulatory arteriovenous structure); ~50% occur subungually. The classic triad is **severe pain, pinpoint tenderness, and cold sensitivity**, often with a bluish subungual discoloration. An **ice-cube test** can reproduce the pain; **MRI or ultrasound** localizes it. Treatment is nail removal and complete surgical excision (examine for multiple tumors).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: The MOST COMMON malignant tumor of the perionychium is:

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma
Subungual melanoma
Basal cell carcinoma
Kaposi sarcoma

questions.explanation: **Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor of the perionychium** (though still uncommon), sometimes associated with HPV or chronic irritation/radiation. It may appear as a raised, red, sometimes verrucous or ulcerated lesion and can masquerade as chronic infection or a wart — persistent/atypical perionychial lesions warrant biopsy. Subungual melanoma is rarer but more lethal.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: In the ABCDEF guidelines for subungual melanoma, the 'E' (extension of pigment onto the surrounding nail-fold skin) corresponds to which classic clinical sign?

options.text: Hutchinson sign
Terry Thomas sign
Wartenberg sign
Froment sign

questions.explanation: In the **ABCDEF** guidelines for subungual melanoma, **'E' = Extension of pigment onto the eponychium/paronychium (surrounding nail-fold skin), the Hutchinson sign** — a worrisome feature for melanoma. The mnemonic also includes Age/African-Asian-Hispanic, Band (Brown-black, Breadth ≥3 mm, irregular Border), Change/lack of nail-plate change, Digit (thumb/great toe/single digit/dominant hand), and Family/personal history. Suspicious lesions require biopsy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A patient has a longitudinal pigmented band in one fingernail. To help distinguish a subungual hematoma from a nevus/melanoma at the bedside, one can:

options.text: Scratch/mark the nail at the proximal and distal edges of the pigment and watch whether the pigment moves distally with the nail (hematoma) or stays fixed (matrix lesion)
Apply an ice cube and check for pain
Perform the Watson shift test
Measure grip strength

questions.explanation: Marking the nail at the proximal/distal borders of the pigment and observing over ~3 weeks distinguishes the source: **a subungual hematoma migrates distally with the growing nail (moving relative to the scratches), whereas a nevus/melanoma in the matrix stays fixed** (the scratches grow away from the pigment). A fixed band — especially a solitary band with Hutchinson sign — warrants biopsy. Subungual hematoma is actually the most common cause of subungual pigmentation in adults.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A rapidly growing, friable, bright-red mass protruding through the nail after a nail puncture is most likely a:

options.text: Pyogenic granuloma (treated with silver nitrate cautery; biopsy if persistent/recurrent)
Glomus tumor
Subungual melanoma
Mucous cyst

questions.explanation: A **pyogenic granuloma** is a rapidly growing, red, elevated, friable lesion of granulation-like tissue, often from a nail perforation/trauma. Treatment is usually **repeated silver nitrate cauterization** (or excision, which may need a nail bed graft). Because **amelanotic melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma can mimic it**, a **persistent or recurrent lesion should be biopsied**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: When exposing the nail bed proximally for repair, incisions at the eponychial corners should be made:

options.text: At 90-degree angles from the eponychial edge (perpendicular), to prevent notch deformity
At acute (30-degree) angles for cosmesis
In a curved arc across the eponychium
Directly through the germinal matrix

questions.explanation: Eponychial release incisions (to expose the proximal nail bed/germinal matrix) should be made **at 90-degree (perpendicular) angles from the eponychial fold**; angled incisions predispose to **notch/corner deformity** of the eponychium. The nail fold is later closed with fine suture (e.g., 6-0 nylon). Perpendicular incisions preserve the eponychial contour.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A fingertip amputation includes both bone and nail bed on the amputated part in a suitable clean injury. This piece can be used as a:

options.text: Composite graft (bone segment fixed to the phalanx, nail bed replaced), preserving length
Free vascularized toe transfer only
Split-thickness skin graft only
It must always be discarded

questions.explanation: When the amputated part contains **both bone and nail bed**, it can serve as a **composite (nonvascularized) graft** — the bone is fixated to the remaining phalanx and the nail bed replaced — to **preserve digit/nail length**. Composite grafting is more reliable in children. Alternatives include using just the amputated nail bed as a graft, V-Y advancement flaps, or (for suitable levels) revision amputation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: Which statement about late (secondary) reconstruction of the nail bed is most accurate?

options.text: Late reconstruction is commonly less successful than desired, so meticulous primary repair is preferable when possible
Late reconstruction reliably restores a perfectly normal nail
Primary repair is unnecessary because late reconstruction is superior
Nail bed scars always resolve spontaneously

questions.explanation: The chapter stresses that **late reconstruction of the nail bed is commonly not as successful as surgeon or patient would like** — scar in the nail bed prevents normal nail growth and grafts have imperfect results. This underscores the value of **careful primary repair** at the time of injury. When reconstruction is needed, thorough scar excision and appropriate (split sterile or full germinal) grafting, usually from a toe, are used.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: For a DIP ganglion causing nail deformity, the KEY step to prevent recurrence is:

options.text: Debridement/excision of the offending DIP osteophyte (cyst-wall excision is unnecessary and risks nail deformity)
Complete excision of the entire nail bed
Amputation of the distal phalanx
Repeated needle aspiration alone

questions.explanation: The **DIP osteophyte drives the ganglion**, so **osteophyte debridement is the key to preventing recurrence**; simply draining the cyst through a T/H-shaped incision plus removing the osteophyte gives low recurrence and less nail deformity than excising the cyst wall (which risks nail bed injury). The nail deformity typically resolves once the osteophyte is removed and the cyst decompressed. An actively draining cyst should be treated for infection first.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: Toenail growth compared with fingernail growth is approximately:

options.text: Four times slower
Four times faster
The same rate
Twice as fast

questions.explanation: **Toenails grow roughly four times more slowly than fingernails.** This is relevant when a toe is used as a donor for germinal/sterile matrix or composite grafts (slower regrowth at the donor) and when counseling on recovery timelines. Fingernails grow ~1 mm/week and reach the tip ~6–9 months after a nail bed injury.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A pigmented subungual nevus is discovered in a child's fingernail. The chapter's general recommendation is:

options.text: Consider incisional biopsy given the potential for malignant degeneration (with informed discussion; delaying until older is an option)
Ignore it permanently; nail nevi never require attention
Immediate ray amputation
Cauterize it with silver nitrate

questions.explanation: Because of the **potential for malignant degeneration within the nail bed**, the chapter generally recommends **incisional biopsy of subungual nevi**, with a discussion of options (observing for change and delaying biopsy until the child is older is also reasonable). If atypia is found, the involved nail bed is excised and reconstructed. Dermoscopy can help select which lesions to biopsy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A felon is:

options.text: A closed-space infection (abscess) of the distal pulp of the fingertip
An infection of the proximal nail fold
A fungal infection of the nail plate
A benign nail bed tumor

questions.explanation: A **felon** is a **closed-space pyogenic infection (abscess) of the distal pulp** of the fingertip, where fibrous septa create multiple small compartments — causing intense throbbing pain and pressure (and risk of skin/bone necrosis if untreated). Treatment is prompt **incision and drainage** of the abscess with septa release, plus antibiotics (commonly Staph aureus). It is distinct from paronychia (nail-fold infection).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: During incision and drainage of a paronychia/nail abscess, if a tourniquet is used, the finger should NOT be exsanguinated by tight wrapping because:

options.text: Exsanguination can push infection proximally
It would injure the germinal matrix
It prevents adequate anesthesia
It causes a hook nail

questions.explanation: The finger should **not be exsanguinated** before drainage because compressing an infected digit can **drive purulent material/infection proximally** along tissue planes. Instead, the tourniquet is applied after simple elevation. (Local anesthesia may also be incomplete because of the acidic infected tissue.) Adequate open drainage plus warm soaks is the mainstay, with antibiotics for cellulitis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: Eponychial marsupialization (Keyser-Eaton) for refractory chronic paronychia involves:

options.text: Excising a 3–4 mm crescent of the proximal nail fold (skin and dorsal roof) down to the nail, preserving the cuticle and germinal matrix, and healing by secondary intention
Removing the entire nail bed
Fusing the DIP joint
Amputating the fingertip

questions.explanation: **Eponychial marsupialization** removes a **3–4 mm crescent of the proximal nail fold (skin and dorsal roof) down to the nail**, taking care **not to injure the germinal matrix** (and preserving the cuticle), then lets it heal secondarily — draining the chronically infected pouch. It is reserved for **refractory chronic (usually Candida) paronychia** after moisture-avoidance and antifungal measures fail.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: Which is the best initial reconstructive choice for a small, full-thickness sterile matrix defect where adjacent nail bed is available?

options.text: Split-thickness sterile matrix graft from the adjacent uninjured nail bed
Leaving it to heal by secondary intention
A full-thickness germinal matrix graft from the toe
A cross-finger flap

questions.explanation: A small full-thickness **sterile matrix defect** is best resurfaced with a **split-thickness sterile matrix graft harvested from adjacent uninjured nail bed** (no donor deformity from a thin graft). Leaving full-thickness losses to secondary healing causes scarring/deformity. Germinal matrix grafts are for germinal defects; flaps are for soft-tissue/skin coverage, not matrix resurfacing.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A composite toenail graft (including germinal matrix, sterile matrix, and dorsal roof) for total nail reconstruction is typically harvested from which donor to best match fingernail width?

options.text: The second toe
The great toe (hallux)
The fifth toe
An adjacent finger

questions.explanation: For composite toenail grafts, the **second toe** is preferred because it is **approximately the width of a fingernail** and produces a more acceptable donor result than sacrificing the great toenail (which would leave a significant deformity). Patients are counseled about expected donor toenail deformity and potentially suboptimal fingernail outcome. The 3rd–5th toes usually lack sufficient germinal matrix.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: Subungual melanoma most commonly involves which digits, and what is a notable epidemiologic feature?

options.text: The thumb and great toe; it comprises a disproportionately larger share of melanomas in patients with darker skin (African American, Asian, Hispanic)
The small finger only; it is exclusive to fair-skinned patients
It never occurs in the thumb
It is always painless and easily diagnosed

questions.explanation: **Subungual melanoma most commonly involves the thumb and great toe.** Although it is only ~0.7–3.5% of all melanomas and occurs across all groups, it makes up a **much larger proportion of melanomas in African American, Asian, and Hispanic patients** (who have lower cutaneous melanoma rates). Hand/foot melanomas carry a poorer prognosis, and delayed diagnosis (mimicking hematoma/infection) is common — a solitary Hutchinson-positive band warrants biopsy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: For a fingertip soft-tissue amputation through the sterile matrix with adequate remaining bone and palmar tissue, a common local coverage option is:

options.text: V-Y advancement flap(s)
Free medial femoral condyle flap
Groin flap
Toe-to-hand transfer

questions.explanation: **V-Y advancement flaps** (volar or bilateral) are workhorse local flaps for fingertip amputations, advancing sensate pulp tissue to cover the defect while preserving length. They can be combined with nail bed grafts to reconstruct the tip. Larger/more complex reconstructions may use cross-finger or thenar flaps; microsurgical transfers are reserved for major tissue loss.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST accurate statement about the perionychium?

options.text: Scarring of the STERILE matrix leads to complete absence of the nail
Scarring of the germinal matrix can lead to absence of the nail
The sterile matrix keeps the nail adherent to the nail bed
The germinal matrix produces about 90% of the nail volume

questions.explanation: The false statement swaps the roles: **germinal matrix scarring causes ABSENCE of nail (it makes ~90% of the nail), whereas sterile matrix scarring causes nail DEFORMITY/nonadherence, not absence.** The other statements are correct: germinal scarring → absent nail, the sterile matrix maintains adherence, and the germinal matrix produces ~90% of nail volume.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A patient asks why the nail should always be inspected (and radiographs obtained) with a nail bed injury. The best rationale is:

options.text: There is a high rate of associated distal phalanx fracture, which changes management (e.g., Seymour fracture, need for reduction/fixation)
To measure grip strength
To assess the scapholunate interval
Radiographs are never indicated for nail injuries

questions.explanation: Nail bed injuries have a **high rate of associated distal phalanx fracture**, so **radiographs (AP/lateral) are obtained**. Identifying a fracture (especially a physeal Seymour fracture with interposed matrix in children) changes management — the fracture may need reduction/fixation and the matrix extraction/repair. Missing this risks malunion, growth disturbance, or osteomyelitis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: During nail bed repair, why is only CONSERVATIVE debridement of the nail bed recommended?

options.text: The nail bed does not regenerate lost matrix, so aggressive debridement creates a permanent defect and nail deformity
The nail bed heals better if left completely unrepaired
Debridement causes carpal tunnel syndrome
The nail bed regrows any amount of removed tissue within a week

questions.explanation: Nail matrix does not regenerate — **removed matrix leaves a permanent gap that scars and deforms the nail** — so debridement must be **conservative**. The surgeon should preserve and reapproximate even small adherent nail-bed fragments ('when in doubt, close rather than leave a defect from aggressive debridement'). Meticulous approximation (7-0 absorbable, loupe magnification) minimizes scar.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: The dorsal roof of the nail fold is important to include when reconstructing a totally absent nail with a composite graft because:

options.text: It produces the nail's shine and a nail fold pouch, contributing to a normal-appearing nail
It produces 90% of the nail volume
It keeps the nail adherent
It has no reconstructive value

questions.explanation: The **dorsal roof produces the nail's shine** and forms the nail-fold pouch, so a **composite toenail graft includes germinal matrix, sterile matrix, AND dorsal roof** to reconstruct a normal-looking nail. (Germinal matrix makes ~90% of nail volume; sterile matrix maintains adherence — a complete reconstruction needs all three components.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: The nail plate itself (as opposed to the perionychium) contributes to hand function primarily by:

options.text: Protecting the fingertip, aiding fine pinch/tactile sensation, and helping regulate peripheral circulation
Producing sweat
Providing the main blood supply to the finger
Serving as the insertion of the flexor tendon

questions.explanation: The nail **protects the fingertip, provides counter-pressure that enhances fine pinch and tactile sensation, aids in picking up small objects and scratching, and contributes to regulation of peripheral circulation/thermoregulation**. Preserving or reconstructing the nail after injury therefore has both functional and cosmetic value, not merely appearance.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A pincer nail deformity (transverse over-curvature/tubing of the nail) can be treated by:

options.text: Elevating the lateral edges of the nail bed and supporting them (e.g., with dermal grafts/bone graft) to flatten the transverse curve
Complete permanent nail ablation in all cases as first-line
A germinal matrix graft from the great toe only
DIP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: A **pincer nail** is a transverse over-curvature ('tubing') of the nail that pinches the underlying tissue. Correction involves **removing the nail, elevating the constricted lateral nail bed edges, and supporting/widening them** (dermal grafts, and sometimes bone graft/tissue under the elevated bed) to restore a flatter transverse contour. Underlying causes (e.g., osteophytes, prior injury) are addressed; ablation is reserved for refractory/severe cases.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: The nail bed's arterial supply is derived mainly from:

options.text: Dorsal branches of the volar (proper) digital arteries
The posterior interosseous artery
The dorsal metacarpal arteries alone
The princeps pollicis artery only

questions.explanation: The **nail bed is supplied by dorsal branches of the volar (proper palmar) digital arteries** (the two terminal digital arteries), with venous drainage into the proximal nail bed/fold and abundant lymphatics paralleling the veins. This rich distal blood supply supports healing of nail bed repairs and grafts. Preserving the digital vessels is important in fingertip reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: For a simple, clean nail bed laceration in a cooperative patient, an accepted alternative to suture repair that reduces operative time is:

options.text: Repair with tissue adhesive (2-octyl cyanoacrylate)
Leaving it open without any approximation
Staple closure of the nail bed
Immediate germinal matrix grafting

questions.explanation: For **simple nail bed lacerations**, studies support repair with **tissue adhesive (2-octyl cyanoacrylate)** as an accepted, faster alternative to fine suture, with comparable cosmetic outcomes. Regardless of method, the nail (or a substitute) is replaced under the nail fold as a stent. More complex stellate/crush/avulsion injuries still generally warrant sutured repair or grafting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: A ganglion (DIP mucous cyst) that is actively DRAINING through the skin should be managed by:

options.text: Treating the infection/achieving skin closure first, then definitively excising the osteophyte before it ruptures again — not operating while actively draining
Immediate excision while draining, regardless of infection
Ignoring it, as draining cysts never cause problems
Amputating the digit

questions.explanation: An **actively draining DIP ganglion should NOT be surgically excised while draining**, due to the increased risk of septic arthritis and permanent deformity. The correct sequence is **antibiotics until the skin closes**, then **definitive osteophyte removal (± cyst drainage) before it ruptures again**. A draining cyst is a portal into the DIP joint, so infection control precedes reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 9 (The Perionychium)

questions.stem: Dupuytren disease is best characterized as:

options.text: The most common heritable fibrotic disease, causing progressive palmar/digital fascial fibrosis and flexion contractures
An infectious tenosynovitis of the flexor tendons
A primary degenerative arthritis of the finger joints
A malignant fibrous tumor of the palm

questions.explanation: **Dupuytren disease (DD) is the most common heritable fibrotic disorder**, a chronic condition producing progressive fibrosis of the palmar/digital fascia and, in some, finger flexion contractures. It is driven by a 'two-hit' (genetic predisposition + local factors) process, with myofibroblasts and abnormal collagen (notably type III) as key players. Most affected people never develop significant contractures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The key cellular effector responsible for the contractile force in Dupuytren tissue is the:

options.text: Myofibroblast
Osteoclast
Mast cell
Schwann cell

questions.explanation: The **myofibroblast** — a fibroblast expressing alpha-smooth-muscle actin — generates the contractile force in Dupuytren nodules/cords. Myofibroblasts differentiate under mechanical tension and TGF-β stimulation, sense and remodel matrix tension, and dedifferentiate when tension is lost. Their density parallels macrophage density in nodules, reflecting the inflammatory-fibrotic interplay.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which collagen abnormality is characteristic of Dupuytren tissue compared with normal palmar fascia?

options.text: Persistently increased type III collagen (30–40% of nodule collagen vs <5% normally)
Complete absence of type I collagen
Replacement of collagen with elastin
A total loss of all collagen

questions.explanation: Dupuytren tissue shows an abnormal, **persistent elevation of type III collagen** — contributing ~30–40% of nodule collagen and ~20–30% of cord collagen, versus <5% in normal fascia. Unlike normal wound healing (where type III rises then falls with scar maturation), this elevation persists indefinitely. Type III collagen contracts faster than type I, and the type III:I ratio is highest in early (proliferative) disease.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which of the following is a recognized ECTOPIC manifestation associated with Dupuytren disease?

options.text: Ledderhose disease (plantar fibromatosis)
Carpal tunnel syndrome
de Quervain tenosynovitis
Kienböck disease

questions.explanation: Ectopic (extrapalmar) fibromatoses correlating with DD include **Ledderhose disease (plantar fibromatosis)**, **Peyronie disease** (penile tunica albuginea), **knuckle pads (Garrod pads)** on the dorsal finger joints, and **frozen shoulder**. Their presence is part of the 'Dupuytren diathesis' — a more aggressive, recurrence-prone phenotype.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The 'Dupuytren diathesis' describes a recurrence-prone phenotype. Which set of features is classically included?

options.text: Family history, onset younger than 50, Ledderhose disease, and knuckle pads (± bilateral disease)
Onset after age 70, unilateral disease, and diabetes only
Female sex and single-digit involvement
Absence of any family history

questions.explanation: The **diathesis** (Hueston) classically comprises **positive family history, young age at onset (<50), ectopic disease (Ledderhose, knuckle pads/Garrod pads, Peyronie), and bilateral disease** — markers of aggressive disease and higher recurrence. Although individual factor correlations are inconsistent in studies, the **strongest biologic predictor of recontracture is younger age at first treatment**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: A patient presents with an isolated palmar Dupuytren nodule and no contracture. Which rough 10-year natural-history estimate is correct?

options.text: ~10% spontaneous involution, ~20% progress to contracture needing treatment, ~70% unchanged or progress to cord without contracture
100% will require surgery within 1 year
All nodules resolve spontaneously
None ever progress to contracture

questions.explanation: For isolated nodules, a rough 10-year prediction is **~10% spontaneous nodule involution, ~20% progression to contracture requiring treatment, and ~70% unchanged or progressing to a cord without contracture**. Because most nodules do not progress to disabling contracture, observation is appropriate for nodules without functional contracture. Knuckle pads correlate with earlier progression.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Why do PIP joint Dupuytren contractures generally progress faster and have a worse prognosis than MCP contractures?

options.text: Cords at the PIP (and lateral cords, more common there) lie closer to the joint's axis of rotation, so a given cord shortening produces a larger angular change
PIP joints have no collateral ligaments
MCP cords never contract
The PIP joint has a richer blood supply

questions.explanation: Angular joint change from linear cord shortening **increases as the cord lies closer to the joint's axis of rotation**. PIP cords (and lateral cords, which are more common at the PIP) sit closer to the PIP axis than MCP/central cords do to the MCP axis, so the same shortening yields a much larger angle at the PIP. This geometry — not diathesis — explains faster PIP contracture (roughly twice the MCP rate) and worse small-finger prognosis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: In the normal digit, the fibrous ligaments surrounding the neurovascular bundle are named such that the fibers PALMAR to the bundle are ___ and those DORSAL to it are ___.

options.text: Grayson ligament ; Cleland ligament
Cleland ligament ; Grayson ligament
Natatory ligament ; retrovascular ligament
Spiral band ; lateral digital sheet

questions.explanation: **Grayson ligament lies palmar (volar) to the neurovascular bundle; Cleland ligament lies dorsal.** A mnemonic: Grayson is on the 'ground' (palmar) side, Cleland is the 'ceiling' (dorsal) side. In Dupuytren disease, the **Grayson ligament fibers are commonly involved** (contributing to cords), whereas Cleland's ligament is typically spared.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: A SPIRAL cord is dangerous during surgery because it displaces the digital neurovascular bundle in which direction?

options.text: Proximally, toward the midline, and superficially (more palmar and central)
Distally and deep, away from the surgeon
Dorsally, out of harm's way
It does not move the neurovascular bundle at all

questions.explanation: As a spiral cord contracts, it winds around the neurovascular bundle and displaces it **proximally, toward the midline (central), and superficially (palmarly)** — placing the nerve/artery in an unexpectedly superficial, central position where it is easily injured. Spiral bundles are more likely with greater PIP contracture and beneath a fleshy palmar prominence; preoperative Doppler or a compression maneuver can help localize them.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The spiral cord is formed from the convergence of which four fascial components?

options.text: Pretendinous band, spiral band, lateral digital sheet, and Grayson ligament
Cleland ligament, natatory ligament, transverse palmar ligament, and A1 pulley
Central cord, retrovascular cord, ADM cord, and natatory cord
Superficial palmar aponeurosis, extensor hood, sagittal band, and volar plate

questions.explanation: The **spiral cord is formed by four confluent structures: the pretendinous band, the spiral band, the lateral digital sheet, and Grayson ligament.** As these shorten, the cord spirals around and displaces the neurovascular bundle superficially, centrally, and proximally — the anatomic basis for the surgical hazard of the spiral cord.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: In Dupuytren disease, a normal palmar fascial band that becomes a diseased 'cord' is the pretendinous band. When it contracts, it primarily produces contracture of which joint?

options.text: The MCP joint
The DIP joint
The wrist
The CMC joint

questions.explanation: The **pretendinous cord** (from the pretendinous band of the palmar aponeurosis) runs longitudinally in the palm and, when it contracts, produces **MCP joint flexion contracture**. Central and pretendinous cords tend to cause isolated MCP contractures, whereas spiral, lateral, and retrovascular cords more often drive PIP contractures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which cord runs dorsal to the neurovascular bundle and, when it contracts, can cause PIP contracture and even DIP hyperextension?

options.text: Retrovascular cord
Central cord
Natatory cord
Pretendinous cord

questions.explanation: The **retrovascular cord** lies dorsal to the neurovascular bundle (derived from retrovascular fascia). Because it passes behind the bundle and inserts distally, its contracture contributes to **PIP flexion contracture** and is a cause of residual PIP contracture after other cords are released; it can also affect the DIP. Its dorsal position keeps the NV bundle relatively protected during its dissection compared with the spiral cord.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: A cord derived from the natatory ligament, spanning the web spaces, characteristically causes:

options.text: Limitation of finger abduction (web-space contracture)
Isolated DIP flexion contracture
Wrist flexion contracture
Thumb IP hyperextension

questions.explanation: The **natatory cord** (from the natatory/interdigital ligament that spans the web spaces) contracts to **limit finger abduction/spread**, drawing the fingers together and narrowing the web spaces. It can coexist with and mask other cords. A cord in the first web space (proximal/distal commissural cords) similarly causes **thumb-index web (adduction) contracture**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Luck described three HISTOLOGIC stages of Dupuytren disease. Which is the correct progression from early to late?

options.text: Proliferative → involutional → residual
Residual → involutional → proliferative
Involutional → residual → proliferative
Nodular → cystic → calcific

questions.explanation: Luck's histologic stages progress **proliferative → involutional → residual**, roughly corresponding to nodules (early, highly cellular/mitotic myofibroblasts, disorganized collagen), nodular cords (active contracture), and non-nodular fibrotic cords (late, acellular). The **proliferative stage has the highest type III:I collagen ratio (>35%)** and the highest recontracture rate after fasciectomy — about twice that of involutional and three times that of residual histology at 8 years.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The Hueston 'tabletop test' is used to help decide when to treat Dupuytren contracture. It is positive when:

options.text: The patient cannot lay the palm and fingers flat on a tabletop
The patient cannot make a full fist
The patient has any palpable palmar nodule
There is pain on palpation of a cord

questions.explanation: The **Hueston tabletop test is positive when the patient cannot place the palm and extended fingers flat on a table** — a practical threshold indicating a functionally significant contracture (roughly ≥30° MCP or any significant PIP contracture) that warrants considering intervention. It reflects that isolated nodules/cords without meaningful contracture are generally observed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Percutaneous needle aponeurotomy (needle fasciotomy, PNF) for Dupuytren contracture:

options.text: Uses a hypodermic needle to divide (not remove) the cord percutaneously; it is minimally invasive but has a higher recurrence rate than open fasciectomy
Removes all diseased fascia through a wide open incision
Dissolves the cord enzymatically
Is the definitive treatment with the lowest recurrence rate

questions.explanation: **Needle aponeurotomy/fasciotomy (PNF)** uses a small (e.g., 25-gauge) hypodermic needle to perforate and divide the cord percutaneously, then the finger is manipulated into extension. It is quick, minimally invasive, and low-morbidity, but **recurrence is higher than open fasciectomy** because the diseased tissue is not removed. It is best for well-defined palpable cords (especially MCP); the main risks are digital nerve/tendon injury and skin tears.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Collagenase clostridium histolyticum (CCH, Xiaflex) treats Dupuytren contracture by:

options.text: Enzymatically lysing the collagen cord, followed by finger extension manipulation (typically the next day) to rupture the weakened cord
Surgically excising the palmar fascia
Injecting corticosteroid into the nodule
Freezing the cord with cryotherapy

questions.explanation: **CCH (collagenase)** is injected into the cord where it enzymatically **digests/weakens the collagen**; the patient returns (usually ~24–48 hours later) for **extension manipulation that ruptures the weakened cord**. Injection is confined to the cord (avoiding tendons/skin) to limit complications. Common adverse effects are skin tears, ecchymosis, swelling, and pain; rare flexor tendon rupture has occurred. Recurrence is comparable to needle fasciotomy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which treatment for Dupuytren contracture is the most invasive but has the LOWEST long-term recurrence rate?

options.text: Dermofasciectomy with full-thickness skin grafting
Percutaneous needle fasciotomy
Collagenase injection
Corticosteroid injection of a nodule

questions.explanation: **Dermofasciectomy** removes the diseased fascia AND the overlying involved skin, replacing it with a **full-thickness skin graft**; the grafted skin appears to resist recurrence beneath it, giving the **lowest long-term recurrence rate**. It is reserved for aggressive/recurrent disease (diathesis) or when skin is diseased. It is the most invasive option with the longest recovery, and repeated aggressive surgery raises amputation risk.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The most commonly performed OPEN surgical treatment for Dupuytren contracture, removing the diseased cord/fascia through incisions, is:

options.text: Regional (limited/segmental) fasciectomy
Radical fasciectomy removing all palmar fascia
Amputation
Total palmar fasciotomy alone

questions.explanation: **Limited (regional) fasciectomy** — excising only the diseased cord/fascia — is the **most common open procedure** and the current standard operative treatment. It has lower recurrence than needle/collagenase but higher permanent complication rates. **Radical fasciectomy** (removing all palmar fascia) is largely abandoned due to high morbidity without a recurrence benefit.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which joint's Dupuytren contracture responds MOST completely to treatment and has the LOWEST recurrence, regardless of technique?

options.text: The MCP joint
The PIP joint
The DIP joint
The small finger PIP joint specifically

questions.explanation: **MCP joint contractures correct more completely and recur less** than PIP contractures, across all techniques — the MCP collateral ligaments do not shorten in flexion, so full extension is more readily restored. **PIP contractures** are harder to correct fully (secondary joint changes: collateral/volar plate/checkrein contracture) and recur more; the **small-finger PIP** has the worst prognosis of all.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The small finger PIP joint has a worse Dupuytren prognosis. What role does abductor digiti minimi (ADM) tendon involvement play?

options.text: ADM involvement is common in small-finger contractures but is NOT an independent risk factor for worse outcome or recurrence
ADM involvement is the strongest predictor of recurrence
ADM involvement makes the contracture easier to correct
ADM involvement never occurs

questions.explanation: An **abductor digiti minimi cord** is common in small-finger disease and can cause a loss of small-finger supination, but studies show **ADM involvement is NOT an independent risk factor** for inferior outcome or recurrence. The worse small-finger PIP prognosis is driven mainly by the joint geometry (cords closer to the axis) and the difficulty of fully correcting PIP contractures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The most serious intraoperative complication to avoid during Dupuytren fasciectomy is:

options.text: Digital nerve (or artery) injury — occurring in at least ~3% of fasciectomies
Fracture of the metacarpal
Rupture of the extensor tendon
Injury to the median nerve at the wrist

questions.explanation: **Digital nerve injury (and digital artery injury) is the key intraoperative risk, occurring in at least ~3% of fasciectomies**, especially where a **spiral cord** displaces the neurovascular bundle superficially and centrally. Careful identification of the bundle (proximal-to-distal dissection, awareness of the spiral cord, Doppler when suspected) minimizes this. Other complications include hematoma, skin necrosis, flare reaction, CRPS, and loss of flexion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: A 'postfasciectomy flare reaction' is characterized by:

options.text: Prolonged swelling, stiffness, redness, and pain — resembling and possibly overlapping with CRPS
Immediate wound dehiscence with pus
Painless recurrence of the cord
A benign transient rash unrelated to the hand

questions.explanation: A **flare reaction** is a prolonged inflammatory response after fasciectomy — swelling, stiffness, erythema, and pain — that can be difficult to distinguish from **complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)**; the two overlap (CRPS can even cause Dupuytren-like palmar thickening). It is more common with more extensive dissection and can worsen contracture; management is supportive with therapy and edema control.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Regarding postoperative night splinting after Dupuytren surgery, current evidence suggests:

options.text: Routine postoperative splinting has no demonstrable long-term benefit
Splinting reliably prevents all recurrence
Splinting is mandatory for wound healing
Splinting cures the underlying disease

questions.explanation: The chapter states that **post-treatment Dupuytren splinting has no demonstrable long-term benefit** — routine prophylactic night extension splinting has not been shown to reduce recurrence or improve final motion in trials. Splinting may still be used selectively (e.g., to maintain a difficult PIP correction), but it should not be assumed to prevent recontracture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which statement about 'recurrence' (recontracture) in Dupuytren disease is most accurate?

options.text: There is no standard definition of recurrence, and early recontracture can be due to residual secondary joint/soft-tissue changes rather than active disease
Recurrence is uniformly defined as any nodule reappearance
Recurrence never occurs after fasciectomy
All recontracture reflects active new disease

questions.explanation: Dupuytren **'recurrence' has no standard definition**, which confounds comparisons. Importantly, **not all recontracture is active disease** — early recontracture (often within months, then plateauing) frequently reflects **residual secondary static changes** (contracted collateral ligaments, volar plate, checkrein, tendon adaptation) from the chronic flexed posture, especially after severe PIP contractures, rather than new fibromatosis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which is the strongest biologic predictor of RECONTRACTURE after treatment of Dupuytren disease?

options.text: Younger age at the first treatment
Male sex alone
Presence of a single MCP cord
Right-hand dominance

questions.explanation: Despite conflicting data on individual diathesis factors, the **strongest biologic predictor of recontracture is younger age at the first treatment** (reflecting more biologically aggressive disease). Proliferative (early) Luck-stage histology also correlates with higher recurrence. These help set expectations and may favor tissue-removing procedures (fasciectomy/dermofasciectomy) in young, aggressive disease.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Knuckle pads (Garrod pads) in Dupuytren disease are:

options.text: Firm fibrous nodules over the dorsal aspect of the finger joints (a dorsal Dupuytren manifestation) correlating with earlier contracture progression
Painful gouty tophi
Osteophytes of the DIP joint (Heberden nodes)
Rheumatoid nodules

questions.explanation: **Knuckle pads (Garrod pads / dorsal Dupuytren nodules)** are firm fibrous masses on the **dorsal (extensor) aspect of the finger joints** — an ectopic dorsal manifestation of Dupuytren disease and part of the diathesis. Their presence **correlates with earlier progression to contracture** in patients presenting with isolated palmar nodules. They are distinct from Heberden nodes (DIP osteoarthritis).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: A cord in the first web space causing thumb-index adduction contracture arises from which structures?

options.text: The proximal and distal commissural (first web) cords / distal first-web fascia
The A1 pulley
The Cleland ligament of the thumb
The extensor pollicis longus

questions.explanation: Thumb-index **first web-space contracture** results from **commissural cords (proximal/distal first-web fascia and the distal commissural ligament)**, drawing the thumb into adduction and narrowing the web. Correcting these often requires first-web release with local flaps (e.g., Z-plasties) to lengthen the contracted skin envelope. Thumb-side Dupuytren is less common than in the ulnar digits.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The 'two-hit' etiologic concept of Dupuytren disease refers to:

options.text: A genetic (heritable) predisposition combined with local/environmental triggering factors producing the phenotype
Two separate traumatic events to the palm
Simultaneous bacterial and viral infection
Two consecutive surgeries

questions.explanation: Dupuytren is conceptualized as a **'two-hit' process: an inherited genetic predisposition ('first hit') plus local/environmental factors ('second hit')** — mechanical tension, microtrauma, ischemia/free radicals, and inflammatory signaling that drive myofibroblast differentiation. Like diabetes, DD is likely not a single disease but a phenotype from multiple genetic/environmental contributions; classic risk associations (alcohol, diabetes, trauma) are, at most, minor.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which statement about the classic clinical risk-factor associations (alcohol, diabetes, local trauma) with Dupuytren disease is most accurate per this chapter?

options.text: They are, at most, minor risk factors, and correlations are confounded by disease-severity and treatment-timing biases
They are the primary cause of the disease
They are completely unrelated in every study
They guarantee progression to contracture

questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that **alcohol, diabetes, and local trauma are at most MINOR risk factors**, and reported associations are confounded — e.g., different comorbidities correlate with different endpoints (diagnosis vs progression vs recontracture), and heavy alcohol use may delay presentation (giving greater contracture at presentation) rather than causing faster progression. So these should not be overstated as causes.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The 'McCash' open-palm technique in Dupuytren surgery refers to:

options.text: Leaving the transverse palmar wound open to heal by secondary intention (reducing hematoma and flare)
A full-thickness skin graft over the entire palm
Radical excision of all palmar fascia
Enzymatic cord dissolution

questions.explanation: The **McCash open-palm technique** leaves the **transverse palmar incision open to heal by secondary intention** after fasciectomy, which reduces hematoma formation, swelling, and flare reaction and allows earlier motion — at the cost of longer wound healing. It remains a useful approach, particularly in extensive palmar disease.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: When a severe chronic PIP flexion contracture does not fully correct after cord removal, the residual contracture is most often due to:

options.text: Secondary changes — contracted volar plate, checkrein ligaments, accessory collateral ligaments, and adapted flexor tendon
A missed metacarpal fracture
Extensor tendon rupture
Median nerve compression

questions.explanation: A stubborn residual PIP contracture after complete cord excision reflects **secondary joint contracture** — shortened **volar plate, checkrein ligaments, and accessory collateral ligaments**, plus adapted flexor tendon length — from the chronically flexed posture. Gentle staged manipulation and, selectively, checkrein/volar plate release may help; however, aggressive open PIP release has generally shown poor results and increased complications, so caution is advised.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: According to the chapter, aggressive open PIP joint release for Dupuytren contracture:

options.text: Has generally shown disappointing results and added complications, so it is approached cautiously
Reliably restores full PIP extension with no downside
Is the first-line treatment for all PIP contractures
Eliminates recurrence entirely

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that **open PIP joint release for Dupuytren has generally been disappointing** — it often fails to durably improve extension and adds complications (stiffness, flare, vascular compromise). Gentle correction (removing the cord and gentle passive extension) achieves results at least as good as aggressive capsular releases, so restraint is favored.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which patient is the BEST candidate for percutaneous needle aponeurotomy or collagenase rather than open fasciectomy?

options.text: An older patient with a well-defined, palpable, isolated MCP cord who prefers minimal downtime
A young patient with aggressive diffuse diathesis and diseased skin
A patient with a poorly defined, diffuse PIP contracture and prior recurrence
A patient needing first-web reconstruction with skin flaps

questions.explanation: Minimally invasive options (**needle aponeurotomy, collagenase**) work best for a **discrete, palpable cord causing MCP contracture** in a patient wanting rapid recovery/low morbidity, accepting a higher recurrence rate. **Young, aggressive/diathesis disease, diseased skin, diffuse or recurrent PIP disease, and cases needing skin replacement** favor open fasciectomy or dermofasciectomy with grafting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: During needle aponeurotomy, a key safety maneuver to avoid tendon injury is to:

options.text: Have the patient gently flex/extend the fingers with the needle in place — tendon movement (transmitted to the needle) warns of tendon proximity
Insert the needle as deeply as possible into the cord
Use the largest gauge needle available
Avoid any patient interaction during the procedure

questions.explanation: A core safety step is to **ask the awake patient to gently move the fingers while the needle is in place**: if the needle is near a flexor tendon, the tendon's excursion moves/tugs the needle, warning the surgeon. Similarly, **paresthesia on needle manipulation warns of nerve proximity**. Keeping the needle superficial (in the cord, not deep toward tendon/nerve), using a short 25-gauge needle, and tensioning the cord maximize control and safety.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Away from the PIP joint, where does the digital neurovascular bundle usually lie relative to a LATERAL cord versus a CENTRAL cord?

options.text: Central to lateral cords and lateral to central cords
Always directly superficial to any cord
Always dorsal to every cord
Its position is completely random and unpredictable

questions.explanation: Away from the PIP (where a spiral cord can displace it superficially), the neurovascular bundle usually lies **central to a lateral cord and lateral to a central cord** — i.e., roughly between the two cord positions. Knowing this default location guides safe dissection, while remaining vigilant for the spiral cord that pulls the bundle superficial and central near fleshy prominences.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which physical maneuver can help detect a spiral cord (superficial neurovascular bundle) before surgery?

options.text: Passively extend the finger to tension the cord while compressing an overlying fleshy prominence — pain/paresthesia suggests the bundle is superficial there
The Finkelstein test
The Watson scaphoid shift test
Allen test of the wrist

questions.explanation: To screen for a spiral cord/superficial neurovascular bundle, **passively extend the finger (tensioning the cord) and firmly compress the overlying palmar prominence against the cord; reproduced pain or paresthesias suggest the bundle runs superficial** at that spot. A **Doppler stethoscope or ultrasound** can also localize a spiral bundle. Spiral bundles are more likely with greater PIP contracture and beneath a fleshy prominence.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Compared with fasciectomy alone, dermofasciectomy with full-thickness skin grafting is specifically indicated when:

options.text: There is diseased/deficient overlying skin or aggressive recurrent disease, aiming to lower recurrence beneath the graft
The patient has a single mild MCP cord
The patient wants the fastest possible recovery
There is no contracture at all

questions.explanation: **Dermofasciectomy + full-thickness skin graft** is chosen when the **overlying skin is diseased/adherent/deficient** or in **aggressive or recurrent disease (diathesis)**, because the grafted skin resists recurrence beneath it (lower long-term recurrence). It is more invasive with longer recovery, so it is not used for simple isolated cords or when minimal downtime is the priority.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: A patient with palmar Dupuytren nodules but NO contracture (negative tabletop test) who is bothered mainly by nodule tenderness may be offered:

options.text: Observation, activity modification, and possibly intralesional corticosteroid injection of a symptomatic nodule
Immediate dermofasciectomy
Amputation of the digit
Radical fasciectomy

questions.explanation: Without functional contracture, **observation** is appropriate (most nodules do not progress to disabling contracture). For a **symptomatic (tender) nodule**, an **intralesional corticosteroid injection** can reduce pain and nodule size, and activity/padding modifications help. Surgery is reserved for functionally significant contractures (positive tabletop test), not isolated nodules.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Repeated aggressive surgery for recurrent Dupuytren disease is important to counsel about because:

options.text: Cumulative complications rise, and amputation rates climb with repeat/aggressive procedures (e.g., ~8% after fasciectomy performed following dermofasciectomy)
Each surgery cures the disease permanently
Recurrence becomes impossible after two operations
There are no added risks with repeat surgery

questions.explanation: The chapter stresses that **recontracture and retreatment complications are the prime drivers of poor outcomes**, and that **repeated aggressive surgery increases complications and amputation risk** (an ~8% amputation rate was reported for fasciectomy performed after dermofasciectomy). This motivates minimizing the lifetime burden of both disease and treatment — favoring the least morbid effective option and realistic expectations.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which demographic/epidemiologic statement about Dupuytren disease is correct?

options.text: It is more common in men and in people of Northern European ancestry, with increasing prevalence with age
It is most common in young women of African ancestry
It affects all populations equally regardless of ancestry
It is exclusively a disease of childhood

questions.explanation: Dupuytren disease is classically more prevalent in **men and in individuals of Northern European descent** ('Viking disease'), with **prevalence rising with age**. It is heritable (family history is common). Prevalence/contracture risk must be interpreted in the context of age, sex, and ancestry — reflecting its strong genetic underpinning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which finding is the sentinel (first-noticed) presentation of Dupuytren disease in a substantial number of patients?

options.text: A cord or contracture, without the patient ever having noticed a preceding nodule
Sudden complete loss of hand sensation
Acute severe hand pain at rest
A rapidly enlarging painful mass over weeks

questions.explanation: While many patients start with a palmar **nodule**, in nearly a quarter of patients a **cord or contracture is the sentinel finding**, without a noticed preceding nodule. DD is generally slowly progressive and painless; a rapidly growing painful mass should prompt consideration of an alternative diagnosis (e.g., a soft-tissue tumor).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which statement about the biology-severity relationship in Dupuytren disease is correct?

options.text: Most patients with contractures actually have mild disease biology, needing only one or two corrective procedures over a lifetime
Every patient with a contracture has aggressive biology requiring lifelong repeated surgery
Contracture severity perfectly predicts biologic aggressiveness
Disease biology is identical in all patients

questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that **most patients with contractures have relatively mild disease biology, needing only one or two corrective procedures** across their lifetime; a smaller subset has aggressive biology (diathesis) driving frequent recurrence. Distinguishing biologic aggressiveness (better reflected by young onset/diathesis) from the mechanical severity of a given contracture is central to counseling and treatment selection.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: TGF-β is implicated in Dupuytren disease because it:

options.text: Drives fibroblast-to-myofibroblast differentiation, collagen synthesis, and matrix remodeling
Dissolves collagen cords
Blocks all fibrosis
Is protective against Dupuytren disease

questions.explanation: **TGF-β** is a key profibrotic cytokine that (with mechanical tension) **stimulates myofibroblast differentiation, collagen synthesis, and matrix metalloproteinase gene expression** in Dupuytren tissue. This signaling, along with macrophage (M1→M2) activity and mechanical feedback via myofibroblast mechanotransduction, sustains the fibrotic, contractile process — the biologic rationale behind investigational anti-fibrotic therapies.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which of the following is the LEAST accurate statement about Dupuytren disease?

options.text: The DIP joint is the joint most commonly and severely contracted in Dupuytren disease
MCP contractures correct more completely than PIP contractures
The spiral cord displaces the neurovascular bundle superficially and centrally
Grayson ligament (palmar to the NV bundle) is commonly involved

questions.explanation: The false statement is about the DIP — Dupuytren primarily contracts the **MCP and PIP joints**, not the DIP (the DIP is only occasionally affected, often via a retrovascular cord causing DIP hyperextension, and is not the most commonly/severely contracted joint). The other statements are correct: MCP contractures correct better than PIP, the spiral cord displaces the NV bundle superficially/centrally, and Grayson ligament is commonly involved.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The lateral digital sheet, a normal fascial layer contributing to Dupuytren cords, is located:

options.text: Along the lateral (side) aspect of the digit, superficial to the neurovascular bundle
Deep within the flexor tendon sheath
On the dorsum of the finger over the extensor tendon
Within the joint capsule

questions.explanation: The **lateral digital sheet** runs along the **lateral border of the digit** (receiving fibers from the natatory ligament and continuous with Grayson ligament/dermis). It is one of the four components that coalesce into a **spiral cord** (with the pretendinous band, spiral band, and Grayson ligament) and contributes to **lateral cords** that cause PIP contracture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: The 'central cord' of a Dupuytren digit is essentially a distal continuation of the pretendinous cord and characteristically causes:

options.text: PIP joint flexion contracture (it does not displace the neurovascular bundle)
MCP hyperextension
Displacement of the neurovascular bundle superficially, like a spiral cord
Web-space narrowing only

questions.explanation: The **central cord** is a distal extension of the pretendinous cord that inserts on the middle phalanx/flexor sheath and causes **PIP flexion contracture**.
