Unlike the spiral cord, the central cord lies superficial and midline and **does not displace the neurovascular bundle**, so the bundle sits lateral to it — making the central cord relatively safer to dissect than a spiral cord.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which statement about flexor tendon rupture as a complication of collagenase (CCH) injection is correct?

options.text: It is a rare but recognized complication, avoided by confining the injection to the cord and away from the flexor tendon (especially at the PIP of the small finger)
It occurs in the majority of injections
It cannot occur because collagenase does not affect tendon
It only occurs with needle aponeurotomy, never collagenase

questions.explanation: **Flexor tendon rupture is a rare but recognized CCH complication** because collagenase can digest tendon collagen if it diffuses out of the cord. It is minimized by **injecting precisely into the cord and away from the underlying flexor tendon** — a particular concern at the **small-finger PIP**, where the cord and flexor tendon are close. Manufacturer guidance limits needle penetration depth for this reason. Skin tears and ecchymosis are the more common adverse effects.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: When treating a first-web-space (thumb-index) Dupuytren contracture surgically, skin shortage is commonly managed with:

options.text: Local skin-lengthening flaps such as Z-plasties
Simple primary closure under tension
Amputation of the thumb
Fusion of the thumb CMC joint

questions.explanation: Correcting a **first-web adduction contracture** requires releasing the commissural cords AND addressing the **contracted skin envelope**, commonly with **Z-plasties** (or other local flaps) to lengthen and widen the web. Closing under tension risks flap necrosis and recurrent contracture. Z-plasties are also used along digital incisions to prevent longitudinal scar contracture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Which of the following best reflects the overall philosophy of Dupuytren management emphasized in this chapter?

options.text: Minimize the lifetime burden of BOTH the disease and the complications of treatment, choosing the least morbid effective intervention
Operate aggressively and early on every nodule to prevent any contracture
Always choose the most invasive option to guarantee no recurrence
Avoid all treatment because recurrence is universal

questions.explanation: The chapter frames the goal as **minimizing the lifetime burden of both the disease AND treatment complications** — since recurrence and retreatment morbidity drive poor outcomes. This favors treating functionally significant contractures (not asymptomatic nodules), selecting the **least morbid effective procedure** for the situation, and counseling realistically about recurrence rather than pursuing maximal intervention.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 4 (Dupuytren Disease)

questions.stem: Osteoarthritic bony enlargement at the DISTAL interphalangeal (DIP) joint is called a ___ node, whereas the same finding at the PROXIMAL interphalangeal (PIP) joint is a ___ node.

options.text: Heberden ; Bouchard
Bouchard ; Heberden
Haygarth ; Osler
Osler ; Janeway

questions.explanation: **Heberden nodes** are the periarticular osteophyte/soft-tissue enlargements at the **DIP joint**; **Bouchard nodes** are the analogous enlargements at the **PIP joint**. A useful mnemonic: 'B' (Bouchard) is higher in the alphabet and located more proximally (PIP). A DIP mucous cyst is another common osteoarthritic manifestation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: In the hand, which interphalangeal joint is the MOST COMMONLY affected by osteoarthritis, and which is most commonly SYMPTOMATIC?

options.text: DIP is most commonly affected; PIP is most commonly symptomatic
PIP is most commonly affected; DIP is most commonly symptomatic
MCP is most commonly affected and symptomatic
The thumb IP joint is both most affected and most symptomatic

questions.explanation: The **DIP joint is the most commonly affected** finger joint by osteoarthritis, but the **PIP joint is most commonly symptomatic** (its arthritis interferes more with grip and function). The thumb CMC (basal) joint is the most common site of surgically treated hand osteoarthritis overall.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: A patient has a small, translucent cyst over the dorsum of an osteoarthritic DIP joint, associated with a longitudinal groove/ridge in the nail. This is a:

options.text: Mucous cyst (a ganglion arising from the osteoarthritic DIP joint, often compressing the germinal matrix)
Epidermal inclusion cyst
Giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath
Glomus tumor

questions.explanation: A **mucous cyst** is a ganglion arising from an osteoarthritic DIP joint (associated with a dorsal osteophyte). Pressure on the **germinal matrix** causes a longitudinal **nail groove/deformity**. Treatment addresses the underlying osteophyte (excision of the cyst and osteophyte); the overlying skin can thin and rupture, risking **septic arthritis** of the DIP. Excision should remove the osteophyte to prevent recurrence.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The most reliable, durable surgical treatment for a painful, unstable, or deformed osteoarthritic DIP joint is:

options.text: DIP arthrodesis (fusion)
DIP silicone arthroplasty
DIP pyrocarbon arthroplasty
Proximal row carpectomy

questions.explanation: **DIP arthrodesis** is the mainstay for symptomatic DIP osteoarthritis (pain, deformity, instability) — it reliably relieves pain and provides stability, and the small DIP joint tolerates fusion well functionally. Contraindications include active infection/septic arthritis or an open wound. The DIP is typically fused in near-full extension to slight flexion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The preferred position for DIP joint arthrodesis is:

options.text: Full extension to slight flexion (near neutral)
45 degrees of flexion
20 degrees of hyperextension
90 degrees of flexion

questions.explanation: The DIP is fused in **full extension to slight flexion (near neutral)**, which optimizes pinch and appearance. Fixation is commonly a **headless compression screw** (giving stable fixation) or longitudinal K-wires; care is taken to avoid 'inside-out' screw contact with the nail bed, especially in the small distal phalanx.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: When performing multiple PIP joint arthrodeses, the recommended fusion angle progresses from radial to ulnar. Approximately what angles are used for the index, long, ring, and small fingers?

options.text: ~30°, 40°, 50°, 60° (increasing flexion toward the ulnar side)
All fingers at 0° (full extension)
~60°, 50°, 40°, 30° (increasing toward the radial side)
All fingers at 90°

questions.explanation: PIP arthrodesis flexion angle **increases from the index to the small finger — roughly 30°, 40°, 50°, and 60°** respectively — mirroring the normal cascade and functional needs (radial digits favor pinch/extension; ulnar digits favor grip/flexion). Some recent data suggest intermediate angles (~40–60° across all digits) may give good results, but the classic teaching is the increasing cascade.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The main advantage of PIP joint ARTHROPLASTY over PIP arthrodesis is:

options.text: Motion preservation
Lower cost
Elimination of any implant complications
It is stronger for heavy manual labor

questions.explanation: **PIP arthroplasty preserves motion**, which is its principal advantage over arthrodesis (which eliminates painful motion but sacrifices it). Arthrodesis, however, is more predictable for pain relief, more durable for high-demand/border digits (index PIP, which needs stability for pinch), and avoids implant complications. The choice balances motion preservation against durability/stability needs.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Why is the INDEX finger PIP joint generally better treated with arthrodesis than arthroplasty in an active patient?

options.text: The index PIP must resist the lateral/pinch forces of key and pulp pinch, for which a stable fusion is more reliable than an implant
The index PIP cannot be fused
Arthroplasty is technically impossible at the index
The index finger has no extensor mechanism

questions.explanation: The **index PIP experiences high radially/ulnarly directed pinch forces** during key and pulp pinch; PIP implants (silicone, pyrocarbon, SRA) can develop **instability, deviation, or lateral laxity** under these loads. A stable **arthrodesis** better withstands pinch demands, so it is often preferred for the index PIP, reserving arthroplasty for the ulnar digits (which are used more for grip and tolerate implant motion).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Which PIP implant arthroplasty design is a constrained/semi-constrained silicone spacer that acts primarily as a flexible hinge-spacer (with encapsulation providing stability)?

options.text: Silicone (Swanson-type) implant
Pyrocarbon surface replacement
Linscheid-Dobyns surface replacement arthroplasty (SRA)
Total metal-on-polyethylene linked hinge

questions.explanation: The **silicone (Swanson) implant** is a one-piece flexible spacer functioning as a hinge; stability comes from the fibrous **encapsulation** that forms around it. **Pyrocarbon** and **surface replacement arthroplasty (SRA, Linscheid-Dobyns)** are unconstrained resurfacing designs relying on soft-tissue/ligament balance for stability. Studies show broadly comparable results, though pyrocarbon/SRA have more complications (instability, squeaking, subsidence) than silicone in some series.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: MCP joint arthroplasty (implant) is MOST commonly indicated for which condition, rather than primary osteoarthritis?

options.text: Rheumatoid arthritis
Primary osteoarthritis (which usually spares the MCP joints)
Gout
Psoriatic arthritis only

questions.explanation: Most **MCP arthroplasties are performed for rheumatoid arthritis** (with its characteristic MCP volar subluxation and ulnar drift), because **primary osteoarthritis tends to spare the MCP joints**. When MCP arthroplasty is done for primary/post-traumatic OA, it is chiefly for pain relief rather than large functional gains, and requires adequate bone stock and a stable soft-tissue envelope.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The recommended position for arthrodesis of the THUMB MCP joint (e.g., for primary osteoarthritis) is approximately:

options.text: About 20 degrees of flexion (with slight pronation/appropriate rotation)
Full extension (0 degrees)
60 degrees of flexion
20 degrees of hyperextension

questions.explanation: The thumb MCP joint is fused in roughly **20 degrees of flexion** (with appropriate rotation/slight pronation) to optimize opposition and pinch. Thumb MCP arthrodesis is a reliable, durable option for primary or post-traumatic MCP arthritis, and is also used to correct a fixed MCP hyperextension deformity accompanying advanced CMC arthritis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The thumb carpometacarpal (trapeziometacarpal) joint is biomechanically predisposed to osteoarthritis because it is:

options.text: A biconcave, reciprocating saddle joint with little inherent bony stability, dependent on ligaments
A rigid ball-and-socket joint
A simple uniaxial hinge like the PIP
A fibrous immobile joint

questions.explanation: The thumb CMC joint is a **biconcave, reciprocating saddle joint with little inherent bony stability**, relying on ~16 surrounding ligaments; the metacarpal articular surface is ~34% smaller than the trapezial surface. This mobility (for prehension/opposition/circumduction) at the cost of stability — combined with high pinch loads — predisposes it to degeneration, making it the most common surgically treated hand OA site.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The PRIMARY stabilizing ligament of the thumb CMC joint, whose incompetence is central to the development of basal joint arthritis, is the:

options.text: Deep anterior oblique ('beak') ligament
Dorsal intermetacarpal ligament
Posterior oblique ligament
Superficial radial collateral ligament

questions.explanation: The **deep anterior oblique ('beak') ligament** — running from the trapezial volar tubercle to the ulnar-volar base of the thumb metacarpal — is classically considered the **primary stabilizer**, tightening with pronation/abduction/extension to resist dorsoradial subluxation. (Note: the **dorsoradial ligament** is now recognized as a major, well-innervated restraint to dorsal subluxation, and the dorsal intermetacarpal ligament also resists proximal metacarpal migration after trapeziectomy.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The CMC 'grind test' for thumb basal joint arthritis is performed by:

options.text: Applying axial load along the thumb metacarpal while gently rotating, reproducing pain and crepitus at the CMC joint
Radially deviating the thumb MCP joint
Percussing over the radial styloid
Passively flexing the wrist

questions.explanation: The **grind test** axially loads (and rotates) the thumb metacarpal against the trapezium, compressing the degenerative surfaces to reproduce **pain and crepitus** at the CMC joint. A related **subluxation/lever test** gently subluxes the joint to elicit pain. Note pinch maneuvers can multiply CMC joint forces ~12-fold, and ~30% of CMC OA patients have concurrent carpal tunnel syndrome.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: In the Eaton radiographic staging of thumb CMC osteoarthritis, what distinguishes STAGE IV from stage III?

options.text: Stage IV adds scaphotrapeziotrapezoid (STT) joint involvement (pantrapezial arthritis)
Stage IV shows only joint-space widening from synovitis
Stage IV has osteophytes less than 2 mm
Stage IV is a normal joint

questions.explanation: **Eaton staging**: Stage I — normal/slightly widened joint (synovitis); Stage II — mild narrowing, osteophytes/loose bodies ≤2 mm; Stage III — marked narrowing, osteophytes >2 mm, subchondral cysts/sclerosis; **Stage IV — stage III changes PLUS scaphotrapeziotrapezoid (STT) joint arthritis (pantrapezial)**. Notably, the staging has not reliably correlated with intraoperative disease extent or outcome.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: A dedicated 'Robert view' radiograph of the thumb CMC joint is:

options.text: A true PA view of the trapeziometacarpal joint (obtained with the forearm hyperpronated so the dorsal thumb lies on the cassette)
A true lateral of the scaphoid
A carpal tunnel view
An oblique view of the hamate hook

questions.explanation: The **Robert view is a true PA of the thumb CMC joint**, obtained with the arm hyperpronated (shoulder internally rotated) so the **dorsum of the thumb rests directly on the cassette**, profiling the trapeziometacarpal joint without overlap. It best shows joint-space narrowing and osteophytes for staging. Advanced imaging (CT/MRI) is seldom needed for CMC surgical decision-making.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: First-line management of early symptomatic thumb CMC osteoarthritis is:

options.text: Nonoperative — splinting (thumb spica/CMC orthosis), activity modification, NSAIDs, and possibly corticosteroid injection
Immediate trapeziectomy in all cases
Primary CMC arthrodesis for everyone
Total wrist fusion

questions.explanation: Early CMC OA is treated **nonoperatively first**: a **thumb (CMC) orthosis/splint**, activity modification, NSAIDs, hand therapy, and selective corticosteroid injections often control symptoms for years. Surgery (osteotomy, ligament reconstruction, trapeziectomy ± LRTI, or arthrodesis) is reserved for patients who fail conservative measures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: An extension (closing-wedge) osteotomy of the thumb metacarpal (Wilson-type) is a described treatment for which stage of CMC arthritis?

options.text: Early (stage I–II) disease, aiming to unload the volar/palmar contact of the joint
Stage IV pantrapezial disease
Only after failed trapeziectomy
Advanced STT arthritis

questions.explanation: A **closing-wedge extension osteotomy of the thumb metacarpal base** is used for **early (stage I–II) CMC OA**: extending the metacarpal shifts joint loading away from the diseased volar articular surface toward healthier dorsal cartilage, and can reduce subluxation tendency. It preserves the joint. Advanced disease (III–IV) is treated with resection/reconstruction procedures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The classic Burton-Pellegrini LRTI procedure for advanced thumb CMC arthritis consists of:

options.text: Trapeziectomy + Ligament Reconstruction and Tendon Interposition (using a slip of the FCR)
CMC arthrodesis with a plate
Silicone trapezial implant alone
Thumb metacarpal extension osteotomy

questions.explanation: **LRTI = trapeziectomy plus Ligament Reconstruction and Tendon Interposition.** A portion of the **flexor carpi radialis (FCR)** tendon is used to reconstruct the beak ligament (through a bone tunnel in the thumb metacarpal base) and the remainder is coiled as interposition in the trapezial void, suspending the metacarpal. It is indicated for **stage III–IV** disease. Notably, RCTs show simple trapeziectomy gives comparable outcomes with fewer complications, though LRTI remains widely used.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: For advanced thumb CMC arthritis, which patient is the BEST candidate for CMC ARTHRODESIS rather than trapeziectomy-based arthroplasty?

options.text: A young, high-demand manual laborer wanting maximal pinch strength and durability (with a healthy STT joint)
An elderly low-demand patient who needs to preserve motion
A patient with stage IV pantrapezial (STT) arthritis
A patient with a fused wrist

questions.explanation: **CMC arthrodesis** trades motion for **strength and durability**, so it best suits a **young, high-demand manual worker** who prioritizes pinch power — provided the **STT joint is healthy** (STT arthritis, i.e., stage IV, contraindicates fusion because load transfers there). Trade-offs include loss of circumduction/palmar flattening for grasping large objects and risk of nonunion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The 'hematoma and distraction' arthroplasty for thumb CMC arthritis refers to:

options.text: Simple trapeziectomy with temporary K-wire distraction/immobilization, without formal ligament reconstruction or interposition
A pyrocarbon total joint replacement
CMC arthrodesis with bone graft
An extension osteotomy with distraction

questions.explanation: **Hematoma and distraction arthroplasty** is essentially a **trapeziectomy alone**, relying on the postoperative hematoma to fill the void and a **temporary K-wire to distract/hold the thumb metacarpal** during healing — no tendon interposition or formal ligament reconstruction. Outcomes are comparable to more complex procedures (LRTI), supporting the trend toward simpler resection arthroplasty.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: In advanced thumb CMC arthritis, a compensatory deformity often develops at the adjacent MCP joint. It is:

options.text: MCP hyperextension (with a first-web/metacarpal adduction contracture)
MCP flexion contracture
MCP ulnar drift
IP joint hyperextension

questions.explanation: As the CMC joint subluxes and the thumb metacarpal adducts (first-web contracture), the patient compensates by **hyperextending the MCP joint** to open the web/oppose the thumb. If MCP hyperextension exceeds ~30°, it must be addressed at surgery — options include **volar capsulodesis, sesamoid arthrodesis, MCP arthrodesis, or temporary pinning** — otherwise the deformity undermines the CMC reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: When correcting significant thumb MCP hyperextension (>~30°) during CMC reconstruction, durable options include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.text: Temporary K-wire fixation alone, which reliably maintains correction long-term
Volar capsulodesis
MCP arthrodesis
Sesamoid arthrodesis

questions.explanation: For MCP hyperextension >~30°, durable correction requires a **structural procedure — volar capsulodesis, sesamoid arthrodesis, or MCP arthrodesis**. **Temporary K-wire fixation alone tends to FAIL** to maintain correction long-term (the hyperextension recurs), so it is not reliable as the definitive correction. Lesser hyperextension may be managed by pinning in flexion, but frank deformity needs a stabilizing procedure.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Roughly what proportion of patients with thumb CMC osteoarthritis have concurrent carpal tunnel syndrome, an important association to screen for?

options.text: About 30%
Less than 1%
About 90%
0% — they are unrelated

questions.explanation: The association of **carpal tunnel syndrome with CMC osteoarthritis approaches ~30%**. Because both are common in the same demographic and can coexist, clinicians should specifically evaluate for median nerve symptoms in CMC OA patients — and may address both at the same operative setting when indicated.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Randomized comparisons of surgical techniques for advanced thumb CMC arthritis (trapeziectomy alone vs LRTI vs trapeziectomy + K-wire) have generally shown:

options.text: No consistent superiority of LRTI or ligament reconstruction over simple trapeziectomy, with more complications in the more complex procedures
LRTI is dramatically superior in every outcome
Arthrodesis is always best regardless of demand
Nonoperative treatment matches surgery in advanced disease

questions.explanation: High-quality comparative studies have found **no consistent advantage of LRTI (or tendon interposition/ligament reconstruction) over simple trapeziectomy** for pain and function, while the **more complex procedures carry more complications** (and longer recovery). This underlies a shift toward simpler resection arthroplasty, though surgeon preference and specific patient factors still guide the choice.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: A mucous cyst over the DIP joint has thinned the overlying skin, which is now draining. Beyond cosmesis, the main concern is:

options.text: Septic arthritis / osteomyelitis of the DIP joint from the direct communication with the joint
Malignant transformation
Distant metastasis
Compartment syndrome

questions.explanation: A draining or ulcerated mucous cyst creates a **direct portal into the DIP joint**, risking **septic arthritis and osteomyelitis** (the chapter shows DIP destruction after an infected mucous cyst requiring arthrodesis). This makes timely treatment — excision of the cyst AND the underlying osteophyte, with skin coverage if needed — important, rather than leaving thin/draining skin over the joint.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Excision of a DIP mucous cyst should include removal of what, to minimize recurrence?

options.text: The associated osteoarthritic dorsal osteophyte at the DIP joint
The entire distal phalanx
The nail matrix
The terminal extensor tendon

questions.explanation: Mucous cysts arise from an osteoarthritic DIP joint and communicate with it via a stalk near a **dorsal osteophyte**; **removing the osteophyte (and the stalk)** at the time of cyst excision reduces recurrence. Simple cyst excision without addressing the osteophyte has a higher recurrence rate. The germinal matrix and terminal tendon are protected, not resected.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: A recognized complication specific to headless compression screw fixation of a DIP arthrodesis in a small distal phalanx is:

options.text: 'Inside-out' screw contact with (perforation of) the nail bed
Radial nerve palsy
Flexor tendon rupture at the wrist
Carpal tunnel syndrome

questions.explanation: In the small distal phalanx, a headless compression screw can breach the dorsal cortex and cause **'inside-out' contact with/perforation of the nail bed**, producing nail deformity or dorsal prominence. Preoperative planning (screw length/diameter) and careful trajectory avoid this; if it occurs, K-wire fixation may be substituted. Headless screws otherwise give high union rates (~96%) for DIP fusion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Compared with silicone PIP implants, pyrocarbon and surface replacement (SRA) PIP arthroplasties in the literature generally show:

options.text: Comparable motion/pain relief but MORE complications (instability, subsidence, squeaking)
Uniformly superior outcomes with fewer complications
No motion at all
Guaranteed elimination of pain in all patients

questions.explanation: Meta-analyses/comparative studies find **pyrocarbon and SRA give comparable pain relief and range of motion to silicone but with MORE complications** — instability, subsidence, radiolucent lines/loosening, intraoperative fracture, and even audible 'squeaking' of pyrocarbon joints. No design is clearly superior; silicone remains a durable, lower-complication option, especially in lower-demand patients.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Which is a CONTRAINDICATION to DIP joint arthrodesis?

options.text: Active infection/septic arthritis of the joint or an open wound at the site
Primary osteoarthritis with pain
A painful chronic mallet with joint degeneration
Post-traumatic DIP arthritis

questions.explanation: **Active infection, septic arthritis of the DIP, or an open wound** at the fusion site contraindicate DIP arthrodesis (fusing over active infection risks persistent osteomyelitis/nonunion). Appropriate indications include painful primary or post-traumatic OA, and degeneration after chronic mallet — situations where a stable, pain-free fusion improves function.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: During pinch/grasp, forces across the thumb CMC joint can be magnified relative to the applied pinch force by a factor of approximately:
questions.explanation: Because of the lever arms across the thumb, a **lateral (key) or tip pinch can increase forces at the CMC joint by roughly 12-fold** relative to the pinch force at the thumb tip. This large mechanical amplification helps explain why the incongruent, ligament-dependent saddle joint degenerates so commonly and why load-altering procedures (osteotomy) or resection arthroplasty relieve symptoms.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The Weilby-type suspension (sling) arthroplasty for thumb CMC arthritis uses a slip of which tendon woven around the APL/ECRL to suspend the metacarpal after trapeziectomy?

options.text: Flexor carpi radialis (FCR)
Palmaris longus
Extensor pollicis longus
Flexor carpi ulnaris

questions.explanation: The **Weilby technique** passes half of the **FCR tendon** as a sling/lattice around the abductor pollicis longus (APL) (and/or ECRL) to suspend and stabilize the thumb metacarpal after trapeziectomy, without a formal bone tunnel. It is one of several resection-suspension arthroplasties; prospective/RCT data show results comparable to other techniques.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: In advanced thumb CMC arthritis, after trapeziectomy, which ligament is credited with helping prevent proximal migration of the thumb metacarpal into the trapezial void?

options.text: The dorsal intermetacarpal ligament
The transverse carpal ligament
The scapholunate interosseous ligament
The terminal extensor tendon

questions.explanation: The **dorsal intermetacarpal ligament** (connecting the thumb and index metacarpal bases) both prevents radial translation of the thumb metacarpal and helps **resist proximal migration of the metacarpal into the trapezial space after trapeziectomy**. This is relevant to why simple trapeziectomy often works despite metacarpal 'settling' — remaining ligaments and interposed hematoma maintain enough suspension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Ligament reconstruction (volar ligament reconstruction, Eaton-Littler type) WITHOUT trapeziectomy is best indicated for:

options.text: Early (stage I–II) CMC instability/arthritis with preserved articular cartilage
Stage IV pantrapezial arthritis
A completely destroyed trapezium
Fixed MCP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: **Volar ligament reconstruction (Eaton-Littler)** re-tensions the beak ligament to restore CMC stability and is indicated for **early (stage I–II) disease with instability but preserved cartilage** (or laxity without advanced arthritis). Once cartilage is destroyed (stage III–IV), ligament reconstruction alone is insufficient and resection/reconstruction (trapeziectomy ± LRTI) or arthrodesis is required.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Which statement about PIP joint stability, relevant to arthroplasty selection, is correct?

options.text: The collateral ligaments are the primary stabilizers; complete sectioning permits ~20° of deviation, greatest in mid-flexion
The PIP has no collateral ligaments
The volar plate is the sole stabilizer of the PIP
PIP stability is provided entirely by the flexor tendons

questions.explanation: The PIP is a uniaxial hinge whose **primary stabilizers are the collateral ligaments** (with the volar plate). Complete collateral sectioning allows up to ~20° of radioulnar deviation, and laxity is **greatest in mid-flexion** (least in full extension/flexion). This is why unconstrained PIP implants depend on competent collateral/soft-tissue balance and can become unstable — a consideration favoring silicone (encapsulation) or arthrodesis in high-demand digits.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: For PIP arthroplasty rehabilitation using a relative-motion / extension-block orthosis, the goal is to:

options.text: Allow protected early active PIP motion while protecting the implant and soft-tissue balance
Immobilize the PIP rigidly for 8 weeks
Force maximal passive hyperextension immediately
Fuse the joint gradually

questions.explanation: PIP arthroplasty rehab aims to **restore motion early while protecting the reconstruction**, using an extension-block/relative-motion orthosis that permits protected active flexion/extension and guards against deviation or extensor lag. Balancing early motion against soft-tissue healing is key, since implants rely on periarticular balance for stability.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Which statement about primary osteoarthritis distribution in the hand is correct?

options.text: It characteristically involves the DIP, PIP, and thumb CMC (and STT) joints while typically sparing the finger MCP joints
It preferentially destroys the finger MCP joints first
It only affects the wrist
It never involves the thumb

questions.explanation: Primary hand OA characteristically affects the **DIP and PIP joints and the thumb basal joints (CMC, and STT in advanced disease)**, while **typically sparing the finger MCP joints** (MCP involvement suggests inflammatory arthritis, hemochromatosis, or CPPD). This distribution guides diagnosis and the selection of joint-specific treatments.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: A limitation of the Eaton radiographic staging system for thumb CMC arthritis, noted in the chapter, is that it:

options.text: Has not reliably correlated with intraoperative disease extent or treatment outcome
Cannot be applied to any radiograph
Requires MRI for every stage
Only applies to inflammatory arthritis

questions.explanation: Although the **Eaton staging** is widely used to describe and communicate CMC OA radiographically, it **has never shown reliable correlation with the intraoperative extent of disease or with treatment outcomes**. Consequently, surgical decision-making relies more on symptoms, function, examination (grind test, MCP compensation), and STT-joint status than on the radiographic stage alone.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Recent ultrastructural analysis of thumb CMC ligaments (Mobargha et al.) found that mechanoreceptors/innervation were most abundant in which ligament, suggesting a proprioceptive role?

options.text: The dorsoradial ligament
The deep anterior oblique (beak) ligament
The transverse carpal ligament
The intermetacarpal ligament of the index

questions.explanation: Mobargha and colleagues found the **dorsoradial ligament to be richly innervated with mechanoreceptors and better-organized collagen**, whereas the deep anterior oblique (beak) ligament in OA patients showed disorganized tissue with little innervation. This has shifted thinking toward the **dorsoradial ligament as a key dynamic/proprioceptive stabilizer** of the CMC joint, informing dorsal ligament reconstruction concepts.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Which fixation gives immediate, stable fixation and high union rates for DIP (or thumb IP) arthrodesis and allows earlier mobilization of adjacent joints?

options.text: An intramedullary headless compression screw
A single loose K-wire left long
Cerclage suture alone
No fixation, cast only

questions.explanation: An **intramedullary headless compression screw** provides **immediate, rigid, compressive fixation** across a DIP/IP arthrodesis (union rates ~96%), allowing early motion of the PIP/MCP/wrist. Alternatives include crossed/longitudinal K-wires or tension-band techniques. Screw fixation requires attention to distal phalanx size to avoid nail-bed perforation ('inside-out').
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: A key disadvantage of thumb CMC ARTHRODESIS that patients should be counseled about is:

options.text: Loss of thumb circumduction/palmar abduction, making it hard to flatten the hand or grasp large objects, plus a risk of nonunion
It uniformly weakens pinch
It cannot relieve pain
It always causes STT arthritis immediately

questions.explanation: CMC arthrodesis provides strong, durable pinch but **eliminates thumb circumduction and full palmar abduction**, so patients may struggle to lay the hand flat or grasp large/flat objects; it also carries a **nonunion risk** and can accelerate adjacent (STT) joint loading over time. These trade-offs make it best for young, high-demand patients rather than those prioritizing motion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Which examination maneuver increases forces across the thumb CMC joint and often reproduces the patient's pain, complementing the grind test?

options.text: Lateral (key) pinch or the CMC subluxation/lever test
Finkelstein test
Phalen test
Allen test

questions.explanation: **Lateral (key) pinch or tip pinch** loads the CMC joint (up to ~12× the pinch force) and often reproduces pain; the **CMC subluxation (lever) test** gently subluxes the joint to elicit pain/crepitus. These complement the grind test. (Finkelstein tests de Quervain's — an important radial-wrist-pain mimic to distinguish — while Phalen/Allen test the median nerve and vascular supply respectively.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The Burton-Pellegrini LRTI reconstructs the beak ligament by passing the FCR slip through a bone tunnel at which site?

options.text: The base of the thumb metacarpal
The scaphoid tubercle
The distal radius metaphysis
The proximal phalanx of the thumb

questions.explanation: In LRTI, after trapeziectomy a slip of **FCR** is routed through a **bone tunnel at the base of the thumb metacarpal** to reconstruct the palmar beak ligament and suspend the metacarpal; the remaining tendon is coiled ('anchovy') as interposition in the trapezial void. This mirrors the Eaton-Littler ligament reconstruction concept applied to advanced (stage III–IV) disease.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST accurate statement regarding treatment of finger osteoarthritis?

options.text: Silicone MCP arthroplasty is the first-line treatment for primary MCP osteoarthritis, which is very common
DIP arthrodesis is a reliable, durable option for DIP OA
PIP arthroplasty preserves motion but risks implant instability, especially at the index
Mucous cyst excision should include the underlying osteophyte

questions.explanation: The false statement is that MCP silicone arthroplasty is first-line for primary MCP OA — in fact **primary OA usually spares the finger MCP joints**, and most MCP arthroplasties are done for **rheumatoid arthritis**. The other statements are correct: DIP fusion is reliable/durable, PIP arthroplasty preserves motion but risks instability (worse at the index), and mucous cyst excision should remove the osteophyte.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with stage II thumb CMC arthritis has failed 6 months of splinting, activity modification, NSAIDs, and an injection. She has good cartilage on the STT joint and wants to preserve motion. A reasonable surgical option is:

options.text: Trapeziectomy-based resection arthroplasty (e.g., simple trapeziectomy ± suspension/LRTI)
Total wrist arthrodesis
Proximal row carpectomy
Darrach distal ulna resection

questions.explanation: For symptomatic CMC arthritis refractory to conservative care in a patient wanting to **preserve motion**, a **trapeziectomy-based resection arthroplasty** (simple trapeziectomy, or with suspension/LRTI/hematoma-distraction) is the mainstay. Arthrodesis is the motion-sacrificing, strength-favoring alternative for young high-demand laborers. Wrist fusion, PRC, and Darrach address different pathologies.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: Intraoperative fracture during small-joint (MCP/PIP) arthroplasty is more likely with which factors?

options.text: Cementless fixation, pyrocarbon implants, and diabetes mellitus
Cemented silicone implants in healthy bone
Use of a dorsal blocking splint
Regional anesthesia

questions.explanation: Intraoperative periprosthetic fracture (occurring in ~3% of MCP arthroplasties) is associated with **cementless fixation, pyrocarbon implants, and diabetes mellitus** — reflecting the press-fit stem preparation and stiffer implant material in potentially compromised bone. Awareness guides careful bone preparation and implant/technique selection, particularly in at-risk patients.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: For a symptomatic osteoarthritic PIP joint in a low-demand elderly patient's ulnar (ring/small) finger where motion preservation is desired, a reasonable option is:

options.text: PIP implant arthroplasty (e.g., silicone)
PIP arthrodesis is mandatory for all PIP OA
Proximal row carpectomy
Wrist denervation

questions.explanation: **PIP arthroplasty (commonly silicone) is well suited to the ulnar digits (ring/small)** of lower-demand patients, where **preserving grip motion** matters more than the high pinch stability required at the index. Arthrodesis remains preferred for the index PIP (pinch stability) and for high-demand or unstable joints. The choice individualizes motion vs stability/durability by digit and demand.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: A key advantage of trapeziectomy-based procedures over CMC arthrodesis for basal thumb arthritis is that trapeziectomy:

options.text: Preserves thumb motion/circumduction and avoids the nonunion risk inherent to fusion
Provides greater pinch strength than fusion
Eliminates any risk of metacarpal subsidence
Is only appropriate for young laborers

questions.explanation: **Trapeziectomy (± suspension/interposition) preserves thumb motion and circumduction and avoids the nonunion risk of arthrodesis**, making it well suited to most patients (especially older/lower-demand). Its trade-offs include some **metacarpal subsidence/settling and potentially less pinch strength than a solid fusion**. Arthrodesis, conversely, maximizes strength/durability at the cost of motion — favored for young high-demand laborers.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: The normal active range of motion of the finger PIP joint (relevant when counseling on arthroplasty vs arthrodesis) is approximately:

options.text: 0 to 100 degrees
0 to 30 degrees
0 to 60 degrees
0 to 160 degrees

questions.explanation: Normal finger joint motion is roughly **MCP 0–90°, PIP 0–100°, and DIP 0–60°**. The PIP contributes the largest arc and is central to grip, which is why PIP arthrodesis (fixed motion) is a bigger functional trade-off than DIP fusion, and why motion-preserving PIP arthroplasty is attractive when stability allows.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: When both symptomatic thumb CMC arthritis and carpal tunnel syndrome are present in the same patient, a reasonable strategy is to:

options.text: Address both at the same operative setting when indicated, since the association approaches 30%
Never treat them together under any circumstances
Assume the CMC arthritis causes the median nerve symptoms and treat only the joint
Defer all treatment indefinitely

questions.explanation: Given the **~30% coexistence of carpal tunnel syndrome with CMC osteoarthritis**, and that both commonly require surgery, it is reasonable to **address both conditions at the same operative setting** when each is independently symptomatic and indicated (e.g., CMC reconstruction plus carpal tunnel release). Each diagnosis should be confirmed on its own merits rather than attributing all symptoms to one.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 11 (Treatment of the Osteoarthritic Hand and Thumb)

questions.stem: In the Verdan/Doyle zone classification of extensor tendon injuries, the ODD-numbered zones correspond to:

options.text: The joints (DIP = zone 1, PIP = zone 3, MP = zone 5)
The regions over the phalanges/metacarpals between joints
The extensor compartments at the wrist
The forearm muscle bellies

questions.explanation: Extensor zones are numbered distal to proximal, with **odd numbers over the joints and even numbers over the intervening segments**. For the fingers: **DIP = zone 1, PIP = zone 3, MP = zone 5** (with zones 2, 4, 6 over the middle phalanx, proximal phalanx, and metacarpal respectively); zone 7 is the wrist/retinaculum, zone 8 the distal forearm, zone 9 the proximal forearm/muscle. For the thumb, the IP joint is zone 1 and the MP joint is zone 3.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: At the MP joint level, the extensor tendon is centered over the joint by which structure?

options.text: The sagittal bands
The central slip
The triangular ligament
The oblique retinacular ligament

questions.explanation: The **sagittal bands** arise from the volar plate and intermetacarpal ligaments and insert on the extensor hood, tethering and centering the EDC over the MP joint. Because the EDC has no firm direct bony insertion at the proximal phalanx, it extends the MP joint largely by this sagittal-band 'sling.' Sagittal band injury allows the EDC to **sublux/dislocate** into the intermetacarpal groove.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Proximal to the PIP joint, the extensor tendon 'trifurcates.' Into what does it divide?

options.text: A central slip (to the middle phalanx base) and two lateral components that join the lateral bands
Two sagittal bands and one central slip
The terminal tendon and two juncturae
The oblique retinacular ligament and two triangular ligaments

questions.explanation: Over the proximal phalanx the extensor mechanism **trifurcates into a central slip** (inserting on the dorsal base of the middle phalanx to extend the PIP) and **two lateral slips** that join the intrinsic lateral bands. The **conjoined lateral bands** coalesce over the middle phalanx and continue as the **terminal tendon**, which inserts on the dorsal distal phalanx to extend the DIP.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The lateral bands are held in their normal dorsal position at the PIP joint by two structures. The triangular ligament prevents ___, and the transverse retinacular ligament prevents ___.

options.text: volar (palmar) subluxation ; dorsal subluxation
dorsal subluxation ; volar subluxation
proximal migration ; distal migration
radial deviation ; ulnar deviation

questions.explanation: The **triangular ligament** (dorsal-distal to the PIP) keeps the lateral bands from sliding **volarly** — its loss (as in boutonnière) lets the lateral bands drop palmar to the PIP axis. The **transverse retinacular ligament** prevents the lateral bands from subluxing **dorsally** — its laxity contributes to dorsal band displacement in swan-neck deformity. There is normal small dorsal-palmar band translation during flexion/extension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The oblique retinacular ligament (ORL) of Landsmeer is significant because it:

options.text: Links PIP and DIP motion (passively extends the DIP as the PIP extends) and is exploited in reconstructions like the SORL
Centers the extensor tendon at the MP joint
Is the primary MP joint flexor
Anchors the flexor tendon to the phalanx

questions.explanation: The **oblique retinacular ligament (Landsmeer)** runs volar to the PIP axis and dorsal to the DIP axis, **coordinating PIP and DIP extension** — as the PIP extends, the ORL tightens and assists DIP extension. This coupling is the basis of the **spiral ORL (SORL) reconstruction** for swan-neck/mallet imbalance and the concept of a passive tendon 'checkrein' for chronic mallet.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The juncturae tendinum are important clinically because:

options.text: Finger extension can be preserved if the EDC is lacerated proximal to a junctura that connects it to an intact adjacent tendon
They are the sole extensors of the index finger
They center the tendon over the MP joint
They connect the flexor tendons to each other

questions.explanation: **Juncturae tendinum** interconnect the EDC tendons on the dorsum of the hand (between communis tendons). If the EDC is cut **proximal to a junctura** that links it to an intact neighboring tendon, the injured finger may still extend (through the junctura), which can **mask an extensor laceration**. Testing individual MP extension with the other fingers flexed helps unmask such injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The six dorsal wrist extensor compartments contain specific tendons. Which pairing is correct?

options.text: First compartment: APL and EPB
First compartment: EPL alone
Third compartment: ECU
Fourth compartment: EDM only

questions.explanation: The compartments are: **1st = APL + EPB** (de Quervain's), 2nd = ECRL + ECRB, **3rd = EPL** (angling around Lister tubercle), 4th = EDC + EIP, 5th = EDM, 6th = ECU. The EPL's course around Lister tubercle explains its attritional rupture after distal radius fractures, and the 6th compartment (ECU) is relevant to ECU subluxation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient cannot actively extend the DIP joint of a finger after it was struck by a ball, and rests with the DIP flexed. There is no laceration. This is a:

options.text: Mallet finger (terminal tendon disruption)
Boutonnière deformity
Sagittal band rupture
Jersey finger

questions.explanation: A **mallet finger** is disruption of the **terminal extensor tendon** at the DIP (with or without a dorsal avulsion fracture), producing an extensor lag at the DIP. It classically follows a sudden forced flexion of an actively extended DIP (ball striking the fingertip). Radiographs are always obtained to assess for a bony mallet fracture and DIP volar subluxation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: In Doyle's classification of mallet finger, a closed injury with or without a small dorsal avulsion fracture is which type?

options.text: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV

questions.explanation: **Doyle Type I** is a **closed mallet** (with or without a small dorsal avulsion fracture) — the most common type. **Type II** is an open injury with a tendon laceration; **Type III** is an open injury with loss of skin/soft-tissue and tendon substance; **Type IV** is a mallet fracture (IVA transepiphyseal in children; IVB hyperflexion fracture 20–50% of surface; IVC hyperextension fracture >50% with volar subluxation).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The standard treatment of an acute closed (Doyle type I) mallet finger is:

options.text: Continuous DIP extension (or slight hyperextension) splinting for 6–8 weeks, keeping the PIP free
Immediate open tendon repair
DIP arthrodesis
Splinting the PIP in flexion

questions.explanation: Acute closed mallet fingers are treated with **continuous full-time DIP extension splinting for ~6–8 weeks** (then weaning), keeping the **DIP from flexing even momentarily** while leaving the PIP free to move. Even late-presenting mallets often respond to prolonged splinting. **Static PIP flexion splinting is not recommended.** Fingers must be kept extended continuously; any DIP flexion resets the clock.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which mallet FRACTURE pattern (Doyle IVC) most strongly warrants consideration of operative treatment?

options.text: A large fragment (>50% of the articular surface) with volar subluxation of the distal phalanx
A tiny dorsal avulsion fleck with a congruent joint
A transepiphyseal fracture in a child that is nondisplaced
Any mallet fracture regardless of size or subluxation

questions.explanation: The classic operative indication is a **large articular fragment (>50%) with volar (palmar) subluxation of the distal phalanx** — an unstable, incongruent joint. Many surgeons still treat mallet fractures without subluxation nonoperatively (splinting) even with sizable fragments, since studies show good painless outcomes; fixation (e.g., extension-block pinning) is reserved chiefly for **subluxation/instability**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The extensor mechanism at the DIP is extremely unforgiving of any tendon lengthening. Approximately how much extensor lag results from just 1 mm of terminal tendon lengthening?

options.text: About 25 degrees
About 2 degrees
About 90 degrees
No measurable lag

questions.explanation: The terminal tendon has a very short moment arm, so **1 mm of lengthening produces roughly a 25-degree DIP extensor lag** (and ~0.5 mm ≈ 10°). This exquisite sensitivity explains why mallet injuries commonly leave a residual lag and why meticulous, gap-free management is essential. It also underlies why over-lengthening at repair or a small gap is so consequential at the DIP.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: An untreated mallet finger can, over time, lead to which secondary deformity?

options.text: Swan-neck deformity (compensatory PIP hyperextension)
Boutonnière deformity
Claw finger
Dupuytren contracture

questions.explanation: In a chronic mallet, the extensor force normally taken up by the terminal tendon is transmitted proximally, and the lateral bands migrate dorsally, causing **PIP hyperextension with the persistently flexed DIP — a swan-neck deformity**. This 'mallet-induced' swan neck can be treated by addressing DIP balance (e.g., terminal tendon reconstruction) and, if needed, restraining PIP hyperextension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient laceration over the dorsal PIP joint injures the central slip. Untreated, the classic resulting deformity is:

options.text: Boutonnière deformity (PIP flexion, DIP hyperextension)
Swan-neck deformity (PIP hyperextension, DIP flexion)
Mallet finger
Claw deformity

questions.explanation: Central slip disruption allows the **lateral bands to sublux volarly** (below the PIP axis) as the triangular ligament attenuates; the lateral bands then flex rather than extend the PIP and hyperextend the DIP — a **boutonnière deformity (PIP flexion + DIP hyperextension)**. It often develops over days to weeks, so early recognition (Elson test) and PIP extension splinting are important.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The Elson test detects an acute central slip rupture. With the PIP flexed 90° over a table edge and the patient extending against resistance, central slip rupture is indicated by:

options.text: Weak PIP extension with a rigid/hyperextended DIP (extension diverted through the lateral bands)
Strong PIP extension with a supple DIP
Inability to flex the DIP passively
Pain only over the volar plate

questions.explanation: In the **Elson test**, the PIP is flexed 90° over an edge and the patient extends the PIP against resistance. With an **incompetent central slip, PIP extension is weak and the extension force is shunted through the lateral bands, making the DIP rigidly extended/hyperextended**. A supple, freely flexible DIP indicates an intact central slip. It is the most reliable clinical test for acute central slip injury.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The recommended treatment of an acute closed central slip (boutonnière) injury is:

options.text: Splint the PIP in full extension for ~6 weeks while allowing/encouraging active DIP flexion
Splint the PIP in flexion
Splint the entire finger including the DIP in extension
Immediate PIP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: Acute closed central slip injuries are treated by **splinting the PIP in full extension for ~6 weeks** to let the central slip heal at length, while **actively flexing the DIP** — DIP flexion draws the lateral bands distally/dorsally, preventing them from contracting volarly and helping restore balance. Splinting the DIP in extension would worsen the deformity by tightening the ORL/lateral bands.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The Fowler central slip tenotomy for a chronic mallet finger works by:

options.text: Dividing the central slip to reduce PIP extension tone and redistribute extensor force distally to the DIP
Reattaching the terminal tendon to the distal phalanx
Fusing the DIP joint
Releasing the oblique retinacular ligament

questions.explanation: A **Fowler central slip tenotomy** divides the central slip (relying on an intact triangular ligament/lateral bands to still extend the PIP) so that **extensor force is shifted distally to help extend the DIP**, correcting a mallet lag. It works best for **modest lags**; larger lags may not correct fully. It also reduces the PIP extension moment, which can help a coexisting swan-neck.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient reports painful snapping of the extensor tendon over the MP joint when making a fist; the EDC subluxes ulnarly into the intermetacarpal groove. The injured structure is:

options.text: The (usually radial) sagittal band
The central slip
The terminal tendon
The junctura tendinum

questions.explanation: Painful snapping/subluxation of the EDC at the MP joint results from a **sagittal band tear** — most commonly the **radial** sagittal band, allowing ulnar subluxation of the tendon. It can be spontaneous ('flicking' a finger) or traumatic (a direct blow — 'boxer's knuckle'). The middle finger is most often involved. Rayan and Murray classify it: type I contusion, type II subluxation/snapping, type III frank dislocation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: An acute closed sagittal band injury with EDC subluxation presenting within 3 weeks is best treated with:

options.text: An MP extension-block ('sagittal band'/yoke/relative-motion) splint holding the MP in relative extension for ~6–8 weeks
Immediate open sagittal band reconstruction in all cases
Full immobilization of the wrist and all fingers in flexion
DIP extension splinting

questions.explanation: Acute (<3 weeks) sagittal band injuries with subluxation are usually managed nonoperatively with an **MP-joint extension-block / relative-motion (yoke) splint** that holds the injured MP in ~25–35° of relative hyperextension compared with adjacent MPs, worn full-time for ~6–8 weeks while allowing active IP motion — permitting the torn band to heal. Chronic or failed cases may need sagittal band reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient sustained a small laceration over the dorsal MP joint during a fist fight (striking another person's teeth). What critical concern must dominate management?

options.text: It is a 'fight bite' (human bite) — a contaminated joint injury needing irrigation, antibiotics, and exploration, not simple closure
It is a benign laceration that can be closed primarily and sent home
It only requires a tetanus shot
It should be splinted without any wound care

questions.explanation: A dorsal MP laceration from a clenched-fist injury is a **'fight bite' (human bite)** — the tooth can inoculate the extensor tendon, joint, and metacarpal head with oral flora (including Eikenella corrodens). It requires **thorough irrigation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and operative exploration/debridement**, with the wound left open (never simply closed). Because the injury occurs with the fist clenched, the tendon/joint damage shifts position when the finger is extended, so the zone of injury must be sought with the MP flexed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Compared with flexor tendons, extensor tendon repair differs biomechanically because extensor tendons in the digits/dorsal hand:

options.text: Are thin and flat, holding core sutures poorly, so many repairs use running/flat-tendon techniques and most heal with less tendency to adhere than zone 2 flexors
Are thick and round, ideal for multistrand core sutures
Run within tight fibro-osseous sheaths like zone 2 flexors
Never require any suture

questions.explanation: The extensor tendons over the phalanges/dorsal hand are **thin and flat** (Doyle measured thickness ~0.65 mm at zone 1 to ~1.75 mm at zone 6), so they **hold conventional core sutures poorly** — distal zones are repaired with running/interlacing techniques (e.g., running-interlocking or figure-of-eight) rather than bulky core sutures. Extensor repairs also generally do less poorly than zone 2 flexor repairs regarding adhesions, but stiffness/lag remain concerns.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The 'relative motion' (yoke) splinting concept (e.g., Merritt) after zone 4–7 extensor repair or for sagittal band injury works by:

options.text: Holding the injured finger's MP in relative extension (~15–25°) versus the adjacent MPs, off-loading the repair while allowing active motion
Immobilizing all fingers rigidly for 6 weeks
Holding the injured MP in relative flexion
Blocking all IP joint motion

questions.explanation: **Relative motion (yoke) splinting** positions the affected MP joint in **relative extension (~15–25°) compared with the neighboring MPs**, which reduces tension/excursion demand on the repaired extensor (or lets a torn sagittal band heal) while **permitting early active hand use**. Reviews suggest relative-motion protocols give outcomes comparable or superior to traditional static/dynamic splinting for select extensor injuries, with better function and satisfaction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient with a prior distal radius fracture (or rheumatoid arthritis) suddenly loses active thumb IP extension and retropulsion. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.text: Attritional rupture of the extensor pollicis longus (EPL)
Rupture of the extensor pollicis brevis
Sagittal band rupture of the thumb
Anterior interosseous nerve palsy

questions.explanation: Sudden loss of thumb IP extension/retropulsion suggests **EPL rupture**, classically an **attritional rupture as the tendon courses around Lister tubercle** (after distal radius fracture, or from tenosynovitis in RA). Because the tendon ends are frayed/retracted and diseased, direct repair is usually not feasible; the standard reconstruction is an **EIP-to-EPL tendon transfer**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The standard reconstruction for a chronic EPL rupture is transfer of which tendon?

options.text: Extensor indicis proprius (EIP) to EPL
Palmaris longus to EPL
Flexor carpi radialis to EPL
Extensor digiti minimi to EPL

questions.explanation: The **EIP-to-EPL transfer** is the workhorse for chronic EPL rupture. The EIP (the most ulnar tendon at the index MP joint) is harvested proximal to the sagittal bands; index MP extension is preserved via the EDC. The EIP has adequate excursion and amplitude to restore thumb IP/MP extension and retropulsion. Loss of the EIP typically causes no functional deficit if the index extensor hood is intact.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Why can loss of the EIP (as a donor for tendon transfer) usually be tolerated without an index extensor lag?

options.text: The EDC to the index continues to extend the MP joint as long as the extensor hood/sagittal bands are intact
The index finger has no extensor tendon
The lumbrical fully extends the index MP joint
The junctura from the small finger takes over

questions.explanation: The index finger normally has **both an EIP and an EDC slip**; the **EDC alone maintains MP extension** provided the extensor hood/sagittal bands are intact. This redundancy is why the EIP is an expendable donor. (A caution applies at the small finger, where the EDC is variable/sometimes absent — harvesting the EDM there could cause a small-finger extensor lag.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The germinal nail matrix, which produces the nail plate, lies approximately how far from the terminal tendon insertion — a relationship relevant to dorsal DIP surgery?

options.text: About 1.2 mm distal to the terminal tendon insertion
About 1 cm proximal to it
Directly deep to the DIP joint
At the level of the PIP joint

questions.explanation: The **germinal matrix begins only ~1.2 mm distal to the terminal tendon insertion** on the dorsal distal phalanx. This tiny margin means surgery or pin placement for mallet injuries risks **injuring the germinal matrix and causing nail deformity**, so care is required when operating at the dorsal DIP.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: In extensor tendon repair, dorsal bony/tendon shortening or malunion at the metacarpal is poorly tolerated. Roughly what MP extensor lag results from ~1 cm of dorsal metacarpal shortening (per experimental data)?

options.text: Only about 7 degrees at the MP joint (relatively tolerant)
About 90 degrees
About 45 degrees
No lag at all

questions.explanation: Experimentally, the extensor mechanism is far more forgiving proximally than distally: metacarpal shortening produces only about a **7-degree MP extensor lag per centimeter**, whereas over the PIP/DIP even tiny tendon lengthening causes large lags (e.g., ~12° PIP lag or ~25° DIP lag per mm). This gradient explains why distal (zone 1–3) extensor injuries are so unforgiving compared with proximal ones.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient sustains a laceration over the dorsal middle phalanx (zone 2) partially dividing the conjoined lateral bands. If less than ~50% is divided and there is no extensor lag, appropriate treatment is:

options.text: Nonoperative — wound care and early protected motion (small partial injuries often need no formal repair)
Mandatory core suture repair for all partial lacerations
DIP arthrodesis
Full-time DIP flexion splinting

questions.explanation: Partial extensor lacerations **(<~50%) without extensor lag** can be treated **nonoperatively** with wound care and early protected motion. Complete lacerations or those with a lag are repaired (running/flat techniques). Zone 2 injuries generally have better prognosis than zone 1 (mallet) because the terminal tendon is still intact distally.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The structure allowing ECU tendon subluxation when torn is the:

options.text: ECU subsheath (linea jugata) of the sixth dorsal compartment
Extensor retinaculum over the third compartment
Sagittal band of the small finger
Triangular ligament

questions.explanation: The **sixth compartment has its own ECU subsheath** (linea jugata) that holds the ECU in its groove on the distal ulna. Rupture of this **ECU subsheath** allows the ECU tendon to **sublux/dislocate** (often with a painful snap during forearm supination and ulnar deviation). It is distinct from the overlying extensor retinaculum, and comparison to the opposite wrist aids diagnosis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Why does a claw finger ('intrinsic-minus') develop with ulnar nerve palsy, in terms of the extensor mechanism?

options.text: Loss of intrinsic contribution lets the MP hyperextend, creating slack distally so the extrinsic extensor can no longer extend the IP joints
The central slip ruptures
The terminal tendon lengthens
The sagittal band subluxes

questions.explanation: The intrinsics (lumbricals/interossei) flex the MP and extend the IP joints via the lateral bands. With **intrinsic loss, unopposed extrinsic extensor tone hyperextends the MP**, which introduces **'slack' distally in the extensor mechanism**, so the extrinsic tendons can no longer extend the PIP/DIP — producing the **claw** (MP hyperextension, IP flexion). MP flexion-block (anti-claw) splinting or intrinsic reconstruction restores balance.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A dorsal hand laceration (zone 6) completely divides the EDC to the ring finger, yet the patient can still weakly extend the ring MP. The most likely explanation is:

options.text: An intact junctura tendinum transmitting extension from adjacent tendons
The injury is actually a sagittal band tear
The lateral bands are extending the MP
The FDP is extending the finger

questions.explanation: A **junctura tendinum** connecting the ring EDC to adjacent intact communis tendons can transmit extension force, producing **weak MP extension despite a complete EDC laceration proximal to the junctura** — a classic pitfall that masks the injury. Careful exam (extending the isolated finger with neighbors flexed) and wound exploration are needed; the laceration is still repaired.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A chronic, supple boutonnière deformity with a fixed extension contracture of the DIP is best addressed first by:

options.text: Restoring passive PIP extension (serial casting/splinting) and DIP flexion exercises before considering surgical reconstruction
Immediate central slip reconstruction regardless of stiffness
DIP arthrodesis as the first step
Fowler tenotomy of the terminal tendon first

questions.explanation: Chronic boutonnière management **first restores passive motion** — regain full **passive PIP extension** (serial casting/dynamic splinting) and mobilize the DIP with **DIP flexion exercises** (which draw the lateral bands dorsally). Only a supple joint benefits from reconstruction (central slip reconstruction, terminal tendon/distal Fowler tenotomy to relieve DIP hyperextension). Operating on a stiff, fixed deformity yields poor results.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A terminal tendon (distal Fowler / 'dolphin') tenotomy is used to treat which chronic deformity?

options.text: The DIP hyperextension component of a chronic boutonnière (or swan-neck imbalance)
An acute mallet finger
A sagittal band rupture
An EPL rupture

questions.explanation: A **terminal tendon (distal Fowler/'dolphin') tenotomy** divides the terminal tendon to relieve **DIP hyperextension** in a chronic boutonnière (where the lateral bands over-extend the DIP), rebalancing the digit. It relies on the ORL/retinacular structures to prevent a resulting mallet. It complements central slip reconstruction and passive-motion restoration in boutonnière treatment.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: In repairing a complete zone 3 (central slip) laceration acutely, the goal is to:

options.text: Restore central slip continuity and splint the PIP in extension, protecting DIP motion, to prevent boutonnière
Excise the central slip and fuse the PIP
Repair only the skin and mobilize immediately
Splint the PIP in flexion

questions.explanation: Acute complete **zone 3 (central slip)** injuries are **repaired** (direct suture, or reattachment to bone if avulsed distally leaving a short stump) and then the **PIP is protected in extension** (with DIP motion allowed) to prevent a boutonnière while healing. Small distal avulsions can sometimes be treated closed with PIP extension splinting, similar to a mallet strategy but at the PIP.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about extensor tendon rehabilitation is best supported by the studies cited?

options.text: Early controlled motion (dynamic or relative-motion) tends to give better early results than static immobilization, with differences often narrowing by ~8 weeks
Static immobilization is clearly superior at all time points
Rehabilitation protocol has no effect on outcome
Extensor repairs never require any splinting

questions.explanation: Comparative studies show **early controlled motion (dynamic extension or relative-motion splinting) generally yields better early range of motion and function than static immobilization**, though the differences frequently **diminish by ~8 weeks**. Relative-motion protocols in particular allow earlier hand use with good outcomes, and are increasingly favored for zones 4–7 and sagittal band injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The transverse retinacular ligament laxity/incompetence contributes to which deformity by allowing the lateral bands to migrate dorsally?

options.text: Swan-neck deformity (dorsal lateral band subluxation with PIP hyperextension)
Boutonnière deformity
Mallet finger
Claw finger

questions.explanation: The **transverse retinacular ligament normally prevents dorsal migration of the lateral bands**. When it is lax/incompetent (as with PIP volar plate laxity or intrinsic tightness), the lateral bands ride **dorsal to the PIP axis**, contributing to **PIP hyperextension — a swan-neck deformity**. Conversely, triangular ligament failure lets bands drop volarly, causing boutonnière.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient presents 6 weeks after an untreated closed mallet finger. What is the most reasonable initial management?

options.text: A trial of continuous DIP extension splinting — even 'chronic' mallets often respond to prolonged splinting
Immediate surgical terminal tendon reconstruction
DIP arthrodesis
No treatment is possible after 4 weeks

questions.explanation: Although mallets presenting >4 weeks are termed 'chronic,' the chapter notes that **even late-presenting mallets (months out) have been treated successfully with prolonged continuous DIP extension splinting**. A splinting trial is therefore reasonable first-line, reserving surgical options (e.g., terminal tendon reconstruction, Fowler tenotomy, or DIP fusion for arthritic/failed cases) for refractory deformities.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: During examination for a suspected extensor tendon laceration over the dorsal hand, which maneuver best unmasks an EDC injury that is being 'bridged' by a junctura tendinum?

options.text: Testing isolated MP extension of the affected finger while the other fingers are held flexed at the MP joints
Testing a full composite fist
Resisted wrist extension
Two-point discrimination testing

questions.explanation: Holding the **adjacent fingers flexed at the MP joints** tensions and thereby neutralizes the juncturae, so any residual MP extension of the affected finger must come from its own (possibly injured) tendon. This unmasks an EDC laceration proximal to a junctura that would otherwise be 'bridged.' It parallels the FDS isolation maneuver on the flexor side.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about the extensor apparatus at the MP joint is correct regarding how the EDC extends the proximal phalanx?

options.text: The EDC extends the proximal phalanx indirectly via the sagittal band 'sling,' not by a firm direct bony insertion
The EDC inserts firmly onto the proximal phalanx base and extends it directly
The lumbrical is the sole extensor of the proximal phalanx
The terminal tendon extends the proximal phalanx

questions.explanation: There is only loose connective tissue between the EDC and the proximal phalanx base; the EDC extends the proximal phalanx **indirectly through the sagittal band system** (which lifts the extensor hood and, through it, the proximal phalanx) rather than a firm direct bony insertion. This is why sagittal band disruption both allows tendon subluxation and can impair MP extension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which of the following is the LEAST accurate statement about mallet finger treatment?

options.text: The PIP joint should be splinted in flexion along with the DIP
The DIP is splinted continuously in full extension for 6–8 weeks
Radiographs are obtained to evaluate for a mallet fracture and subluxation
Even momentary DIP flexion during splinting can compromise healing

questions.explanation: The false statement is splinting the PIP in flexion — **static PIP flexion splinting is NOT recommended** for mallet fingers, and the PIP should remain free. Correct principles: splint the **DIP continuously in full extension for 6–8 weeks**, always obtain **radiographs** (assess fracture/subluxation), and warn the patient that **any DIP flexion resets healing**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The EIP and EDM are considered the 'independent' extensors of the index and small fingers. Where does the EIP typically insert relative to the EDC at the index MP joint?

options.text: Ulnar to the EDC tendon
Radial to the EDC tendon
Volar to the volar plate
Into the flexor sheath

questions.explanation: The **EIP typically lies ulnar to the EDC** tendon at the index MP joint (analogously, the EDM lies ulnar to the small-finger EDC).
