Knowing the EIP is the more ulnar of the two index extensors is important when harvesting it for transfer (e.g., EIP-to-EPL) — it is transected proximal to the sagittal bands, preserving index extension through the EDC.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops progressive inability to extend the ring and small finger MP joints, but passive extension is full and the tendons can be pulled proximally at the wrist. Besides tendon rupture, an important alternative cause is:

options.text: Extensor tendon subluxation into the intermetacarpal gutters from sagittal band/MP joint disease (or PIN palsy) — causes that mimic rupture
A mallet finger
A boutonnière deformity
de Quervain tenosynovitis

questions.explanation: Loss of MP extension in RA can result not only from **extensor tendon rupture** (attrition over the distal ulna — Vaughan-Jackson) but also from **ulnar subluxation of the extensor tendons off the MP joints** (from sagittal band/MP disease) or a **posterior interosseous nerve palsy** (from elbow synovitis) — mimics that must be distinguished, since their treatments differ (tendon relocation/repair vs transfer vs nerve issues). A tenodesis test and careful exam help differentiate.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: When repairing a zone 6 (dorsal hand) extensor laceration, the tendon is thicker than distally and can hold a stronger repair. Compared with distal zones, early active motion here is:

options.text: More feasible because the thicker tendon holds a stronger repair and can tolerate controlled early motion
Impossible because the tendon cannot hold suture
Contraindicated in all cases
Identical in every respect to zone 1 management

questions.explanation: In **zone 6 the extensor tendon is thicker (~1.75 mm)**, holding a more secure core/interlacing repair, so **controlled early active or relative-motion rehabilitation is more feasible** than in the thin distal zones. This supports the use of relative-motion/yoke splinting for zone 4–7 repairs, allowing early hand use while protecting the repair.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: In the Rayan-Murray classification of sagittal band injury, which type describes frank dislocation of the extensor tendon into the intermetacarpal groove?

options.text: Type III
Type I
Type II
Type IV

questions.explanation: Rayan and Murray graded sagittal band injuries: **Type I = contusion without tear/instability; Type II = tear with tendon snapping/subluxation but no complete dislocation; Type III = frank tendon dislocation** into the groove between the metacarpal heads. Higher grades and chronic/failed cases are more likely to need operative reconstruction; acute injuries often respond to relative-motion (yoke) splinting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The most important reason radiographs are ALWAYS obtained for a mallet finger is to:

options.text: Identify a mallet fracture and any volar subluxation of the distal phalanx (which changes management)
Rule out a scaphoid fracture
Assess bone density
Evaluate the flexor tendon

questions.explanation: Radiographs are essential to detect a **bony mallet (avulsion fracture)** and, critically, **volar subluxation of the distal phalanx** — the finding that shifts management toward operative fixation. In children, a **transepiphyseal (Salter) fracture** may be present. A purely soft-tissue mallet is splinted; a subluxated large-fragment mallet fracture may need surgery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient has a chronic swan-neck deformity from PIP volar plate laxity. Which reconstruction specifically uses the extensor/retinaculum concept to restrain PIP hyperextension while coupling DIP motion?

options.text: Spiral oblique retinacular ligament (SORL) reconstruction
Fowler central slip tenotomy
EIP-to-EPL transfer
Darrach procedure

questions.explanation: The **spiral ORL (SORL) reconstruction** recreates the oblique retinacular ligament (e.g., with a tendon graft passing volar to the PIP axis and dorsal to the DIP), **restraining PIP hyperextension while linking DIP extension** — correcting swan-neck (and mallet-related) imbalance. It leverages the ORL's role in coupling PIP-DIP motion. Fowler tenotomy and EIP-EPL transfer address different problems (mallet lag and EPL rupture respectively).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which extensor tendon angles around Lister tubercle, making it prone to attritional rupture after a distal radius fracture?

options.text: Extensor pollicis longus (EPL), in the third compartment
Extensor carpi radialis brevis, in the second compartment
Extensor digiti minimi, in the fifth compartment
Extensor carpi ulnaris, in the sixth compartment

questions.explanation: The **EPL runs in the third compartment and hooks sharply around Lister tubercle** before crossing to the thumb. This angulation, plus a watershed vascular zone at the tubercle, makes it vulnerable to **attritional rupture** — classically after a (often minimally displaced) distal radius fracture, or from dorsally protruding plate screws. Reconstruction is typically an EIP-to-EPL transfer.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: For an acute open extensor laceration in zone 5 (over the MP joint), before repair the surgeon must specifically evaluate for:

options.text: A human bite (fight bite) with joint penetration, since zone 5 lacerations are commonly tooth injuries
A scaphoid fracture
A flexor tendon avulsion
Carpal instability

questions.explanation: **Zone 5 (over the MP joint)** lacerations are frequently **human bite ('fight bite') injuries** from striking a mouth. Because of the high infection risk (Eikenella, oral flora) and joint penetration, these require irrigation, antibiotics, and exploration/debridement with the wound left open — NOT primary closure and repair. The zone of tendon/capsule injury shifts with finger position (injury occurred with the fist clenched), so it must be sought with the MP flexed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The lumbrical is unique among hand muscles because it:

options.text: Originates from the FDP (flexor) tendon and inserts into the extensor mechanism (radial lateral band)
Originates from bone and inserts on the flexor tendon
Has no tendinous insertion
Only extends the MP joint

questions.explanation: The **lumbrical originates from the FDP tendon in the palm and inserts into the radial lateral band of the extensor mechanism** — the only muscle spanning from a flexor to an extensor system. This arrangement lets it simultaneously flex the MP and extend the IP joints, and underlies the **lumbrical-plus** phenomenon (paradoxical PIP extension) when FDP tension is abnormal after injury/reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: When is a patient considered to have a 'chronic' mallet finger, per the timing definition used in the chapter?

options.text: Presenting later than 4 weeks after injury
Presenting later than 1 week after injury
Presenting later than 6 months after injury
Only after failed surgery

questions.explanation: By the chapter's convention, mallet fingers presenting **within 4 weeks are 'acute' and later than 4 weeks are 'chronic.'** This distinction guides expectations, but even chronic mallets often still respond to a trial of prolonged continuous DIP extension splinting before surgical options (terminal tendon reconstruction, Fowler tenotomy, or DIP fusion) are considered.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 5 (Extensor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: In the five-zone (Verdan/Kleinert) classification of flexor tendon injuries, Zone 2 ('no man's land') extends between:

options.text: The proximal edge of the A1 pulley and the insertion of the FDS on the middle phalanx
The FDS insertion and the fingertip
The muscle-tendon junction and the carpal tunnel
Within the carpal tunnel

questions.explanation: **Zone 2** runs from the **proximal edge of the A1 pulley to the FDS insertion** on the middle phalanx — the region where FDS and FDP run together within the tight fibro-osseous sheath, historically 'no man's land' because repairs adhered so readily. **Zone 1** is distal to the FDS insertion (FDP only); **Zone 3** is the lumbrical origin (palm); **Zone 4** is the carpal tunnel; **Zone 5** is proximal to the carpal tunnel.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A laceration in Zone 1 of a finger, by definition, injures which tendon?

options.text: Only the FDP (flexor digitorum profundus)
Only the FDS
Both FDP and FDS
The lumbrical tendon

questions.explanation: **Zone 1 is distal to the FDS insertion**, so a laceration there injures **only the FDP**. This is why an isolated loss of active DIP flexion with preserved PIP flexion localizes to zone 1 (or an FDP avulsion). Zone 2 injuries, in contrast, can involve FDP and/or one or both slips of the FDS.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: To isolate and test the FDS tendon of a single finger, the examiner should:

options.text: Hold the other fingers in full extension and ask the patient to flex the finger at the PIP joint
Hold the middle phalanx and ask for DIP flexion
Ask the patient to make a full fist
Stabilize the wrist and test resisted wrist flexion

questions.explanation: Because the FDP tendons share a common muscle belly, **holding the adjacent fingers in full extension neutralizes the profundus**, so any active **PIP flexion of the tested finger must come from the FDS**. Active DIP flexion (with the middle phalanx stabilized) tests the FDP. Note: preserved PIP flexion does not exclude a partial FDS laceration.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which two annular pulleys are considered biomechanically the most important to preserve to prevent flexor tendon bowstringing?

options.text: A2 and A4
A1 and A3
A3 and A5
A1 and A5

questions.explanation: The **A2 (proximal third of the proximal phalanx) and A4 (middle phalanx)** pulleys are the most critical for maintaining tendon mechanical advantage; their loss causes **bowstringing** and loss of efficient excursion. The A1, A3, and A5 pulleys arise from the palmar plates of the MCP, PIP, and DIP joints respectively and are more expendable. Modern data show A2 and A4 can be partially vented to allow repair passage without bowstringing.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The 'Camper chiasm' refers to:

options.text: The point where the two decussating slips of the FDS reunite (deep to the FDP) before inserting on the middle phalanx
The bifurcation of the FDP into two slips
The junction of the lumbrical and FDP
The crossing of the digital nerves over the flexor sheath

questions.explanation: In the proximal sheath the **FDS splits into two slips that decussate around the FDP** (passing dorsal to it), then **reunite at the Camper chiasm** (over the PIP volar plate) before inserting as two slips on the volar middle phalanx. This anatomy explains why the FDP lies superficial (palmar) to the FDS distally and is relevant to tendon retrieval and repair sequencing in zone 2.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The intrasynovial flexor tendon in zones 1–2 has a dual nutritional supply consisting of:

options.text: Vascular perfusion (via the vincula) and synovial diffusion (imbibition)
Only vincular blood supply
Only muscular perfusion from the forearm
Periosteal blood supply from the phalanges

questions.explanation: Intrasynovial flexor tendons are nourished by **both vascular perfusion (the vincular system) and synovial fluid diffusion (imbibition)**. Notably, the **palmar surface of the tendon in zones 1–2 is relatively avascular** (relying on diffusion), while the dorsal surface has richer vincular supply. This diffusion-based nutrition is the biologic rationale for early controlled motion, which promotes healing and reduces adhesions.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The four vincula of a finger's flexor tendons carry segmental blood supply. The vinculum longum to the profundus (VLP) arises from:

options.text: The FDS at the level of the PIP joint
The floor of the sheath over the proximal phalanx
The distal phalanx near the FDP insertion
The A1 pulley

questions.explanation: The **vinculum longum profundus (VLP) arises from the FDS at the PIP joint level**. The vinculum longum superficialis (VLS) arises from the floor of the sheath over the proximal phalanx, and the vincula brevia (VBS, VBP) are small triangular mesenteries near the FDS and FDP insertions. This vincular arrangement is clinically important in FDP avulsions (Leddy classification), where the level of retraction reflects which vincula remain intact.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: In the Leddy classification of FDP avulsions ('jersey finger'), which type has the tendon retracted into the PALM (with disruption of both vincula) and therefore requires the MOST urgent repair?

options.text: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV

questions.explanation: **Leddy Type I**: the FDP retracts **into the palm**, disrupting both vincula and its blood supply — this is the most time-sensitive, best repaired **within ~7–10 days (before ~3 weeks)** to avoid tendon necrosis/contracture. **Type II**: tendon retracts to the PIP level with the vinculum longum intact (more time available). **Type III**: a large bony fragment is caught at the A4 pulley, limiting retraction. (A type IV describes a bony fragment plus tendon avulsion off that fragment.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A rugby player cannot actively flex the DIP joint of the ring finger after his finger caught in a jersey. The most likely injury and its typical mechanism are:

options.text: FDP avulsion ('jersey finger') — forced extension of an actively flexed DIP
Central slip rupture — forced flexion of an extended PIP
Mallet finger — forced flexion of an extended DIP
Sagittal band rupture — direct blow to the MCP

questions.explanation: **Jersey finger** is an FDP avulsion, classically in the **ring finger**, from **forced extension of a maximally flexed DIP** (grabbing a jersey). It presents with loss of active DIP flexion. The **ring finger** is most vulnerable because of its relative prominence in grip and its FDP anatomy. Early recognition matters — a Leddy type I (palm retraction) needs prompt repair.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: When reattaching an avulsed FDP to the distal phalanx, over-advancing and inserting the tendon too tightly (>~1 cm advancement) risks:

options.text: A 'quadriga' effect — limited flexion of the adjacent uninjured fingers
A lumbrical-plus finger
A swan-neck deformity
A Stener lesion

questions.explanation: Because the FDP tendons share a common muscle belly, over-advancing one FDP effectively shortens it; when the repaired finger reaches full flexion, the other FDP tendons cannot pull through, causing incomplete flexion and weak grip of the adjacent fingers — the **quadriga effect**. Therefore FDP advancement should be limited (repair to bone if <1 cm of stump remains, but avoid excessive shortening).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: During flexor tendon healing, repair-site GAP formation is important because gaps greater than approximately how much predict failure to gain tensile strength and worse outcomes?

options.text: 3 mm
10 mm
0.5 mm
20 mm

questions.explanation: Repairs with **gaps <3 mm accrue tensile strength during healing**, whereas **gaps >3 mm fail to gain strength** and are associated with adhesions, triggering at the repair, and rupture. Minimizing gap (adequate core suture purchase/tension, adding a peripheral epitendinous suture) is a central goal — the epitendinous suture also tidies the repair and reduces gliding resistance.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The tensile strength of a flexor tendon core suture repair is most directly proportional to:

options.text: The number of core suture strands crossing the repair (and suture caliber/material)
The number of skin sutures used
The length of the skin incision
The color of the suture

questions.explanation: Repair strength correlates with the **number of core suture strands crossing the repair** (a 4-strand repair is roughly twice as strong as a 2-strand), plus **suture caliber and material** (e.g., 3-0 stronger than 4-0). Multistrand repairs (4- to 6-strand: Strickland, cruciate, Savage, etc.) provide the strength needed for early active motion, though more strands can increase bulk/gliding resistance and handling difficulty.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Adding a peripheral (epitendinous/circumferential) suture to a core suture flexor tendon repair primarily serves to:

options.text: Increase repair strength, reduce gap formation, and smooth the repair to lower gliding resistance
Provide the entire tensile strength of the repair
Serve only a cosmetic purpose with no mechanical benefit
Replace the need for any core suture

questions.explanation: The **epitendinous (peripheral) suture** adds meaningful strength (often 10–50%), **resists gap formation**, and **tidies/smooths the repair surface to reduce gliding resistance** through the pulleys. It complements — but does not replace — the core suture, which provides the bulk of the tensile strength. Together they make a repair robust enough for early active motion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: For a partial flexor tendon laceration involving LESS than ~50–60% of the tendon cross-section, the recommended management is generally to:

options.text: Not place a formal core repair; smooth/trim the edges (or leave alone) and mobilize, since core repair adds bulk without benefit
Always place a full core suture repair as for a complete laceration
Excise the entire tendon and graft
Fuse the adjacent joint

questions.explanation: Partial lacerations under ~50–60% generally do **not need a core repair**; the flap may be trimmed/beveled or left alone, avoiding the bulk and triggering that a formal repair could cause. Lacerations **>50–60%** are repaired (or the frayed edge debrided) because they risk **late rupture, triggering, or entrapment**. Some surgeons place an epitendinous suture on larger partial injuries to prevent triggering.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The modern consensus for a sharp complete zone 2 flexor tendon laceration in a clean wound is:

options.text: Primary (or delayed primary) repair with early controlled motion rehabilitation
Routine tendon excision and staged grafting for all cases
Immobilization only, never repair (it is still 'no man's land')
Immediate DIP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: Although zone 2 was once deemed 'no man's land' where primary repair was avoided, **improved suture techniques and early-motion rehabilitation have made primary (or delayed primary) repair the preferred treatment**. Delayed primary repair (within ~1–2 weeks) yields results similar to immediate repair. Emergency repair is reserved for injuries requiring microvascular repair of compromised digital perfusion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The only clear indication for truly EMERGENT (immediate) flexor tendon exploration/repair, rather than delayed primary repair, is:

options.text: Compromised digital perfusion requiring microvascular arterial (and nerve) repair
Any complete tendon laceration
A partial laceration
An isolated FDS laceration with intact FDP

questions.explanation: Flexor tendon repair itself is not an emergency and can be done as a **delayed primary** procedure with equal results. The exception is **impaired digital perfusion** (e.g., both digital arteries injured), which mandates **urgent exploration and microvascular repair** of the artery (and nerve) — the tendon is then repaired at the same setting. A clean isolated tendon laceration can safely wait days.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: 'Venting' (partial division) of the A2 or A4 pulley during zone 2 repair is now considered acceptable because:

options.text: Limited venting improves tendon gliding without causing clinically significant bowstringing
The A2 and A4 pulleys have no mechanical role
Complete excision of both pulleys is harmless
Venting increases repair strength

questions.explanation: Biomechanical/clinical work (Lieber and others) shows that **partial venting of the A2 or A4 pulley (or A4 division) can be done to allow the repaired tendon to glide** without producing clinically significant bowstringing. This pragmatic modification prevents the repair from catching at the pulley edge. It does not add strength; the goal is smooth intraoperative excursion on passive motion testing.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The Kleinert rehabilitation protocol after flexor tendon repair uses:

options.text: A dorsal blocking splint with rubber-band traction producing active extension and passive (elastic) flexion
Complete immobilization for 6 weeks
Immediate unrestricted active flexion and extension
Serial casting in progressive flexion

questions.explanation: The **Kleinert protocol** uses a **dorsal blocking splint** with **rubber-band traction on the fingernail**: the patient actively extends the finger against the elastic, which then passively flexes the digit — protecting the repair while promoting gliding. The **Duran protocol** is passive flexion and extension performed by the therapist/other hand. Modern strong (4-strand+) repairs increasingly use **early active motion / place-and-hold** protocols.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The Duran rehabilitation method after flexor tendon repair is best described as:

options.text: Controlled passive motion (passive flexion and extension within a dorsal blocking splint)
Rubber-band dynamic traction for active extension/passive flexion
Early active place-and-hold flexion
Rigid immobilization until 4 weeks

questions.explanation: The **Duran protocol** is **controlled passive motion**: within a dorsal blocking splint, the tendon is moved by passive flexion and extension (originally to produce a few millimeters of tendon excursion) to prevent adhesions while protecting the repair. It contrasts with Kleinert's dynamic rubber-band method and with modern early-active-motion (place-and-hold) protocols that require stronger multistrand repairs.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Early ACTIVE motion (e.g., place-and-hold) protocols after flexor tendon repair became feasible primarily because of:

options.text: Stronger multistrand (4- to 6-strand) core repairs with epitendinous augmentation that resist gap and rupture
The abandonment of dorsal blocking splints
Routine tenolysis at 2 weeks
Use of absorbable core sutures

questions.explanation: Early **active** motion generates higher forces than passive protocols, so it requires a repair strong enough to resist gapping and rupture — hence the shift is enabled by **multistrand (4- to 6-strand) core repairs plus a peripheral epitendinous suture**. Active-motion protocols improve tendon excursion/gliding and functional results but demand meticulous, robust repair technique.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The WALANT (wide-awake local anesthesia, no tourniquet) technique offers which specific advantage in flexor tendon surgery?

options.text: Intraoperative active testing of tendon gliding and repair integrity by the awake patient before closure
It eliminates the need for any suture repair
It guarantees no adhesion formation
It allows repair without any core suture

questions.explanation: **WALANT** uses lidocaine with epinephrine for anesthesia/hemostasis without a tourniquet, allowing the **awake patient to actively flex and extend the finger intraoperatively** so the surgeon can confirm smooth gliding, adequate repair strength, and absence of catching/triggering at the pulleys before closing — and adjust (e.g., vent a pulley) if needed. It has become popular for tendon repair for this reason.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient develops a stiff finger with an adherent flexor tendon graft/repair that fails to glide despite adequate therapy. The prerequisite for proceeding with flexor TENOLYSIS is:

options.text: Full or nearly full PASSIVE digital range of motion (supple joints)
Complete absence of any active motion
A fixed joint contracture
Immediate surgery within 2 weeks of the injury

questions.explanation: **Tenolysis requires supple joints — full or near-full passive motion** — because releasing adhesions only helps if the joints can move; a fixed contracture must be corrected first. Tenolysis is considered when **serial measurements show a plateau of active motion despite adequate therapy** (typically several months out — often ~4 months after repair, or ~6 months after a free graft). Immediate postoperative active motion is essential to preserve the gains.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: When a flexor tendon cannot be primarily repaired and the sheath/bed is scarred, a two-stage (Hunter) reconstruction is used. The purpose of the FIRST stage (silicone rod) is to:

options.text: Create a smooth, pseudosynovial gliding tunnel (and reconstruct pulleys) before grafting
Permanently replace the tendon
Fuse the finger joints
Deliver antibiotics to the sheath

questions.explanation: In **staged (Hunter) reconstruction**, a **silicone rod is placed first to induce a smooth pseudosynovial sheath (gliding tunnel)** and to allow pulley reconstruction, while the passive motion keeps joints supple. At the **second stage** (~3 months later), the rod is replaced by a **free tendon graft** that runs in the newly formed gliding bed. Single-stage grafting is reserved for a supple finger with an adequate, unscarred sheath.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which finding is a recognized poor-prognostic factor for functional gain after flexor tenolysis?

options.text: Associated nerve repair/graft, patient age >40, late tenolysis (>1 year), or need for prolonged operative time
Supple joints with full passive motion
A localized single adhesion
Early tenolysis in a compliant patient

questions.explanation: Poor prognostic factors for tenolysis include **associated nerve repair/graft, age older than 40, late tenolysis (>1 year post-injury), and a technically difficult, prolonged procedure** (extensive adhesions). Favorable candidates have **isolated/localized adhesions, supple joints, and good motivation** for aggressive immediate postoperative motion (which is essential to preserve the surgical gains).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: During zone 2 repair, the retracted proximal FDP stump is best retrieved atraumatically by:

options.text: Gentle milking/passive wrist-and-finger flexion, or a catheter/suture technique, avoiding repeated blind grasping that damages the tendon and sheath
Repeated blind grasping with a clamp until it is caught
Widely excising the A2 pulley for exposure
Leaving it retracted and grafting instead

questions.explanation: The retracted proximal stump is delivered atraumatically — **milking the tendon distally, flexing the wrist/MCP, or using a small catheter/feeding tube (the tendon sutured to it) to shuttle it** through the sheath. **Repeated blind grasping damages the tendon surface and sheath, increasing adhesions**; a proximal counter-incision or the Sourmelis-McGrouther retrieval technique helps. The stump can be held with a transverse needle while the core suture is placed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Bowstringing after flexor tendon injury/surgery most directly results from:

options.text: Loss/incompetence of critical annular pulleys (especially A2 and A4)
Over-tightening of the core suture
Excessive early passive motion
Repair of a partial laceration

questions.explanation: **Bowstringing** — the flexor tendon lifting away from the phalanges during flexion — occurs when the **key annular pulleys (A2, A4) are lost or incompetent**, reducing mechanical efficiency and flexion arc. It is a rationale for preserving/reconstructing A2 and A4 (pulley reconstruction using tendon graft or extensor retinaculum). Complications after flexor repair also include quadriga, triggering, swan-neck, and lumbrical-plus deformity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A 'lumbrical-plus' finger produces paradoxical PIP EXTENSION on attempted finger flexion. It can arise after flexor tendon injury/reconstruction because:

options.text: A divided/lengthened FDP (or an over-long graft) transmits tension through the intact lumbrical to the extensor mechanism
The central slip is ruptured
The A1 pulley is contracted
The FDS is over-tightened

questions.explanation: The lumbrical originates from the FDP and inserts into the radial lateral band (extensor mechanism). If the **FDP is divided distal to the lumbrical origin or a graft is too long/loose**, attempted flexion pulls the FDP proximally, tensioning the lumbrical, which **paradoxically extends the PIP** — the **lumbrical-plus** phenomenon. Correct graft tensioning and, if needed, lumbrical release address it.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: When repairing an FDP avulsion to bone, direct end-to-end tendon repair (rather than repair to bone) is preferred when:

options.text: There is at least ~1 cm of distal tendon stump available for a tendon-to-tendon repair
There is less than 1 cm of distal stump
The tendon has retracted into the palm
There is an associated distal phalanx fracture

questions.explanation: If **≥1 cm of distal FDP stump** remains, a **direct tendon-to-tendon (end-to-end) repair** is preferable. If **<1 cm** of stump remains, the tendon is advanced and **repaired to bone** (e.g., suture anchor or pull-out suture over a button) — but excessive advancement (>1 cm) must be avoided to prevent the quadriga effect on the other fingers.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which suture material property combination is generally favored for the CORE suture of a flexor tendon repair?

options.text: A stronger caliber (e.g., 3-0 or 4-0) non-absorbable, low-friction braided or looped suture
A fine 6-0 absorbable monofilament
Plain catgut
Steel wire for all repairs

questions.explanation: The **core suture is typically a strong, non-absorbable material of 3-0 or 4-0 caliber** (larger caliber = stronger repair; 3-0 stronger than 4-0), chosen to match tendon size. Looped sutures ease placement of multistrand configurations. The peripheral epitendinous suture is finer (e.g., 6-0). Absorbable/fine sutures lack the durability needed to withstand early motion forces.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The FPL (flexor pollicis longus) tendon poses a unique challenge in repair because:

options.text: Its proximal end tends to retract far into the forearm (no restraining vinculum), often requiring retrieval via a separate incision
It has no muscle belly
It cannot be repaired primarily
It lies dorsal to the extensor tendons

questions.explanation: The **FPL lacks a restraining vinculum**, so its proximal stump **retracts markedly, often into the distal forearm**, and may need retrieval through a separate proximal incision (e.g., delivering it with a silicone feeding tube). Otherwise, thumb flexor repair principles mirror zone 2, and its repair is protected postoperatively (thumb included in the splint). Overtightening should be avoided.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The three layers of an annular pulley each have a strategic function. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The inner layer secretes hyaluronic acid for gliding; the collagen-rich middle layer resists palmar tendon translation; the outer areolar layer aids nutrition
The outer layer secretes synovial fluid and the inner layer resists translation
All three layers only provide vascular supply
The pulley is a single homogeneous layer of collagen

questions.explanation: Structural analysis shows the **innermost pulley layer secretes hyaluronic acid to facilitate gliding**, the **collagen-rich middle layer resists palmar (volar) translation of the tendon** (the pulley's mechanical role), and the **outer areolar layer supports nutrition** of the pulley. The cruciform pulleys are collapsible ('accordion') to permit flexion without deforming the annular system.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The A2 and A4 pulleys are distinguished from A1, A3, and A5 by their bony origins. From where do A2 and A4 arise?

options.text: A2 from the proximal third of the proximal phalanx; A4 from the middle phalanx
A2 from the MCP volar plate; A4 from the DIP volar plate
Both from the metacarpal
A2 from the middle phalanx; A4 from the distal phalanx

questions.explanation: **A2 originates from the proximal third of the proximal phalanx and A4 from the middle phalanx** (both arise from bone). In contrast, **A1, A3, and A5 arise from the palmar plates** of the MCP, PIP, and DIP joints. The bony (phalangeal) origin and greater length of A2 and A4 underlie their mechanical importance in preventing bowstringing.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The palmar (volar) surface of the flexor tendon in zones 1–2 is relatively avascular. What is the practical implication?

options.text: It relies heavily on synovial diffusion, supporting early controlled motion to enhance healing and reduce adhesions
It means the tendon cannot heal and must always be grafted
It requires the repair suture to be placed only palmarly
It has no relevance to rehabilitation

questions.explanation: Because the **palmar tendon surface in zones 1–2 is relatively avascular and depends on synovial fluid diffusion**, healing is favored by mechanisms that promote diffusion and gliding — namely **early controlled motion**, which improves nutrition, reduces adhesions, and enhances intrinsic tendon healing. This biology is a key rationale for modern early-motion protocols over prolonged immobilization.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A patient with an isolated FDS laceration (FDP intact) but a laceration to only one FDS slip near the Camper chiasm can present with:

options.text: Preserved active PIP flexion despite a partial FDS injury (so preserved flexion does not exclude FDS injury)
Complete loss of DIP flexion
A mallet finger
Loss of MCP extension

questions.explanation: Because the FDS has two slips, a **partial FDS injury can still allow active PIP flexion** — so **preserved PIP flexion does NOT rule out an FDS laceration**. Careful wound exploration (ideally with the finger moved through its arc, e.g., under WALANT) is needed to identify partial FDS injuries, which if large may need repair to prevent triggering.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A dorsal blocking splint after flexor tendon repair typically positions the wrist and MCP joints how?

options.text: Wrist in slight/neutral-to-mild flexion and MCP joints flexed, with the IP joints allowed to extend within the splint
Wrist in maximal extension and MCP joints extended
Wrist and all finger joints in full extension
Wrist in neutral with the MCPs hyperextended

questions.explanation: The **dorsal blocking splint** holds the **wrist in mild/neutral flexion and the MCP joints flexed**, which relaxes the flexor system and prevents full extension that would stress the repair, while permitting protected IP motion. Newer protocols favor a more wrist-neutral position with early active place-and-hold. The exact position varies by protocol, but the principle is to protect the repair while allowing controlled gliding.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A single-stage free tendon graft (rather than a staged reconstruction) is appropriate when:

options.text: The finger has supple joints and a relatively intact, unscarred sheath with adequate pulleys
The sheath is heavily scarred with destroyed pulleys
There are fixed joint contractures
There is active infection in the sheath

questions.explanation: **Single-stage free tendon grafting** works when the digit has **supple joints and a preserved, relatively unscarred sheath with adequate pulleys** to allow the graft to glide. If the **sheath is scarred and pulleys are deficient** (or joints stiff), a **two-stage (Hunter) reconstruction** with a silicone rod (to form a pseudosheath and reconstruct pulleys) followed by grafting is required.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which of the following is the LEAST accurate statement about zone 2 flexor tendon repair?

options.text: Primary repair should be avoided in zone 2 because it is 'no man's land'
Both FDP and one or both FDS slips may be involved
Early controlled motion improves gliding and outcomes
Pulley venting can aid tendon gliding without significant bowstringing

questions.explanation: The false (outdated) statement is that primary repair should be avoided in zone 2. Historically called 'no man's land,' zone 2 was thought unsuitable for primary repair, but **modern technique and rehabilitation have made primary (or delayed primary) repair the standard**. The other statements are correct: zone 2 can involve FDP and FDS slips, early motion helps, and judicious pulley venting aids gliding.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: In Leddy Type II FDP avulsion, the tendon typically retracts to the level of the PIP joint and is held there by:

options.text: An intact vinculum longum profundus (VLP)
A bony fragment caught at the A4 pulley
The intact A1 pulley
The lumbrical origin

questions.explanation: In **Leddy Type II**, the FDP retracts to the **PIP level**, tethered by the **intact vinculum longum profundus (VLP)** (which arises from the FDS at the PIP), preserving some blood supply. This gives more time for repair than Type I (palm retraction, both vincula disrupted). **Type III** has a bony fragment caught at the A4 pulley, limiting retraction further and preserving vincular supply.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which anatomic fact about the FDP muscle is correct and clinically relevant to the quadriga phenomenon?

options.text: The FDP tendons to the fingers share a common muscle belly (especially the ulnar three digits)
Each finger FDP has a completely independent muscle belly
The FDP is innervated solely by the radial nerve
The FDP has no tendons in the fingers

questions.explanation: The **FDP tendons (particularly to the ulnar three fingers) share a common muscle belly**, so they move together — the anatomic basis of the **quadriga effect** (over-advancing/tethering one FDP limits excursion of the others). The FDP is innervated by the **ulnar nerve (medial half) and the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve (lateral half, index/middle)**, with its blood supply largely from the ulnar artery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Postoperatively, a repaired flexor tendon is weakest (most prone to rupture) at approximately what time, guiding rehabilitation caution?

options.text: Around days 5–21, during the inflammatory/softening phase before collagen remodeling strengthens the repair
Immediately at day 0, then it only gets weaker
At 6 months, when it is fully healed
The repair strength never changes over time

questions.explanation: Tendon repairs commonly experience a **'softening' phase in roughly the first ~1–3 weeks** where the repair strength dips before collagen remodeling and revascularization progressively strengthen it (repairs with <3 mm gap gain strength thereafter). This early vulnerable window is why controlled-motion protocols carefully limit forces, and why patient compliance is critical to avoid rupture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Why must a distal phalanx (or associated bony) fracture be considered when repairing an FDP avulsion?

options.text: A bony avulsion fragment (Leddy III/IV) changes the level of retraction and the fixation strategy (fragment fixation vs tendon-to-bone)
It always contraindicates any repair
It converts the injury into a mallet finger
It has no effect on management

questions.explanation: An FDP avulsion may carry a **bony fragment (Leddy type III, or type IV with tendon avulsed off the fragment)**. The fragment limits retraction (often caught at the A4 pulley) and dictates whether to **fix the bony fragment** (screw/wire/suture) versus perform **tendon-to-bone repair**. Recognizing associated fractures on imaging is essential to plan the correct fixation and avoid missing a displaced fragment.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about the timing of tenolysis after flexor tendon repair or grafting is most consistent with the chapter?

options.text: Allow adequate healing first — often ~4 months after primary repair and ~6 months after a free tendon graft — once active motion has plateaued despite therapy
Perform tenolysis routinely at 2 weeks postoperatively
Tenolysis should never be performed
Tenolysis is only appropriate in the first postoperative week

questions.explanation: Tenolysis is delayed until **soft tissues have healed and stabilized and active motion has plateaued despite adequate therapy** — commonly cited as **~4 months after primary repair** and **~6 months after a free tendon graft** (opinions range from 3 to 9 months). The joints must be supple (full passive motion), and immediate aggressive postoperative active motion is required to preserve the gains.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Pulley reconstruction (e.g., after loss of A2/A4) can be performed using which graft materials?

options.text: A tendon graft (e.g., a strip of FDS/palmaris) or a segment of extensor retinaculum wrapped around the phalanx
Only synthetic mesh, which is mandatory
The volar plate transferred proximally
A silicone rod left permanently

questions.explanation: Critical pulleys (A2, A4) are reconstructed with **autograft — a tendon graft strip (e.g., from FDS or palmaris longus) looped around the phalanx, or a segment of extensor retinaculum**. Restoring these pulleys prevents bowstringing and improves excursion efficiency, and is a key step during staged flexor reconstruction (over a silicone rod) before grafting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which principle best summarizes why early controlled mobilization is favored over prolonged immobilization after flexor tendon repair?

options.text: Controlled motion promotes intrinsic tendon healing/gliding and reduces adhesions, improving final range of motion
Motion eliminates the need for a strong repair
Immobilization has no effect on adhesions
Motion prevents the tendon from ever gaining strength

questions.explanation: **Early controlled motion improves tendon gliding, promotes intrinsic (rather than adhesive extrinsic) healing, enhances diffusion-based nutrition, and reduces peritendinous adhesions**, producing better final motion. It does, however, **require a repair strong enough** (multistrand + epitendinous) to withstand the applied forces without gapping or rupture — the balance that defines modern flexor tendon rehabilitation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A laceration over the distal palm/proximal finger injures the flexor tendon at the level of the lumbrical origin from the FDP. This corresponds to which flexor zone?

options.text: Zone 3
Zone 1
Zone 2
Zone 5

questions.explanation: **Zone 3** is the region of the palm between the distal edge of the carpal tunnel (distal to zone 4) and the proximal edge of the A1 pulley — it contains the **origin of the lumbricals from the FDP tendons**. Repairs in zone 3 (and zone 5, proximal to the carpal tunnel) generally have better outcomes than zone 2 because the tendons are outside the tight digital sheath.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: A laceration within the carpal tunnel that injures multiple flexor tendons and possibly the median nerve is classified as which zone, generally associated with a relatively favorable tendon-repair prognosis?

options.text: Zone 4
Zone 2
Zone 1
Zone 3

questions.explanation: **Zone 4** is the segment **within the carpal tunnel**. Injuries here often involve multiple tendons and risk **median nerve** injury; the transverse carpal ligament may need partial release/repair considerations. Because the tendons lie outside the constrictive digital sheath, tendon-repair prognosis is generally better than in zone 2, though tendon adherence within the tunnel and nerve injury can complicate recovery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about where the core suture 'grasp' or 'lock' should be positioned within the tendon is best supported by biomechanical data?

options.text: Adequate purchase (roughly ~0.7–1 cm from the cut end) with locking loops improves strength and resistance to pull-through
The core suture should be placed as close as possible (<1 mm) to the cut edge
Locking configurations weaken the repair compared with simple grasping loops in all cases
Purchase length has no effect on repair strength

questions.explanation: Repair strength improves with **adequate core-suture purchase from the cut end (on the order of ~7–10 mm)** and with **locking loops**, which resist suture pull-through and gap formation better than simple grasping loops. Too short a purchase pulls out; excessively long purchase adds little. This is why locked, adequate-purchase multistrand techniques are favored for early active motion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Digital triggering or catching AFTER a flexor tendon repair most commonly results from:

options.text: A bulky repair or unrepaired large partial laceration catching at a pulley edge
Excessive tendon nutrition
Too many core suture strands producing weakness
Complete pulley preservation

questions.explanation: **Post-repair triggering/catching** typically arises when a **bulky repair or a large unrepaired partial laceration flap catches at a pulley edge** (commonly A2 or A4). Prevention includes tidy repair with an epitendinous suture, repairing/trimming large partial injuries, judicious pulley venting, and confirming smooth gliding intraoperatively (e.g., under WALANT). Persistent triggering may require pulley venting or repair revision.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the recommended approach to a flexor tendon laceration presenting 2 weeks after a clean injury (no repair yet performed)?

options.text: Delayed primary repair is still reasonable, with results comparable to earlier repair if the tendon ends can be approximated
It is far too late; only staged reconstruction is possible
The tendon should never be repaired after 24 hours
Immediate amputation is indicated

questions.explanation: A **delayed primary repair** (up to roughly 2–3 weeks) can give results comparable to earlier repair as long as the tendon ends can be mobilized and approximated without excessive tension. Beyond that window, myostatic muscle contracture and tendon retraction/gap may preclude direct repair and necessitate grafting/staged reconstruction. So a 2-week delay does not doom the repair.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: Which tendon is a commonly used donor for a free flexor tendon graft when the palmaris longus is absent?

options.text: Plantaris (or a long toe extensor / a segment of FDS)
Flexor carpi ulnaris
Extensor carpi radialis brevis
Abductor pollicis longus

questions.explanation: When the **palmaris longus is absent** (~15% of people) or insufficient, common free-graft donors include the **plantaris tendon, a long toe extensor (EDL to a lesser toe), or a segment of an expendable FDS**. These provide adequate length and appropriate caliber for a flexor graft. Wrist/finger prime movers (FCU, ECRB, APL) are not used as expendable free grafts.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 6 (Flexor Tendon Injury)

questions.stem: The stability of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint is provided by a three-sided 'box' complex. Which structures form this complex?

options.text: The two collateral ligaments and the volar plate
The central slip, lateral bands, and terminal tendon
The A2 and A4 pulleys and the flexor tendons
The dorsal capsule and the two sesamoids

questions.explanation: PIP stability derives from a three-sided **'box' complex: the radial and ulnar collateral ligaments on each side and the volar plate as the floor**. This rigid three-dimensional construct strongly resists displacement; to dislocate the PIP, the complex must be disrupted in **at least two planes**. The collaterals are the primary restraints to lateral stress, and the volar plate is the primary restraint to hyperextension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: The proximal portion of the PIP volar plate thickens into paired 'checkrein' ligaments. What is their function?

options.text: They are secondary restraints to hyperextension while still permitting full flexion
They are the primary restraint to lateral deviation
They flex the DIP joint
They anchor the flexor tendon to bone

questions.explanation: The proximal volar plate thickens into paired **checkrein ligaments**, which act as **secondary restraints to hyperextension** but permit full flexion. Pathologic contracture/scarring of the checkreins is a cause of PIP flexion contracture; their release is part of treating a stiff PIP. The distal fibrocartilaginous volar plate is the primary hyperextension restraint.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: The PIP joint is the most common site of ligamentous injury in the hand. When testing PIP collateral ligament stability, examination in 30–40° of FLEXION primarily assesses:

options.text: The proper collateral ligaments
The accessory collateral ligaments only
The central slip
The flexor tendon integrity

questions.explanation: Stress testing the PIP in **flexion (~30–40°) isolates the proper collateral ligaments** (taut in flexion), whereas testing in full extension reflects the secondary stability from the accessory collaterals, volar plate, and bony contours. Biomechanically the ligament is under maximal tension around 40° of flexion, which is the best position to test collateral competence.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: The most common mechanism producing a DORSAL PIP dislocation is:

options.text: Hyperextension with axial (longitudinal) compression — classically a ball striking the fingertip
Pure lateral (radial or ulnar) force
Forced flexion with rotation
A crush injury to the fingertip

questions.explanation: A **dorsal PIP dislocation** results from **hyperextension plus axial compression** (a ball striking the extended fingertip). The volar plate is sheared off the base of the middle phalanx (often with a small avulsion fracture — ~44% in one series). In a pure dislocation the collaterals split longitudinally, and the middle phalanx displaces dorsally on the proximal phalangeal head.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: After closed reduction of a simple dorsal PIP dislocation that is stable, the recommended treatment is:

options.text: Brief dorsal extension-block splinting and early active motion / buddy taping
Continuous full-extension splinting for 6 weeks
Immediate open volar plate repair in all cases
PIP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: A reduced, **stable** simple dorsal PIP dislocation is treated with a brief **dorsal extension-block splint and early active motion** (or buddy taping) — the usual sequela of PIP ligament injury is **stiffness, not instability**, so prolonged rigid immobilization is avoided. If the joint requires flexion beyond ~30° to stay reduced/congruent, it is unstable and operative stabilization should be considered.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: The single most important factor determining the STABILITY of a dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation is:

options.text: The percentage of the volar articular surface of the middle phalanx involved (the collateral attachments)
The patient's age
The finger involved
The presence of a subungual hematoma

questions.explanation: Stability depends on **how much of the volar articular base of the middle phalanx is fractured**: with **<40% involvement the joint is usually stable** in all positions (collaterals remain on the intact dorsal fragment); with **40–60% it is stable only in flexion**; and with **>60% it is unstable**. This drives the choice between extension-block splinting (stable) and operative reconstruction (unstable).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation involving 25% of the volar articular surface reduces concentrically and is stable at less than 30° of flexion. The best initial treatment is:

options.text: Dorsal extension-block splinting with early active flexion
Hemihamate autograft arthroplasty
Volar plate arthroplasty
PIP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: A fracture-dislocation with **<40% articular involvement that maintains a concentric reduction within ~30° of flexion** is well managed with **dorsal extension-block splinting and early motion**. The block is progressively decreased weekly. Reconstructive procedures (hemihamate arthroplasty, volar plate arthroplasty) are reserved for larger (>40–50%), comminuted, or unstable/chronic patterns.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: For an unstable, comminuted dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation with a large (>40–50%) volar fragment not suitable for ORIF, a favored reconstructive option that resurfaces the volar base with vascularized-appearing bone/cartilage is:

options.text: Hemihamate autograft arthroplasty
Extension-block splinting
Simple buddy taping
Central slip tenotomy

questions.explanation: **Hemihamate autograft arthroplasty** harvests an osteochondral graft from the dorsal-distal hamate to reconstruct the comminuted volar articular base of the middle phalanx, restoring the volar buttress and allowing early motion. Many authors prefer it over **volar plate arthroplasty** for unstable PIP fracture-dislocations, especially with large defects (>40–50%). Volar plate arthroplasty (Eaton) is an alternative for smaller/chronic defects.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Eaton's volar plate arthroplasty for a PIP fracture-dislocation works by:

options.text: Advancing the volar plate into the defect of the middle phalangeal base to resurface it and restore a stable buttress
Fusing the PIP joint in functional flexion
Transferring the FDS to the extensor mechanism
Replacing the joint with a silicone implant

questions.explanation: In **volar plate arthroplasty (Eaton and Malerich)**, the volar plate is advanced distally and sutured into the debrided defect of the middle phalangeal base to **resurface the volar articular deficiency and restore a stable buttress**, with the joint pinned in ~20–30° flexion and early protected motion. It is most reliable for defects up to ~40–50%; it tends to fail with larger involvement, where hemihamate grafting is preferred.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: In a LATERAL dislocation of the PIP joint, what are the critical anatomic lesions?

options.text: Rupture of one collateral ligament plus at least partial avulsion of the volar plate
Isolated central slip rupture
Bilateral collateral rupture with intact volar plate
Flexor tendon avulsion

questions.explanation: A **lateral PIP dislocation** requires disruption in two planes: **complete rupture of one collateral ligament and at least partial avulsion of the volar plate** from the middle phalanx. More than **20° of lateral deformity** on stress suggests complete collateral rupture. Most are treated closed (reduction, buddy taping, early motion) because stiffness — not chronic instability — is the usual outcome; acute repair is selective.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A VOLAR PIP dislocation (or rotatory volar subluxation) is important to recognize because the injured structure is:

options.text: The central slip — risking a boutonnière deformity, and a lateral band/collateral may block reduction
The terminal extensor tendon — risking a mallet finger
The A2 pulley — risking bowstringing
The flexor digitorum superficialis — risking loss of PIP flexion

questions.explanation: A **volar PIP dislocation** ruptures the **central slip**, so it carries a high risk of **boutonnière deformity** if the PIP is not held in extension during healing. In the rotatory variant, the proximal phalangeal condyle buttonholes between the central slip and a lateral band, which can **block reduction** (an irreducible pattern needing open reduction). Even after easy reduction, central slip competence must be checked (Elson test) and the PIP splinted in extension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: The Elson test assesses central slip integrity. With the PIP flexed 90° over a table edge and the patient extending against resistance, which finding indicates central slip RUPTURE?

options.text: A rigidly extended (or hyperextended) DIP joint, because extension force is diverted through the lateral bands
A supple, freely flexible DIP joint
Complete inability to flex the PIP
Pain over the volar plate only

questions.explanation: In the **Elson test**, with the PIP flexed 90° and the patient attempting PIP extension against resistance, an **incompetent central slip diverts all extension force through the lateral bands, producing a rigidly extended/hyperextended DIP**. A **supple DIP** indicates the central slip is intact. This detects central slip injury before a fixed boutonnière develops, prompting extension splinting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: After reduction of a volar PIP dislocation (central slip injury), the joint should be splinted:

options.text: PIP in full extension for ~6 weeks, while the DIP is left free for active flexion
PIP in 60° flexion continuously
Entire finger in extension including the DIP
PIP in extension-block flexion allowing PIP flexion

questions.explanation: Central slip injuries (volar PIP dislocation) are splinted with the **PIP in full extension for ~6 weeks** to allow the central slip to heal at length and prevent boutonnière, while the **DIP is left free** and actively flexed to keep the lateral bands mobile and prevent DIP extension contracture (which would worsen a boutonnière). This is the opposite of the extension-block strategy used for dorsal (volar plate) injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A dorsal PIP dislocation is IRREDUCIBLE by closed means. The most likely interposed structure blocking reduction is:

options.text: The volar plate (avulsed and drawn into the joint)
The extensor central slip
The flexor digitorum profundus
A sesamoid bone

questions.explanation: Rarely, the **volar plate ruptures proximally and is drawn into the joint**, blocking reduction of a dorsal PIP dislocation. Repeated forceful closed attempts can trap the volar plate and convert a reducible into an irreducible dislocation. Open reduction (Bruner volar approach, reflecting the A3 pulley/flexors, extricating and repairing the volar plate) is then required.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A chronic hyperextension deformity of the PIP joint following an untreated volar plate injury (with the DIP flexed) is called a:

options.text: Swan-neck deformity (with the pseudoboutonnière being its flexion-contracture counterpart)
Boutonnière deformity
Mallet finger
Claw deformity

questions.explanation: Volar plate insufficiency permits PIP **hyperextension**, producing a **swan-neck deformity** (PIP hyperextension, DIP flexion). Its counterpart, a **pseudoboutonnière deformity**, is a PIP flexion contracture from volar plate scarring after a hyperextension injury (distinguished from a true boutonnière, which stems from central slip injury). Flexible swan-neck from volar plate laxity can be treated with FDS tenodesis or lateral band relocation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: DIP joint dislocations are usually dorsal and typically reduce easily. When a DIP (or thumb IP) dislocation is IRREDUCIBLE, a commonly interposed structure is:

options.text: The volar plate or an interposed flexor tendon / sesamoid
The central slip
The extensor terminal tendon only
The A1 pulley

questions.explanation: DIP dislocations are rarely irreducible, but when they are, the block is usually the **volar plate**, an **entrapped flexor tendon** (the condyles can buttonhole through a longitudinal rent), or an interposed **sesamoid**. Open reduction is then needed. After reduction, stable DIP dislocations are splinted in extension for several weeks; associated large articular fractures (>40%) may need ORIF.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A patient has a dorsally dislocated index MCP joint. The finger is only slightly hyperextended, there is puckering of the palmar skin, and a sesamoid is seen within the widened joint space. This is a:

options.text: Complex (complete, irreducible) dislocation — the volar plate is interposed
Simple (subluxation) dislocation that will reduce with longitudinal traction
Lateral dislocation from collateral rupture
A volar MCP dislocation

questions.explanation: The **complex (complete/irreducible) MCP dislocation** is paradoxically only slightly hyperextended (bayonet posture), shows **palmar skin puckering** and a **sesamoid within the joint space** on radiographs — signs the **volar plate is avulsed and interposed** (Kaplan's lesion) over the metacarpal head, trapped between the flexor tendons and lumbrical. A **simple** dislocation is markedly hyperextended and reduces with flexion-based maneuvers.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Why can longitudinal traction and hyperextension WORSEN a simple (subluxated) MCP dislocation, converting it to a complex irreducible one?

options.text: It pulls the volar plate over the metacarpal head into the joint, trapping it
It ruptures the collateral ligaments
It fractures the metacarpal neck
It divides the flexor tendon

questions.explanation: In a simple (reducible) dorsal MCP dislocation, the volar plate is still out of the joint. **Forceful longitudinal traction/hyperextension drags the avulsed volar plate dorsally over the metacarpal head and into the joint**, where it becomes trapped between the metacarpal head and the flexor tendons/lumbrical — converting a reducible subluxation into an **irreducible complex dislocation**. The correct maneuver instead flexes the wrist and pushes the phalanx base over the head.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Which MCP joints are most commonly involved in complex dorsal dislocations, and through which approach can the interposed volar plate be released?

options.text: The index (and small) finger 'border' digits; via a dorsal or volar approach to extract/split the volar plate
Only the middle finger; via a midaxial approach
Only the thumb; via a Wagner approach
The ring finger exclusively; via a volar zigzag

questions.explanation: Complex MCP dislocations most often involve the **border digits (index most commonly, then small finger)**. Open reduction can be done via a **dorsal approach** (splitting the interposed volar plate longitudinally to free it from the metacarpal head) or a **volar approach** (extracting the plate, but with the digital nerves at risk as they are tented over the prominent metacarpal head). Early protected motion with a dorsal extension-block follows.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A young skier falls while gripping a pole and injures the thumb. The mechanism producing an ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) tear of the thumb MCP joint is:

options.text: Sudden forced radial deviation (abduction) of the thumb MCP joint
Forced ulnar deviation (adduction)
Axial compression along the thumb
Hyperflexion of the IP joint

questions.explanation: **'Skier's thumb'** (acute thumb MCP UCL injury) results from **sudden forced radial deviation/abduction** — e.g., the ski pole handle levering the thumb into abduction during a fall. UCL injuries are ~10× more common than RCL injuries. The tear is most often **distal (at the proximal phalangeal insertion)**, and the small avulsion fracture, when present, is at the ulnar base of the proximal phalanx.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A Stener lesion is:

options.text: Interposition of the adductor aponeurosis between the distally avulsed thumb UCL and its insertion, preventing healing
An avulsion fracture of the radial base of the proximal phalanx
A partial tear of the thumb UCL
Interposition of the volar plate in the MCP joint

questions.explanation: A **Stener lesion** occurs when the completely torn, distally avulsed thumb **UCL retracts and the proximal edge of the adductor aponeurosis becomes interposed between the ligament and its insertion**. Because the ligament is no longer in contact with its footprint, it **cannot heal with immobilization**, resulting in chronic instability — hence a Stener lesion is a firm indication for **surgical repair**. It does not occur in partial tears.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Which clinical finding on stress testing is most consistent with a COMPLETE (rather than partial) thumb UCL tear?

options.text: ~30° or more of radial laxity with NO firm endpoint, or ≥15° more laxity than the contralateral thumb
A firm endpoint with mild pain
Laxity only in full extension but a firm endpoint in flexion
No laxity in any position

questions.explanation: Common criteria for a **complete UCL tear** are **≥30° of radial (valgus) laxity when stressed in ~30–40° of MCP flexion**, or **≥15° more laxity than the uninjured thumb**, and — most usefully — the **absence of a firm endpoint**. Testing in flexion is key because the volar plate provides substantial stability in full extension and can mask a complete tear. Absent endpoint suggests a complete tear ± Stener lesion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Why is stress testing of the thumb UCL performed in ~30° of MCP FLEXION rather than full extension?

options.text: In full extension the volar plate provides substantial lateral stability that can mask a complete tear
Flexion tenses the extensor pollicis longus
Extension is too painful to test
Flexion relaxes the collateral ligament

questions.explanation: In **full MCP extension the volar plate and accessory collateral contribute substantial lateral stability**, so a complete proper-UCL tear can appear falsely stable. Testing in **~30–40° flexion isolates the proper collateral ligament** (and relaxes the volar plate), unmasking a complete tear. Comparing to the contralateral thumb helps account for physiologic laxity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: The term 'gamekeeper's thumb' most accurately refers to:

options.text: Chronic attritional instability of the thumb MCP UCL
An acute complete UCL rupture from a single event
A radial collateral ligament injury
A Bennett fracture

questions.explanation: Campbell coined **'gamekeeper's thumb'** for the **chronic UCL instability** originally seen in Scottish gamekeepers who repetitively stressed the ulnar side of the thumb (breaking rabbits' necks). Strictly, gamekeeper's thumb denotes **chronic** attritional instability, whereas the acute traumatic UCL rupture (e.g., from skiing) is better called **'skier's thumb.'** The terms are often used interchangeably in practice.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A patient has a complete thumb UCL tear with a confirmed Stener lesion. The appropriate management is:

options.text: Surgical repair (e.g., suture anchor reinsertion) — the interposed aponeurosis prevents healing with casting
Thumb spica cast for 4 weeks
Immediate MCP arthrodesis
Buddy taping and early motion

questions.explanation: A **Stener lesion mandates surgical repair** because the interposed adductor aponeurosis keeps the avulsed ligament from contacting its insertion, so it cannot heal with immobilization. Repair typically reinserts the distally avulsed UCL to the proximal phalangeal base with a **suture anchor** (or repairs a large displaced avulsion fragment), followed by protection and avoidance of radially directed stress for ~12 weeks.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A small, minimally displaced avulsion fracture at the ulnar base of the proximal phalanx accompanies a thumb UCL injury but the joint is stable with a firm endpoint. Reasonable initial treatment is:

options.text: Thumb spica cast immobilization, with ORIF reserved for displacement ≥2 mm or joint incongruity/instability
Immediate open repair in every case
No immobilization and immediate return to sport
MCP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: A **small, minimally displaced (<2 mm) avulsion fracture with a stable joint and firm endpoint** is generally treated with **thumb spica immobilization**. Operative fixation is indicated if the fragment is **displaced ≥2 mm, involves a significant portion of the articular surface with incongruity, or the joint is unstable (Stener lesion / no endpoint)**. Note that some series report persistent pain even after casting small avulsions, occasionally requiring later ORIF.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Why is a Stener lesion much LESS likely to occur with a radial collateral ligament (RCL) injury of the thumb than with a UCL injury?

options.text: The abductor/dorsal apparatus covers most of the radial side broadly, whereas the narrow adductor aponeurosis on the ulnar side is easily interposed
The RCL never tears completely
The radial side has no aponeurosis at all
The RCL is intraarticular

questions.explanation: On the ulnar side, the **narrow adductor aponeurosis** is readily interposed between a torn UCL and its insertion (creating a Stener lesion). On the radial side, the broader **abductor pollicis brevis expansion/dorsal apparatus covers most of the RCL**, making interposition (a radial-sided Stener-equivalent) uncommon — though it has been reported. RCL injuries are also far less frequent overall.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: In an isolated complete thumb MCP UCL rupture, the proximal phalanx tends to rotate in which direction, using the intact RCL as the axis?

options.text: Supination (volar rotation on the ulnar/torn side)
Pronation
Pure dorsal translation without rotation
Radial translation only

questions.explanation: Smith observed that the thumb MCP collaterals also resist volar subluxation; when one is torn, the proximal phalanx rotates volarly on that side. With an **isolated UCL rupture, the proximal phalanx rotates into supination around the intact RCL** (and pronates if the RCL is the torn one). This rotatory/volar subluxation contributes to the instability and can be a clinical clue.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: During surgical repair of a thumb UCL, which nerve is most at risk and must be identified/protected?

options.text: The dorsal (radial) sensory branch supplying the thumb
The recurrent motor branch of the median nerve
The deep motor branch of the ulnar nerve
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve

questions.explanation: The **dorsoradial sensory branch (superficial radial nerve)** crosses the operative field over the dorsoulnar thumb MCP joint and is the structure most at risk during UCL exposure/repair; it must be identified and protected to avoid a painful neuroma and sensory loss. The repair involves incising and later repairing the adductor aponeurosis over the reconstructed ligament.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: For CHRONIC thumb UCL instability (chronic gamekeeper's thumb) with good cartilage but an irreparable ligament, an appropriate reconstruction is:

options.text: Free tendon graft reconstruction of the UCL (e.g., palmaris longus)
Simple re-immobilization in a cast
Volar plate arthroplasty
Hemihamate autograft

questions.explanation: **Chronic** UCL insufficiency with **preserved cartilage** and an unrepairable native ligament is reconstructed with a **free tendon graft** (palmaris longus, or alternatives like a strip of ECRL/EDM/APL) to recreate the ligament. If there is significant **degenerative arthritis** of the MCP joint, **MCP arthrodesis** is preferred instead for reliable pain relief.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Which sign on a stress radiograph or during examination best confirms a complete thumb CMC (trapeziometacarpal) ligament injury / instability?

options.text: A stress view (both thumbs' distal phalanges pressed together) showing abnormal radial/dorsal subluxation of the metacarpal base
A widened scapholunate interval
A positive Watson scaphoid shift
A sesamoid within the MCP joint

questions.explanation: Thumb CMC ligament instability is assessed with a **stress radiograph** — a PA view of both thumbs with the distal phalanges pressed together — looking for **abnormal subluxation of the metacarpal base** relative to the trapezium compared with the opposite side. The dorsoradial and anterior (beak) oblique ligaments are the key restraints; injury/laxity predisposes to instability and later basal joint arthritis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Which ligament is now considered a (if not the) primary restraint to dorsal subluxation of the thumb CMC joint during pinch?

options.text: The dorsoradial ligament
The anterior oblique (volar beak) ligament alone
The intermetacarpal ligament
The ulnar collateral ligament

questions.explanation: Although the **anterior (volar) oblique ('beak') ligament** was classically emphasized, more recent anatomic/biomechanical work identifies the **dorsoradial ligament** as a primary restraint to the **dorsal subluxation force inherent to pinch** at the thumb CMC joint (reinforced by the expanded APL insertion). Both are relevant to CMC instability and the development of basal joint arthritis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: An acute, IRREDUCIBLE dislocation of the thumb CMC joint is best treated by:

options.text: Open reduction and ligament reconstruction/pinning
Prolonged casting alone
Immediate trapeziectomy
Buddy taping to the index

questions.explanation: A pure thumb CMC dislocation is uncommon; an **acute irreducible CMC dislocation** (or one that is grossly unstable after reduction) is treated with **open reduction, temporary pinning, and ligament reconstruction** (e.g., a volar ligament reconstruction using a slip of FCR to restore the beak/dorsoradial restraints). Closed reduction with casting is prone to recurrent instability, predisposing to early basal joint arthritis.
