references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: The most common sequela of PIP joint ligament injuries and dislocations — even when appropriately reduced — is:

options.text: Joint stiffness (loss of motion), often with a residual flexion contracture and fusiform swelling
Recurrent chronic instability
Avascular necrosis
Nonunion

questions.explanation: **Stiffness — not chronic instability — is the usual sequela of PIP injuries.** Patients frequently have a residual flexion contracture, loss of terminal extension, and persistent fusiform swelling for months. This is precisely why treatment emphasizes the **shortest safe immobilization and early protected motion**, and why routine acute collateral ligament repair is not favored for most closed PIP dislocations.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: In the assessment of any PIP fracture-dislocation, besides the percentage of articular involvement, which factor is emphasized as critical to choosing treatment?

options.text: Whether a concentric (congruent) reduction can be maintained and at what degree of flexion
The patient's dominant hand
The presence of a subungual hematoma
The ambient temperature during reduction

questions.explanation: The chapter stresses that **maintenance of a concentric (congruent) reduction — and the flexion angle required to hold it — is as important as fragment size**. If the joint stays concentrically reduced within a modest flexion arc, extension-block splinting can work even with borderline fragment size; if concentricity is lost or excessive flexion (>~30°) is needed, operative reconstruction is indicated. A congruent joint remodels better than an incongruent one.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A dynamic external fixator (e.g., pins-and-rubber-band traction) is useful for certain PIP fracture-dislocations primarily because it:

options.text: Applies ligamentotaxis to maintain reduction and joint space while permitting early active motion
Rigidly immobilizes the joint to allow bony fusion
Replaces the need for any reduction
Is used only for the thumb IP joint

questions.explanation: **Dynamic external fixation/traction** uses **ligamentotaxis** to maintain a reduced, distracted joint surface and concentric alignment for comminuted PIP fracture-dislocations (pilon patterns), while critically **allowing early active motion** to mold the articular surface and prevent stiffness. It can be combined with ORIF or volar plate arthroplasty for very comminuted injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: During open reduction of a complex dorsal MCP dislocation through a VOLAR approach, which structures are at particular risk because they are displaced and tented?

options.text: The digital neurovascular bundles, drawn tightly over the prominent metacarpal head
The extensor tendon central slip
The deep palmar arch
The recurrent motor branch of the median nerve

questions.explanation: In the **volar approach** to a complex MCP dislocation, the metacarpal head buttonholes volarly and the **digital nerves and vessels are stretched/tented tightly over it (often displaced to the sides)**, making them very vulnerable to iatrogenic injury during skin incision and dissection. This risk is a reason some surgeons prefer the **dorsal approach** (splitting the interposed volar plate) for these dislocations.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Isolated complete ruptures of a FINGER (non-thumb) MCP collateral ligament are uncommon; when they occur, which is more frequently torn?

options.text: The radial collateral ligament (RCL) is more commonly injured than the ulnar in the fingers
The ulnar collateral ligament, as in the thumb
Both are torn equally in all cases
The volar plate is always the sole injury

questions.explanation: In the fingers, isolated MCP UCL ruptures are extremely rare; **isolated radial collateral ligament (RCL) ruptures are the more commonly encountered** finger MCP collateral injury (the digits are more often forced ulnarward). Most are treated with immobilization in ~30° flexion for ~3 weeks; surgical repair is reserved for gross instability or displaced avulsions with locking.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: In a dorsal MCP fracture-dislocation, the deep transverse intermetacarpal ligament is relevant because it:

options.text: Connects the volar plates and stabilizes the metacarpal heads; the volar plate is most securely attached to the proximal phalanx
Is the primary flexor of the MCP joint
Supplies the blood to the metacarpal head
Is the terminal insertion of the extensor tendon

questions.explanation: The **deep transverse intermetacarpal ligament links the volar plates** across the metacarpal heads, and because the **volar plate is most securely attached distally to the proximal phalanx**, this ligamentous complex primarily supports the proximal phalanges. In complex MCP dislocations, this arrangement contributes to the way the avulsed volar plate becomes trapped over the metacarpal head, blocking reduction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: After open reduction of an irreducible (complex) MCP dislocation, rehabilitation typically involves:

options.text: Early active motion with a dorsal extension-block splint (blocking terminal extension)
Continuous immobilization in full MCP extension for 6 weeks
Immediate unrestricted hyperextension exercises
MCP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: Following reduction (closed or open) of an MCP dislocation, the joint is typically protected in slight flexion (~30° initially) and then started on **early active motion with a dorsal extension-block splint** (e.g., blocking the last ~10° of extension) to protect the healing volar plate while preventing stiffness. Timely treatment of these injuries generally yields good functional outcomes.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Slight asymmetry of the PIP condyles imparts a small amount of which motion through the arc of PIP flexion, which is relevant when assessing rotational alignment?

options.text: Up to about 9 degrees of supination
Up to 30 degrees of pronation
45 degrees of abduction
No rotation occurs at the PIP

questions.explanation: The PIP is a hinge joint, but **slight condylar asymmetry produces up to ~9° of supination through the full arc of PIP motion**. This normal rotational subtlety is worth appreciating when judging digital rotation after injury/fixation, so that a normal physiologic rotation is not mistaken for pathologic malrotation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A flexible swan-neck deformity resulting from PIP volar plate laxity (with a supple joint) can be corrected by:

options.text: FDS tenodesis or volar transposition/relocation of a lateral band to restrain PIP hyperextension
Terminal extensor tenotomy
A1 pulley release
DIP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: A **flexible swan-neck** from volar plate insufficiency is treated by re-creating a volar checkrein: an **FDS tenodesis** (using one slip of the superficialis as a static restraint to PIP hyperextension) or **volar transposition of a lateral band**. The joint is then rested in ~20–30° of flexion. These procedures require a supple, passively correctable deformity; fixed deformities need release/other measures first.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Which statement about acute primary REPAIR of collateral ligaments after a simple closed lateral PIP dislocation is most accurate?

options.text: It is generally NOT required, since most heal well with closed treatment and stiffness (not instability) is the main risk
It is mandatory for all lateral PIP dislocations to prevent chronic instability
It reliably improves final range of motion over nonoperative care
It should always be combined with volar plate arthroplasty

questions.explanation: Although acute collateral repair has been reported (e.g., in athletes/manual laborers) and can restore stability, the chapter notes that **most simple closed lateral PIP dislocations do well with closed treatment**, and the principal risk is **stiffness rather than chronic instability**. Routine acute repair is therefore not required; it is reserved for select cases (gross instability, displaced avulsions, interposition, high-demand patients).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: When reconstructing the volar base of the middle phalanx with a hemihamate autograft, the graft is harvested from the:

options.text: Dorsal-distal articular surface of the hamate (its 4th/5th metacarpal facets)
Volar hook of the hamate
Proximal pole of the scaphoid
Distal radius metaphysis

questions.explanation: The **hemihamate osteochondral graft** is taken from the **dorsal-distal articular surface of the hamate** (the ridge between its 4th and 5th metacarpal facets), which matches the concave contour of the middle phalangeal base. It reconstructs the comminuted volar buttress with true articular cartilage, restoring stability and permitting early motion — the preferred option for many unstable/chronic PIP fracture-dislocations with large defects.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: The most reliable radiographic clue distinguishing a COMPLEX (irreducible) from a SIMPLE MCP dislocation is:

options.text: A sesamoid seen within the widened MCP joint space (indicating interposed volar plate)
Marked hyperextension of the proximal phalanx
An avulsion fracture of the metacarpal neck
Soft-tissue swelling alone

questions.explanation: On radiographs, a **sesamoid visualized within the widened MCP joint space** signals that the **volar plate (which carries the sesamoids) is interposed** — the hallmark of a **complex, irreducible** dislocation. Clinically the complex dislocation shows only slight hyperextension (bayonet) with palmar puckering. In contrast, a **simple** dislocation is markedly hyperextended and lacks an intraarticular sesamoid.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A thumb IP joint dislocation that is irreducible after a crush/hyperextension injury is most often blocked by:

options.text: An interposed volar plate or sesamoid (or entrapped flexor pollicis longus)
The extensor pollicis longus
The princeps pollicis artery
The A1 pulley

questions.explanation: Thumb IP (and finger DIP) dislocations are usually easily reduced; when irreducible, the block is typically an **interposed volar plate, a sesamoid, or an entrapped flexor tendon (FPL)**. Open reduction is required. After reduction, stable IP dislocations are splinted in extension; large associated articular fractures may need fixation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: Which of the following is the LEAST correct statement regarding thumb MCP UCL injuries?

options.text: Proximal (metacarpal-side) tears are far more common than distal tears
UCL injuries are roughly 10 times more common than RCL injuries
A Stener lesion occurs only with complete tears, not partial tears
Absence of a firm endpoint on valgus stress suggests a complete tear

questions.explanation: The false statement is that proximal tears predominate — in fact **distal tears (avulsion from the proximal phalangeal insertion) are MORE common** than proximal (metacarpal) tears, and it is the distally avulsed ligament that retracts and can become a Stener lesion. The other statements are correct: UCL injuries ≈10× RCL injuries, Stener lesions occur only with complete tears, and loss of a firm endpoint indicates a complete tear.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: A patient sustains a dorsal PIP dislocation and, on the post-reduction lateral view, the joint shows a 'V-sign' (dorsal V-shaped widening) rather than congruent parallel surfaces. This indicates:

options.text: A non-concentric (subluxated) reduction that predicts instability and possible need for operative treatment
A perfectly concentric, stable reduction
An isolated central slip injury
A normal finding after reduction

questions.explanation: A congruently reduced PIP shows the middle phalanx base and proximal phalanx condyles as **parallel, concentric surfaces**. A dorsal **'V sign'** — dorsal widening/gapping between the surfaces on the true lateral — indicates **residual dorsal subluxation (non-concentric reduction)**, which predicts instability and dorsal fracture-dislocation behavior. It is a signal to reassess fragment size/stability and consider operative reduction or dynamic fixation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: For a stable, reduced simple dorsal PIP dislocation, roughly how long should immobilization typically last before progressing to buddy taping and motion, to minimize stiffness?

options.text: A short period (about 1–2 weeks or less) of protected splinting, then early motion
At least 6 weeks of rigid immobilization
3 months of continuous casting
No immobilization and no follow-up

questions.explanation: Because **stiffness is the dominant risk**, a stable simple dorsal PIP dislocation is protected only **briefly (roughly ≤1–2 weeks)** with an extension-block splint before transitioning to buddy taping and active motion. Prolonged rigid immobilization predictably produces flexion contracture and loss of motion. Early controlled motion optimizes the functional result.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: In the surgical treatment of a chronic thumb UCL Stener lesion with a large, displaced avulsion FRACTURE fragment (rather than a purely ligamentous avulsion), the preferred fixation is:

options.text: Open reduction and fixation of the fragment (e.g., screw/K-wire or suture) restoring the ligament's bony insertion
Excision of the fragment and cast immobilization only
Immediate MCP arthrodesis regardless of cartilage status
Dynamic external fixation of the MCP joint

questions.explanation: When a complete UCL injury includes a **large, displaced avulsion fragment**, restoring the ligament means **reducing and fixing the bony fragment** (screw, K-wire, or suture through bone), re-establishing the UCL's insertion and joint congruity, and then repairing the adductor aponeurosis over it. Excision plus casting risks persistent instability; arthrodesis is reserved for chronic instability with significant MCP arthritis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 8 (Dislocations and Ligament Injuries of the Digits)

questions.stem: What is the single most commonly fractured bone in the hand?

options.text: The distal phalanx of the middle (long) finger
The fifth metacarpal neck
The proximal phalanx of the index finger
The thumb metacarpal base

questions.explanation: Metacarpal and phalangeal fractures are the most common upper-extremity fractures, and the **distal phalanx of the middle (long) finger** is the single most commonly fractured bone in the hand — it is the most prominent/exposed fingertip. Distal phalanx fractures overall are the most frequently encountered hand fracture, with the thumb and middle finger most vulnerable during work.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old punches a wall and sustains a fifth metacarpal neck fracture ('boxer's fracture'). The characteristic deformity is:

options.text: Apex dorsal angulation
Apex volar angulation
Radial angulation of the shaft
Pure rotational deformity without angulation

questions.explanation: A metacarpal neck fracture (boxer's fracture) classically has **apex dorsal angulation**. This occurs because the axial punching force comminutes the volar cortex, and the **intrinsic muscles crossing the MCP joint lie volar to the axis of rotation**, creating a flexion (apex dorsal) bending moment on the distal fragment. The metacarpal head is thereby driven into the palm.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Regarding acceptable angulation of metacarpal NECK fractures, which statement is correct?

options.text: The ulnar (ring/small) metacarpals tolerate far more angulation than the radial (index/middle), owing to greater CMC mobility
The index and middle metacarpals tolerate the most angulation
All metacarpals tolerate an identical amount of angulation
No metacarpal neck fracture can tolerate any angulation

questions.explanation: The **ulnar (ring and small finger) metacarpals have mobile carpometacarpal joints (~20–30° of flexion), so they tolerate substantial neck angulation** — commonly cited as acceptable up to ~40° (ring) and ~70° (small finger) in the absence of pseudoclawing or rotation. The **index and middle CMC joints are essentially rigid**, so those metacarpals tolerate only ~10–15°. This is why fifth metacarpal neck fractures are usually managed nonoperatively.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Which finding is the strongest indication to operatively correct an angulated metacarpal neck fracture, rather than accept it?

options.text: Rotational malalignment or significant pseudoclawing
Any measurable angulation on the lateral radiograph
A palpable loss of knuckle contour alone
Mild dorsal hand swelling

questions.explanation: Numerous studies show angulation alone correlates poorly with function/grip. The true indications for intervention are **rotational malalignment (digital scissoring)** and **significant pseudoclawing** (compensatory MCP hyperextension with PIP flexion from dynamic instability due to shortening/angulation). A loss of knuckle prominence is cosmetic and usually well tolerated.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: The Jahss maneuver is used to reduce a metacarpal neck fracture. It involves:

options.text: Flexing the MCP joint 90° and pushing dorsally on the flexed proximal phalanx while stabilizing the metacarpal shaft
Longitudinal traction with the MCP joint fully extended
Direct volar pressure over the metacarpal head with the finger extended
Ulnar deviation of the wrist with the fingers flexed

questions.explanation: The **Jahss maneuver** flexes the MCP joint to ~90° (which tightens the collateral ligaments and uses the proximal phalanx base as a lever), then pushes the flexed proximal phalanx dorsally to reduce the apex-dorsal deformity while downward pressure is applied to the metacarpal shaft. The reduction is then held (often in intrinsic-plus position). Note that immobilizing in extreme MCP flexion (the Cotton-Loder-like position) is discouraged.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: The 'bouquet' (Foucher) technique for a displaced small-finger metacarpal neck fracture involves:

options.text: Antegrade intramedullary insertion of several blunt prebent Kirschner wires down the medullary canal into the subchondral head
Retrograde transarticular pinning through the metacarpal head
Open plating through a dorsal tendon-splitting approach
External fixation across the MCP joint

questions.explanation: The **bouquet (Foucher) technique** is a closed, antegrade intramedullary osteosynthesis: through a window at the metacarpal base, several **blunt, prebent K-wires are passed down the medullary canal across the fracture into the subchondral bone of the head**, splaying like a bouquet to maintain reduction. It avoids the joint and extensor mechanism. A single larger IM wire/nail is a variation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: In metacarpal SHAFT fractures, how much rotational malalignment is generally considered unacceptable because of the resulting digital overlap at the fingertips?

options.text: About 5 degrees of malrotation (which can cause ~1.5 cm of fingertip overlap)
Up to 30 degrees is always acceptable
Only rotation greater than 45 degrees matters
Rotation is never clinically significant

questions.explanation: Rotation is poorly tolerated in the hand: as little as **5 degrees of metacarpal malrotation can produce roughly 1.5 cm of overlap (scissoring)** at the fingertips during flexion. Rotational alignment is assessed by having the fingers flex toward the scaphoid tubercle and checking that the nail planes are parallel and there is no crossover — malrotation, not angulation, is often the key operative indication.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Cadaveric studies of metacarpal SHORTENING found that for every 2 mm of shortening there is approximately:

options.text: 7 degrees of extensor lag
1 degree of extensor lag
20 degrees of extensor lag
No change in extensor mechanics

questions.explanation: Cadaveric work showed that **each 2 mm of metacarpal shortening produces about a 7-degree extensor lag** (from relative laxity of the extensor mechanism), and digital flexion force declines with shortening beyond ~5 mm. Clinically, however, several studies found even ~2–5 mm of shortening is well tolerated without meaningful loss of motion or grip, so modest shortening is often accepted.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: The 'intrinsic-plus' (safe / clam-digger) position for immobilizing hand fractures places the joints in:

options.text: Wrist ~30° extension, MCP joints flexed ~70–90°, IP joints in extension
Wrist flexed, MCP joints extended, IP joints flexed
Wrist neutral, all finger joints fully extended
Wrist extended, MCP joints extended, IP joints flexed 90°

questions.explanation: The **intrinsic-plus (safe) position** is **wrist ~30° extension, MCP joints flexed ~70–90°, and IP joints in full extension**. Flexing the MCPs keeps the collateral ligaments at maximal length (taut) and extending the IPs keeps the volar plates stretched, which minimizes the joint contractures that develop with prolonged immobilization.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: The deforming forces in a proximal phalanx SHAFT fracture typically produce which angulation, and why?

options.text: Apex volar — the proximal fragment is flexed by the interossei and the distal fragment extended by the central slip pull
Apex dorsal — from the pull of the flexor tendons
Pure radial angulation from the lumbricals
No consistent deformity occurs

questions.explanation: Proximal phalanx fractures classically angulate **apex volar (apex palmar)**: the **interosseous (intrinsic) muscles flex the proximal fragment**, while the **central slip/extensor mechanism extends the distal fragment**, creating a volar apex. Reduction requires MCP flexion (to relax the intrinsics/tension the extensor) and correction with the flexed digit as a lever.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: London (1971) classified phalangeal condylar fractures. A displaced UNICONDYLAR fracture corresponds to which type, and what is its behavior?

options.text: Type II — unstable; prone to displacement and frequently missed
Type I — always stable and never displaces
Type III — always nondisplaced and benign
It is not included in the London classification

questions.explanation: London's condylar classification: **Type I = stable, nondisplaced; Type II = unicondylar, unstable; Type III = bicondylar or comminuted**. Unicondylar (type II) fractures are notoriously **unstable and easily missed** (Stark) and tend to displace even when initially nondisplaced. Displaced unicondylar fractures are therefore best treated operatively (K-wires or interfragmentary screws) with a dorsal approach between central slip and lateral band.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A nondisplaced unicondylar fracture of the proximal phalangeal head is discovered. The safest management principle is:

options.text: Treat as potentially unstable — anticipate displacement; consider fixation or very close radiographic follow-up rather than simple splinting
Simple buddy taping and immediate unrestricted motion
Cast for 8 weeks and expect union without displacement
Ignore it, as unicondylar fractures never displace

questions.explanation: Even **nondisplaced unicondylar fractures are potentially unstable**; simple splinting is risky and displacement should be anticipated. Options are percutaneous or open fixation (K-wire/screw) or, if truly nondisplaced and reliably monitored, splinting with **very close serial radiographs** to catch early displacement. Displaced (>1 mm intraarticular step) condylar fractures warrant operative fixation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: An avulsion fracture of the DORSAL base of the middle phalanx represents detachment of which structure, and if displaced >2 mm can lead to which deformity?

options.text: Central slip insertion; boutonnière deformity
Terminal extensor tendon; mallet finger
Flexor digitorum superficialis; swan-neck deformity
Collateral ligament; lateral instability only

questions.explanation: A **dorsal base of the middle phalanx** avulsion is a bony **central slip** injury; untreated displaced (>2 mm) fractures allow the lateral bands to sublux volarly, producing a **boutonnière deformity** (PIP flexion, DIP hyperextension). Preferred treatment is open reduction through a dorsal approach (between central slip and lateral band), preserving the central slip insertion, with small-screw fixation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A comminuted intraarticular fracture of the BASE of the middle phalanx with axial impaction of the articular surface is termed a:

options.text: Pilon fracture
Bennett fracture
Seymour fracture
Rolando fracture

questions.explanation: A **pilon fracture** of the middle phalangeal base is a comminuted intraarticular fracture with **articular depression and metaphyseal impaction** from an axial load. Simple splinting causes stiffness; better outcomes come from restoring the articular surface and length — **skeletal traction (dynamic external fixation) and/or ORIF**. It is analogous to a pilon fracture of the distal tibia.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A tuft fracture of the distal phalanx is associated with a tense, painful subungual hematoma. Appropriate management includes:

options.text: Nail-plate trephination (decompression) for pain relief, and repairing associated nail matrix/pulp lacerations
Rigid internal fixation of the tuft with a plate
Immediate DIP arthrodesis
Amputation of the fingertip

questions.explanation: Most **tuft fractures** are stable crush injuries treated symptomatically. A tense **subungual hematoma is decompressed (trephination)** for dramatic pain relief, and any **nail matrix/pulp lacerations are repaired** to reduce nail deformity. Tuft fractures often go to fibrous (not bony) union but rarely cause functional problems; hardware is generally unnecessary.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A 'Seymour fracture' is:

options.text: An open physeal (Salter-Harris) fracture of the distal phalanx in children with interposed nail matrix, the nail plate lying superficial to the eponychial fold
A comminuted articular fracture of the thumb metacarpal base
A volar avulsion of the FDP from the distal phalanx
A dorsal chip fracture of the middle phalanx

questions.explanation: A **Seymour fracture** is a pediatric **open physeal (typically Salter-Harris I/II) fracture of the distal phalanx** with a juxta-epiphyseal deformity; the germinal matrix is often interposed in the fracture, and the **nail plate sits superficial to (out of) the proximal nail fold** — a pathognomonic sign of the open physeal injury. Treatment requires irrigation/antibiotics, removal of interposed matrix, reduction, nail matrix repair, and replacing the nail plate as a stent; missed injuries risk infection/osteomyelitis and growth disturbance.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A patient cannot actively extend the DIP joint after a forced flexion injury; radiographs show a small dorsal avulsion fragment at the distal phalanx base. This is a:

options.text: Bony mallet finger (terminal extensor tendon avulsion)
Jersey finger (FDP avulsion)
Boutonnière injury
Seymour fracture

questions.explanation: A **mallet finger** is avulsion of the **terminal extensor tendon** from the dorsal distal phalanx (± a bony fragment), producing an extensor lag at the DIP. Most (including many bony mallets) are treated with **continuous DIP extension splinting for ~6–8 weeks**. Operative fixation is considered for large fragments (often >1/3 of the articular surface) or volar (palmar) subluxation of the distal phalanx.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A Bennett fracture is best described as:

options.text: An intraarticular fracture-subluxation of the base of the thumb metacarpal, with a volar-ulnar fragment retained and the shaft subluxating
A comminuted (Y/T) intraarticular fracture of the thumb metacarpal base
An extraarticular transverse thumb metacarpal shaft fracture
A fracture of the trapezium

questions.explanation: A **Bennett fracture** is a **two-part intraarticular fracture-subluxation of the thumb metacarpal base**. A small **volar-ulnar (beak) fragment** stays anchored to the trapezium by ligaments, while the metacarpal shaft subluxates. A comminuted (Y/T-shaped) version is instead a **Rolando fracture**. It is 'really a fracture subluxation' from axial loading of a partially flexed thumb.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: In a Bennett fracture, which deforming muscle pulls the metacarpal SHAFT proximally, radially, and dorsally (into subluxation)?

options.text: Abductor pollicis longus (APL)
Adductor pollicis
Flexor pollicis brevis
Opponens pollicis

questions.explanation: The **abductor pollicis longus (APL)** pulls the metacarpal shaft **proximally, radially, and dorsally**, subluxating it away from the retained volar-ulnar (beak) fragment; the **adductor pollicis** adds a flexion/supination deforming force. Closed reduction is achieved by **longitudinal traction, palmar abduction, and pronation** ('screw-home torque'), then pinning (often metacarpal-to-trapezium, without needing to pin the small fragment).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Recent anatomic work (Kang et al.) revised the classic teaching about the Bennett fragment. Which ligament is now identified as the PRIMARY ligament attached to the volar-ulnar fragment?

options.text: The ulnar collateral ligament
The anterior (volar) oblique ligament
The dorsoradial ligament
The intermetacarpal ligament

questions.explanation: Classically the **anterior (volar) oblique ('beak') ligament** was thought to tether the Bennett fragment, but Kang et al. demonstrated that the **ulnar collateral ligament is actually the primary ligament attached to the fragment**. Either way, the fragment stays with the trapezium while the shaft subluxates, and reduction aims to restore CMC stability and articular congruity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A Rolando fracture is:

options.text: A comminuted (classically Y- or T-shaped) intraarticular fracture of the thumb metacarpal base, with a generally worse prognosis than a Bennett fracture
A two-part fracture-subluxation of the thumb metacarpal base
An extraarticular epibasal thumb metacarpal fracture
A stress fracture of the thumb metacarpal shaft

questions.explanation: A **Rolando fracture** is a **comminuted intraarticular thumb metacarpal base fracture** (originally a Y/T pattern; now the term covers any comminuted basal articular fracture). Prognosis is **worse than a Bennett fracture**. A simple three-part pattern can be treated with ORIF (K-wires or L/T-plate); severely comminuted patterns are often best managed with traction/external fixation (± limited fixation and bone graft), accepting some articular irregularity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: For a severely comminuted Rolando fracture that is not amenable to stable internal fixation, a favored low-complication approach is:

options.text: Traction / external fixation (e.g., oblique traction pin or a mini-external fixator), with limited fixation and bone graft as needed
Primary trapeziometacarpal arthrodesis in all cases
Immediate trapeziectomy
Long-arm casting alone for 12 weeks

questions.explanation: For **highly comminuted Rolando fractures**, anatomic ORIF is difficult and prone to failure; **oblique skeletal traction or a mini-external fixator** (spanning thumb-index metacarpals) with limited K-wire/screw fixation and metaphyseal bone graft gives good results with a low complication rate (Gelberman, Büchler). The goal is to restore length/alignment and a congruent-enough joint while avoiding extensive dissection.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: An extraarticular fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the thumb metacarpal base is called an 'epibasal' fracture. Compared with Bennett/Rolando fractures, it is:

options.text: Extraarticular and usually stable after closed reduction (traction, downward pressure, mild pronation/extension)
Always intraarticular and unstable
Managed only with open plating
Associated with the worst prognosis of all thumb base fractures

questions.explanation: An **epibasal fracture is extraarticular** (at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction). Because it spares the joint, it usually reduces easily and is **stable** — longitudinal traction, downward pressure on the fracture apex, and mild pronation/extension achieve reduction, held in a thumb spica. This benign behavior contrasts with the intraarticular Bennett and comminuted Rolando fractures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Rotational alignment of the fingers after a metacarpal or phalangeal fracture is best assessed clinically by:

options.text: Flexing the fingers and confirming they all point toward the scaphoid tubercle with parallel nail planes and no crossover
Measuring the angulation on a lateral radiograph only
Checking grip strength with a dynamometer
Assessing two-point discrimination

questions.explanation: Rotation is a **clinical** determination: with the fingers flexed, they should all **point toward the scaphoid tuberosity**, the **nail plates should be parallel**, and there should be **no scissoring/overlap**. Radiographs poorly show rotation. Small degrees of malrotation are magnified into fingertip crossover during flexion, which is why this exam is essential before accepting a reduction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: The most common complication after articular (intraarticular) fractures of the metacarpal HEAD is:

options.text: Stiffness (from extensor adhesions, collateral/capsular contracture, or articular incongruity)
Nonunion
Avascular necrosis of the metacarpal shaft
Chronic infection

questions.explanation: **Stiffness is the most common complication of metacarpal head fractures**, resulting from extensor tendon adhesions, collateral ligament or dorsal capsular contracture, and/or articular incongruity. Because of this, anatomic reduction, stable fixation, and early motion are emphasized. Nonunion of the metacarpal is rare; malunion and stiffness are the practical concerns.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A 'baby Bennett' (reverse Bennett) fracture refers to:

options.text: An intraarticular fracture-subluxation of the base of the FIFTH metacarpal, with the shaft displaced by the pull of the ECU
A pediatric Bennett fracture of the thumb
A fracture of the trapezoid
A tuft fracture in an infant

questions.explanation: A **'baby Bennett' (reverse Bennett)** is an intraarticular fracture-dislocation of the **base of the fifth metacarpal** at the hamate-metacarpal joint. Analogous to the thumb Bennett, the shaft is displaced (proximally/dorsally) by the pull of the **extensor carpi ulnaris**, while a fragment remains attached. It is often unstable and, like a Bennett, frequently requires reduction and pinning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Regarding the necessity of anatomic articular reduction in Bennett fractures, cadaveric/clinical data cited in the chapter suggest:

options.text: As long as CMC stability is restored and fragments heal in close apposition, minor articular incongruity may not be biomechanically significant
Even 1 mm of articular step-off inevitably causes disabling arthritis
Articular reduction is irrelevant and no reduction is ever needed
Only perfect anatomic reduction prevents any subluxation

questions.explanation: A cadaveric study simulating a Bennett fracture with 2-mm articular displacement found that **as long as the shaft and fragment healed in close apposition and CMC stability was restored, the lack of perfect articular restoration was not biomechanically significant**. Long-term clinical series similarly show many patients do well despite some incongruity — so restoring **joint stability** is the priority, though large steps/gaps are still reduced.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Biomechanically, which fixation construct provides the GREATEST rigidity for a transverse metacarpal fracture, allowing the earliest motion?

options.text: Dorsal locked plating
Crossed Kirschner wires
A single intramedullary screw
Cerclage wiring alone

questions.explanation: **Locked plating provides the greatest stiffness/stability** among common constructs (greater than nonlocked plating, crossed K-wires, or a single IM screw), permitting early motion — at the cost of a more invasive approach and possible hardware/tendon irritation. **IM screws and crossed K-wires are biomechanically similar** to each other and offer less invasive alternatives. Construct choice balances rigidity against soft-tissue insult.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: For displaced fifth metacarpal neck and shaft fractures, comparative studies (e.g., Westbrook, Zong meta-analysis) found that nonoperative treatment:

options.text: Was superior or equivalent to pinning/plating, with the lowest complication rate
Was clearly inferior in grip strength and union
Always led to nonunion
Should be abandoned in favor of routine plating

questions.explanation: The literature repeatedly shows **nonoperative management of small-finger metacarpal neck (and many shaft) fractures is superior or equivalent** — Westbrook found it better than pinning/plating in DASH and esthetics with similar grip/union, and a Zong meta-analysis found conservative care had the **lowest complication rate** vs pinning, plating, and IM nailing. Surgery is reserved for malrotation, pseudoclawing, multiple fractures, or open injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A transverse laceration of the germinal (nail) matrix with the nail plate avulsed from beneath the proximal nail fold, seen together with a distal phalanx fracture, most classically accompanies which associated injury pattern in adults?

options.text: It signals an open fracture requiring irrigation and nail-bed repair
It is always a purely closed, benign injury
It indicates a stable tuft fracture needing no care
It confirms a flexor tendon rupture

questions.explanation: When the nail plate lies superficial to (out of) the nail fold with an underlying distal phalanx fracture and a torn nail matrix, the injury is **open** (the fracture communicates with the lacerated matrix). It requires **irrigation, antibiotics, nail-bed (matrix) repair, and replacing/stenting the nail plate** to reduce nail deformity and infection — the same principles that apply to the pediatric Seymour fracture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Nonunion is characteristically RARE in metacarpal neck fractures. What is the more typical concern with these fractures?

options.text: Malunion (e.g., loss of knuckle contour, prominent metacarpal head in the palm)
Avascular necrosis
Growth arrest
Chronic osteomyelitis

questions.explanation: Metacarpal neck fractures essentially **never go to nonunion**; the practical issue is **malunion** — loss of the normal knuckle prominence, a metacarpal head palpable/prominent in the palm, and occasionally pseudoclawing or rotational malalignment. Most malunions are cosmetic and well tolerated; a symptomatic malunion can be corrected with an osteotomy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: The surgical approach recommended for open reduction of a displaced unicondylar fracture of the proximal phalanx uses which interval to protect the extensor mechanism?

options.text: Between the central slip and the lateral band
Splitting directly through the central slip
A midaxial volar (Bruner) approach through the flexor sheath
Transecting the lateral band

questions.explanation: Displaced condylar fractures of the proximal phalanx are exposed **dorsally between the central slip and the lateral band**, taking care to **preserve the central slip insertion** on the middle phalangeal base. The fragment is reduced and fixed with K-wires or small interfragmentary screws, and the interval is repaired. This protects the extensor apparatus and PIP function.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A patient has a malunited SUBcondylar (phalangeal neck) fracture that blocks PIP flexion. The mechanism of the flexion block is:

options.text: Loss of the subcondylar (volar) recess and dorsal displacement of the head, which impinges and blocks flexion
Extensor tendon adhesion only
Collateral ligament rupture
Volar plate hyperlaxity

questions.explanation: Phalangeal **neck (subcondylar) malunions** — common in children — heal with the head displaced dorsally and loss of the normal **subcondylar fossa (volar recess)** that normally accommodates the base of the next phalanx in flexion; the malunited head then mechanically **blocks flexion**. Corrective osteotomy (or, in remodeling children, observation) restores the recess and motion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A displaced volar (palmar) base fracture of the middle phalanx associated with dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation is best conceptualized as an injury to which structure, dictating stability?

options.text: The volar plate/volar articular base — the amount of articular surface involved determines dorsal dislocation stability
The central slip only
The terminal extensor tendon
The A2 pulley

questions.explanation: In a **dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation**, the fracture involves the **volar base of the middle phalanx (volar plate/volar buttress)**. Stability depends on how much of the volar articular arc is fractured: small fragments (<~30–40%) are usually stable and treated with extension-block splinting, whereas larger fragments (>~40–50%) are unstable and need volar-plate arthroplasty, ORIF, or dynamic external fixation to maintain concentric reduction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Which deforming forces act on the thumb metacarpal SHAFT fracture to produce its typical apex-dorsal (adduction/flexion) deformity?

options.text: Thenar intrinsics (APB, FPB) and adductor pollicis flex/adduct the distal fragment while APL extends the proximal fragment
The extensor pollicis longus flexes the distal fragment
The flexor carpi radialis pulls the proximal fragment volarly
No muscle forces act on the thumb metacarpal

questions.explanation: In a thumb metacarpal **shaft** fracture, the **abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, and adductor pollicis flex/adduct the distal fragment**, while the **abductor pollicis longus extends the proximal fragment** — producing an apex-dorsal deformity. Reduction uses traction, extension, and pronation; malunited hyperextension deformity can be corrected by closing-wedge osteotomy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: For an unsalvageable, comminuted OPEN metacarpal HEAD fracture (e.g., from a gunshot), reasonable reconstructive options include all EXCEPT:

options.text: Acute rigid plate fixation restoring the native head, which reliably restores full motion
Silicone (implant) arthroplasty
Volar plate (Tupper) interposition arthroplasty
Delayed MCP arthrodesis

questions.explanation: For a **nonsalvageable open metacarpal head**, described options include immediate **silicone arthroplasty**, **volar plate interposition ('Tupper') arthroplasty**, or subsequent **MCP fusion** — these are the intended answers as legitimate strategies. The statement that 'acute rigid plating reliably restores full motion' is the false/least-correct choice: a destroyed comminuted head cannot simply be plated back to normal, and stiffness is the dominant problem.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: During dorsal plating of a metacarpal shaft fracture, why are prominent screw heads/K-wire ends and plate edges a concern?

options.text: They cause extensor tendon irritation, adhesion, or rupture over the dorsum of the metacarpal
They injure the median nerve
They compress the ulnar artery
They disrupt the flexor pulleys

questions.explanation: The **extensor tendons lie directly dorsal to the metacarpals**, so prominent hardware causes **extensor tendon irritation, adhesions, tenosynovitis, and occasionally rupture**. K-wires are cut flush to the dorsal cortex, plates are low-profile, and hardware removal is sometimes required. Extensor adhesions are also a leading cause of postoperative stiffness after dorsal approaches.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: For proximal phalangeal shaft fractures, the acceptable amount of angulation and rotation is generally STRICTER than for metacarpals because:

options.text: The phalanx is intimately related to the flexor/extensor apparatus, so malalignment quickly causes tendon imbalance, extensor lag, and functional loss
The phalanges have no blood supply
Phalangeal fractures never unite
The metacarpals are intraarticular and phalanges are not

questions.explanation: Phalangeal fractures are **less forgiving** because the phalanges are enveloped by the **flexor and extensor tendon apparatus** — malunion (angulation, shortening, or rotation) rapidly produces tendon imbalance, extensor lag/pseudoclaw, and adhesions with stiffness. Small degrees of malrotation and apex-volar angulation are thus less well tolerated than comparable metacarpal deformities.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: An avulsion fracture of the DORSAL base of the index metacarpal (with the wrist forcibly flexed) usually represents avulsion of which tendon?

options.text: The extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL)
The flexor carpi radialis (FCR)
The abductor pollicis longus (APL)
The extensor indicis proprius (EIP)

questions.explanation: Dorsal base avulsion fractures of the index (and middle) metacarpals typically represent avulsion of the wrist extensor insertions — the **ECRL inserts on the index metacarpal base** (and ECRB on the middle). Recognizing these as extensor tendon bony avulsions matters because significant displacement can weaken wrist extension and may warrant fixation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A symptomatic malunion of a metacarpal or phalangeal fracture producing functional impairment is best addressed by:

options.text: Corrective osteotomy (e.g., closing- or opening-wedge, or rotational osteotomy) tailored to the deformity
Routine amputation of the digit
Immediate joint replacement
Indefinite splinting

questions.explanation: A **symptomatic malunion** (angular, rotational, or shortening) causing pain, scissoring, or motion loss is corrected with a **targeted osteotomy** — closing-wedge (may shorten), opening-wedge (needs graft), or a rotational osteotomy (often at the metacarpal base). Asymptomatic malunions with acceptable function are generally left alone, since many hand malunions are well tolerated.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A 'true lateral' radiograph of the thumb trapeziometacarpal joint (Billing-Gedda / Robert-type technique) is important in a Bennett fracture to:

options.text: Accurately assess CMC joint congruity and the degree of subluxation/step-off
Evaluate the scapholunate interval
Measure ulnar variance
Visualize the hook of the hamate

questions.explanation: A dedicated **true lateral of the trapeziometacarpal joint** (Billing-Gedda technique: hand pronated ~15–35°, tube angled ~15°) profiles the CMC joint to accurately judge **articular congruity, subluxation, and fragment step-off** — standard AP/lateral hand films obscure this. CT is used when comminution/displacement is unclear (especially for Rolando fractures).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Which statement about intramedullary (IM) fixation of small-finger metacarpal neck fractures is best supported?

options.text: Antegrade IM nailing/pinning avoids the extensor mechanism and gives outcomes comparable to transverse pinning, though the literature is somewhat conflicting
IM nailing requires opening the fracture and splitting the extensor tendon
IM nailing has been proven vastly superior to all other methods in every study
IM fixation cannot maintain length or rotation

questions.explanation: **Antegrade IM fixation** (bouquet or single nail) is minimally invasive, spares the extensor apparatus, and gives results **broadly comparable to transverse percutaneous pinning** — the literature is mixed (some show equivalence, some favor transverse pinning for time/complications, some favor IM). Locked IM nails maintain length, alignment, and rotation. Limitations include possible implant removal and MCP joint/extensor irritation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: A displaced FDP avulsion ('jersey finger') associated with a distal phalanx bony fragment is important to recognize because:

options.text: The tendon (± fragment) may retract, and the level of retraction dictates urgency and reconstructive options
It is always treated with a simple extension splint
It never requires surgery
It causes loss of DIP extension

questions.explanation: An **FDP avulsion (jersey finger)** — loss of active DIP flexion — often carries a bony fragment; the **level of tendon retraction** (Leddy-Packer classification) determines urgency: retraction into the palm (with vinculae disruption) risks the blood supply and needs prompt repair, whereas a large bony fragment caught at the A4 pulley may be more stable. It is fixed by tendon reinsertion (suture anchor/pull-out) ± fragment fixation. It causes loss of DIP flexion (not extension).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: After closed reduction of a boxer's fracture, the wrist and hand are typically immobilized with:

options.text: An ulnar gutter cast/splint with the wrist ~30° extended and the ring/small MCP joints flexed ~70°
A radial gutter splint with the MCP joints in full extension
A thumb spica cast
A volar slab with the wrist in full flexion

questions.explanation: A reduced fifth (± fourth) metacarpal neck fracture is held in an **ulnar gutter** with the **wrist ~30° extended and the ring/small MCP joints flexed ~70°** (intrinsic-plus), which maintains the reduction (flexed MCP tensions the collaterals) and prevents stiffness. The flexed proximal phalanx also acts as a 'crank' to control rotation during casting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Which statement about acceptable angulation of metacarpal SHAFT fractures (as opposed to neck fractures) is correct?

options.text: Shaft fractures tolerate LESS angulation than neck fractures, because there is more shortening for a given angle and the deformity is farther from the CMC compensation
Shaft fractures tolerate more angulation than neck fractures
Shaft and neck fractures have identical tolerances
Angulation of shaft fractures is never clinically relevant

questions.explanation: For a **given angle, shaft fractures cause more shortening than neck fractures** and their deformity is less compensated by CMC motion, so **less angulation is acceptable in the shaft** (roughly ≤10° for index/middle, and less than the generous neck allowances even for ring/small). This is why apex-dorsal shaft angulation and any rotation are scrutinized more closely.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Phalangeal NECK fractures (of the proximal or middle phalanx) are particularly important in which population, and why?

options.text: Children — they are easily missed, often displace/rotate, and malunion blocks IP flexion by obliterating the subcondylar recess
Elderly — because of osteoporosis causing nonunion
They only occur in adults and always heal uneventfully
They are irrelevant because they never affect motion

questions.explanation: **Phalangeal neck (subcondylar) fractures are notably a pediatric injury** and account for a meaningful share of phalangeal fractures. They are easily missed, tend to displace/rotate (the head often rotates and displaces dorsally), and malunion **obliterates the volar subcondylar recess, mechanically blocking IP flexion**. Close follow-up and, when displaced, reduction/fixation are important; corrective osteotomy treats established blocks.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: Which fracture is most appropriately managed with early protected motion / 'buddy taping' as a primary strategy in the majority of cases?

options.text: A stable, nondisplaced, non-rotated proximal phalanx shaft fracture
A displaced unicondylar fracture of the proximal phalanx
A Bennett fracture-subluxation
A displaced dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation with a large volar fragment

questions.explanation: **Stable, nondisplaced, non-rotated phalangeal shaft fractures** do well with early protected motion (buddy taping to an adjacent digit) which limits stiffness while the fracture heals. The other options are unstable/intraarticular injuries (displaced unicondylar, Bennett, unstable dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation) that require reduction and fixation to avoid malunion, subluxation, or arthritis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: In a dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation, an 'extension-block' splinting protocol is used for stable (small-fragment) patterns because it:

options.text: Maintains concentric reduction by blocking the terminal degrees of extension while permitting active flexion
Immobilizes the PIP in full extension continuously
Holds the DIP in flexion while the PIP is free
Prevents all PIP motion for 6 weeks

questions.explanation: **Dorsal extension-block splinting** keeps the PIP flexed enough to hold the middle phalanx concentrically reduced (the dorsal dislocating force is greatest near full extension), while **allowing active flexion**; the block is gradually reduced weekly. It applies to stable dorsal PIP fracture-dislocations (small volar fragment, concentric reduction maintained). Unstable large-fragment injuries instead need volar plate arthroplasty, ORIF, or dynamic external fixation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: The most common complication overall after phalangeal fractures — often the main determinant of a poor result — is:

options.text: Stiffness from tendon adhesions and joint contracture
Deep infection
Avascular necrosis
Compartment syndrome

questions.explanation: Because the phalanges are enveloped by the flexor and extensor tendons and their sheaths, **stiffness — from tendon adhesions, capsular contracture, and prolonged immobilization — is the dominant complication** of phalangeal fractures and the usual cause of a poor outcome. This drives the emphasis on stable-enough fixation and early motion, and on avoiding unnecessary immobilization.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: The 'pseudoclaw' deformity that can result from an excessively angulated/shortened metacarpal neck fracture is characterized by:

options.text: MCP hyperextension with PIP flexion during attempted extension, from relative intrinsic weakness/dynamic instability
Fixed PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension (true boutonnière)
DIP flexion deformity from terminal tendon rupture
Thumb IP hyperextension

questions.explanation: **Pseudoclawing** occurs when marked apex-dorsal angulation/shortening of a metacarpal neck fracture creates **relative intrinsic weakness and dynamic imbalance**: on attempted extension the finger shows **MCP hyperextension with compensatory PIP flexion**. Unlike a true intrinsic-minus claw, it stems from the fracture geometry — and significant, functionally impairing pseudoclawing is one of the clear indications to correct the fracture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 7 (Fractures of the Metacarpals and Phalanges)

questions.stem: In the widely used classification of carpal instability, a lesion producing dysfunction BETWEEN bones of the SAME carpal row (e.g., scapholunate dissociation) is termed:

options.text: Carpal instability dissociative (CID)
Carpal instability nondissociative (CIND)
Carpal instability complex (CIC)
Carpal instability adaptive (CIA)

questions.explanation: **CID (carpal instability dissociative)** involves ligament disruption **between bones of the same row** — most commonly scapholunate (SL) or lunotriquetral (LT). **CIND** is nondissociative proximal-row instability (dysfunction at the radiocarpal and/or midcarpal joints with intact interosseous ligaments). **CIC** combines features of both (e.g., perilunate fracture-dislocations/axial injuries), and **CIA (adaptive)** is carpal malalignment driven by a problem OUTSIDE the carpus (classically a distal radius malunion).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: A patient develops carpal malalignment (e.g., a DISI-like posture) purely as a consequence of a malunited distal radius fracture, with intact interosseous ligaments. This is classified as:

options.text: Carpal instability adaptive (CIA)
Carpal instability dissociative (CID)
Carpal instability nondissociative (CIND)
Carpal instability complex (CIC)

questions.explanation: **Carpal instability adaptive (CIA)** describes carpal malalignment caused by a condition OUTSIDE the carpus — the most frequent being the **carpal malalignment adapting to a distal radius malunion** (e.g., dorsal tilt driving a compensatory midcarpal posture). Correcting the extrinsic deformity (radial osteotomy) typically corrects the adaptive instability.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Linscheid and colleagues (1972) defined the lunate as the 'intercalated segment.' In dorsal intercalated segment instability (DISI), the lunate is:

options.text: Extended (tilted dorsally), typically with a scapholunate angle >60 degrees
Flexed (tilted palmarly), with a scapholunate angle <30 degrees
Translated ulnarly with a normal scapholunate angle
Rotated into pronation only, with no sagittal change

questions.explanation: In **DISI**, the lunate tilts into **extension (dorsiflexion)** — because with SL dissociation the scaphoid flexes and the lunate, freed from the scaphoid, follows the triquetrum into extension. This produces an abnormally increased **scapholunate angle (>60°)**. In **VISI**, the lunate flexes (palmar tilt), classically from lunotriquetral insufficiency.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The normal scapholunate angle (measured on a true lateral radiograph) is approximately:

options.text: 30 to 60 degrees (mean ~47 degrees)
0 to 15 degrees
70 to 90 degrees
90 to 120 degrees

questions.explanation: The normal **scapholunate angle ranges ~30–60 degrees** (the scaphoid normally sits at ~45° of flexion relative to the radius). An angle **>60°** suggests DISI/SL dissociation, while an angle **<30°** suggests VISI. The capitolunate angle (normal <15°) and radiolunate angle are complementary measurements.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: On a PA radiograph, an abnormally widened gap between the scaphoid and lunate is called the:

options.text: Terry Thomas sign (a unilateral gap >3–5 mm suggests SL dissociation)
Gilula sign
Fat pad sign
Sail sign

questions.explanation: The **Terry Thomas sign** (named for the actor's dental diastema) is an abnormally wide SL gap, measured at the middle of the flat ulnar facet of the scaphoid. A **unilateral gap >5 mm is diagnostic of SL dissociation** (comparison to the contralateral wrist is essential, since constitutional widening is usually bilateral). Dynamic stress views (clenched-fist PA) unmask dynamic instability.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The 'scaphoid ring sign' on a PA wrist radiograph indicates:

options.text: An abnormally flexed/pronated (foreshortened) scaphoid — its tuberosity projected as a dense ring
A scaphoid waist fracture
Avascular necrosis of the lunate
A normal, well-aligned scaphoid

questions.explanation: The **ring sign** appears when the scaphoid rotates into **flexion and pronation**, foreshortening it in the PA view so the palmar tuberosity is seen end-on as a radiodense ring over the distal scaphoid. It signals abnormal scaphoid flexion — seen in SL dissociation but also in dissociative or nondissociative VISI, so it is not by itself pathognomonic of SLD.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The Watson scaphoid shift test is performed by:

options.text: Pressing on the palmar scaphoid tuberosity while moving the wrist from ulnar to radial deviation
Ballotting the pisiform against the triquetrum
Axially loading the thumb metacarpal
Percussing over the distal radioulnar joint

questions.explanation: In the **Watson scaphoid shift test**, the examiner presses on the **palmar scaphoid tuberosity** while moving the wrist from **ulnar to radial deviation**. Normally the scaphoid cannot flex against the thumb pressure; with SL incompetence (or a lax wrist) the proximal scaphoid **subluxates dorsally out of the fossa**, and releasing pressure produces a painful clunk as it relocates. Comparison to the opposite wrist is important because lax wrists can test positive without pathology.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Watson described SLAC (scapholunate advanced collapse) as a three-stage degenerative progression. Where does arthritis begin (stage I)?

options.text: The radial styloid–distal scaphoid articulation
The proximal scaphoid–scaphoid fossa
The midcarpal (capitolunate) joint
The radiolunate joint

questions.explanation: In **SLAC**, arthritis starts at the **radial styloid–distal scaphoid** articulation (stage I, with breaking of the styloid tip), progresses to the **proximal scaphoid–scaphoid fossa** (stage II), then to the **midcarpal (capitolunate) joint** (stage III). The **radiolunate joint is characteristically spared**, which is what makes proximal row carpectomy and four-corner fusion viable motion-sparing salvage options.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Which region of the scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL) is the strongest and most important biomechanically?

options.text: The dorsal region
The palmar region
The proximal (membranous) region
All three regions are equal in strength

questions.explanation: The **dorsal region of the SLIL is the thickest and strongest**, providing the greatest resistance to SL rotation and palmar-dorsal translation. The proximal membranous portion is the weakest (and often perforated with age without instability). This is why SL repairs and capsulodeses focus on restoring dorsal SL competence, and why the dorsal SL ligament is targeted on MRI.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Mayfield's cadaveric study described progressive perilunate instability in four stages. Which structure fails FIRST (stage I)?

options.text: The scapholunate ligament (radial side)
The lunotriquetral ligament (ulnar side)
The radioscaphocapitate ligament
The dorsal radiocarpal ligament

questions.explanation: In **Mayfield's progressive perilunate instability** (from wrist hyperextension, ulnar deviation, midcarpal supination), failure proceeds radial-to-ulnar around the lunate: **Stage I = scapholunate disruption**, **Stage II = capitolunate (through the space of Poirier)**, **Stage III = lunotriquetral disruption** (perilunate dislocation), and **Stage IV = lunate dislocation** (the lunate is extruded volarly). A reverse (ulnar-to-radial) pattern also exists.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The 'space of Poirier' is clinically important because:

options.text: It is a relatively weak interligamentous zone (palmar capsule) through which most perilunate dislocations occur
It is the strongest ligamentous condensation of the wrist
It carries the main blood supply to the lunate
It is the origin of the extensor tendons

questions.explanation: The **space of Poirier** is a relatively weak sulcus in the palmar capsule between the radioscaphocapitate and the long radiolunate ligaments, at the level of the capitolunate joint. Because it is a zone of weakness, **most perilunate dislocations propagate through it** (stage II of Mayfield), allowing the capitate to dislocate dorsally and, ultimately, the lunate to extrude palmarly.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: A patient sustains a high-energy wrist hyperextension injury; the lateral radiograph shows the capitate dislocated dorsal to the lunate but the lunate still articulating with the radius. This is a:

options.text: Perilunate dislocation
Lunate dislocation
Isolated scapholunate dissociation
Midcarpal instability (nondissociative)

questions.explanation: In a **perilunate dislocation**, the carpus (capitate) dislocates — usually dorsally — while the **lunate remains seated in the radial fossa**. If the lunate itself is extruded (typically volarly, the 'spilled teacup' sign) with the capitate realigned to the radius, it is a **lunate dislocation** (Mayfield stage IV). Both are surgical emergencies (watch for acute median nerve compression) requiring reduction and ligament repair/fixation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: A perilunate/lunate dislocation is often accompanied by which acute neurologic complication that must be actively sought?

options.text: Acute median nerve compression (acute carpal tunnel syndrome)
Radial nerve palsy
Posterior interosseous nerve palsy
Axillary nerve injury

questions.explanation: The volarly displaced lunate/fracture fragments compress the **median nerve** in the carpal tunnel, so **acute carpal tunnel syndrome** is common with perilunate/lunate dislocations. Progressive or severe median symptoms warrant urgent reduction and often a carpal tunnel release. This is why the exam and history must specifically assess median nerve function.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The lunotriquetral (LT) ballottement test (Reagan) and the shear test (Kleinman) are used to diagnose:

options.text: Lunotriquetral instability
Scapholunate dissociation
Distal radioulnar joint instability
First CMC joint arthritis

questions.explanation: For **LT instability**, the **ballottement test (Reagan)** stabilizes the lunate while displacing the triquetrum (pisotriquetral unit) dorsal-palmar, and the **shear test (Kleinman)** applies opposing forces across the LT joint — both reproduce pain/laxity. LT injury classically produces a **VISI** posture (palmar-flexed lunate). Note: purely dorsal triquetral chip fractures don't produce this.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: In the reverse-perilunate (ulnar-to-radial) mechanism, the FIRST ligament complex to fail is the:

options.text: Lunotriquetral ligament complex
Scapholunate ligament
Radioscaphocapitate ligament
Dorsal intercarpal ligament

questions.explanation: In the **reverse perilunate** pattern, high load applied to the hypothenar area forces the triquetrum dorsally relative to the constrained lunate, rupturing the **lunotriquetral ligaments first (stage I)**, then the ulnocarpal (UL/UT/UC) ligaments and lunocapitate (stage II), and finally the SL ligament (stage III) — the mirror image of Mayfield's radial-to-ulnar progression.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: A lunotriquetral dissociation classically produces which static carpal malalignment pattern on the lateral radiograph?

options.text: VISI (volar/palmar-flexed lunate)
DISI (dorsally extended lunate)
Ulnar translocation only
No malalignment is ever possible

questions.explanation: Complete LT dissociation lets the lunate follow the scaphoid into **flexion**, producing a **VISI** posture (palmar-tilted lunate, reduced scapholunate angle). A key distinction is that VISI can be **dissociative** (true LT tear) or **nondissociative** (CIND-VISI, proximal-row laxity); the triquetral axis alignment helps differentiate the two, which matters because treatment differs (LT stabilization vs midcarpal/radiolunate procedures).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: A patient reports a painful 'clunk' as the wrist moves into ulnar deviation, reproduced by the midcarpal shift ('catch-up clunk') test, with normal interosseous ligaments and generalized laxity. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.text: Nondissociative midcarpal instability (CIND)
Scapholunate dissociation (CID)
SLAC wrist
Kienböck disease

questions.explanation: **Nondissociative midcarpal instability** (a form of CIND) typically occurs in **lax wrists** with intact SL/LT ligaments; the proximal row snaps from a flexed to an extended position during ulnar deviation, producing the palpable/audible **'catch-up clunk.'** Louis' CLIP maneuver assesses the capitolunate variant. Treatment is initially nonoperative (activity modification, therapy), with soft-tissue reconstruction or limited fusion reserved for refractory cases.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: When evaluating a suspected SL widening on radiographs, why are bilateral comparison views essential?

options.text: Constitutional (often bilateral) SL widening from hyperlaxity or conditions like CPPD can mimic traumatic dissociation
SL widening is invisible unless both wrists are imaged simultaneously
Radiation dose is halved with bilateral imaging
The contralateral wrist always has an identical fracture

questions.explanation: An SL gap can be **constitutionally increased (usually bilateral)** in hyperlax individuals, or bilaterally widened by **rheumatoid arthritis, gout, or CPPD (calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease)**. A **unilateral** gap >5 mm on comparison stress views is what indicates a **traumatic** SL disruption — hence the need to image both wrists (e.g., bilateral clenched-fist views).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Which radiographic view is most useful for dynamically unmasking a reducible scapholunate dissociation?

options.text: Clenched-fist (loaded) PA view
Carpal tunnel view
Robert (true AP thumb) view
Oblique 45-degree pronated view

questions.explanation: The **clenched-fist PA view** axially loads the carpus, driving the capitate proximally between the scaphoid and lunate and **widening a dynamically unstable SL interval** that may look normal on a static film. Loaded ulnar-deviation or AP grip views serve the same purpose. Static films may miss dynamic (reducible) SL instability, which is why stress views or arthroscopy are used.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The Garcia-Elias 'three-ligament tenodesis' (a modification of the Brunelli procedure) reconstructs chronic reducible SL dissociation using a strip of which tendon?

options.text: Flexor carpi radialis (FCR)
Palmaris longus
Extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU)
Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU)

questions.explanation: The **three-ligament tenodesis** uses a distally based strip of the **FCR** tendon passed through a bone tunnel in the distal scaphoid, across the dorsum to reconstruct the dorsal SL ligament, and anchored to correct scaphoid flexion and SL alignment. The original Brunelli used a strip crossing the radiocarpal joint; Garcia-Elias modified it to avoid crossing that joint (limiting flexion loss). It is indicated for **reducible chronic SL dissociation without arthritis**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The Blatt dorsal capsulodesis for scapholunate instability works by:

options.text: Advancing a dorsal radiocarpal capsular flap onto the distal scaphoid to check scaphoid flexion (a non-anatomic tether)
Fusing the scaphoid to the lunate
Excising the proximal scaphoid pole
Replacing the SL ligament with a free tendon graft alone

questions.explanation: A **Blatt dorsal capsulodesis** advances a proximally based flap of the dorsal radiocarpal (radioscaphoid) capsule and secures it to the distal scaphoid, acting as a **non-anatomic checkrein that limits scaphoid flexion/rotatory subluxation**. It is used to reinforce a repair or in reducible instability; a downside is some loss of wrist flexion. It does not restore true SL ligament anatomy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: For an ACUTE, complete, repairable scapholunate ligament tear (well-reduced, no chondral wear), the preferred treatment is:

options.text: Direct SL ligament repair (often with suture anchors) protected with K-wires and/or dorsal capsulodesis
Immediate proximal row carpectomy
Four-corner fusion
Long-term casting without reduction

questions.explanation: An **acute, complete, repairable SL tear** is best treated with **direct ligament repair** (typically suture anchors to the dorsal SLIL footprint), protected with temporary **K-wires or a temporary SL screw**, and frequently reinforced with a **dorsal capsulodesis**. Salvage procedures (PRC, four-corner fusion) are reserved for established arthritis (SLAC), not acute repairable tears.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The RASL procedure for scapholunate instability refers to:

options.text: Reduction and Association of the Scaphoid and Lunate, held with a (usually headless) screw
Radial Styloidectomy And Scaphoid Levelling
Radioscaphoid Arthrodesis with Soft-tissue Lengthening
Reverse Advancement of the Scapholunate Ligament

questions.explanation: **RASL = Reduction and Association of the Scaphoid and Lunate**, in which the SL joint is reduced and stabilized with a screw (often headless) placed across the scaphoid into the lunate, allowing a fibrous/pseudoligamentous union to form. It is one of several options for chronic reducible SL dissociation; results and hardware complications vary, and it is contentious compared with tenodesis techniques.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: For a SLAC (or SNAC) stage II–III wrist with a preserved radiolunate (lunate fossa) joint and intact capitate head cartilage, appropriate motion-preserving salvage options include:

options.text: Proximal row carpectomy OR scaphoid excision with four-corner (midcarpal) fusion
Direct scapholunate ligament repair
Three-ligament tenodesis
Simple immobilization only
