questions.explanation: Once **SLAC/SNAC arthritis** is established (stage II–III), reconstructive ligament procedures are futile; motion-preserving **salvage** is chosen: **proximal row carpectomy** (requires an intact capitate head and lunate fossa cartilage; relies on the RSC ligament to prevent ulnar translocation) or **scaphoid excision + four-corner fusion**. Total wrist fusion is reserved for pancarpal (including radiolunate) arthritis or failed salvage.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: A proximal row carpectomy relies on which articulation becoming the new radiocarpal joint, and therefore requires intact cartilage on which surfaces?

options.text: The capitate head articulating with the lunate fossa of the radius
The scaphoid articulating with the scaphoid fossa
The hamate articulating with the radial styloid
The trapezium articulating with the sigmoid notch

questions.explanation: After **proximal row carpectomy** (excision of scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum), the **capitate head migrates into the lunate fossa of the radius**, forming a new radiocarpal articulation. Therefore intact cartilage on the **capitate head and the lunate fossa** is required — if the capitate head is arthritic (SLAC/SNAC III), PRC is contraindicated and four-corner fusion (or capitate resurfacing) is preferred. The RSC ligament must be preserved to prevent ulnar translocation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The radioscaphocapitate (RSC) ligament must be carefully preserved during a proximal row carpectomy because it:

options.text: Prevents ulnar translocation of the carpus
Supplies blood to the capitate
Is the main dorsal stabilizer of the DRUJ
Provides thumb opposition

questions.explanation: The **RSC ligament** is a key palmar extrinsic ligament; if it is sacrificed during PRC (along with the long radiolunate, which is removed with the lunate), the carpus can **translate ulnarly**. Preserving the RSC as a sling supporting the capitate maintains carpal alignment after the proximal row is removed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) and its central articular disc are often perforated with age. A central TFCC perforation communicating the radiocarpal and DRUJ compartments:

options.text: Is common and does not necessarily indicate instability
Always indicates lunotriquetral dissociation
Is pathognomonic of a perilunate dislocation
Confirms DRUJ instability by itself

questions.explanation: Age-related **central TFCC perforations are common and often asymptomatic**, and communication between the radiocarpal and DRUJ compartments **does not by itself indicate instability**. Clinical correlation, comparison views, and cartilage-sensitive imaging are needed before attributing symptoms to such a finding — an incidental perforation should not be over-treated.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The 'dart-thrower's motion' (DTM) of the wrist is clinically important because:

options.text: It occurs largely through the midcarpal joint with minimal proximal-row (SL/LT) motion, and is exploited in rehabilitation to protect SL repairs
It occurs entirely at the radiocarpal joint
It maximizes scapholunate motion and should be avoided in all patients
It is a pathologic movement seen only in unstable wrists

questions.explanation: The **dart-thrower's motion** (radial extension to ulnar flexion) is a functional oblique arc that occurs **predominantly through the midcarpal joint with minimal scaphoid/lunate motion at the proximal row**. Because it minimizes stress across the SL and LT intervals, DTM-based rehabilitation protocols are used to **protect SL/LT repairs and reconstructions** while allowing early motion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Which finding best distinguishes a dissociative (true LT tear) VISI from a nondissociative CIND-VISI on radiographs?

options.text: The alignment of the triquetral axis relative to the lunate helps discriminate the two
The presence of any lunate flexion, which occurs only in true LT tears
A scapholunate gap greater than 5 mm
A positive Watson scaphoid shift test

questions.explanation: Because **VISI can be dissociative (LT tear) or nondissociative (CIND)**, lunate flexion alone doesn't distinguish them. The chapter notes that assessing the **triquetral axis relative to the lunate** helps: in normal and CIND-VISI wrists the triquetrum-lunate relationship differs from that seen in true LT dissociation. This distinction matters because CIND-VISI is treated differently (e.g., radiolunate or midcarpal procedures) than an isolated LT tear.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: A meta-analysis and comparative data cited in the chapter suggest that isolated lunotriquetral ARTHRODESIS for LT dissociation:

options.text: Has a substantial nonunion rate and persistent pain, and may merely convert a dissociative VISI into a nondissociative VISI
Is the gold-standard first-line treatment with near-100% union
Reliably restores normal carpal kinematics
Eliminates the need to address ulnar variance

questions.explanation: **LT fusion** is plagued by a **high nonunion rate and persistent pain**, and biomechanically it may only convert a dissociative VISI into a **nondissociative VISI** (the malalignment persists). For these reasons many surgeons prefer LT ligament reconstruction, or for a static VISI deformity, a **radiolunate (or midcarpal) fusion**. Associated positive ulnar variance may warrant ulnar shortening to offload the LT joint.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Positive ulnar variance is relevant to lunotriquetral instability because:

options.text: Ulnar shortening osteotomy can offload/tension the ulnar carpus and augment LT stability
It has no relationship to LT instability
It always requires a Darrach resection
It is a contraindication to any wrist surgery

questions.explanation: In LT instability associated with **positive ulnar variance / ulnocarpal abutment**, an **ulnar shortening osteotomy** both relieves ulnocarpal impaction and **tightens the extrinsic ulnocarpal ligaments**, augmenting LT stability. Reagan and colleagues noted ulnar shortening can be used to reinforce LT immobilization. This addresses the mechanical driver rather than fusing or reconstructing the joint alone.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The proximal carpal row is described as an 'intercalated segment' primarily because:

options.text: It has no direct tendon insertions and is positioned between the radius and the distal row, controlled indirectly by ligaments and joint geometry
It contains the strongest muscles of the wrist
It is fused to the distal radius
It is the only part of the carpus with a blood supply

questions.explanation: The proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum) is an **intercalated segment**: it lies interposed between the fixed radius and the distal row and has **no direct tendon/muscle insertions** (the pisiform, an FCU sesamoid, is the exception). Its position is dictated by ligament balance and articular geometry — which is why interosseous ligament failure produces the abnormal DISI/VISI postures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Dorsal scaphoid translation (proximal scaphoid riding onto the dorsal rim of the distal radius) on the lateral view is a sign of:

options.text: Advanced scapholunate instability
Early Kienböck disease
A stable, well-aligned carpus
Isolated pisotriquetral arthritis

questions.explanation: As SL instability advances, the proximal scaphoid **translates dorsally onto the dorsal rim of the distal radius**, best seen on the lateral view (detectable with the dorsal tangential line technique). It reflects loss of the normal constraint on the scaphoid and is part of the progression toward rotatory subluxation and, ultimately, SLAC changes.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Geissler reported that up to what proportion of distal radius fractures are associated with some degree of carpal (interosseous) ligament disruption?

options.text: Up to about 30%
Less than 1%
About 90%
Essentially 0% — they are unrelated

questions.explanation: Per Geissler, **up to ~30% of distal radius fractures** have associated carpal ligament disruption of variable degree, which is one reason SL injuries are frequently missed when masked by an obvious fracture. Recognizing this prompts scrutiny of the SL interval (and arthroscopy in selected cases) when treating distal radius fractures, especially high-energy intraarticular patterns.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Which of the following is a recognized IATROGENIC cause of scapholunate ligament injury?

options.text: Excessive dorsal capsular excision during dorsal wrist ganglion removal
Simple carpal tunnel release
Trigger finger release
de Quervain first dorsal compartment release

questions.explanation: Overly aggressive **dorsal capsular excision during dorsal wrist ganglion resection** can disrupt the dorsal SL/dorsal intercarpal ligaments and precipitate SL instability. The chapter also lists ligament attenuation from inflammatory, crystalline, or septic arthritis as non-traumatic causes. This underscores conservative dorsal capsulotomy technique near the SL interval.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: A study of complete SL ligament sectioning found that isolated SL division does NOT immediately produce a static DISI deformity because:

options.text: The lunate has multiple secondary stabilizers (dorsal, palmar, radiocarpal, and midcarpal), so several must fail before static malalignment appears
The SL ligament is functionally unimportant
The scaphoid is rigidly fixed to the radius
The lunate has no ligamentous attachments

questions.explanation: The lunate is buttressed by an array of **secondary stabilizers — two dorsal, two palmar, two radiocarpal, and two midcarpal** ligamentous restraints. Because of this redundancy, **isolated SL sectioning often produces only dynamic instability**; a **static DISI** requires attenuation/failure of these secondary stabilizers over time. This explains the spectrum from occult/dynamic to static/reducible to fixed SL instability.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Cartilage-sensitive MRI is emphasized as a critical part of SL/carpal instability workup because:

options.text: Cartilage status determines whether a reconstructive (ligament) vs a salvage (fusion/PRC) procedure is appropriate
It replaces the need for any physical examination
It is the only way to see an SL gap
It is used solely to measure ulnar variance

questions.explanation: Assessing **articular cartilage integrity** is decisive: intact cartilage permits **ligament repair/reconstruction**, whereas established chondral wear (SLAC changes) mandates a **salvage** procedure (PRC, four-corner fusion, or total wrist fusion). High-resolution (≥1.5 T, dedicated coil) MRI with cartilage-sensitive sequences complements ligament assessment to guide this fork in management.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Why is restoration of NORMAL scapholunate kinematics considered impossible with a single screw or a single graft strand across the SL joint?

options.text: The SL joint has a complex, off-center axis of rotation that a single rigid element cannot replicate
Screws cannot be placed in the carpus
The scaphoid and lunate never move relative to each other
Grafts always fail immediately

questions.explanation: The SL joint rotates about a **complex, eccentrically located axis**; a single screw or single graft strand cannot reproduce the multiplanar constrained motion between scaphoid and lunate. This biomechanical reality is why reconstructions increasingly aim to recreate multiple ligamentous restraints (e.g., dorsal and volar components) rather than a single tether, and why no technique fully restores normal kinematics.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The ulnar (medial) 'rotational column' of the carpus — the triquetrum-hamate articulation — is important because it:

options.text: Converts compressive load into a rotational/shear moment that drives lunate flexion-extension (helping control the proximal row)
Provides the sole blood supply to the lunate
Has no effect on proximal row motion
Is rigidly fused and immobile

questions.explanation: The helicoid **triquetrohamate articulation** converts compressive forces of the ulnar 'control column' into a **rotational/shear moment**, driving lunotriquetral (and thus lunate) sagittal alignment during radioulnar deviation. This is why LT integrity and the ulnar column are central to proximal-row balance, and why LT dissociation flips the lunate into VISI.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: A neglected, chronic SL dissociation is left untreated. Which is the LEAST accurate statement about its natural history?

options.text: Every case rapidly and inevitably progresses to SLAC within weeks
Increased shear and compressive stress develops at the SL level
It can progress through the SLAC stages over time
Some partial injuries produce functional sequelae without radiographic SLAC changes at intermediate follow-up

questions.explanation: The false statement is that SLAC develops within weeks in every case — progression is **variable and often takes years**, and not all injuries reach SLAC. The chapter cites a cohort with SL injury (without SL widening/DISI) that at ~7 years had functional sequelae and pain but **no SLAC changes**. SLD does increase abnormal shear/compressive stress and *can* progress to SLAC, but the rate and inevitability vary with injury completeness.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: In a chronic complete perilunate injury that presents late (>6 weeks) and cannot be anatomically reduced/repaired, a reasonable option is:

options.text: Proximal row carpectomy or salvage arthrodesis, depending on cartilage status
Simple splinting with no surgery ever indicated
Immediate total wrist arthroplasty in all cases
Isolated pisiform excision

questions.explanation: **Chronic, unreconstructable perilunate injuries** (late presentation, fixed deformity, or chondral damage) are managed with **salvage** — proximal row carpectomy when the capitate head/lunate fossa are preserved, or partial/total wrist arthrodesis when they are not. Acute injuries are reduced and repaired/fixed; the window for anatomic ligament repair narrows substantially after ~6 weeks.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Which physical exam sign is most specific for SCAPHOLUNATE (rather than lunotriquetral) pathology?

options.text: Dorsal SL-interval tenderness (distal to Lister tubercle) with a positive Watson scaphoid shift test
A positive Reagan ballottement test
A positive Kleinman shear test
Pisotriquetral grind pain

questions.explanation: **SL pathology** localizes to the **dorsal SL interval (just distal to Lister tubercle)** with tenderness and a positive **Watson scaphoid shift**. In contrast, the **Reagan ballottement** and **Kleinman shear** tests localize to the **lunotriquetral** joint (ulnar side), and pisotriquetral grind pain points to that joint — helping the examiner distinguish radial-sided (SL) from ulnar-sided (LT) instability.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Rotatory subluxation of the scaphoid describes:

options.text: Abnormal flexion/pronation of the scaphoid due to SL incompetence, producing the ring sign and increased SL angle
A fracture through the scaphoid waist
Dorsal dislocation of the entire carpus
Avascular necrosis of the proximal scaphoid pole

questions.explanation: **Rotatory subluxation of the scaphoid** (a term popularized by Watson) is the abnormal **flexion and pronation of the scaphoid** that occurs when the SL ligament is incompetent — the scaphoid is no longer held in extension by the lunate. Radiographically it produces the **cortical ring sign, increased SL angle (>60°), and SL gap widening**. It is essentially the clinical/radiographic expression of SL dissociation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: First-line management of symptomatic nondissociative midcarpal instability (CIND) in a hyperlax patient is generally:

options.text: Nonoperative — activity modification, proprioceptive/strengthening therapy, and bracing
Immediate four-corner fusion
Proximal row carpectomy
Total wrist arthrodesis

questions.explanation: Because CIND midcarpal instability usually reflects **ligamentous laxity rather than a discrete tear**, initial treatment is **nonoperative**: activity modification, therapy emphasizing proprioception and dynamic (ulnar-column) muscle control, and bracing. Surgery — soft-tissue reconstruction/capsular tightening or limited (e.g., midcarpal) fusion — is reserved for refractory, disabling cases.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: A 'carpal instability complex' (CIC) pattern, such as a perilunate fracture-dislocation or an axial (dorsopalmar crush) carpal disruption, is characterized by:

options.text: Coexisting dissociative AND nondissociative dysfunction (features of both CID and CIND)
Pure ligament laxity with no bony injury
Malalignment driven solely by an extracarpal deformity
Isolated single-ligament failure within one row

questions.explanation: **CIC** combines **dissociative and nondissociative** components — the dysfunction spans both within-row and between-row (radiocarpal/midcarpal) derangement. Classic examples are **perilunate fracture-dislocations** and **axial carpal disruptions** (from dorsopalmar crush), which flatten the transverse carpal arch and can injure neurovascular structures. Inadequately treated carpal dislocations can also evolve into CIC patterns.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: During the Mayfield sequence, at the point of a complete perilunate dislocation (before lunate extrusion), which ligament typically remains intact and tethers the lunate to the radius?

options.text: The radioscaphocapitate / short radiolunate palmar ligaments (the volar radiolunate attachment)
The dorsal intercarpal ligament
The scapholunate interosseous ligament
The extensor retinaculum

questions.explanation: As the injury progresses (stage III–IV), the **volar radiolunate ligaments** (notably the short radiolunate, with the RSC acting on the capitate) remain the final tether. In stage IV the lunate is levered by the still-intact RSC and rotates/extrudes palmarly ('spilled teacup'). Recognizing which restraints remain guides reduction maneuvers and the sequence of ligament repair.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: For a symptomatic, chronic LT dissociation with a STATIC VISI deformity that has failed conservative care, the chapter's preferred surgical option over isolated LT fusion is often:

options.text: Radiolunate (or midcarpal) fusion
Total wrist arthroplasty
Isolated pisiform excision
Repeat casting for 6 months

questions.explanation: Because isolated **LT fusion has high nonunion and persistent pain** and may just convert a dissociative VISI into a nondissociative one, for a **static VISI deformity** the authors favor **radiolunate fusion** (others prefer midcarpal fusion). Ligament reconstruction (± ulnar shortening) is considered for reducible LT dissociation without fixed deformity; triquetrum excision is an option in select degenerative situations.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: Gilula's arc lines are used on a PA wrist radiograph to detect carpal malalignment. A disruption (step-off) in these smooth arcs suggests:

options.text: Carpal malalignment, dislocation, or intercarpal instability
Normal carpal alignment
A distal radioulnar joint problem only
Soft-tissue swelling with intact bones

questions.explanation: **Gilula's arcs** are three smooth curved lines drawn along the proximal and distal margins of the proximal carpal row and the proximal margins of the capitate/hamate. **Disruption or step-off of an arc** indicates malalignment, overlap, or dislocation (e.g., the abnormal capitate-lunate overlap of a perilunate dislocation). Preserving smooth arcs is a quick screen for carpal congruity on the PA film.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: In an acute perilunate/lunate dislocation, the recommended definitive treatment is:

options.text: Open reduction, ligament repair, and internal fixation (with carpal tunnel release if median nerve compromised)
Closed reduction and casting alone as definitive care
Immediate proximal row carpectomy in all cases
Primary total wrist fusion

questions.explanation: Although **urgent closed reduction** is performed to relieve median nerve pressure and soft-tissue tension, **closed treatment alone gives poor results**; the standard of care is **open reduction, repair of the disrupted ligaments (SL and LT), and internal fixation** (K-wires or screws), often through combined dorsal ± volar approaches, with **carpal tunnel release** if there is median nerve compromise. Salvage is reserved for late/unreconstructable injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: In a normal wrist, the proximal carpal row moves as a coordinated unit. During RADIAL deviation, the scaphoid characteristically:

options.text: Flexes (palmar-flexes), shortening its PA projection
Extends and elongates
Does not move at all
Translates dorsally out of the fossa

questions.explanation: With **radial deviation**, the scaphoid **flexes (palmar-flexes)** and the whole proximal row flexes; with **ulnar deviation** the scaphoid extends and the row extends. The SL and LT ligaments transmit these coupled motions. Loss of this coupling (SL dissociation) lets the scaphoid flex independently into rotatory subluxation, which is the basis of the Watson shift test and the ring sign.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 13 (Carpal Instability)

questions.stem: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Its blood supply is described as predominantly retrograde, entering mainly through which structure?

options.text: Branches of the radial artery entering distally through the dorsal ridge
The anterior interosseous artery entering the proximal pole
The ulnar artery entering through the waist
The posterior interosseous artery entering the tubercle

questions.explanation: About **70–80% of the intraosseous and proximal-pole blood supply** comes from **branches of the radial artery entering distally through the dorsal ridge** of the scaphoid. Because flow is **retrograde** (distal-to-proximal), the more proximal the fracture, the more dysvascular the proximal fragment and the higher the risk of AVN and nonunion. The distal pole/tubercle also receives palmar branches supplying ~20–30% of the bone.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A proximal-pole scaphoid fracture carries a substantially higher risk of avascular necrosis than a distal fracture. The reported incidence of AVN in proximal pole fractures is approximately:

options.text: Less than 1%

questions.explanation: Because the proximal pole depends almost entirely on retrograde flow from distally entering radial artery branches, **proximal pole fractures have a reported AVN incidence of ~13–50%**. This is why proximal pole fractures are generally treated operatively (often via a dorsal approach with a headless compression screw), and why increased proximal-pole radiodensity on imaging signals dysvascularity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man falls on an outstretched hand and has anatomic snuffbox tenderness, scaphoid tubercle tenderness, and pain on axial compression of the thumb, but initial radiographs are normal. The most appropriate management is:

options.text: Immobilize in a thumb spica cast and re-image (repeat radiographs, or advanced imaging with MRI/CT) in 10–14 days
Discharge with reassurance that there is no fracture
Immediate open reduction and internal fixation
Begin immediate wrist range-of-motion exercises

questions.explanation: The combination of snuffbox tenderness, tubercle tenderness, and a positive axial compression test is highly suggestive of a scaphoid fracture even with normal initial films. The standard approach is to **immobilize (thumb spica) and repeat imaging in ~10–14 days**, or obtain **MRI** (highly sensitive/specific for occult fractures) or CT. Missing an occult scaphoid fracture risks displacement and nonunion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: For a nondisplaced scaphoid WAIST fracture treated in a cast, the reported nonunion rate is approximately:

options.text: Less than 1%

questions.explanation: Nonunion rates for **nondisplaced waist fractures treated with casting are ~5–12%**. Rates rise substantially for displaced fractures. This favorable healing potential is why nondisplaced waist fractures can reasonably be treated in a cast OR with percutaneous screw fixation (the latter allowing faster return to work/sport), with union rates similar between the two.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A neglected displaced scaphoid waist fracture resorbs at its volar aspect, producing a flexion deformity of the scaphoid. This deformity is called:

options.text: Humpback deformity
Fishtail deformity
Boutonnière deformity
Madelung deformity

questions.explanation: The **humpback deformity** is volar collapse/flexion of the scaphoid (intrascaphoid angle >45°, normally ~40°). Radial column shortening and extension of the proximal pole releases the lunate to rotate into **DISI** (scapholunate angle >60°, capitolunate angle >15°) under the pull of the triquetrum. Correcting a humpback nonunion requires restoring scaphoid length/alignment, typically with a volar wedge (interposition) graft.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: The pattern of degenerative arthritis that develops from a chronic scaphoid nonunion is abbreviated SNAC. The EARLIEST (stage I) arthritic change occurs at which articulation?

options.text: The radial styloid–distal scaphoid articulation
The scaphocapitate joint
The midcarpal (capitolunate) joint
The radiolunate joint

questions.explanation: In **scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse (SNAC)**, arthritis begins at the **radial styloid–distal scaphoid articulation (stage I)**, progresses to the **scaphocapitate joint (stage II)**, and ultimately the **midcarpal joint (stage III)**. The radiolunate joint is characteristically spared — mirroring the SLAC-wrist pattern — which is what makes proximal row carpectomy or four-corner fusion viable salvage options.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Which imaging modality does the chapter consider most useful for evaluating scaphoid fracture displacement, gapping, sclerosis, and confirming union after surgery (since plain radiographs frequently give indeterminate results)?

options.text: CT with thin overlapping cuts and reconstructions along the scaphoid long axis
Plain radiographs at 3 months
Bone scintigraphy
Ultrasound

questions.explanation: **CT** (thin cuts reformatted along the scaphoid long axis) best assesses displacement, gapping, sclerosis, cysts and, importantly, healing — radiographs often can't reliably determine union even at 3 months. CT also shows that radiographs frequently *underestimate* displacement (26–33% of 'nondisplaced' films were displaced on CT). MRI is preferred when occult fracture is suspected or cartilage status is in question.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: When comparing percutaneous screw fixation with cast immobilization for acute nondisplaced scaphoid waist fractures, the principal advantage cited for percutaneous fixation is:

options.text: Faster return to work/sport with high union rates and relatively few complications
A dramatically higher union rate that casting cannot approach
Elimination of any need for postoperative CT
Guaranteed prevention of avascular necrosis

questions.explanation: For nondisplaced waist fractures, union rates are **similar** whether treated by cast or surgery; the main benefit of **percutaneous screw fixation** is **earlier return to work or athletics** (avoiding months of cast immobilization) with relatively few complications. Displacement <2 mm may be casted; the choice often reflects patient demands and preferences.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: For a scaphoid WAIST fracture requiring fixation, biomechanical studies show a headless compression screw is strongest when placed:

options.text: Along the central axis of the scaphoid, as perpendicular as possible to the fracture plane
Eccentrically along the volar cortex
Parallel to the fracture line
Through the dorsal ridge to preserve blood supply

questions.explanation: Screws placed along the **central axis** of the scaphoid and **perpendicular to the fracture plane** provide the strongest, most stable fixation and best compression; deviation more than ~10° from perpendicular weakens the construct. Preoperative CT helps plan a central, perpendicular trajectory. Proximal pole nonunions are approached dorsally; distal/waist often volarly.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Which is the primary intrinsic ligamentous stabilizer connecting the scaphoid to the lunate?

options.text: The scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL), whose dorsal portion is the strongest region
The radioscaphocapitate ligament
The long radiolunate ligament
The scaphotrapeziotrapezoid ligament

questions.explanation: The **scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL)** is the primary stabilizer between scaphoid and lunate. Its **dorsal region is the stoutest** and most important for resisting palmar-dorsal translation and rotation; the palmar region resists rotational forces. The RSC is an extrinsic ligament acting as the fulcrum around which the scaphoid rotates (and around which it may fracture at the waist).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: The radioscaphocapitate (RSC) ligament plays a special mechanical role relevant to scaphoid fractures. What is it?

options.text: It acts as a fulcrum around which the scaphoid rotates and around which the waist may fracture
It is the primary blood supply to the proximal pole
It resists dorsal subluxation of the lunate
It is the main restraint to distal radioulnar translation

questions.explanation: The **RSC ligament** crosses the volar concavity of the scaphoid waist and runs toward the capitate, acting as a **fulcrum for scaphoid rotation** — the scaphoid can fracture at the waist around this fulcrum. It is also critical to preserve during a proximal row carpectomy because it prevents ulnar translocation of the carpus.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: The 1,2 intercompartmental supraretinacular artery (ICSRA) pedicled vascularized bone graft (Zaidemberg graft) for scaphoid nonunion is harvested from which location?

options.text: The dorsal distal radius, between the first and second extensor compartments
The volar distal radius near the pronator quadratus
The iliac crest
The medial femoral condyle

questions.explanation: The **1,2 ICSRA (Zaidemberg) graft** is a pedicled vascularized bone graft taken from the **dorsal distal radius**, based on the artery running superficial to the extensor retinaculum **between the 1st and 2nd extensor compartments**. It has a relatively short pedicle. Alternatives include the volar carpal artery graft (Mathoulin), dorsal capsular pedicle (Sotereanos), and free grafts such as the medial femoral condyle.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: In a scaphoid nonunion with proven avascular necrosis of the proximal pole, comparative studies suggest the highest union rates are achieved with which graft?

options.text: Free vascularized medial femoral condyle graft
Non-vascularized iliac crest graft
Distal radius cancellous autograft
Allograft cancellous chips alone

questions.explanation: In the setting of **AVN**, the **free vascularized medial femoral condyle graft** has shown superior union — e.g., a study where 12/12 medial femoral condyle grafts healed versus only 4/10 1,2 ICSRA grafts. Vascularized bone restores biology to the avascular proximal pole. Non-vascularized grafts are generally reserved for nonunions with adequate vascularity and no significant AVN.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A scaphoid waist nonunion with a humpback deformity and DISI but preserved cartilage is best reconstructed with:

options.text: A volar interposition (wedge) bone graft to restore length/alignment plus headless screw fixation
Proximal row carpectomy
Total wrist arthrodesis
Simple cast immobilization

questions.explanation: A humpback nonunion with DISI but healthy cartilage needs correction of the flexion/shortening deformity — a **volar (palmar) interposition wedge graft** restores scaphoid length and corrects the humpback and DISI, fixed with a headless compression screw. Salvage procedures (PRC, four-corner fusion, total wrist fusion) are reserved for nonunions that already have significant SNAC arthritis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Which approach is generally preferred for fixing a scaphoid PROXIMAL POLE fracture or nonunion?

options.text: Dorsal approach
Volar (palmar) approach
Ulnar (Guyon canal) approach
Transverse carpal tunnel approach

questions.explanation: **Proximal pole** fractures/nonunions are best accessed via a **dorsal approach**, which gives direct access to the proximal pole and allows antegrade central screw placement. Distal pole and waist fractures are more commonly approached **volarly** (which also facilitates volar wedge grafting for humpback correction). Care is taken dorsally to protect the SLIL and dorsal scaphoid blood supply.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: After the scaphoid, which carpal bone is most commonly reported as the second most frequently fractured?

options.text: Triquetrum
Lunate
Capitate
Pisiform

questions.explanation: In most large series, the **triquetrum is the second most commonly fractured carpal bone** (roughly 15% of carpal fractures; Garcia-Elias reported 64 triquetral fractures among 249 carpal fractures, second only to 153 scaphoid). The trapezium is typically third and the capitate fourth. The scaphoid vastly predominates, comprising the majority of all carpal fractures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: The most common type of triquetral fracture is a:

options.text: Dorsal cortical (chip) fracture
Triquetral body fracture
Palmar cortical fracture
Comminuted proximal pole fracture

questions.explanation: The **dorsal cortical (chip) fracture** is by far the most common triquetral fracture (reported up to ~93%). Mechanisms include dorsal ligament avulsion (extreme palmar flexion/radial deviation) or impaction/shear by the ulnar styloid or hamate during a fall in dorsiflexion and ulnar deviation. Most are treated nonoperatively in a splint/cast for 4–6 weeks; symptomatic nonunions can have the dorsal fragment excised.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A patient has a triquetral BODY fracture. Beyond the fracture itself, what should this alert the surgeon to look for?

options.text: Associated perilunate fracture-dislocation and/or carpal ligamentous instability
An occult scaphoid tubercle fracture
A distal radius Barton fracture
A Bennett fracture of the thumb

questions.explanation: Triquetral **body** fractures generally require higher energy and are seen in **12–25% of triquetral injuries as part of perilunate fracture-dislocations**. They should prompt a search for **associated ligamentous injury and carpal instability** (e.g., scapholunate widening or VISI). Small proximal-pole/volar avulsions from the lunotriquetral ligament carry a worse prognosis than isolated dorsal chips.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A trapezial body fracture is classically associated with which concomitant injury, given the shared mechanism of axial loading through the thumb metacarpal?

options.text: Bennett fracture of the thumb metacarpal base
Hook of hamate fracture
Dorsal triquetral chip fracture
Lunate fracture

questions.explanation: A fall onto an outstretched thumb drives the thumb metacarpal base axially into the trapezium, producing a **vertical intraarticular shear fracture** — and depending on the compression angle, either a trapezial fracture, a **Bennett fracture**, or both. The trapezial ridge is a separate consideration: it anchors the transverse carpal ligament and is best seen on a carpal tunnel view; tip (type II) ridge fractures often go to nonunion and may need excision.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A patient has base-of-thumb pain and a suspected trapezial RIDGE fracture, but standard PA and lateral radiographs are unremarkable. Which view best demonstrates the trapezial ridge?

options.text: Carpal tunnel view
Standard lateral view
Clenched-fist AP view
Robert (true AP thumb) view

questions.explanation: The **trapezial ridge** projects palmarly and is poorly seen on PA and lateral films; a **carpal tunnel view** best profiles it (CT is definitive). Palmer classified ridge fractures: **type I at the base** (usually heals in a thumb spica cast) and **type II at the tip** (high nonunion rate; excise if symptomatic). The FCR runs in a groove along the ridge and is at risk during excision.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: During a volar approach to fix or excise a trapezium fracture, which structure is most at risk and must be protected?

options.text: The radial artery (and the FCR tendon)
The ulnar nerve
The posterior interosseous nerve
The superficial palmar arch's ulnar contribution

questions.explanation: The trapezium is approached volarly by elevating the thenar musculature; the **radial artery is at risk during this exposure** and must be identified and protected. The **FCR tendon**, which runs in a groove along the trapezial ridge, is also easily injured (and can be a source of chronic tendinopathy/rupture with trapezial fractures) and must be protected during fragment excision.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: The 'scaphocapitate syndrome' (Fenton syndrome) refers to which injury pattern?

options.text: A transscaphoid transcapitate perilunate injury in which the proximal capitate fragment rotates 180 degrees
A combined scaphoid tubercle and trapezial ridge avulsion
A scaphoid fracture with a concurrent Bennett fracture
A pisiform fracture with hook of hamate fracture

questions.explanation: **Scaphocapitate (Fenton) syndrome** is a transscaphoid transcapitate perilunate fracture in which the fractured **proximal capitate fragment rotates 180 degrees** (fracture surface faces the lunate). Fenton attributed it to the radial styloid acting as a 'chisel'; Stein and Siegel later proposed a hyperextension mechanism. The malrotated capitate cannot reduce closed, so **ORIF (headless screws via a dorsal approach)** is required.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Why do fractures of the proximal pole/neck of the capitate behave similarly to proximal pole scaphoid fractures with respect to healing?

options.text: The capitate head is largely covered by cartilage and its blood supply is retrograde, so proximal fractures risk delayed/nonunion and AVN
The capitate has no blood supply at all
The capitate is entirely extraarticular
The capitate head receives its supply antegrade from the third metacarpal

questions.explanation: Like the proximal pole scaphoid (or femoral head), the **capitate head is nearly completely covered by articular cartilage and has a retrograde blood supply**, so proximal fractures are prone to **delayed union, nonunion, and AVN**. This favors ORIF for displaced fractures/delayed diagnoses, and re-establishing carpal height (corticocancellous graft) when treating established capitate nonunions.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A right-handed golfer complains of chronic ulnar-sided palm pain and ulnar nerve paresthesias after his club struck the ground. Point tenderness is ~2 cm distal and radial to the pisiform, worse with resisted small/ring finger flexion. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.text: Fracture of the hook of the hamate
Pisotriquetral arthritis
Distal ulna stress fracture
Scaphoid waist fracture

questions.explanation: The **hook of the hamate** is fractured by racket/club/bat sports (direct compression against the handle) and often presents late with **hypothenar pain, ulnar nerve paresthesias, and reduced grip**. Tenderness lies ~2 cm distal-radial to the pisiform; pain worsens with resisted ring/small finger flexion in ulnar deviation. Note: in golfers/baseball the **non-dominant** hand is typically injured, whereas in tennis/racquetball the **dominant** hand is.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Which imaging study is the preferred modality to diagnose a suspected hook of the hamate fracture?

options.text: CT scan (sensitivity ~100%)
Standard PA radiograph
Bone scintigraphy
Ultrasound

questions.explanation: **CT is the preferred and most accurate** test for hook of hamate fractures (sensitivity ~100%, specificity ~94%, accuracy ~97%), markedly better than plain radiographs (sensitivity ~72%). A carpal tunnel view or 45-degree supinated lateral can show the hook but requires wrist extension that is painful acutely. PA clues include absence of the hook's cortical ring or sclerosis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A patient has a chronic, displaced, symptomatic hook of the hamate fracture. The most widely recommended treatment and its key intraoperative hazard are:

options.text: Excision of the hook fragment; protecting the motor branch of the ulnar nerve, which lies at the fracture base
ORIF with a plate; protecting the radial artery
Total wrist fusion; protecting the median nerve
Pisiform excision; protecting the posterior interosseous nerve

questions.explanation: For displaced or chronic symptomatic hook fractures, most authors recommend **excision of the hook fragment** (studies show no adverse effect on ROM or grip). The chief hazard is the **motor branch of the ulnar nerve**, which runs immediately near the base of the hook and 'almost always lies at the fracture site' — it must be identified and protected. Ulnar nerve motor branch injury is the most common complication of excision.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A chronic, unrecognized hook of the hamate fracture can lead to which tendon complication?

options.text: Attritional rupture of the small or ring finger flexor tendon
Rupture of the extensor pollicis longus
Rupture of the abductor pollicis longus
Rupture of the flexor carpi radialis

questions.explanation: A fractured hamate hook creates a rough bony surface adjacent to the ulnar flexor tendons; chronic friction can cause **attritional rupture of the small (or ring) finger flexor tendons (FDP/FDS)**. This is analogous to how a prominent Lister tubercle or hardware can rupture the EPL/FPL. It underscores prompt diagnosis and, for displaced/chronic cases, excision.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A dorsal coronal fracture of the hamate BODY is most commonly associated with which concomitant injury?

options.text: Fourth and fifth metacarpal (carpometacarpal) fracture-dislocation
Scaphoid waist fracture
Distal radius Barton fracture
Radial styloid fracture

questions.explanation: **Dorsal coronal hamate body fractures** result from axial forces through the metacarpals and are frequently associated with **4th and 5th CMC fracture-dislocations**. These fractures are best seen on lateral and 45-degree pronated oblique views (CT confirms). Displaced CMC-involving fractures are treated with reduction and pinning, miniscrews, or a small plate; the ulnar nerve motor branch is at risk when drilling dorsal-to-palmar near the hook.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: The pisiform is best described anatomically as:

options.text: A sesamoid bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, articulating with the triquetrum
The central keystone of the distal carpal row
A bone with no tendinous attachments
An intraarticular ossicle of the radiocarpal joint

questions.explanation: The **pisiform is a sesamoid bone within the FCU tendon**, articulating with a facet on the triquetrum (the pisotriquetral joint) and giving origin to the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments and the abductor digiti minimi. Because of its many soft-tissue attachments it can fracture by avulsion or direct blow. Symptomatic nonunions, comminuted, or widely displaced fractures are treated by **pisiform excision** (shelled from the FCU, which is then repaired), with little functional loss.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: The trapezoid is the least commonly fractured carpal bone largely because:

options.text: It is wedge-shaped, well-recessed, and firmly bound by strong ligaments between the trapezium, scaphoid, capitate, and index metacarpal
It has no articular surfaces
It has an unusually robust independent blood supply
It is the largest carpal bone

questions.explanation: The **trapezoid** is wedge-shaped (dorsal surface twice as wide as volar) and sits in a well-protected recess, firmly bound by strong ligaments to the trapezium, scaphoid, capitate, and index metacarpal. This stable, recessed position makes it the **least frequently fractured carpal bone**; injury usually requires high-energy axial load through the index metacarpal and is often a fracture-dislocation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A patient with an acute transscaphoid perilunate fracture-dislocation reports numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers. This finding should prompt:

options.text: Urgent reduction and a low threshold for carpal tunnel release (acute median nerve compression)
Reassurance, as median symptoms are expected and self-limited
Immediate wrist arthrodesis
Observation for 6 weeks before any intervention

questions.explanation: Perilunate injuries commonly cause **acute median nerve compression** as the lunate/fracture displaces volarly into the carpal tunnel. Untreated, this risks permanent median nerve dysfunction. Management includes **urgent reduction** and often an **extended carpal tunnel release** — indicated when there are signs of acute carpal tunnel syndrome (or when a volar approach is used for ligament repair). The chapter stresses specifically asking about median nerve symptoms.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Garcia-Elias described several general characteristics common to carpal (non-scaphoid) fractures. Which of the following is one of them?

options.text: They are frequently missed at initial presentation
They almost always occur in elderly osteoporotic patients
They rarely have any associated ligamentous injury
The large size of the bones makes fixation straightforward

questions.explanation: Garcia-Elias noted carpal fractures tend to occur in **young, high-demand individuals**, are **frequently missed initially**, involve **small bones that complicate reduction and can compromise vascular supply**, may cause **articular incongruity and post-traumatic arthritis**, are **often associated with adjacent ligament injury**, and can cause **secondary entrapment neuropathies or tendon ruptures** from unreduced fragments. High clinical suspicion and CT are key.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Carpal fractures in general are conceptualized as occurring in three broad mechanistic groups. Which of the following is one of these groups?

options.text: Perilunate-pattern injuries
Physeal (growth plate) injuries
Pathologic (tumor-related) injuries
Insufficiency (osteoporotic) injuries

questions.explanation: The chapter groups carpal fractures into **perilunate-pattern injuries, axial-pattern injuries, and local avulsion/impaction injuries**. Perilunate 'lesser arc' (purely ligamentous) and 'greater arc' (with fractures — e.g., transscaphoid) injuries arc around the lunate. Recognizing the pattern helps predict associated ligament disruption and guides fixation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: The scaphoid is unique among the carpal bones because it:

options.text: Bridges both the proximal and distal carpal rows, acting as a 'tie-rod' linking the carpus
Is the only carpal bone with no articular cartilage
Has the most robust, non-retrograde blood supply
Lies entirely within the distal carpal row

questions.explanation: The **scaphoid spans the proximal and distal carpal rows**, coordinating their motion like a 'tie-rod' — the reason its fractures and nonunions so profoundly disturb carpal kinematics and stability (e.g., DISI, SNAC). Roughly **80% of its surface is covered by cartilage**, which limits ligamentous/vascular attachment and contributes to its precarious retrograde blood supply.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Which examination finding, if ALL are absent, makes an acute scaphoid fracture very unlikely?

options.text: Snuffbox tenderness, scaphoid tubercle tenderness, and a positive scaphoid axial compression test
Tinel sign at the wrist, Phalen test, and Durkan test
Finkelstein test, grind test, and Watson shift
Allen test, Adson test, and Roos test

questions.explanation: The three classic clinical tests for scaphoid fracture are **anatomic snuffbox tenderness, scaphoid tubercle tenderness, and pain on axial (longitudinal) thumb compression**. When all three are positive, sensitivity for fracture is very high; when all three are negative, a fracture is very unlikely — this triad guides whether to immobilize and re-image a radiographically occult injury.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: For a symptomatic scaphoid nonunion with established advanced SNAC arthritis involving the midcarpal joint but a preserved radiolunate joint, appropriate SALVAGE options include:

options.text: Proximal row carpectomy or scaphoid excision with four-corner (midcarpal) fusion
Volar interposition wedge grafting with screw fixation
Percutaneous screw fixation without grafting
Simple thumb spica casting

questions.explanation: Once SNAC arthritis is advanced (radial styloid + scaphocapitate ± midcarpal), reconstruction of the scaphoid is futile, and motion-preserving **salvage** is indicated: **proximal row carpectomy** (requires an intact capitate head and lunate fossa cartilage, and relies on the RSC ligament to prevent ulnar translocation) or **scaphoid excision with four-corner fusion**. Total wrist fusion is reserved for pancarpal arthritis or failed salvage.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Approximately 29% of the population is at particular risk for osteonecrosis of the hook of the hamate after fracture. Why?

options.text: In ~29% the hook lacks a nutrient vessel entering at its tip, leaving a watershed area at the base prone to nonunion/osteonecrosis
In ~29% the hook has no blood supply whatsoever
In ~29% the ulnar artery is congenitally absent
In ~29% the hook is supplied only by the radial artery

questions.explanation: Failla's vascular study found that while all hamates have a nutrient vessel at the radial base, **only ~71% have a vessel entering at the tip** of the hook. The remaining **~29% have a poorly vascularized watershed zone at the base**, so a fracture there — if not immobilized acutely — is prone to **nonunion and osteonecrosis**. This anatomy supports early diagnosis/immobilization or excision of displaced/chronic hooks.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: For a displaced, unstable transverse scaphoid waist fracture in a young laborer, the preferred management is generally:

options.text: Open (or percutaneous) reduction and internal fixation with a headless compression screw
Long-arm thumb spica casting for 12 weeks
Immediate proximal row carpectomy
Bone stimulator alone

questions.explanation: **Displaced scaphoid fractures** have high nonunion rates with casting (and carry DISI/humpback risk), so **reduction and internal fixation with a headless compression screw** is preferred, restoring alignment and allowing earlier rehabilitation. Displacement, comminution, perilunate fracture-dislocation, DISI, and proximal pole location are all accepted indications for operative fixation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: During the hyperextension mechanism that produces a scaphoid waist fracture, the fracture typically begins:

options.text: At the volar waist as a tensile failure, propagating dorsally
At the dorsal proximal pole as a compression failure
At the distal tubercle
At the scaphotrapezial joint surface

questions.explanation: With wrist **hyperextension**, the scaphoid fails first on its **volar waist under tension**, and the fracture then propagates dorsally. In extreme dorsiflexion/ulnar deviation the scaphoid impinges on the dorsal radial rim (waist fracture), while forced hyperextension with dorsal subluxation tends to produce proximal fractures. Understanding this helps explain why volar cortical integrity/alignment matters in reduction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Distal pole (tubercle) scaphoid fractures generally behave more favorably than proximal fractures because:

options.text: The distal pole is well vascularized, so these fractures heal reliably with short-arm cast immobilization
The distal pole has no articular involvement and never affects the wrist
They are always intraarticular and thus stable
They receive their blood supply retrograde from the proximal pole

questions.explanation: The **distal pole/tubercle is well vascularized** (direct palmar branches supply 20–30% of the bone distally), so distal scaphoid fractures **heal reliably in a short-arm cast** with low nonunion risk — in contrast to the dysvascular, retrograde-supplied proximal pole. Long-term series show excellent function with occasional STT-joint arthritis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Which statement about the Herbert and Russe classifications of scaphoid fractures is most accurate?

options.text: They describe fracture stability/geometry, but studies show neither reliably predicts union with closed treatment
The Herbert classification reliably predicts union in every case
Both systems are based purely on the patient's age
The Russe classification is used only for pediatric fractures

questions.explanation: **Russe** categorized fractures by plane (horizontal oblique, transverse, vertical oblique — the last least stable/highest nonunion). **Herbert** classified fractures by stability (type A stable/incomplete or tubercle; type B unstable acute; type C delayed union; type D nonunion). Despite their utility, studies found **neither reliably predicts union** with closed treatment, so displacement and location remain the key operative determinants.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A comminuted or widely displaced pisiform fracture with persistent pisotriquetral symptoms is best treated by:

options.text: Pisiform excision (shelling it out of the FCU, which is then repaired)
Headless screw ORIF of the pisiform
Pisotriquetral joint arthrodesis
Total wrist fusion

questions.explanation: Acute nondisplaced pisiform fractures are casted, but **comminuted, widely displaced transverse fractures, or symptomatic nonunions** are treated by **pisiform excision**. It is shelled from the FCU tendon (preserving the tendon fibers, then side-to-side repair) via a volar zigzag approach with the ulnar neurovascular bundle protected. Excision causes little functional loss and reliably relieves pisotriquetral pain.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Which associated vascular complication is specifically linked to hook of hamate/ulnar-sided carpal injury from repetitive blunt trauma?

options.text: Ulnar artery thrombosis (hypothenar hammer syndrome)
Radial artery aneurysm
Anterior interosseous artery thrombosis
Subclavian vein thrombosis

questions.explanation: Repetitive blunt trauma to the hypothenar region (where the ulnar artery passes near the hook of the hamate through Guyon's canal) can cause **ulnar artery thrombosis — hypothenar hammer syndrome**. It is listed among the complications of hamate/pisiform-region injury and presents with cold intolerance, digital ischemia, or ulnar nerve symptoms.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: In managing established capitate NONUNION, why is a corticocancellous interposition bone graft often required rather than simple screw fixation?

options.text: To re-establish carpal height and prevent carpal collapse and overload of adjacent joints
Because the capitate cannot accept a screw
To lengthen the third metacarpal
Because cancellous graft is contraindicated in the wrist

questions.explanation: An established capitate nonunion tends to have bone loss/collapse, so a **corticocancellous interposition graft is used to restore carpal height**, preventing carpal collapse and secondary overload of the scaphotrapeziotrapezoid and triquetrohamate joints. Simply compressing across a collapsed nonunion would shorten the central column and worsen mechanics.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A patient has an isolated triquetral body fracture and the proximal carpal row initially looks intact. What follow-up is appropriate?

options.text: Close follow-up with radiographs (or MRI) watching for scapholunate instability or VISI
No follow-up is needed once the cast is applied
Immediate four-corner fusion
Routine excision of the entire triquetrum

questions.explanation: Because triquetral body fractures can accompany occult ligamentous disruption, a patient whose proximal row 'looks intact' should have **close follow-up with repeat radiographs or MRI**, watching for developing **scapholunate instability or nondissociative VISI**. If instability is confirmed (e.g., LT ligament disruption), the joint is pinned/repaired in addition to fixing the fracture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Which of the following is the LEAST accurate statement about scaphoid fracture management?

options.text: Standard radiographs at 3 months reliably confirm union, making CT unnecessary
MRI is highly sensitive and specific for occult scaphoid fractures with normal radiographs
Radiographs frequently underestimate displacement compared with CT
Proximal pole fractures are typically fixed via a dorsal approach

questions.explanation: The false statement is that plain radiographs at 3 months reliably confirm union — the chapter states **scaphoid healing cannot be reliably determined by standard radiographs at 3 months**, so **CT is used to confirm union**. The other statements are correct: MRI is highly sensitive/specific for occult fractures, radiographs underestimate displacement vs CT, and proximal pole fractures are approached dorsally.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A displaced hamate body fracture involving the 4th/5th CMC joints is exposed operatively. During the dorsal approach and dorsal-to-palmar drilling near the hook, which nerve is most at risk?

options.text: The ulnar nerve (including its dorsal sensory branch and motor branch)
The median nerve recurrent motor branch
The superficial radial nerve
The posterior interosseous nerve

questions.explanation: The dorsal approach to the hamate body passes between the 4th/5th EDC tendons, where the **dorsal (sensory) branch of the ulnar nerve** must be protected; and when drilling **dorsal-to-palmar in the hamate**, the **ulnar neurovascular bundle and the motor branch of the ulnar nerve** (which lies close to the hook) are at risk. Careful protection of the ulnar nerve is emphasized throughout hamate surgery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: A true lateral radiograph confirming adequate scaphoid reduction/alignment is best obtained with which specialized view, in which the palmar cortices of the distal scaphoid pole and capitate are aligned?

options.text: The scaphoid-pisiform-capitate (SPC) lateral view
The Robert (true AP thumb) view
The Betts view
The clenched-fist PA view

questions.explanation: A true **scaphoid-pisiform-capitate (SPC) lateral** aligns the palmar cortex of the distal scaphoid pole with the palmar cortex of the capitate, allowing accurate assessment of scaphoid flexion/alignment and intrascaphoid angle. The Robert and Betts views are for the thumb/trapezium, and the clenched-fist PA is a stress view for scapholunate widening.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: The normal intrascaphoid angle in the sagittal (lateral) plane is approximately 40 degrees. A humpback scaphoid nonunion deformity is defined by an intrascaphoid angle greater than:

options.text: 45 degrees
15 degrees
60 degrees
90 degrees

questions.explanation: The normal lateral intrascaphoid angle averages ~40° (± a few degrees); a **humpback flexion deformity** is defined by an intrascaphoid angle **>45°**. Associated carpal malalignment is quantified by the **scapholunate angle >60°** and **capitolunate angle >15°** (DISI). Restoring the intrascaphoid angle toward normal is a goal of volar wedge grafting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: Acute nondisplaced hook of the hamate fractures are most likely to heal without surgery when:

options.text: They are diagnosed and immobilized early (within the first week)
Immobilization is deliberately delayed to allow swelling to resolve
The patient continues sports during treatment
They are treated with early aggressive range of motion

questions.explanation: Acute nondisplaced hook fractures **may heal with cast immobilization, but results are markedly less favorable if treatment starts after the first week** — reflecting the tenuous watershed vascularity at the hook base. Displaced or chronic fractures are generally treated by **excision** rather than prolonged immobilization or ORIF, since excision reliably relieves symptoms without functional loss.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 16 (Fractures of the Carpal Bones)

questions.stem: On a posteroanterior (PA) radiograph of a normal wrist, radial inclination of the distal radius averages approximately:

options.text: 23 degrees
11 degrees
45 degrees
5 degrees

questions.explanation: **Radial inclination** averages about **23 degrees**, measured on the PA film as the angle between a line tangential to the distal radial articular surface and a line perpendicular to the radial shaft. The other two key radiographic parameters are **volar (palmar) tilt ~10–15 degrees** (lateral view) and **ulnar variance** (averaging just under 1 mm negative). Loss of radial inclination (radial compression) is one of the deformities produced by a displaced distal radius fracture and is a target of reduction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The normal volar (palmar) tilt of the distal radial articular surface on the lateral radiograph is approximately:

options.text: 10 to 15 degrees volar
23 degrees volar
30 to 40 degrees dorsal
0 degrees (neutral)

questions.explanation: The normal distal radius has an anatomic **10- to 15-degree volar tilt**. Because of this, on a properly centered lateral the dorsal rim appears slightly distal to the joint line. A Colles' fracture reverses this into dorsal tilt. Restoring tilt toward neutral (dorsal tilt <10 degrees, which correlates with realignment of the capitate with the radial axis) is an important reduction goal.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The radiographic 'teardrop' of the distal radius represents the volar projection of the lunate facet. What is its normal teardrop angle relative to the longitudinal axis of the radius?

options.text: 70 degrees
23 degrees
45 degrees
90 degrees

questions.explanation: The **teardrop angle** normally measures about **70 degrees**, drawn tangential to the subchondral bone of the articular surface through the tip of the teardrop. Even subtle dorsal rotation of an extraarticular fracture decreases this angle, and an impaction injury splitting the lunate facet drives the lunate into the metaphysis and rotates the teardrop. The teardrop is narrow (~5 mm wide), which makes stable fixation of the volar lunate facet difficult with standard volar plates.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: On the lateral view, the anteroposterior (AP) distance between the distal dorsal and volar rims of the lunate facet averages 18–20 mm. A pathologic WIDENING of this distance should raise suspicion of:

options.text: A coronal-plane split of the lunate fossa
Scapholunate ligament rupture
An extraarticular metaphyseal bending fracture
A distal ulna styloid tip fracture

questions.explanation: A **widened AP distance** of the lunate facet suggests a **coronal split** of the lunate fossa (separation of the volar and dorsal lunate-facet fragments), which can be hard to see on the plain lateral and often needs CT. This is important because an uncorrected coronal split with increased AP distance correlates with degenerative change, and the volar (die-punch/volar-rim) fragment can allow volar subluxation of the carpus.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman falls on an outstretched hand. Radiographs show a dorsally displaced, dorsally angulated extraarticular metaphyseal fracture of the distal radius with dorsal comminution. This classic pattern is eponymously known as a:

options.text: Colles' fracture
Smith fracture
Barton fracture
Chauffeur (Hutchinson) fracture

questions.explanation: A **Colles' fracture** is the dorsally displaced/angulated extraarticular (bending) fracture, typically with dorsal comminution and often a radial shortening ('bayonet' malunion) and ulnar styloid fracture. A **Smith** fracture is the volarly displaced mirror image. A **Barton** fracture is an intraarticular shear/fracture–dislocation of the volar or dorsal rim, and the **chauffeur** fracture is a radial styloid shear fracture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A volar rim intraarticular shear fracture of the distal radius that allows the carpus to subluxate volarly with the fragment is best termed a:

options.text: Volar Barton fracture
Colles' fracture
Die-punch fracture
Chauffeur fracture

questions.explanation: A **volar Barton** fracture is a volar-rim intraarticular shear fracture–dislocation in which the volar fragment and the carpus displace together volarly. It is inherently unstable (Fernandez type II shearing pattern) and requires a **volar buttress plate**. A **die-punch** fracture is a depressed central lunate-facet fragment; the **chauffeur/Hutchinson** fracture is a radial styloid shear injury.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The Fernandez classification of distal radius fractures is a mechanism-based system. A fracture caused by a bending force with one cortex failing in tension and the opposite cortex comminuted (Colles' or Smith type; AO A) corresponds to which Fernandez type?

options.text: Type I — metaphyseal bending fracture
Type II — shearing fracture of the joint surface
Type III — compression of the articular surface
Type IV — avulsion / radiocarpal fracture-dislocation

questions.explanation: The **Fernandez classification** is mechanism/dynamic-based: **Type I = bending** (metaphyseal, one cortex tensile failure with opposite comminution — Colles'/Smith), **Type II = shearing** (Barton, reverse Barton, chauffeur), **Type III = compression** of the articular surface (die-punch), **Type IV = avulsion / radiocarpal fracture–dislocation**, and **Type V = combined/high-energy** with metaphyseal–diaphyseal comminution. It is favored because it links injury pattern to treatment.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: In the Fernandez classification, a high-energy die-punch injury with pure axial impaction and depression of the articular surface is which type?

options.text: Type III — compression of the articular surface
Type I — bending
Type II — shearing
Type V — combined

questions.explanation: **Fernandez type III** is axial **compression** of the articular surface (the die-punch pattern, AO type C impaction), where the lunate is driven into the metaphysis. It frequently needs elevation of the depressed fragment with bone graft/void filler and stable fixation. Type IV is a fracture–dislocation and Type V is the combined high-energy pattern.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: Which classification of distal radius fractures is the AO/OTA system based on, dividing fractures into types A (extraarticular), B (partial articular), and C (complete articular)?

options.text: A = extraarticular, B = partial articular, C = complete articular (metaphyseal fracture with articular involvement)
A = complete articular, B = partial articular, C = extraarticular
A = dorsal, B = volar, C = radial
A = stable, B = unstable, C = fracture-dislocation

questions.explanation: In the widely used **AO classification**, **Type A = extraarticular**, **Type B = partial articular** (part of the joint remains in continuity with the shaft, e.g., shear/Barton or radial styloid), and **Type C = complete articular** with metaphyseal involvement. Increasing letter and subtype numbers denote increasing comminution/complexity (27 subtypes total). It is the most commonly used system in research.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The Melone classification (1984) of intraarticular distal radius fractures highlighted the importance of which key anatomic fragment?

options.text: The medial (lunate-facet) complex / intermediate column
The radial styloid fragment
The distal ulna
The dorsal Lister tubercle

questions.explanation: The **Melone classification** drew attention to the **medial (lunate-facet) complex** — corresponding to the radiographic teardrop and the 'intermediate column' of the later columnar theory — and described the four major fragments (radial shaft, radial styloid, dorsomedial and volcomedial lunate-facet fragments). Recognizing these fragments guides fixation of the critical lunate facet.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: Lafontaine and colleagues identified five instability parameters predicting redisplacement of distal radius fractures treated closed. Which of the following is NOT one of the five Lafontaine criteria?

options.text: Ulnar variance greater than 3 mm
Initial dorsal angulation greater than 20 degrees
Dorsal metaphyseal comminution
Age greater than 60 years

questions.explanation: The five **Lafontaine criteria** are: (1) **dorsal angulation >20°**, (2) **dorsal comminution**, (3) **intraarticular radiocarpal involvement**, (4) **associated ulnar fracture**, and (5) **age >60 years**. Lafontaine recommended surgery when **≥3** are present. Ulnar variance ≥3 mm is a predictor in MacKenney's later weighted formula (Edinburgh Wrist Calculator), not in the original Lafontaine list.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: According to Lafontaine's model, a patient with how many of the five instability parameters should be considered for early surgical intervention?

options.text: Three or more
One or more
All five
Two or fewer

questions.explanation: Lafontaine recommended that patients with **three or more** of the five parameters be considered for **early surgical intervention**, because the risk of collapse with closed treatment rises roughly linearly with the number of parameters present. Subsequent authors emphasize 'relative stability' as a combination of factors rather than any single threshold.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: When several authors attempted to validate the Lafontaine criteria, which single factor emerged as the strongest independent predictor of late redisplacement of a distal radius fracture?

options.text: Advanced patient age (surrogate for osteoporosis)
Initial dorsal angulation
The presence of an ulnar styloid fracture
Male sex

questions.explanation: **Age** (a surrogate for osteoporosis/bone quality) is repeatedly the strongest independent predictor of redisplacement. Nesbitt found age the only significant predictor — patients over 58 years had ~50% failure vs ~17% at age 30. **Metaphyseal comminution** (especially volar cortical comminution) and increased ulnar variance are also important; interestingly, initial dorsal angulation alone was NOT independently predictive once comminution was accounted for.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: McQueen and colleagues found that failure to restore which single radiographic parameter was the most predictive factor for deterioration of functional outcome after distal radius fracture?

options.text: Carpal (capitate) malalignment in the sagittal plane
Radial inclination
Ulnar styloid union
Volar tilt exceeding physiologic values

questions.explanation: McQueen showed that **failure to restore carpal alignment** — realigning the capitate's center of rotation with the radial axis (the capitate shift) in the **sagittal plane** — was the single most predictive factor for poor function and strength, and the most important indication for correction. Restoring a dorsal tilt of less than ~10 degrees correlates strongly with realigning the capitate with the radial axis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A newly emphasized reduction parameter describing ULNAR translation of the radial shaft relative to the distal fragment (a step in the ulnar border of the radius proximal to the DRUJ) is called:

options.text: Coronal shift
Ulnar variance
Radial inclination
Teardrop angle

questions.explanation: The **coronal shift** describes ulnar translation of the radial shaft relative to the distal fragment, seen as a step in the ulnar border of the radius proximal to the DRUJ on the PA view. It matters because it slackens the **distal oblique bundle (DOB)** of the interosseous membrane, and if the fracture heals shifted, contracture with the pronator quadratus can cause painful, restricted forearm rotation. It should be assessed alongside tilt, inclination, and variance.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The distal oblique bundle (DOB) is a thickened distal portion of which structure, and it contributes to stability of which joint?

options.text: The interosseous membrane; it adds static stability to the DRUJ
The triangular fibrocartilage; it stabilizes the ulnocarpal joint
The extensor retinaculum; it stabilizes the ECU
The volar radiocarpal ligament; it stabilizes the radiocarpal joint

questions.explanation: The **DOB** is the thickened, most distal portion of the **interosseous membrane**, stretching from the distal ulnar metaphysis to the radius (inserting proximal to the DRUJ). Present in roughly 40% of people, it acts as a **static stabilizer of the DRUJ** and, together with the pronator quadratus (the main dynamic stabilizer), maintains stability during forearm rotation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)
