questions.stem: Which muscle is described in this chapter as the main DYNAMIC stabilizer of the distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) during forearm rotation, and by which nerve is it innervated?

options.text: Pronator quadratus — median nerve (anterior interosseous branch)
Extensor carpi ulnaris — radial (posterior interosseous) nerve
Flexor carpi ulnaris — ulnar nerve
Supinator — radial nerve

questions.explanation: The **pronator quadratus (PQ)** is the principal **dynamic stabilizer of the DRUJ**, relying on articular congruity and competent static stabilizers (the radioulnar ligaments/TFCC and DOB). It is innervated by the **median nerve** via the anterior interosseous branch. During volar plating, repairing the PQ over the plate can help protect the flexor tendons (notably the FPL).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A young patient has a dorsally displaced extraarticular Colles' fracture reduced in the ED. For a dorsally angulated metaphyseal fracture, the recommended position of cast immobilization is:

options.text: Neutral to slight extension, 20–30 degrees ulnar deviation, neutral rotation
Extreme wrist flexion and ulnar deviation (Cotton-Loder position)
Full wrist extension and radial deviation
90 degrees flexion with full pronation

questions.explanation: The recommended immobilization for a dorsally angulated metaphyseal fracture is **neutral to slight extension, 20–30 degrees of ulnar deviation, and neutral rotation**, using three-point (Sarmiento-type) support. Notably, the historic extreme-flexion **Cotton-Loder position** is avoided because it risks acute carpal tunnel syndrome and stiffness. A short-arm cast or Sarmiento slab is typically worn 4–6 weeks with interval radiographs.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: For a Fernandez type I dorsally displaced bending fracture, integrity of which cortex most strongly predicts maintenance of a closed reduction?

options.text: The volar cortex
The dorsal cortex
The radial styloid cortex
The ulnar cortex of the sigmoid notch

questions.explanation: Restoring **volar cortical continuity** at reduction is the strongest predictor of maintaining volar/dorsal tilt and carpal alignment — even in dorsally displaced fractures. Wadsten et al. showed ~96% radiographic failure with volar cortical comminution. When the volar cortices are well aligned and the biomechanical axis is normal, a three-point cast can hold the reduction; if the volar cortex is comminuted, the fracture is inherently unstable.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A dorsally displaced distal radius fracture is treated in a cast. At the 1-week follow-up the volar cortices are NOT realigned and there is early loss of position. The best interpretation is that this fracture is:

options.text: Unstable — surgical stabilization should be strongly considered
Stable — continue casting for 6 weeks
Adequately reduced — no further imaging needed
A candidate for a second manipulation and re-casting, which is reliably effective

questions.explanation: Loss of position with unrestored volar cortices signals **instability**. The chapter warns against the 'slippery slope' of repeated inadequate follow-up: a second closed reduction and re-casting is generally **ineffective** in this situation, especially in younger active patients. Early operative stabilization avoids healing in malposition (and later osteotomy).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: Closed reduction with percutaneous Kirschner-wire pinning is best suited for which fracture type?

options.text: Reducible extraarticular fractures and simple articular fractures without metaphyseal comminution
Highly comminuted intraarticular fractures with metaphyseal bone loss in an osteoporotic patient
Volar shear (Barton) fracture–dislocations
Fractures with a large depressed die-punch fragment

questions.explanation: **Percutaneous pinning** is a simple, effective method ideal for **reducible extraarticular fractures and simple articular fractures without metaphyseal comminution**. It relies on intact cortical buttressing, so it is poorly suited to comminuted/osteoporotic metaphyseal bone (which needs load-bearing fixation such as a locked volar plate or external fixation) or to shear fractures (which need a buttress plate).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The conceptual principle by which a bridging external fixator achieves and maintains reduction of a distal radius fracture is:

options.text: Ligamentotaxis
Direct interfragmentary compression
Fixed-angle subchondral support
Buttressing of the volar rim

questions.explanation: Bridging external fixation works by **ligamentotaxis** — traction across the wrist tensions the capsule and ligaments to indirectly reduce and hold the fragments. Its weaknesses are that it cannot reduce impacted intraarticular fragments (which are not attached to ligaments) and that **overdistraction** causes stiffness and can contribute to CRPS. Augmenting with percutaneous pins improves fixation strength.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A recognized complication specifically associated with OVERDISTRACTION of a bridging external fixator for a distal radius fracture is:

options.text: Finger stiffness and complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)
Flexor pollicis longus rupture from a prominent plate
Screw penetration of the extensor pollicis longus groove
Nonunion of the radial shaft

questions.explanation: **Overdistraction** of an external fixator produces excessive tension across the carpus, leading to **finger stiffness, intrinsic tightness, and a higher risk of CRPS**. The classic teaching is to reduce with traction but then relax to a neutral, anatomic position. FPL rupture and EPL groove screw penetration are complications of **volar/dorsal plating**, not distraction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: Multiple randomized trials and meta-analyses comparing volar locked plating with external fixation for unstable distal radius fractures generally show that volar plating:

options.text: Gives better early (3–6 month) DASH scores and grip strength, with differences narrowing by 12 months
Is uniformly inferior at all time points
Has no complications compared with external fixation
Produces worse outcomes at every follow-up interval

questions.explanation: Fixed-angle **volar locked plating** tends to give **better early functional scores (DASH) and grip strength at 3–6 months**, with the differences narrowing by 12 months; several meta-analyses/Cochrane reviews find it difficult to declare one method superior for the whole spectrum. Volar plating does carry meaningful hardware and tendon complications, so it is not complication-free.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The 'watershed line' is a critical landmark for volar plate placement. Placing the distal edge of a volar plate DISTAL to this line increases the risk of:

options.text: Flexor tendon irritation and rupture (especially FPL)
Extensor pollicis longus rupture
Radial artery laceration
Scapholunate ligament injury

questions.explanation: The **watershed line** is the most volar/distal ridge of the distal radius; plates placed distal to it sit prominently against the **flexor tendons (notably the FPL)**, increasing flexor tenosynovitis and rupture. The **Soong grade** quantifies plate prominence (Grade 1 ≥2 mm volar to the critical line; Grade 2 distal to the volar rim = higher rupture risk). Keep the plate proximal to the watershed line and repair the PQ over it.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The Soong grading system is used to describe:

options.text: Prominence/positioning of a volar plate relative to the volar critical (watershed) line
Severity of articular comminution
Degree of DRUJ instability
Grade of scapholunate interosseous ligament tear

questions.explanation: The **Soong classification** grades **volar plate prominence**: Grade 0 (plate not distal to the volar critical line and not prominent), **Grade 1** (plate ≥2 mm volar to the critical line but proximal to the volar rim), and **Grade 2** (plate at/distal to the volar rim). Higher Soong grade correlates with increased **flexor tendon rupture** risk, and Grade 1–2 positioning is an indication for plate removal after healing.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: When measuring screw length for the distal row of a volar locking plate, the recommended practice to avoid extensor tendon complications is to:

options.text: Subtract at least 2 mm from the measured length and avoid bicortical (dorsal) penetration distally
Always aim for bicortical purchase for maximal strength
Use screws 2 mm longer than measured for subchondral support
Leave the distal screws out entirely

questions.explanation: Distally, screws that protrude dorsally endanger the extensor tendons — classically the **EPL** in its groove at Lister tubercle. The chapter advises **subtracting at least 2 mm** from the measured length and NOT aiming for bicortical purchase distally; biomechanically the shorter length does not weaken fixation. 'Better to stay short than long.' A CT is preferred postoperatively if screw protrusion is suspected.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A patient treated in a cast for a minimally displaced distal radius fracture develops painful loss of thumb extension a few weeks later, with an irregularity near Lister tubercle. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.text: Rupture of the extensor pollicis longus (EPL) tendon
Rupture of the flexor pollicis longus (FPL)
Anterior interosseous nerve palsy
Trigger thumb

questions.explanation: Spontaneous **EPL rupture** classically follows minimally displaced/nondisplaced distal radius fractures (reported in up to ~5% in some series), attributed to attritional/vascular compromise as the tendon runs around Lister tubercle. Loss of thumb IP extension/retropulsion with an irregularity near Lister tubercle is the clue; treatment is typically an **EIP-to-EPL tendon transfer**. FPL rupture instead follows prominent volar plates and causes loss of thumb flexion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: Following volar plating of a distal radius fracture, flexor tendon rupture most commonly involves which tendon, and typically occurs on what time course?

options.text: Flexor pollicis longus (FPL); often late, averaging around 9 months postoperatively
Flexor digitorum profundus to the index; within the first week
Flexor carpi radialis; immediately intraoperatively
Flexor digitorum superficialis to the small finger; at 5 years

questions.explanation: After volar plating, the **FPL** is the predominant flexor tendon to rupture (~0.6% of volarly fixed fractures), because it lies closest to a prominent plate. Rupture is often **late** — averaging about **9 months** in a systematic review, and reported as late as 10 years. Prevention: keep the plate proximal to the watershed line, avoid distal prominence, and cover it with a repaired pronator quadratus.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A patient presents to the ED with an acute displaced distal radius fracture and progressive median nerve paresthesias. After adequate closed reduction under anesthesia, the reduction is well maintained. The best next step is:

options.text: Observation with careful serial neurologic follow-up over the next 24–48 hours
Immediate open carpal tunnel release regardless of the neurologic course
High-dose corticosteroids and discharge without follow-up
Wrist immobilization in the extreme flexion (Cotton-Loder) position

questions.explanation: Acute median nerve symptoms from a distal radius fracture are usually due to **contusion/stretch or hematoma** within the carpal tunnel. If closed reduction is satisfactory and maintained, most improve substantially over **24–48 hours** with observation. **Early operative stabilization plus carpal tunnel release** is indicated only if symptoms worsen or fail to improve, or if the reduction cannot be obtained/maintained. Extreme wrist flexion is avoided because it aggravates carpal tunnel pressure.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: When both a volar (Henry) approach for a distal radius fracture and a carpal tunnel release are performed, why must the two incisions never be connected as a single longitudinal incision?

options.text: To protect the palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve, which runs in that skin bridge
To avoid injuring the radial artery
To prevent flexor tendon bowstringing
To preserve the superficial palmar arch

questions.explanation: A skin bridge must be left because the **palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve** runs across that region; connecting a Henry incision directly to a carpal tunnel incision risks transecting it, causing painful neuroma and pillar/scar-region hypersensitivity. The branch is 'always found if looked for,' and its position can be aberrant, so both the Henry retractor and incision planning must respect it.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: Is there evidence supporting ROUTINE prophylactic carpal tunnel release at the time of operative fixation in a distal radius fracture patient WITHOUT preoperative median nerve symptoms?

options.text: No — there are no data supporting routine release in patients without preoperative median nerve signs
Yes — routine release is strongly recommended for all operative cases
Yes — but only in patients under age 40
Yes — routine release reliably prevents CRPS

questions.explanation: The chapter states there are **no data to support routine carpal tunnel release** at the time of fixation in patients **without preoperative evidence of median nerve injury**. Release is reserved for those with acute or progressive median nerve compression, or when reduction cannot be maintained with ongoing compression.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: Arthroscopic studies of distal radius fractures show associated intercarpal ligament injuries are common. The reported incidence of partial or complete SCAPHOLUNATE tears with distal radius fractures is approximately:

options.text: Less than 1%

questions.explanation: Arthroscopy documents associated **scapholunate (SL) tears in ~30–78%** and lunotriquetral tears in ~15–54% of distal radius fractures. However, long-term data show that untreated low-grade (Geissler I–III) SL tears often remain asymptomatic and do not progress to SLAC. Complete **Geissler IV** tears are the concern, as they can progress to a SLAC wrist and warrant acute repair — arthroscopy is superior for detection since they may be radiographically occult.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A displaced radial styloid ('chauffeur') fracture whose fracture line exits at the ridge between the scaphoid and lunate fossae is particularly associated with which occult injury?

options.text: Scapholunate interosseous ligament tear
Lunotriquetral ligament tear only
Foveal TFCC avulsion
Extensor pollicis longus rupture

questions.explanation: A radial styloid shear fracture entering the **interfossa ridge (between the scaphoid and lunate facets)** is a red flag for an associated **scapholunate ligament injury**, especially in younger patients with high-energy intraarticular fractures. If SL widening is provoked intraoperatively (ulnar/radial deviation under fluoroscopy) after fixation, closed or open pinning is recommended; arthroscopy is the most sensitive way to detect an occult Geissler IV tear.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: After fixation of a distal radius fracture, intraoperative DRUJ stability is assessed by which maneuver?

options.text: A manual 'shuck' (Schuck) test of the radioulnar joint, comparing to the contralateral side
The Watson scaphoid shift test
The Finkelstein test
The Durkan carpal compression test

questions.explanation: DRUJ stability is tested with a manual **'shuck' test** (dorsopalmar translation of the ulna relative to the radius), ideally comparing to the uninjured side. Gross instability after anatomic radius fixation may indicate a foveal TFCC tear needing repair — though the secondary stabilizers (especially the DOB and PQ) often stabilize a moderately unstable DRUJ, so not every positive shuck requires TFCC repair.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: Regarding ulnar styloid fractures accompanying a distal radius fracture, which statement best reflects current management?

options.text: Fix a basilar styloid fracture if the DRUJ is unstable; styloid TIP fractures are essentially always left alone
All ulnar styloid fractures require ORIF to prevent nonunion
An ulnar styloid fracture always mandates immediate Darrach resection
Ulnar styloid fractures should be fixed only in patients under 30

questions.explanation: Management is dictated by **DRUJ stability, not the styloid fracture itself**. A **basilar (base) styloid fracture with an unstable DRUJ** may be fixed (it can represent a foveal/TFCC avulsion), whereas **styloid tip fractures are essentially always left untreated**. Meta-analyses show the presence of an ulnar styloid fracture generally does not worsen outcome after radius plate fixation when the DRUJ is stable.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: For an inactive, low-demand 'super-elderly' patient with a displaced distal radius fracture, the chapter's stated preference is generally:

options.text: Nonoperative (closed) treatment, accepting some malunion, because functional outcomes are often equivalent
Routine volar locked plating in every case
Primary total wrist arthroplasty
Immediate wrist arthrodesis

questions.explanation: For the **inactive, low-demand super-elderly**, the stated preference is **nonoperative treatment**: several prospective studies show a lack of significant functional differences at 1 year even when radiographic parameters are not restored, and osteopenic bone makes fixation harder. However, recent high-quality RCTs show that **active elderly** patients who meet radial reduction parameters achieve better outcomes with surgery, so the 'elderly' should not be treated as one homogeneous group.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A dorsally displaced fracture–dislocation of the dorsal rim of the distal radius in which the carpus subluxates dorsally with the fragment is called a:

options.text: Dorsal Barton fracture
Smith fracture
Galeazzi fracture
Essex-Lopresti injury

questions.explanation: A **dorsal Barton** fracture is an intraarticular shear fracture of the **dorsal rim** with dorsal subluxation of the carpus. Like its volar counterpart, it is unstable and requires buttress (or fragment-specific) fixation. A **Galeazzi** fracture is a radial shaft fracture with DRUJ disruption (Chapter 21 territory), and **Essex-Lopresti** is a radial head fracture with longitudinal forearm instability.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A patient sustains a distal radius fracture with volar displacement and a volar-angulated apex. This pattern (the mirror image of a Colles') is eponymously a:

options.text: Smith fracture
Colles' fracture
Chauffeur fracture
Die-punch fracture

questions.explanation: A **Smith fracture** is the volarly displaced/angulated extraarticular distal radius fracture — the reverse (mirror image) of a Colles'. Because the volar cortex fails, these are inherently unstable and usually require a **volar buttress/locked plate**; casting rarely holds them.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The small, unstable VOLAR-ULNAR (volar lunate-facet) fragment is notorious because inadequate capture leads to:

options.text: Volar subluxation/translation of the carpus
Dorsal intercalated segment instability (DISI) only
Radial styloid nonunion
Extensor tendon adhesion

questions.explanation: The **volar-ulnar (volar lunate-facet) fragment** is critical: it anchors the short radiolunate ligament and buttresses the lunate. If it is too small/distal to be captured by a standard volar plate and is left unfixed, the **carpus subluxates/translates volarly** with the fragment. Small fragments (<15 mm) often need **fragment-specific fixation** (buttress pin, wireform, tension band, or hook/rim plate) rather than a standard volar plate.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A distal radius fracture heals with axial (radial) shortening and positive ulnar variance. The most likely resulting symptomatic problem is:

options.text: Ulnocarpal (ulnar) impaction with painful forearm rotation and ulnar-sided wrist pain
Trigger finger
First dorsal compartment tenosynovitis
Anterior interosseous nerve palsy

questions.explanation: Radial shortening/positive ulnar variance after malunion drives the ulnar head against the carpus — **ulnocarpal (ulnar) impaction** — causing ulnar-sided wrist pain and painful rotation. Treatment options include **ulnar shortening osteotomy** (or a corrective radial osteotomy to restore length) once symptomatic. This is one of the commonest sequelae of a malunited distal radius fracture treated conservatively.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A patient develops CRPS-like symptoms after a distal radius fracture with disproportionate pain and a positive Tinel over the carpal tunnel. Beyond standard CRPS care, the surgeon should specifically consider:

options.text: That an irritated/entrapped median nerve may be the driver — with a low threshold for carpal tunnel release
Immediate wrist arthrodesis
Long-term rigid immobilization to rest the limb
Routine sympathectomy in all cases

questions.explanation: The chapter notes that **an irritated or entrapped median nerve is frequently the cause of CRPS** after distal radius fracture; the surgeon should have a **low threshold for carpal tunnel release** in these patients. Prolonged rigid immobilization actually worsens stiffness and CRPS — early motion, therapy, and (in some) vitamin C prophylaxis are favored, with frequent follow-up until symptoms resolve.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: During the volar (Henry/FCR) approach to the distal radius, which two structures are the 'known knowns' that must be protected by careful retractor placement?

options.text: The median nerve and the radial artery
The ulnar nerve and ulnar artery
The posterior interosseous nerve and cephalic vein
The superficial radial nerve and EPL

questions.explanation: In the volar FCR/Henry approach, the **median nerve** (deep, ulnar to the FCR) and the **radial artery** (radial side) are the two structures at direct risk from retraction — the 'known knowns.' The **palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve** is the 'known unknown' (always present if sought), and an aberrant palmar cutaneous branch is the 'unknown unknown.' The FCR sheath is opened and the FPL and PQ are retracted to expose the radius.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A distal radius malunion is being corrected with a corrective osteotomy. Which combination of goals best defines a successful osteotomy?

options.text: Restore length and joint orientation, rebalance the midcarpal joint, and normalize DRUJ relationships
Maximize radial shortening to unload the radiocarpal joint
Increase dorsal tilt beyond 20 degrees to improve grip
Fuse the radiocarpal joint to eliminate motion

questions.explanation: A corrective osteotomy should **reorient the joint surfaces to restore normal load distribution, reestablish the mechanical balance of the midcarpal joint, and normalize the anatomic relationships of the DRUJ** (restoring radial length, inclination, and tilt). Increasing dorsal tilt or deliberately shortening the radius would worsen carpal malalignment and ulnocarpal impaction. Arthrodesis is a salvage, not the osteotomy goal.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has a failed, collapsed distal radius fixation with a destroyed DRUJ, severely shortened radius, and a poor-quality articular surface. An appropriate SALVAGE strategy is:

options.text: Wrist arthrodesis combined with a distal ulna (Darrach) resection
Repeat closed reduction and casting
Isolated carpal tunnel release
Observation only

questions.explanation: For a **destroyed DRUJ with a radically shortened radius and unsalvageable articular surface**, **wrist arthrodesis plus distal ulna resection (Darrach)** is a reliable salvage that reliably relieves pain — in the case example the patient became pain-free and returned to strenuous work. Other DRUJ salvage options include Sauvé-Kapandji or a DRU prosthesis depending on demand and radiocarpal status.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The dorsal spanning ('bridge') plate for a distal radius fracture is most useful in which scenario?

options.text: Highly comminuted intraarticular/metaphyseal fractures (or polytrauma patients needing to load the extremity), used as internal distraction
Simple extraarticular bending fractures in young patients
Isolated ulnar styloid tip fractures
Stable nondisplaced fractures

questions.explanation: The **dorsal spanning (bridge) plate** functions as internal distraction (ligamentotaxis without external hardware) and is favored for **severely comminuted intraarticular/metaphyseal fractures** and in **polytrauma** patients who need to bear weight through the wrist (e.g., using a walker), potentially with fewer complications than an external fixator. It spans from the radial shaft to a metacarpal and is removed after healing.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: The MacKenney/Edinburgh weighted formula (Edinburgh Wrist Calculator) for predicting distal radius fracture instability found which factors most predictive of malunion?

options.text: Advanced age, dorsal comminution, and increased ulnar variance (≥3 mm)
Initial dorsal angulation and male sex
Presence of an ulnar styloid tip fracture and radial artery injury
Handedness and occupation

questions.explanation: MacKenney's quantitative weighted formula (from 3559 patients) found **advanced age, dorsal comminution, and increased ulnar variance (≥3 mm)** most predictive of malunion; interestingly, **initial dorsal angulation was not independently predictive** (confounded by dorsal comminution). The online Edinburgh Wrist Calculator is based on this formula, though its predictive value varies across populations.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: In the Fernandez classification of DRUJ injuries associated with distal radius fractures, a Type II injury represents an avulsion fracture of the base of the ulnar styloid. What does this typically imply for stability?

options.text: It represents a TFCC (foveal) avulsion and is potentially unstable, warranting reassessment of DRUJ stability after radius fixation
It is always stable and never needs treatment
It mandates immediate Darrach resection in every case
It indicates an intraarticular sigmoid notch fracture

questions.explanation: In the **Fernandez DRUJ classification**, a **base-of-ulnar-styloid avulsion (Type II)** corresponds to a **TFCC/foveal avulsion** and is **potentially unstable**. After anatomic radius fixation, DRUJ stability is retested (shuck test); if still grossly unstable, options include immobilization in a stable position, K-wire fixation of the radius/ulna, ulnar styloid base fixation, or open/arthroscopic **foveal TFCC repair**. A sigmoid notch/ulnar head intraarticular fracture is instead the Type III pattern.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: Which of the following is the LEAST appropriate indication for operative fixation of a distal radius fracture?

options.text: A truly nondisplaced extraarticular fracture in an active young patient with an intact volar cortex
An open distal radius fracture
A displaced fracture with progressive median nerve compression not relieved by reduction
A comminuted intraarticular fracture with articular step-off in a young active patient

questions.explanation: A **truly nondisplaced extraarticular fracture with an intact volar cortex** can be treated in a cast/splint and typically does not need interval radiographs — surgery adds risk without benefit. In contrast, **open fractures, unrelenting/progressive median nerve compression, and displaced intraarticular fractures with step-off in active patients** are accepted operative indications (as are compartment syndrome and unstable/irreducible patterns).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: Systematic-review data cited in the chapter put the overall extensor tendon rupture rate after distal radius plating at roughly:

options.text: About 1.5% for volar plates and 1.7% for dorsal plates
About 20% for both
Less than 0.01%
About 50% for dorsal plates

questions.explanation: In a systematic review of 6278 patients, **extensor tendon rupture** occurred in about **1.5% with volar plates and 1.7% with dorsal plates**. EPL rupture specifically was ~0.7% (volar) and ~0.3% (dorsal), and EDC rupture ~0.05% (volar) vs ~1.3% (dorsal) — reflecting that dorsal hardware endangers the finger extensors more, while the EPL is chiefly at risk from dorsally protruding screws in volar plating.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 15 (Distal Radius Fractures)

questions.stem: A laceration divides a peripheral nerve's axon but leaves the surrounding **endoneurium intact**. Which injury grade does this represent?

options.text: Sunderland II (Seddon axonotmesis)
Sunderland I (Seddon neurapraxia)
Sunderland IV (Seddon axonotmesis)
Sunderland V (Seddon neurotmesis)

questions.explanation: **Sunderland II** = axon disruption with preserved endoneurium. Distal Wallerian degeneration occurs, but because the endoneurial tube is intact, regeneration is straightforward and predictable, so recovery is expected **without surgery**. Sunderland I (neurapraxia) is a conduction block with intact axon; III–V involve progressive loss of endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: In the Sunderland/Seddon schemes, **Seddon neurapraxia** corresponds to which Sunderland grade, and what is its natural history?

options.text: Sunderland I — a conduction block that typically recovers fully within 3–4 months
Sunderland III — usually requires surgical reconstruction
Sunderland V — no spontaneous recovery
Sunderland II — recovers but only after grafting

questions.explanation: **Neurapraxia = Sunderland I**, a focal conduction block (segmental demyelination/ischemia) with an intact axon. Even severe neurapraxia restores normal physiology within **3–4 months** with an excellent prognosis. No surgery is required.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Which Sunderland grades **generally require surgical reconstruction** rather than expectant observation?

options.text: Third, fourth, and fifth degree
First and second degree
First degree only
Second and third degree

questions.explanation: **Third-, fourth-, and fifth-degree** injuries disrupt the endoneurium (III), perineurium (IV), or produce complete transection (V), so spontaneous, well-directed regeneration is severely limited or impossible and surgical reconstruction is generally required. First- and second-degree injuries recover spontaneously.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: The Mackinnon-added **Sunderland sixth-degree** injury describes which pattern?

options.text: A mixed injury where some fascicles are normal or recovering while others are severely disrupted
Complete transection of all connective tissue layers
A pure conduction block with no axonal loss
Injury confined to the perineurium with intact axons

questions.explanation: **Sixth-degree (Mackinnon)** is a *mixed* injury — different fascicles sustain different grades (I–V) within the same nerve trunk. This is clinically common and difficult, producing partial, often functionally unsatisfactory recovery, and a neuroma-in-continuity that may need internal neurolysis to sort viable from non-viable fascicles.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: After axonotmesis, the cell body undergoes nuclear marginalization and dissolution of Nissl bodies. This response is termed:

options.text: Chromatolysis
Wallerian degeneration
Apoptosis
Demyelination

questions.explanation: **Chromatolysis** is the cell-body 'damage-control' response — the nucleus marginalizes and Nissl bodies dissolve as the neuron shifts to a regenerative metabolic program. Wallerian degeneration refers to breakdown of the *distal* axon segment, a separate process.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Following a proximal axotomy, approximately what proportion of **sensory neurons fail to survive**?

options.text: Less than 5%
Essentially 100%

questions.explanation: Despite upregulation of neuroprotectants such as heat-shock protein-27 (HSP27), **20%–50% of sensory neurons die** after axotomy — one reason sensory recovery is often incomplete even after technically excellent repair.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: During regeneration, Schwann cells align in longitudinal columns within the cleared endoneurial tubes to guide elongating axons. These columns are called:

options.text: Bands of Büngner
Nodes of Ranvier
Renaut bodies
Pacinian lamellae

questions.explanation: The **bands of Büngner** are Schwann-cell columns laying down basal-lamina channels rich in laminin that direct regenerating axons. Loss of these bands with Schwann-cell senescence (long grafts, chronic denervation) is a key barrier to recovery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: What is the commonly cited **rate of axonal regeneration** in an unobstructed nerve?

options.text: About 1 mm/day (range 1–3 mm/day)
About 1 cm/day
About 0.1 mm/day
About 5 mm/day

questions.explanation: Axons regenerate at roughly **1–3 mm/day, averaging ~1 mm/day** (~1 inch/month). This underlies the Tinel-advance rate and the clinical timing of expected reinnervation and the '18-month' muscle-viability window for proximal injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: The tendency for regenerating **motor axons to selectively enter motor endoneurial tubes** is known as:

options.text: Preferential motor reinnervation
Saltatory conduction
Collateral sprouting
Neurotropism to non-neural tissue

questions.explanation: **Preferential motor reinnervation** describes the (imperfect) bias of motor axons toward motor pathways, while sensory axons elongate more randomly. Misdirected axons are eventually pruned — a highly inefficient process that limits recovery, especially for mixed nerves.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: A bulbous mass at the proximal end of an **unrepaired distal nerve stump** (which contains Schwann cells and fibroblasts but **no axons**) is called a:

options.text: Glioma
End-bulb neuroma
Neuroma-in-continuity
Schwannoma

questions.explanation: The distal-stump mass is a **glioma** — a Schwann-cell/fibroblast response *without* axons. It must be distinguished from a proximal-stump **neuroma** (disorganized regenerating axons trapped in scar). Both may require resection before repair.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: In a rodent model, delaying nerve repair beyond **6 months** degraded axonal regeneration by approximately:
questions.explanation: Fu and Gordon showed repairs delayed >6 months produced a **~65% degradation** in axonal regeneration, driven by distal-stump Schwann-cell senescence, endoneurial tube degeneration, and loss of guidance cues — a core argument for early reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Denervated muscle loses roughly what fraction of its **cross-sectional area within 2–3 months**?

options.text: Up to 50%
Up to 10%
Up to 90%
None — mass is preserved until 18 months

questions.explanation: Denervated muscle catabolizes rapidly, losing **up to 50% of cross-sectional area within 2–3 months**. Satellite cells preserve fiber viability for a time, but with end-stage atrophy (average ~18 months in humans) endplates are walled off and the muscle becomes permanently silent, replaced by fibrofatty tissue.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Beyond approximately what interval does **denervated muscle** have a statistically low chance of regaining function, so that nerve reconstruction is generally abandoned in favor of tendon transfer or free functioning muscle transfer?

options.text: 18 months
3 months
6 weeks
5 years

questions.explanation: After ~**18 months** of denervation the motor endplates degrade irreversibly and reinnervation rarely restores useful strength. Reconstruction then shifts to **tendon transfer or free functioning muscle transfer**; most nerve surgery beyond this point is for pain (e.g., neuroma management).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: On the modified MRC motor scale, **M3** corresponds to which finding?

options.text: Active movement through a full arc against gravity
Movement only with gravity eliminated
Trace (flicker) contraction only
Movement against strong resistance

questions.explanation: **M3 = active movement against gravity** (full arc). M2 is movement with gravity eliminated, M1 a trace contraction, and M4 grades add increasing resistance (M4−/M4/M4+) up to M5 (full strength). 'Meaningful' motor recovery in outcome studies is usually defined as ≥M3.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: A regenerating nerve's advancing **Tinel sign** should progress distally from the repair site at approximately what rate?

options.text: ~1 inch per month
~1 inch per week
~1 cm per day
It does not move once established

questions.explanation: A percussion (Tinel) sign marking the leading edge of regenerating sensory axons advances at roughly **1 inch/month** (~1 mm/day). Testing should start distally and move proximally. Failure to advance may indicate failed regeneration or neuroma — though the sign is imperfect and can persist at the repair site.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Why should nerve conduction studies/EMG generally **not** be obtained in the first few days after an acute nerve transection?

options.text: Wallerian degeneration (7–10 days) and denervation changes on EMG (2–3 weeks) have not yet developed, so studies are misleading
The nerve cannot be stimulated at all during this period
Early studies overestimate the severity of injury
Muscle fibrillations appear immediately and confound the study

questions.explanation: Distal Wallerian degeneration takes **7–10 days**, and the characteristic denervation EMG pattern (fibrillations, positive sharp waves) appears around **2–3 weeks**. Testing before then is a common error that yields uninterpretable/false-negative results. After this window, NCS can distinguish neurapraxia (conduction block) from axonotmesis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: With stimulating and recording electrodes both placed **distal** to the injury site, a signal is still recordable. This finding best indicates:

options.text: Neurapraxia (conduction block) — the distal axon is intact
Complete axonotmesis with Wallerian degeneration
Neurotmesis with nerve rupture
A normally functioning nerve at all levels

questions.explanation: In **neurapraxia** the distal axon is intact, so it still conducts when both stimulation and recording are distal to the block. In axonotmesis/neurotmesis, distal Wallerian degeneration abolishes the distal response. Neither conducts *across* the lesion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Which statement about sensory testing after nerve injury is correct?

options.text: Two-point discrimination assesses innervation (axonal) density, whereas Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments are a threshold test
Semmes-Weinstein testing measures axonal density
Two-point discrimination is most reliable outside the hand
‘Can you feel this?’ is the most reliable initial question

questions.explanation: **2PD reflects axonal/innervation density** (reliable in hand dermatomes), while **Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments are a threshold test** better suited to compressive neuropathy. Initial screening should use comparative questions ('Does this feel the same as the other side?') and sharp–dull discrimination.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: A patient sustains a **sharp glass laceration** of the volar wrist with an anatomically matched complete median nerve deficit. What is the recommended timing of exploration/repair?

options.text: Urgent exploration within a few days
Observe 3–6 months for spontaneous recovery
Wait 3 weeks for the zone of injury to demarcate
Delay 12 months, then consider tendon transfers

questions.explanation: A **sharp laceration with a correlated deficit** is a clean transection — explore and repair **within a few days**. Early repair improves alignment, limits retraction/fibrosis, and avoids neuroma/glioma formation. The '3-week demarcation' wait applies to *ragged/traction* ruptures, not sharp cuts.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: After a **ragged traction rupture** of a nerve, why is a short delay of roughly 3 weeks before definitive repair often recommended?

options.text: To allow the zone of injury to demarcate so debridement reaches healthy nerve
To allow Wallerian degeneration to reverse
To let the muscle recover strength first
To permit the neuroma to mature for grafting

questions.explanation: With stretch/avulsion injuries the true zone of damage extends beyond the visible rupture and is initially indistinct. A **~3-week equilibration** lets the injury demarcate, so debridement can reach healthy endoneurial tubes — repairing damaged-to-damaged nerve is doomed to fail.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Which medication is an **antiseizure agent** commonly used first-line for neuropathic pain after nerve injury?

options.text: Gabapentin
Amitriptyline
Duloxetine
Tramadol

questions.explanation: **Gabapentin** (and pregabalin) are **antiseizure** neuropathic-pain agents. Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant (helpful for sleep), duloxetine is an SNRI used as second-line, and tramadol/narcotics are used sparingly given tolerance and abuse potential.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: A closed nerve injury shows no clinical or electrodiagnostic recovery by **3–6 months**. The nerve is explored and a firm, scarred, **non-conducting neuroma-in-continuity** is found. What is appropriate?

options.text: Resect the non-conducting segment and reconstruct the gap
Perform neurolysis alone and close, expecting recovery
Leave it undisturbed and observe another 12 months
Apply fibrin glue over the neuroma without resection

questions.explanation: A neuroma-in-continuity that **fails to conduct** across the lesion contains scar rather than viable fascicles and will not recover — it should be **resected and reconstructed** (graft/allograft or nerve transfer). Conducting or soft, well-vascularized fascicular tissue that twitches to low-amperage stimulation (0.05–2 mA) is left alone.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: What are the three primary principles of direct nerve repair?

options.text: Adequate debridement, precise end-to-end alignment, and tension-free atraumatic coaptation
Wide resection, joint immobilization, and early tension
Fascicular repair, nerve wrapping, and prolonged casting
Grafting, conduit placement, and steroid injection

questions.explanation: The three principles are **debridement of damaged nerve to healthy tissue, precise end-to-end (fascicular) alignment, and atraumatic, tension-free coaptation**. Tension impairs regeneration, intraneural vascularity, and Schwann-cell activity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: When freshening (debriding) a nerve stump before repair, what intraoperative finding indicates the resection has reached **healthy nerve**?

options.text: A clear fascicular pattern with pouting fascicles and healthy punctate bleeding
A firm, glistening scar with no bleeding
Uniform grey tissue without visible fascicles
Complete absence of any bleeding to confirm hemostasis

questions.explanation: Debride until a **clear fascicular pattern (fascicles pouting from the cut surface) and healthy bleeding** appear. Repairing damaged-to-damaged nerve fails to juxtapose viable endoneurial tubes. Serial thin slices with a razor/nerve-cutting forceps minimize crush.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Which suture caliber is typically appropriate for microsurgical nerve coaptation?

options.text: 11-0 only, never larger

questions.explanation: One or two **8-0 or 9-0** epineurial sutures (caliber chosen by nerve size) generally maintain stump approximation. The **fewest, smallest** sutures that give stable coaptation are preferred to limit intraneural trauma and foreign-body burden; fibrin glue or a connector can supplement.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: In which situation is a **grouped fascicular repair** most likely to be advantageous over a simple epineurial repair?

options.text: Distal median or ulnar nerve at the wrist, where motor/sensory fascicular topography is well known
A small digital sensory nerve
A very proximal brachial plexus lesion
Any repair, since it consistently improves outcomes

questions.explanation: Grouped fascicular repair helps where the **internal topography is predictable** — e.g., the **distal median/ulnar nerves at the wrist**. Elsewhere it adds manipulation/scarring without proven benefit; full fascicular (perineurial) repair has **not** been shown to improve clinical outcomes over epineurial repair.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Which statement about **fibrin glue** at a nerve coaptation is correct?

options.text: It can augment or, in some cases, replace microsutures and is efficient when doing multiple repairs
It is contraindicated because it blocks axonal regeneration
It provides more tensile strength than sutures
It must fully encase the entire graft to work

questions.explanation: **Fibrin glue** is a coaptation aid that can supplement or partly replace sutures and speeds multiple repairs. However, grafts should **not** be fully immersed (this blocks inosculation/nutrient diffusion). For acellular allograft, even tiny connector-assisted gaps should be avoided because allograft does not form the fibrin exudate scaffold.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Typical postoperative immobilization after a tension-appropriate nerve repair or graft is approximately:

options.text: 3 weeks
3 days
8 weeks
6 months

questions.explanation: Repairs/grafts are generally protected for about **3 weeks** to allow initial connective-tissue healing (nerve regains ~50%–65% of tensile strength within a few weeks). Extreme joint positioning to relieve tension is discouraged as the sole strategy; approximation should hold in a near-neutral posture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: For a median nerve defect in the forearm, roughly how much length can be gained by **mobilizing the proximal and distal stumps** to allow a tension-free primary repair?

options.text: About 4–6 cm
About 15 cm
Less than 5 mm
None — mobilization does not add usable length

questions.explanation: Careful stump mobilization can gain **~4–6 cm** for a forearm median nerve repair. Anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve at the elbow gains a few centimeters proximally but adds little for a forearm-level laceration. Persistent gaps need bridging (conduit/allograft/autograft) or a nerve transfer.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Hollow **nerve conduits** are best reserved for which situation?

options.text: Short gaps (roughly ≤5–6 mm to ~1.5 cm) in small-diameter sensory nerves
Large motor nerve gaps of 5–7 cm
Any gap regardless of length or nerve diameter
Only for reconstructing complete brachial plexus avulsions

questions.explanation: Conduits rely on a **fibrin bridge** that becomes unstable in longer/larger tubes, so they work best for **short gaps in small sensory nerves** (reliably ~5–6 mm, good results generally <1.5–2 cm). They fail across 2–3 cm gaps in major nerves. Autograft/allograft are used for longer or larger defects.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Which set of properties characterizes commercially available absorbable nerve conduits?

options.text: Semipermeable, semirigid (to resist collapse), and bioabsorbable
Impermeable, rigid, and permanent
Fully permeable, floppy, and non-absorbable
Metallic and radiopaque

questions.explanation: Conduits (polycaprolactone, polyglycolic acid, or processed bovine collagen) are **semipermeable** (nutrient diffusion), **semirigid** (prevent collapse), and **absorbable**. Early silicone tubes worked but were non-absorbable and caused irritation, requiring removal.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Regarding conduit sizing, which statement is correct?

options.text: An oversized conduit worsens the regenerative microenvironment and functional recovery
A grossly oversized conduit is ideal because it gives axons more room
Conduit diameter has no effect on outcome
The nerve should be left flush with the conduit end, not inserted

questions.explanation: Both under- and **over-sized conduits impair recovery** — gross oversizing prevents an optimal fibrin-scaffold microenvironment. The nerve should slide in easily and be inserted ~one nerve-diameter into each end, with the conduit sized to the stump.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Processed **acellular nerve allograft (ANA)** differs from a hollow conduit chiefly because it:

options.text: Retains the native three-dimensional internal scaffold (basal lamina/endoneurial architecture)
Contains living donor Schwann cells at implantation
Requires systemic immunosuppression
Is a rigid, non-absorbable tube

questions.explanation: **ANA** is decellularized (rendered immunotolerant) but **keeps the internal 3-D scaffold** with fragmented basal lamina/laminin, providing guidance cues a hollow conduit lacks. Host Schwann cells must migrate in to support regeneration; no immunosuppression is needed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Commercial ANA undergoes an enzymatic step to remove **chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans**. Why?

options.text: These proteoglycans bind laminin and inhibit axon regeneration; removing them lengthens the graft's effective supportive length
To make the graft radiopaque
To add living Schwann cells
To increase graft rigidity for suturing

questions.explanation: **Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans inhibit regeneration** (they bind laminin). Enzymatic removal roughly doubled the length axons could traverse in rodent models. Even so, ANA has a **critical length limitation** (axons cross ~20 mm reliably but falter at 40–60 mm) due to Schwann-cell senescence.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Commercially available acellular nerve allograft is supplied in lengths of approximately:

options.text: 1.5 cm to 7 cm
0.1 cm to 0.5 cm
10 cm to 20 cm
Only a single fixed 3-cm length

questions.explanation: ANA comes in diameters (1–2, 2–3, 3–4, 4–5 mm) and **lengths from 1.5 to 7 cm**. The strongest clinical evidence supports **small-diameter sensory** reconstruction up to ~3 cm; use for long or motor gaps remains less proven pending a prospective comparison with autograft.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: What remains the **gold-standard** material for bridging a nerve defect?

options.text: Nerve autograft
Hollow collagen conduit
Acellular nerve allograft
Autologous vein alone

questions.explanation: **Autograft** most closely mimics native nerve — optimal 3-D scaffold, guidance cues, and viable Schwann cells that need no repopulation — and remains the gold standard, especially for longer and motor gaps.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: The **sural nerve**, the 'workhorse' graft, provides approximately what length and diameter per leg?

options.text: About 30–40 cm of 2–3 mm diameter graft
About 5 cm of 5–6 mm diameter graft
About 60 cm of 4–5 mm diameter graft
About 10 cm of <1 mm diameter graft

questions.explanation: Each leg yields roughly **30–40 cm of relatively uniform 2–3 mm** sural nerve with minimal, well-tolerated donor morbidity. It is identified between the lateral malleolus and Achilles tendon, alongside the lesser (short) saphenous vein.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Why are large-diameter 'trunk' autografts (e.g., a whole major nerve segment) avoided as graft material?

options.text: They exceed the ~2 mm limit of nutrient diffusion, risking central necrosis; donors >3 mm are generally not used
They cannot be reversed in polarity
They regenerate too quickly and overshoot the target
They provoke systemic rejection

questions.explanation: Graft survives by **diffusion until revascularization**, which is limited to a depth of ~**2 mm**. Thick 'trunk' grafts undergo **central necrosis**, so most surgeons avoid donor nerves **>3 mm** and instead build **cable grafts** from thin strands to match a large recipient.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: When harvesting autograft for a **cable graft**, how should length be planned relative to the measured gap?

options.text: Harvest ~10%–20% longer than the gap and reverse the graft's polarity
Harvest exactly the gap length under maximum tension
Harvest 50% shorter and stretch to fit
Harvest same polarity as the recipient to align branches

questions.explanation: Cut grafts **10%–20% longer** than the measured defect to allow for retraction/preparation and ensure a **tension-free** coaptation, and **reverse polarity** so regenerating axons are not diverted out of side branches. Strands are stacked to match recipient diameter.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: The **medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve** graft can be found at which reliable landmark, and what is a notable drawback of its harvest?

options.text: ~2 fingerbreadths anterior/distal to the medial epicondyle (with the basilic vein); persistent neuroma pain in up to ~25%
Dorsal first web space; painless donor site in all cases
Between lateral malleolus and Achilles tendon; risk of foot drop
Radial styloid; risk of thumb weakness

questions.explanation: The anterior division of the **MABC** lies ~two fingerbreadths anterior and distal to the **medial epicondyle**, running with the **basilic vein** proximally. It provides ~3 mm × 30 cm of graft but carries a notable rate of **symptomatic donor neuroma (up to ~25%)**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Which principle makes an ideal **distal nerve transfer** donor, analogous to tendon transfer planning?

options.text: A redundant/synergistic donor whose loss causes minimal deficit, coapted close to the target to shorten reinnervation distance
The largest available motor nerve regardless of its function
A donor placed as proximal as possible to maximize regeneration length
A donor within the zone of injury to keep the incision small

questions.explanation: Like tendon transfers, ideal nerve-transfer donors are **redundant/synergistic with minimal donor morbidity**, and the transfer is done **close to the target and outside the zone of injury** — shortening regeneration time, giving a single coaptation, and matching pure motor-to-motor (or sensory-to-sensory) when possible.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: For a **high ulnar nerve injury** with poor prognosis for intrinsic recovery by conventional repair, which distal nerve transfer is classically used to reinnervate the ulnar-innervated intrinsics?

options.text: Distal anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) to the ulnar motor branch
Superficial radial nerve to the ulnar motor branch
Musculocutaneous nerve to the median nerve
Ulnar motor branch to the AIN

questions.explanation: The **distal AIN-to-ulnar-motor transfer** (often end-to-side or end-to-end at the wrist) 'supercharges'/replaces intrinsic reinnervation in high ulnar injuries, since regeneration over the long distance from a proximal repair usually arrives too late to save the intrinsics.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: To restore **critical sensation in the first web space / ulnar side of the thumb** after median nerve injury, a commonly described sensory transfer uses a donor branch from which nerve?

options.text: The ulnar nerve's fourth web space common digital nerve, transferred to the first web space
The posterior interosseous nerve
The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve to the small finger
The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve to the median palm

questions.explanation: A classic sensory transfer routes an **ulnar-innervated common digital nerve (e.g., 4th web space) to the first web space** to restore protective/critical sensation to the pinch surfaces after median injury. Non-critical donor territory is chosen so its sensory loss is tolerable.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: A painful end-neuroma of an above-elbow ulnar nerve persists 8 years after a failed repair, with no reconstructable distal target. Which strategy specifically treats the pain by giving the axons a 'new target muscle'?

options.text: Targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR)
Simple neuroma excision and burial in bone
Epineurial neurolysis
Sural nerve cable grafting to skin

questions.explanation: **TMR** coapts the neuromatous nerve to a nearby expendable motor nerve/muscle, giving regenerating axons 'somewhere to go' and markedly reducing neuroma pain (RPNI — regenerative peripheral nerve interface — is an analogous strategy using a free muscle graft). Passive burial does not provide a physiologic target.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Primary repair of an isolated **digital nerve** in an adult generally yields good (though not perfect) sensory recovery in approximately what proportion of cases?

options.text: About 50%–70%
Essentially 100%
Under 10%
Exactly 25%

questions.explanation: Digital/small sensory primary repairs achieve good but imperfect recovery in about **50%–70%** (e.g., average static 2PD ~10–11 mm vs 4–6 mm normal), with a low (~2%) rate of painful neuroma. Major mixed nerve repairs fare worse but still better than grafted repairs.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Which factor is consistently one of the **most powerful negative predictors** of functional nerve recovery?

options.text: Advancing patient age
A sharp mechanism of injury
A very distal level of injury
Early (rather than delayed) repair

questions.explanation: **Advancing age** is among the most consistent negative influences — older patients have diminished regenerative capacity and reduced cortical plasticity to adapt to new innervation. Children do best. Sharp mechanism, distal level, and early repair are all *favorable* factors.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: For bridging a nerve gap, which reconstruction is **LEAST** appropriate as described in Green's?

options.text: A hollow collagen conduit across a 3-cm gap in a major mixed motor nerve
Autograft cable graft across a 6-cm ulnar nerve gap
Acellular allograft across a 2-cm digital sensory gap
A conduit across a 6-mm digital sensory gap

questions.explanation: Hollow **conduits fail across ~2–3 cm gaps in major nerves** (unstable fibrin bridge) — Moore et al. reported 4/4 failures. Long/large or motor gaps need **autograft** (or allograft up to ~7 cm with caveats); conduits/allograft suit **short small-sensory** gaps.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: A cadaveric analysis of epineurial repairs found that precise end-to-end **fascicular alignment was NOT achieved** in up to what proportion of repairs, underscoring the difficulty of alignment?

options.text: Up to ~40%
Under 5%
About 90%
0% — alignment is always accurate

questions.explanation: Two cadaver studies showed fascicular malalignment in **up to ~40%** of epineurial repairs, and repair quality was better under the **operating microscope** than loupes. Surface vessels and fascicular patterns aid orientation, but alignment ultimately depends heavily on surgeon skill.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Nerve connective-tissue healing after coaptation is relatively quick — approximately what fraction of native tensile strength returns within a few weeks?

options.text: About 50%–65%
About 5%–10%
0% until 6 months

questions.explanation: Roughly **50%–65%** of native tensile strength is restored within a few weeks (small-animal data), which supports the customary **~3-week** protective immobilization before graduated motion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: Which statement about the biology of **tension at a nerve coaptation** is correct?

options.text: Excessive tension impairs axonal regeneration, intraneural vascularity, and Schwann-cell activity and should be avoided
Moderate tension is beneficial because it stimulates axon growth
Tension only matters for sensory, not motor, nerves
Tension can be permanently neutralized by extreme joint flexion

questions.explanation: **Nonphysiologic tension is detrimental** — it reduces local blood flow, impairs Schwann-cell function and regeneration, and risks postoperative disruption. If tension-free repair is impossible, bridge the gap (graft/allograft) or use a nerve transfer rather than relying on extreme joint positioning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 30 (Nerve Repair)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old laborer had a low median nerve laceration at the wrist repaired 18 months ago. He now has fixed thenar atrophy and cannot bring the thumb pulp to the small finger; sensation has partially returned. Passive thumb mobility is full. What is the most appropriate reconstruction?

options.text: Opponensplasty (e.g., EIP or ring FDS transfer)
Trapeziometacarpal arthrodesis
Repeat median nerve grafting
Continued observation and therapy

questions.explanation: Low median palsy denervates the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, opponens, superficial head of FPB) so **palmar abduction/opposition is lost**. With fixed atrophy 18 months out, further nerve recovery will not occur, and because the joints are supple the correct treatment is an **opponensplasty** to restore the abduction–pronation vector of the thumb. Fusion sacrifices motion and is not needed when joints are mobile.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Which opponensplasty donor has the advantage of NOT requiring a palmaris longus, sacrifices an expendable muscle, and does not weaken grip — making it a versatile 'workhorse' choice?

options.text: Extensor indicis proprius (EIP)
Ring-finger flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS IV)
Palmaris longus (Camitz)
Abductor digiti minimi (Huber)

questions.explanation: The **EIP opponensplasty** uses an expendable independent index extensor (the index still extends via EDC), needs no palmaris, and does not compromise grip strength — advantages over FDS (which weakens a finger and is unreliable in high median palsy) and Camitz (which gives abduction, not true opposition). The EIP is routed around the ulnar border of the wrist to reproduce the opposition vector.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman has long-standing severe carpal tunnel syndrome with marked thenar wasting and inability to abduct the thumb from the plane of the palm. At carpal tunnel release you plan a simultaneous opponensplasty. Which transfer is classically paired with the release in this scenario, and what is its main limitation?

options.text: Camitz transfer (palmaris longus prolonged with a palmar aponeurosis strip) — it restores palmar abduction but not true opposition/pronation
Huber (ADM) transfer — it fails to add thenar bulk
Ring FDS transfer — it cannot be routed around a pulley
EPL rerouting — it produces excessive thumb flexion

questions.explanation: The **Camitz transfer** elongates the palmaris longus with a strip of palmar aponeurosis and is convenient at the time of carpal tunnel release (same exposure). It reliably restores **palmar abduction** so the thumb clears the palm, but it does **not** reproduce true opposition (pronation), because its line of pull is more radial than a pisiform-based opponensplasty. It is chosen for its simplicity in older CTS patients rather than for optimal opposition.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with type II thumb hypoplasia has an absent/deficient thenar musculature and poor opposition. Which opponensplasty is particularly favored in this congenital setting because it also restores thenar bulk?

options.text: Huber transfer (abductor digiti minimi opponensplasty)
Camitz transfer
EPL rerouting opponensplasty
FPL (Makin) opponensplasty

questions.explanation: The **Huber transfer** mobilizes the abductor digiti minimi on its neurovascular pedicle and rotates it across the palm to the thumb. Besides restoring opposition it **adds soft-tissue bulk to the deficient thenar eminence**, which is cosmetically and functionally valuable in congenital thumb hypoplasia — its classic pediatric indication.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: For an opponensplasty to reproduce true opposition (abduction + pronation of the thumb), around what structure is the transfer classically routed to create the correct oblique line of pull?

options.text: A pulley at the pisiform / distal FCU
Lister's tubercle
The radial styloid
The dorsal carpal retinaculum (third compartment)

questions.explanation: Routing the transfer through a **pulley at the pisiform (using the distal FCU)** directs the tendon obliquely across the palm toward the thumb MCP, reproducing the abduction–pronation vector of opposition. A pulley placed too radially yields abduction without pronation (as with Camitz). Getting the pulley position right is the key technical determinant of a good opposition result.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A patient has a HIGH median nerve palsy (injury at the elbow). Compared with a low median palsy, which additional deficits will he have?

options.text: Loss of thumb IP flexion (FPL) and index DIP flexion (FDP to index), plus loss of forearm pronation and FCR
Loss of small-finger abduction and ring/small DIP flexion
Wrist drop and loss of finger MCP extension
Only sensory loss, with no additional motor deficit

questions.explanation: A **high median palsy** adds the forearm muscles: **FPL** (no thumb IP flexion), **FDP to index (±long)** (no index DIP flexion), **FCR**, and **pronator teres/quadratus**. Attempted fist gives the classic **'benediction' posture** — the index (and long) stay extended. Reconstruction therefore also addresses thumb and index flexion, not just opposition.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: In reconstructing a high median nerve palsy, why is the flexor digitorum superficialis a poor opponensplasty donor, and what is preferred instead?

options.text: The FDS is median-innervated and therefore weak/paralyzed; EIP (or ADM/Huber) is preferred
The FDS has too little excursion; the FCU is preferred
The FDS would cause wrist drop; the ECRL is preferred
The FDS is too strong and would hyperextend the thumb; the EPL is preferred

questions.explanation: In high median palsy the **FDS is itself denervated**, so it cannot serve as a donor. An **EIP opponensplasty** (radial-nerve innervated) or a **Huber (ADM, ulnar-innervated)** transfer is used instead. Choosing donors *outside* the paralyzed nerve's territory is a core tendon-transfer principle.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A patient with a high median nerve palsy cannot flex the thumb interphalangeal joint. Which transfer is the standard choice to restore thumb IP flexion?

options.text: Brachioradialis to flexor pollicis longus (BR-to-FPL)
EIP to FPL
ECU to FPL
FCU to FPL

questions.explanation: **BR-to-FPL** restores thumb IP flexion in high median palsy. The brachioradialis is expendable, radial-nerve innervated (intact), and has adequate strength; its relatively short excursion is improved by freeing it up proximally. ECRL-to-FDP (or side-to-side tenodesis of the index FDP to the intact ulnar FDPs) restores index flexion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A high median palsy patient lacks active index-finger DIP flexion. Besides an ECRL-to-FDP transfer, what simple alternative restores index distal flexion?

options.text: Side-to-side tenodesis of the index FDP to the intact ulnar-innervated long/ring FDP
FCR to index FDP
EIP to index FDP
PT to index FDP

questions.explanation: Because the **ulnar-innervated FDP to the ring/small (and often long) fingers is intact**, suturing the paralyzed index FDP **side-to-side** to these working profundus tendons gives the index composite flexion driven by the intact mass. It is simpler than an ECRL transfer and works well when independent index control is not essential.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old sustained a low ulnar nerve laceration at the wrist. Months later he has hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion of the interphalangeal joints of the RING and SMALL fingers. What is this deformity and its cause?

options.text: Claw hand (intrinsic-minus) from paralysis of the ulnar-innervated interossei and ulnar two lumbricals
Swan-neck deformity from FDS insufficiency
Boutonnière deformity from central slip rupture
Intrinsic-plus contracture from interosseous fibrosis

questions.explanation: Loss of the **intrinsics** (interossei + ulnar two lumbricals) removes MCP flexion/IP extension, so the unopposed long extensors hyperextend the MCPs and the FDP/FDS flex the IPs — the **claw (intrinsic-minus) hand**. It affects the **ring and small fingers** because the **radial two lumbricals (index, long) are median-innervated and preserved**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: In a clawed hand, you passively block MCP hyperextension of the ring and small fingers and the patient can then fully actively extend the PIP joints. This positive 'Bouvier' maneuver implies:

options.text: The extensor mechanism is intact, so a procedure that simply prevents MCP hyperextension (static block/capsulodesis or FDS lasso) will correct the claw
The extensor mechanism is incompetent, so a four-tailed FDS transfer to the lateral bands is required
A PIP joint fusion is required
The FDP tendons are ruptured

questions.explanation: A **positive Bouvier** (IP extension restored once MCP hyperextension is blocked) means the extrinsic extensor can extend the IP joints if the MCP is stabilized. Such 'simple' claws are corrected by **static MCP-flexion procedures** (Zancolli volar-plate capsulodesis, Parkes/Fowler tenodesis) or a **Zancolli 'lasso'** (FDS looped through the A1/A2 pulley). A **negative** Bouvier needs a transfer that also actively extends the IPs.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A clawed ulnar-palsy hand has a NEGATIVE Bouvier test — blocking MCP hyperextension does NOT allow the PIP joints to extend. Which reconstruction is therefore indicated?

options.text: A dynamic transfer that flexes the MCP and extends the IP, e.g., an FDS (Stiles-Bunnell) transfer to the lateral bands
Isolated Zancolli volar-plate capsulodesis
Static Parkes tenodesis alone
MCP arthrodesis in extension

questions.explanation: A **negative Bouvier** means the extensor mechanism cannot extend the IPs even with the MCP stabilized, so a simple MCP-block procedure will fail. A **dynamic intrinsic substitution** is needed — an **FDS transfer routed to the lateral bands (Stiles-Bunnell type)** or an ECRL/ECRB transfer extended with grafts to the lateral bands — providing both MCP flexion and active IP extension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: The Zancolli 'lasso' procedure corrects claw deformity by which mechanism?

options.text: The FDS is divided, looped back around the A1 (±A2) pulley, and sutured to itself so its pull flexes the MCP joint
The FDS is transferred to the extensor lateral bands to extend the IP joints
The volar plate is advanced proximally to block MCP hyperextension
The extensor tendons are shortened over the MCP

questions.explanation: In the **Zancolli lasso**, the FDS is transected distally, brought out at the A1 pulley, looped around the pulley, and sutured to itself. Contraction now produces **active MCP flexion**, preventing the hyperextension that drives the claw. It relies on an intact extensor mechanism (positive Bouvier) to then extend the IPs.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A patient with ulnar palsy is asked to pinch a key between the thumb and radial index finger. The thumb IP joint flexes sharply to maintain the pinch. What is this sign, and which muscle is deficient?

options.text: Froment's sign — weakness of the adductor pollicis is compensated by FPL (median) flexing the IP joint
Wartenberg's sign — weakness of the third palmar interosseous
Jeanne's sign — weakness of the first dorsal interosseous
Bunnell's sign — intrinsic tightness

questions.explanation: **Froment's sign** reflects loss of the **adductor pollicis** (ulnar): to hold a lateral (key) pinch the patient substitutes the median-innervated **FPL**, flexing the thumb IP. Associated **MCP hyperextension** during pinch is **Jeanne's sign**. Restoring strong pinch may require an adductorplasty (e.g., ECRB or FDS extended with a graft to the adductor).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: An ulnar-palsy patient holds the small finger persistently abducted and catches it on things (e.g., pockets). This 'Wartenberg sign' results from:

options.text: Unopposed extensor digiti minimi with loss of the third palmar interosseous (small-finger adductor)
Loss of the abductor digiti minimi
Contracture of the first dorsal interosseous
Rupture of the small-finger FDP

questions.explanation: **Wartenberg's sign** is persistent small-finger abduction from the **unopposed EDM (radial nerve) with paralysis of the third palmar interosseous** (the small-finger adductor, ulnar nerve). It can be corrected by transferring part of the EDM (or a slip) to add an adduction force to the small finger.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Counter-intuitively, a HIGH ulnar nerve injury (at the elbow) produces LESS finger clawing than a LOW (wrist) ulnar injury. This 'ulnar paradox' occurs because:

options.text: The high lesion also paralyzes the ring/small FDP, reducing the unopposed IP flexion that produces the claw
The high lesion spares the interossei
The high lesion preserves the lumbricals
The high lesion strengthens the long extensors

questions.explanation: The **'ulnar paradox'**: with a **low** lesion the ring/small **FDP is intact**, so its pull flexes the IPs and the claw is marked; with a **high** lesion the **FDP to ring/small is also paralyzed**, so IP flexion is weak and the clawing is *less* obvious. Paradoxically, recovery/reconstruction can make the claw look worse before pinch and grasp are addressed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: In a high ulnar nerve palsy with absent ring- and small-finger DIP flexion, a common adjunct to claw/pinch reconstruction is:

options.text: Side-to-side tenodesis of the ring/small FDP to the intact median-innervated index/long FDP
BR to ring/small FDP
EIP to ring/small FDP
ECU to ring/small FDP
