questions.explanation: Because the **index and long FDP are median-innervated and intact**, suturing the paralyzed **ring/small FDP side-to-side** to them restores composite distal flexion of the ulnar digits — a simple, reliable step that complements procedures addressing clawing and key pinch in high ulnar palsy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: To restore strong lateral (key) pinch in an ulnar-palsy hand with a weak adductor pollicis, which is a recognized adductorplasty option?

options.text: ECRB lengthened with a tendon graft passed through the second/third intermetacarpal space to the adductor insertion
FPL to the adductor insertion
APL to the adductor insertion
EDM to the adductor insertion

questions.explanation: A common **adductorplasty** transfers the **ECRB extended with a graft** (or an FDS, or BR) across the palm to the adductor pollicis insertion to reproduce a strong key-pinch vector. Restoring the first dorsal interosseous (index abduction) with an APL slip or EIP is a complementary pinch-improving transfer.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A patient is unable to extend the wrist ('wrist drop') and cannot extend the finger MCP joints or extend/abduct the thumb after a mid-humeral injury. Sensory loss is limited to the dorsal first web space. Which nerve is injured?

options.text: Radial nerve
Posterior interosseous nerve
Ulnar nerve
Median nerve

questions.explanation: This is a **radial nerve palsy** — loss of wrist extensors (ECRL/ECRB/ECU), finger MCP extensors (EDC/EIP/EDM), and thumb extensors/abductor (EPL/EPB/APL), with sensory loss over the **dorsal first web space**. A pure PIN palsy would spare wrist extension (ECRL intact) and cause no sensory loss.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A patient can extend the wrist but does so with marked RADIAL deviation, and cannot extend the fingers or thumb; sensation is entirely normal. Which lesion, and which principle follows for transfer selection?

options.text: Posterior interosseous nerve palsy — the PT transfer is unnecessary, and FCR is favored over FCU to avoid worsening radial deviation
High radial nerve palsy — PT-to-ECRB plus FCU transfer are required
C7 radiculopathy — no transfers are indicated
Low ulnar palsy — claw correction is required

questions.explanation: In **PIN palsy** the ECRL (innervated by the radial nerve proper) is spared, so the wrist extends but deviates **radially** (unopposed ECRL with paralyzed ECU); sensation is normal. Wrist extension is preserved, so **PT-to-ECRB is not needed**. Because the only remaining ulnar deviator should be preserved, the **FCR (not FCU)** is the preferred donor for finger extension to avoid aggravating radial deviation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Across essentially all accepted transfer sets for radial nerve palsy, which single transfer is used universally to restore wrist extension?

options.text: Pronator teres to ECRB
FCU to EDC
Palmaris longus to EPL
FDS to EIP

questions.explanation: **Pronator teres → ECRB** is the universally accepted component — it restores active wrist extension, the loss of which most impairs power grip. Debate concerns only how to restore finger and thumb extension (FCU vs FCR vs FDS sets), not the PT transfer for the wrist.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem:
Which of the following correctly lists the components of the commonly used 'FCU set' of transfers for a complete radial nerve palsy?

| Function restored | Transfer |
|---|---|
| Wrist extension | ? |
| Finger extension | ? |
| Thumb extension | ? |

options.text: PT→ECRB; FCU→EDC; PL→rerouted EPL
FCR→ECRB; PT→EDC; FDS→EPL
PT→EDC; FCU→ECRB; BR→EPL
ECRL→EDC; PT→EPL; PL→ECRB

questions.explanation: The classic **FCU set**: **PT→ECRB** (wrist), **FCU→EDC** (finger MCP extension), and **PL→rerouted EPL** (thumb extension/abduction). Rerouting the EPL out of the third compartment gives a combined extension–abduction vector. The FCR set and the Boyes superficialis (FDS) set are the two main alternatives.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Brand argued against using the FCU as the finger-extension donor in radial palsy for which reasons (even though outcome studies show no grip loss)?

options.text: The FCU has short excursion and is too strong, and it is the prime ulnar wrist stabilizer that should be preserved
The FCU is radial-nerve innervated and would also be paralyzed
The FCU cannot reach the dorsum of the forearm
The FCU has excessive excursion for the finger extensors

questions.explanation: Brand objected that the **FCU's excursion is short (~33 mm) relative to the finger extensors (~50 mm)**, that it is a very strong muscle, and that it is the **key ulnar-deviating wrist stabilizer** worth preserving. Leaving one wrist flexor intact is a widely held principle; nonetheless, clinical series show the FCU set does not measurably reduce power grip.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A key theoretical advantage of the Boyes superficialis (FDS) transfer set for radial nerve palsy over the FCU/FCR sets is that:

options.text: The FDS has greater excursion (~70 mm), allowing simultaneous wrist and finger extension without relying on wrist-flexion tenodesis
It avoids any tendon juncture
It does not require a functioning pronator teres
It restores sensation to the dorsal hand

questions.explanation: Wrist flexors have limited excursion (~33 mm) versus finger extensors (~50 mm), so with an FCU/FCR-to-EDC transfer full finger extension requires **wrist flexion (tenodesis effect)**. The **FDS (~70 mm excursion)** provides enough amplitude for more **independent, simultaneous wrist and finger extension**, and allows separate thumb/index control — at the cost of sacrificing superficialis flexors.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: After an FCU-to-EDC transfer for radial palsy, a patient achieves full finger extension only when the wrist is flexed, and makes a strong fist only when the wrist is extended. This behavior reflects:

options.text: Normal expected tenodesis effect from the excursion mismatch between wrist flexor donor and finger extensors
Rupture of the transfer
Excessive tension requiring immediate revision
A missed PIN injury

questions.explanation: This is the **expected tenodesis effect**: because the wrist-flexor donor has less excursion than the finger extensors, active finger extension is augmented by wrist flexion, and finger flexion by wrist extension. It is a normal functional characteristic of FCU/FCR extensor transfers, not a complication.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: During a PT-to-ECRB transfer, which technical point is emphasized to obtain a secure, adequately long juncture?

options.text: Harvest the PT insertion with a long strip of periosteum and weave true tendon (not just periosteum) into the ECRB
Insert the PT into both the ECRL and ECRB for redundancy
Divide the PT at its muscular origin to maximize length
Set the tension with the wrist in full flexion

questions.explanation: The **PT is lengthened by taking a periosteal strip with its radial insertion**, but the periosteum alone is not strong enough — actual **tendon must be woven into the ECRB** (Pulvertaft), ±a free graft if needed. Suture is into the **ECRB only** (just distal to the musculotendinous junction), tensioned with the **wrist ~45° extended** and PT at maximum tension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: When setting tension in extensor tendon transfers for radial palsy, the general guidance is to:

options.text: Err on the tighter side, because extensor transfers tend to stretch out over time
Err on the looser side to preserve finger flexion
Set the wrist in full flexion during suturing
Leave the thumb in adduction under minimal tension

questions.explanation: Extensor transfers **stretch over time**, so it is better to set them **slightly too tight** than too loose. The construct should still permit passive finger flexion with the wrist extended, and the MCPs should pull into full (not hyper-) extension with the wrist flexed — the synergistic check performed intraoperatively.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A patient has a good primary radial nerve repair at the mid-humeral level. When is proceeding to tendon transfers generally considered if no recovery is evident?

options.text: After roughly 5–6 months, once clinical and electrodiagnostic evidence shows inadequate reinnervation
Immediately, in all cases
Only after 3 years
Never — transfers are contraindicated after nerve repair

questions.explanation: After a good repair, most surgeons **wait ~5–6 months** (accounting for regeneration distance) and monitor clinically/electrodiagnostically before deciding on transfers. If the prognosis is poor from the outset (large gap >~4 cm, extensive scarring, skin loss), some proceed **directly to transfers** to spare the patient prolonged disability.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Burkhalter advocated an 'internal splint' concept in radial nerve palsy. What did this entail?

options.text: An early end-to-side PT-to-ECRB transfer to restore power grip while leaving the ECRB in continuity for possible later reinnervation
Wrist arthrodesis at the time of nerve repair
A dynamic outrigger splint replacing all transfers
Immediate transfer of all three donors at injury

questions.explanation: Burkhalter's **'internal splint'** is an **early PT-to-ECRB transfer performed end-to-side** (often with the nerve repair). It restores wrist extension/power grip immediately and eliminates external splinting, while the **ECRB remains in continuity** so it can still function if the radial nerve recovers.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Rerouting the extensor pollicis longus out of the third dorsal compartment during a PL-to-EPL transfer accomplishes what?

options.text: It redirects the EPL's pull to combine thumb extension with abduction, in line with the first metacarpal
It converts the EPL into a wrist extensor
It prevents the thumb from extending at all
It is done only to lengthen the tendon

questions.explanation: Freeing the EPL from Lister's tubercle and passing it across the snuffbox aligns it with the first metacarpal, so the transfer produces **extension plus radial abduction** of the thumb (rather than pure extension with adduction). This gives a more functional thumb position for grasp.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Which statement about the immediate loss of strength when a muscle is used as a tendon transfer is correct?

options.text: A transferred muscle typically loses about one MRC grade of power, so a donor of at least grade 4 (preferably 5) should be chosen
A transferred muscle gains one grade of strength after transfer
Donor strength is irrelevant to the outcome
Only grade 3 donors should be used

questions.explanation: Transfer costs roughly **one MRC grade** of strength, so donors should be **≥ grade 4 (ideally 5)** to leave useful power. This is one of the classic tendon-transfer prerequisites, alongside adequate excursion/amplitude, a straight line of pull, expendability of the donor, synergism, and supple passive joints.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Before performing tendon transfers, which prerequisite condition of the joints must be satisfied?

options.text: The joints to be moved must have full, supple passive range of motion
The joints should be stiff to protect the transfer
The joints must be fused first
Joint condition does not affect transfer outcome

questions.explanation: A tendon transfer can only move a joint that is **passively supple** — no transfer overcomes a fixed contracture. Achieving **full passive ROM (and soft-tissue/tissue equilibrium)** through therapy or prior release is a prerequisite. Other principles: one tendon–one function, synergism, adequate amplitude and strength, straight line of pull, expendable donor.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: The principle that a transfer works best when it is inserted into a single recipient to perform 'one tendon–one function' is illustrated by which refinement in radial palsy surgery?

options.text: Scuderi's PL-to-rerouted-EPL, where the donor drives only the thumb rather than multiple recipients
Using both FCU and FCR simultaneously
Inserting the PT into ECRL and ECRB together
Adding EDM to every EDC juncture

questions.explanation: Directing a donor to **one function/recipient** yields cleaner, more predictable control. Scuderi refined the thumb transfer to **PL → rerouted EPL only**, and most avoid overloading a single donor with many recipients. (Where donors are scarce, exceptions occur, but the principle guides standard practice.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A synergistic donor is preferred for a tendon transfer because:

options.text: Synergistic muscles naturally fire together (e.g., wrist flexors with finger extensors), making re-education after transfer easier
Synergistic muscles are always stronger
Synergism guarantees no loss of donor function
Only synergistic transfers avoid the need for therapy

questions.explanation: **Synergistic donors** (e.g., wrist flexors that normally co-contract with finger extension) are **easier to retrain** to their new role, improving functional outcomes. Non-synergistic transfers can still succeed but demand more motor re-education. Synergism, adequate amplitude, expendability, and one-tendon–one-function together define good transfer planning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Postoperatively after a standard set of radial-palsy transfers, the wrist is typically immobilized in which position?

options.text: About 45° of wrist extension, MCPs in slight flexion, thumb extended/abducted, with PIP joints left free
Full wrist flexion with fingers curled
Neutral wrist with thumb adducted
Wrist extension with all IP joints immobilized in extension

questions.explanation: Transfers are protected in a position that offloads the junctures: **~45° wrist extension, MCPs slightly flexed, thumb extended and abducted**, with **PIP joints free**. Immobilization runs ~4 weeks before a supervised, therapist-guided mobilization program; good control is usually achieved by ~3 months (up to 6 for maximum recovery).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Which pairing of nerve injury and its classic clinical hand posture is correct?

options.text: High median palsy → 'benediction' hand (index/long stay extended on attempted fist)
Low ulnar palsy → wrist drop
Radial palsy → clawing of ring and small fingers
Low median palsy → benediction hand

questions.explanation: **High median palsy** loses FPL and index/long FDP, so on attempted fist those digits remain extended — the **'benediction' (pointing-index)** posture. Clawing of ring/small is **ulnar** palsy; wrist drop is **radial** palsy; **low** median palsy affects thumb opposition, not composite finger flexion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A patient has a combined LOW median and ulnar palsy at the wrist. Which best summarizes the functional deficit?

options.text: Clawing of all four fingers, loss of thumb opposition and key pinch, and anesthesia of the entire volar hand
Wrist drop with preserved sensation
Isolated loss of thumb IP flexion
Clawing of only the index and long fingers

questions.explanation: Combined low median + ulnar palsy paralyzes **all intrinsics** (complete four-finger claw), removes **thumb opposition** (median thenar) and **adduction/key pinch** (ulnar adductor), and denervates **all volar sensation**. Reconstruction is staged and prioritizes sensibility, a stable pinch, opposition, and claw correction; restoring protective sensation is often the first priority.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Which donor is expendable and commonly available for reconstruction because its loss is well tolerated, making it a frequent choice (e.g., BR, PL, EIP, EDM)?

options.text: A muscle with a redundant/duplicated function so its sacrifice leaves no important deficit
The strongest muscle in the forearm regardless of function
A muscle that is the sole mover of an essential joint
Any paralyzed muscle within the injured nerve's territory

questions.explanation: Ideal donors are **expendable** — their function is **duplicated** elsewhere (e.g., PL, EIP, EDM, BR), so harvest causes no meaningful loss. A donor must also lie **outside the paralyzed nerve's territory** (i.e., still innervated) and have adequate strength/excursion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: In the radial nerve's motor innervation sequence, which muscle is typically the FIRST to be reinnervated after a proximal injury (and thus watched as an early sign of recovery)?

options.text: Brachioradialis
Extensor indicis proprius
Extensor pollicis longus
Extensor carpi ulnaris

questions.explanation: The radial nerve innervates muscles in a roughly proximal-to-distal order — **BR, then ECRL**, then (via the PIN) ECRB, EDC, ECU, EDM, APL, EPL, EPB, EIP. Return of **brachioradialis** function is an early recovery marker; the distal muscles (EIP last) recover latest.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Why must the FCU dissection during transfer NOT be carried too far proximally (beyond ~4 cm from the medial epicondyle region)?

options.text: Its motor innervation enters proximally; over-dissection would denervate the donor
The radial artery would be injured
The pisiform would be destabilized
The ulnar nerve sensory branch would be cut

questions.explanation: The **FCU's nerve supply enters its proximal ~4 cm**, so dissection to fully mobilize the muscle for a straight line of pull must **stop short of the neurovascular entry** to avoid denervating the transfer. Extensive but not excessively proximal release is the technical balance.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A patient with an isolated inability to actively extend the thumb IP joint (dropped thumb) after a distal radius fracture (delayed EPL rupture) requests reconstruction. Which transfer is standard?

options.text: Extensor indicis proprius (EIP) to EPL
FCU to EPL
PT to EPL
FDS to EPL

questions.explanation: For an isolated **EPL loss** (classically delayed rupture after a distal radius fracture), the **EIP-to-EPL transfer** is the standard reconstruction — the EIP is expendable, adjacent, and of appropriate excursion, and independent index extension is retained via the EDC. This is distinct from the multi-tendon sets used for complete radial palsy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Which of the following is the LEAST appropriate action when planning tendon transfers?

options.text: Transferring a muscle across a joint with a fixed flexion contracture, expecting the transfer to correct it
Choosing an expendable donor of at least grade 4 strength
Selecting a donor with adequate excursion for the intended function
Restoring supple passive joint motion before transfer

questions.explanation: A tendon transfer **cannot overcome a fixed contracture** — the joint must first be made passively supple, so relying on the transfer to correct a contracture is the least appropriate plan. The other three are sound principles (expendable donor of adequate strength, matched excursion, supple joints before transfer).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: The 'Merle d'Aubigné' variant of radial palsy transfers differs from the standard FCU set mainly in that it:

options.text: Uses FCU→EDC and EPL, with PL→EPB and APL (a slightly different distribution to the thumb)
Replaces the PT transfer with a wrist fusion
Uses the FDS for all recipients
Omits thumb reconstruction entirely

questions.explanation: The **Merle d'Aubigné** (French) variant distributes the donors slightly differently — **FCU to EDC and EPL, and PL to EPB and APL** — but retains the core PT-to-ECRB for the wrist. It illustrates that several donor–recipient distributions achieve comparable outcomes, with the PT-for-wrist component constant.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: In restoring index-finger abduction (first dorsal interosseous function) to improve pinch in ulnar palsy, a recognized transfer is:

options.text: A slip of APL (extended with a graft) or EIP transferred to the first dorsal interosseous insertion
FDP index to the first dorsal interosseous
FPL to the first dorsal interosseous
ECU to the first dorsal interosseous

questions.explanation: Index radial abduction (first dorsal interosseous) can be restored with an **APL slip lengthened by a graft** or an **EIP transfer** to the first dorsal interosseous insertion, stabilizing the index for a strong lateral pinch against the thumb — complementary to adductorplasty in ulnar-palsy pinch reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A patient with ulnar palsy demonstrates MCP hyperextension of the thumb during attempted key pinch (in addition to a positive Froment's sign). This associated finding is called:

options.text: Jeanne's sign
Wartenberg's sign
Masse's sign
Bunnell's sign

questions.explanation: **Jeanne's sign** is **thumb MCP hyperextension** during pinch, accompanying Froment's IP flexion — both reflect adductor pollicis (and first dorsal interosseous) weakness with FPL substitution. Recognizing the combination guides adductor/pinch reconstruction and sometimes thumb MCP stabilization.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Which best describes the rationale for often deferring or avoiding wrist arthrodesis in favor of the PT-to-ECRB transfer in radial palsy?

options.text: Preserving active wrist motion enhances the tenodesis-assisted grasp/release and overall hand function
Arthrodesis is technically impossible after radial palsy
The PT cannot be used for any other purpose
Wrist motion is unimportant for hand function

questions.explanation: Most surgeons **preserve wrist motion** (PT-to-ECRB) rather than fuse the wrist, because active wrist flexion/extension augments finger grasp and release through tenodesis and yields more natural function. Arthrodesis is reserved for select cases (e.g., inadequate donors).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A patient develops radial nerve palsy in association with a closed humeral shaft fracture. What is the generally recommended initial management of the nerve?

options.text: Observation, since most closed fracture-associated radial palsies are neurapraxic and recover spontaneously
Immediate tendon transfers
Immediate nerve grafting
Primary wrist arthrodesis

questions.explanation: Radial palsy with a **closed humeral shaft fracture** is usually a **neurapraxia/traction injury that recovers spontaneously**, so initial **observation** (with splinting and therapy to keep joints supple) is appropriate; recovery is monitored clinically and electrodiagnostically. Exploration is considered for open fractures, high-energy injury, or failure to recover in the expected window; tendon transfers are reserved for established, non-recovering palsy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: While awaiting recovery or reconstruction of a radial nerve palsy, what is the key nonoperative priority?

options.text: Splinting and therapy to maintain supple passive joint motion (a dynamic MCP-extension/outrigger or wrist splint)
Strict immobilization of all joints to prevent stretch
Early aggressive strengthening of denervated muscles
No intervention until surgery

questions.explanation: Maintaining **supple passive joints** with **splinting (e.g., a dynamic outrigger for MCP extension or a simple wrist support) and therapy** is essential so that, if transfers become necessary, no contractures compromise the result — and it improves function in the interim. Denervated muscles are not strengthened by early resistance.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: For claw correction, static procedures such as Zancolli volar-plate capsulodesis or Parkes/Fowler tenodesis are appropriate ONLY when:

options.text: The Bouvier test is positive (intact extrinsic IP extension once MCP hyperextension is blocked)
The Bouvier test is negative
The FDP tendons are ruptured
There is a fixed PIP flexion contracture

questions.explanation: Static MCP-flexion blocks (capsulodesis, tenodesis) merely **prevent MCP hyperextension**; they rely on the extrinsic extensor to then extend the IPs — i.e., a **positive Bouvier**. They also tend to **stretch out over time**, a recognized limitation. A negative Bouvier or the desire for a durable active result favors a **dynamic tendon transfer**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: Some months after a four-tailed FDS (Stiles-Bunnell) transfer to the lateral bands for claw correction, a patient develops PIP-joint hyperextension with the fingers assuming a 'swan-neck' posture. What is the mechanism of this complication?

options.text: Over-tensioning of the intrinsic substitution over-extends the PIP joints (intrinsic-plus / swan-neck)
Rupture of the transferred FDS
Recurrence of the original claw deformity
Central slip attenuation from the transfer

questions.explanation: A recognized pitfall of the **Stiles-Bunnell FDS-to-lateral-band transfer** is **over-correction**: excessive intrinsic-substitution force hyperextends the PIP joints, producing an **intrinsic-plus / swan-neck** deformity. Inserting the transfer into the A1/A2 pulley (Zancolli lasso) or the proximal phalanx instead of the lateral bands, and careful tensioning, help avoid this — a reason the lasso is often preferred when the Bouvier test is positive.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 31 (Tendon Transfers)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with spastic hemiplegic cerebral palsy is referred for upper-limb evaluation. Which statement best characterizes the underlying pathology of cerebral palsy?

options.text: A static, non-progressive injury to the immature/developing brain, though the peripheral deformities evolve with growth
A progressive degenerative disease of the anterior horn cells
A peripheral demyelinating neuropathy
An acquired brain injury in a previously normal mature brain

questions.explanation: Cerebral palsy is a **static (non-progressive) encephalopathy of the immature brain**. The brain lesion itself does not worsen, but the *clinical picture* changes as the child grows — dynamic spasticity gives way to fixed myostatic contractures and bony deformity, which is why surgery is timed to development and 'fine-tuning' procedures are common. This contrasts with traumatic brain injury, which is acquired in a formerly normal brain and may recover over time.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A patient sustained a severe traumatic brain injury 3 months ago and has a spastic, posturing upper limb. Regarding the timing of reconstructive tendon surgery, what is the appropriate approach?

options.text: Delay definitive reconstruction (generally ~12–18 months) until neurologic recovery plateaus, using splinting/therapy and botulinum toxin meanwhile
Proceed immediately with tendon transfers to prevent contracture
Perform tendon lengthenings within the first month
Never operate on a TBI limb

questions.explanation: Unlike the static lesion of CP, **TBI is an evolving injury that can continue to recover for a year or more**. Definitive reconstruction is therefore **deferred until the neurologic status plateaus (commonly ~12–18 months)**. In the interim, contracture is prevented with splinting, serial casting, therapy, and adjuncts such as botulinum toxin or nerve blocks. Operating too early risks reconstructing a limb whose tone and voluntary control are still changing.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: The most common physiologic type of cerebral palsy affecting the upper limb, characterized by velocity-dependent increased tone and a 'clasp-knife' catch, is:

options.text: Spastic (pyramidal) type
Dyskinetic/athetoid (extrapyramidal) type
Ataxic type
Hypotonic type

questions.explanation: **Spasticity (pyramidal/corticospinal involvement) is the most common** form and the one most amenable to tendon surgery, because the deforming forces are relatively predictable. **Athetoid/dyskinetic** CP has fluctuating, unpredictable tone and involuntary movements and generally responds poorly to tendon transfers. **Ataxic** CP involves coordination/balance. Recognizing the movement-disorder type is central to surgical candidacy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: During examination you slowly, then rapidly, move a spastic wrist through its arc and note a clear 'catch' at a specific angle only with fast movement, with the angle differing between slow and fast stretch. Which assessment tool are you applying, and what does it capture?

options.text: Modified Tardieu Scale — it is velocity-dependent and compares the catch angle at slow vs fast stretch (R1/R2)
Modified Ashworth Scale — it measures velocity-dependent catch angles
House Functional Classification — it grades tone
MACS — it measures the angle of catch

questions.explanation: The **Modified Tardieu Scale** is explicitly **velocity-dependent**: it records the angle of muscle reaction ('catch') at slow versus fast stretch (R2 vs R1). A large R2–R1 difference indicates a dynamic spastic component (potentially responsive to tone reduction), whereas a small difference suggests fixed contracture. The **Modified Ashworth Scale** grades resistance to passive movement (0–4) but is not velocity-quantified.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A child with spastic hemiplegia is being considered for a functional (rather than purely hygienic) tendon transfer. Which patient factor most favors a good FUNCTIONAL outcome?

options.text: Preserved voluntary control, adequate sensation/stereognosis, and cognitive ability to participate in rehabilitation
Athetoid movement pattern
Absent stereognosis with dense sensory loss
Severe cognitive impairment

questions.explanation: Good functional candidates have **voluntary motor control (can initiate and release grasp), useful sensation — especially stereognosis — and the cognition/motivation to engage in therapy**. Poor sensation predicts the hand will be neglected even if repositioned, and athetosis makes results unpredictable. When these are lacking, goals shift to **hygienic/positional** improvement (e.g., opening the palm, accessing the axilla) rather than active function.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Stereognosis is tested with a set of common objects while the child is blinded. Why is this assessment emphasized before functional hand surgery in CP?

options.text: Intact stereognosis predicts the hand will be incorporated into use; poor stereognosis predicts neglect despite good positioning
It measures grip strength
It quantifies spasticity velocity
It determines the degree of fixed contracture

questions.explanation: **Stereognosis** (recognizing objects by feel) reflects the cortical sensory integration needed for a hand to be *used*. A child with poor stereognosis tends to **ignore the hand** even after a technically successful transfer, so functional surgery yields little benefit. Testing with familiar objects with and without vision helps set realistic goals (functional vs hygienic).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: The Manual Ability Classification System (MACS) describes cerebral palsy hand function on a 5-level scale. What does MACS actually measure?

options.text: How a child handles objects in everyday activities (I = easily/successfully … V = does not handle objects)
The velocity-dependent catch angle of spastic muscles
Gross motor walking ability
The degree of fixed elbow contracture

questions.explanation: **MACS grades everyday manual ability** from **Level I** (handles objects easily and successfully) to **Level V** (does not handle objects; severely limited). It is an *activity-limitation* measure (WHO-ICF) complementary to the House classification. It differs from **GMFCS**, which grades gross-motor/ambulation, and from tone scales like Ashworth/Tardieu.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: On the House Functional Classification of upper-limb use in CP, a hand graded as a 'good passive assist' (can hold an object and stabilize it for use by the other hand) corresponds to which general level, and what does the scale's high end (7–8) denote?

options.text: A low-mid passive-assist level; the high end (7–8) denotes spontaneous partial-to-complete independent use
An active-assist level; the high end denotes no functional use
The highest level; the high end denotes hygienic use only
The lowest level (does not use); the high end denotes passive assist

questions.explanation: The **House scale (0–8)** ascends from **0 (does not use)** → passive assist (poor/fair/good, holds and stabilizes) → active assist (poor/fair/good) → **7–8 (spontaneous use, partial then complete independent use)**. It is a validated way to describe preop function and measure change after surgery — a 'good passive assist' still relies on the other hand, whereas 7–8 uses the hand independently.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: In planning spastic upper-limb surgery, the 'hierarchy of hand function' (reconstruction ladder) places which movement as the highest priority to restore?

options.text: Wrist extension (enables tenodesis grasp and lateral pinch)
Coordinated fine dexterity
Digital opening for object acquisition
Shoulder external rotation

questions.explanation: **Wrist extension is the pivotal function** — it produces a **tenodesis grasp/pinch** (fingers and thumb close as the wrist extends) and aligns the finger flexors on the length-tension (Blix) curve for stronger grip. The ladder then descends: lateral pinch → grasp → digital opening (lowest, since wrist flexion passively opens the digits) → coordinated dexterity (hardest to achieve surgically).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: The surgical 'toolbox' for the spastic upper limb comprises four categories of technique. Which set correctly lists them?

options.text: Soft-tissue release/lengthening, tendon transfer, bone/joint stabilization (osteotomy/fusion), and neurectomy
Arthroscopy, arthroplasty, amputation, and grafting
Nerve graft, nerve transfer, free muscle transfer, and replantation
Casting, bracing, injection, and observation only

questions.explanation: The four surgical categories are **(1) soft-tissue release/lengthening (myotomy, tendon lengthening), (2) tendon transfer, (3) bone/joint procedures (osteotomy, arthrodesis), and (4) neurectomy (selective/hyperselective)**. These are applied region by region (shoulder → thumb), frequently combined in a single anesthetic to minimize the number of operations a child undergoes.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A spastic biceps muscle-tendon unit requires lengthening. Compared with a long forearm flexor, why is a Z-plasty (rather than fractional) lengthening generally chosen for the biceps tendon?

options.text: The biceps has a short muscle-tendon junction, so fractional lengthening cannot provide enough length without discontinuity
The biceps cannot tolerate any lengthening
Fractional lengthening of the biceps risks nerve injury
Z-plasty is always preferred for every muscle

questions.explanation: Lengthening options are **Z-plasty, fractional (incising the tendon within the muscle-tendon junction and stretching), muscle-origin slide, or myotomy**. Muscles with a **short muscle-tendon junction (e.g., biceps)** cannot be fractionally lengthened enough without separating muscle from tendon, so a **Z-plasty** is used; the adjacent **brachialis** (broad MTJ) is well suited to fractional lengthening. Technique choice depends on the required amount and the muscle's anatomy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with spastic hemiplegia has an elbow flexion posture limiting extension and interfering with gait and reach. Surgical release typically addresses which structures?

options.text: Lengthening of biceps and brachialis (± lacertus fibrosus release), sometimes with musculocutaneous neurectomy
Triceps lengthening
Anconeus release
Pronator teres rerouting only

questions.explanation: Elbow flexion spasticity is addressed by **lengthening the biceps (Z-plasty) and brachialis (fractional), and releasing the lacertus fibrosus**; a **musculocutaneous neurectomy** may be added to reduce flexor tone. EMG can help decide whether biceps and/or brachialis are the dominant offenders. Care is taken not to over-lengthen and create an extension deficit or lose active elbow flexion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: The forearm has been called 'the forgotten joint' in cerebral palsy. What is the typical deforming posture, and why is it functionally important?

options.text: Spastic pronation, which impairs supination-dependent tasks (feeding, carrying a tray, catching a ball)
Fixed supination, impairing keyboard use
Neutral rotation with no functional impact
Excessive external rotation of the forearm

questions.explanation: The spastic forearm characteristically rests in **pronation** (initially dynamic, later a fixed myostatic contracture). This blocks **supination**, hindering activities like feeding, carrying, obtaining soap, catching a ball, and perineal hygiene. It is addressed by **pronator teres release** (or **rerouting** to convert it into an active supinator when there is a dynamic component), ± pronator quadratus release.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: When is pronator teres REROUTING (rather than simple release/lengthening) preferred to manage spastic forearm pronation?

options.text: When active supination is a goal and there is a dynamic (supple) pronation component the rerouted PT can actively correct
When there is a fixed bony deformity requiring osteotomy
When the patient has no voluntary control at all
Only in traumatic brain injury, never in cerebral palsy

questions.explanation: **PT rerouting** redirects the pronator around the radius so it becomes an **active supinator**, useful when the surgeon wants to *restore active supination* in a limb with dynamic pronation and reasonable voluntary control. Simple **release/lengthening** only weakens the deforming force (helpful for a mainly contractural, less functional limb). Severe fixed rotational deformity may instead need a **rotational osteotomy**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A child with spastic hemiplegia has a flexed, ulnarly deviated wrist but useful finger control. Which tendon transfer is the classic 'workhorse' to correct wrist flexion while harnessing a deforming muscle?

options.text: Flexor carpi ulnaris to extensor carpi radialis brevis (Green transfer)
Extensor carpi radialis brevis to flexor carpi ulnaris
Flexor digitorum superficialis to profundus
Pronator teres to flexor carpi radialis

questions.explanation: The **FCU-to-ECRB (Green) transfer** removes a strong wrist flexor/ulnar deviator (a deforming force) and converts it into a **wrist extensor**, correcting the posture and improving tenodesis grasp. It also tends to improve forearm supination. Alternatives include **ECU-to-ECRB** or **FCU-to-EDC** (chosen when improving finger extension is also desired).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Before transferring the FCU to a wrist extensor in a spastic hand, why must you assess whether the fingers can extend with the wrist held in neutral?

options.text: If active finger extension depends on wrist flexion (tenodesis), correcting wrist flexion can leave the child unable to open the fingers
To confirm the FCU is paralyzed before transfer
Because finger extension is irrelevant to wrist transfers
To decide whether to fuse the wrist instead

questions.explanation: Many spastic hands open the fingers only **passively via wrist flexion (tenodesis)**. If you eliminate the wrist-flexion posture without ensuring the child has (or will gain) active finger extension in a neutral/extended wrist, the transfer can produce a hand that **grasps but cannot release**. This is why finger-extension capacity with the wrist stabilized guides whether to add an extensor transfer and how much to correct.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A child with severe spastic quadriplegia has a tightly clenched, non-functional hand with poor voluntary control and hygiene problems in the palm. The goal is hygienic, not functional. Which procedure is most appropriate?

options.text: Superficialis-to-profundus (STP) transfer, sacrificing active grip to relax the clenched fingers for hygiene
FCU-to-ECRB transfer to restore active grasp
Opponensplasty
Pronator rerouting for active supination

questions.explanation: For a **severely clenched, non-functional hand where the goal is hygiene/positioning**, the **superficialis-to-profundus (STP)** transfer lengthens the flexor system (the FDS tendons are divided and sutured to the lengthened FDP) to open the palm for cleaning and skin care. It deliberately **sacrifices active grip**, so it is reserved for hands without useful function. A flexor-pronator slide is an alternative for combined wrist/finger flexion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A flexor-pronator slide is used in the spastic upper limb to address:

options.text: Combined wrist and finger flexion contracture, by releasing the flexor-pronator origin from the medial epicondyle/proximal ulna and letting it slide distally
Thumb-in-palm deformity alone
Elbow extension contracture
Shoulder internal rotation contracture

questions.explanation: The **flexor-pronator slide** releases the common origin of the flexor-pronator mass, allowing it to migrate distally and thereby lengthen multiple wrist/finger flexors (and pronator) simultaneously. It suits **combined myostatic wrist and digital flexion contractures**, adjusting tension across several muscles at once rather than lengthening each individually.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: The House classification of thumb-in-palm deformity guides treatment. Which component defines a Type I deformity, and how does treatment escalate with higher types?

options.text: Type I = simple metacarpal adduction contracture (first web); higher types add MCP flexion, MCP instability/hyperextension, and IP/extrinsic involvement, each requiring added release, tendon rebalancing, and joint stabilization
Type I = IP joint contracture only; higher types add wrist deformity
Type I = MCP hyperextension; higher types reduce to simple adduction
Type I always requires CMC fusion

questions.explanation: House **Type I** is an isolated **first-web (metacarpal adduction) contracture** from a tight adductor pollicis/first dorsal interosseous — treated by web release ± adductor/FPB release and augmenting extension/abduction (e.g., EPL rerouting, EPB reinforcement). Higher types add **MCP flexion (II), MCP instability/hyperextension (III), and IP/extrinsic (FPL) involvement (IV)**, so treatment escalates to include **MCP stabilization (capsulodesis/fusion)** and **FPL lengthening**. Matching the procedure to the deformity components is the key principle.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: In releasing a thumb-in-palm deformity, augmenting thumb extension/abduction is often achieved by rerouting which tendon?

options.text: Extensor pollicis longus (rerouted radially, out of Lister's tubercle)
Flexor pollicis longus
Abductor pollicis brevis
Extensor carpi ulnaris

questions.explanation: **EPL rerouting** (releasing it from the third compartment/Lister's tubercle and redirecting it radially) converts its pull into combined **extension and abduction**, helping lift the thumb out of the palm. It is combined with **first-web/adductor release**, and — depending on House type — **MCP stabilization** to prevent recurrent collapse and **FPL lengthening** if the extrinsic flexor is tight.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: During thumb-in-palm reconstruction, why is metacarpophalangeal joint stabilization (capsulodesis or fusion) frequently required in the higher House types?

options.text: An unstable MCP will collapse into hyperextension (or flexion) after release/rebalancing, so it must be stabilized for a durable, functional pinch
To lengthen the FPL
To restore CMC opposition
Because the MCP is the only joint that ever needs surgery in CP

questions.explanation: A lax/unstable **thumb MCP** will deform after the balancing procedures (e.g., collapse into **hyperextension**, undermining pinch). **Volar-plate capsulodesis** (or **MCP arthrodesis** if severe) provides the stable post needed for effective lateral pinch. Failing to address MCP instability is a common cause of persistent deformity after thumb-in-palm surgery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Botulinum toxin type A has an important role in the spastic upper limb. Which use is correct?

options.text: A temporary, reversible tone reducer that can serve as a 'trial' to predict the effect of weakening/lengthening a muscle before committing to surgery
A permanent replacement for tendon surgery
A treatment that increases muscle strength
Only useful after fixed contractures have formed

questions.explanation: **Botulinum toxin** temporarily weakens a target muscle (effect ~3–4 months), useful for reducing dynamic tone, aiding therapy/serial casting, and as a **diagnostic 'test dose'** to preview what surgically weakening or lengthening that muscle would do. It does **not** correct fixed myostatic contractures and is not a substitute for definitive surgery, but it helps select muscles and set expectations.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A key counseling point for families before spastic upper-limb surgery in CP is that:

options.text: Surgery can improve position and function, but no operation restores a normal hand; goals must be shared and realistic
Surgery will normalize the limb
A single procedure reliably corrects all deformities permanently
Recurrence with growth never occurs

questions.explanation: Surgery **improves alignment and specific functions but cannot restore normal control** to a brain-injured limb. Multiple simultaneous procedures are common, later 'fine-tuning' may be needed as the child grows, and outcomes depend on voluntary control, sensation, and motivation. **Setting shared, realistic goals** (e.g., via the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure) is essential to satisfaction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with spastic hemiplegia has a nonfunctional, malpositioned wrist with a severe fixed flexion deformity and no useful voluntary hand control. Which salvage option addresses position when tendon balancing alone is inadequate?

options.text: Wrist arthrodesis (± proximal row carpectomy for shortening) to give a stable, better-positioned wrist
FCU-to-ECRB transfer alone
Botulinum toxin injection alone
Pronator teres rerouting

questions.explanation: For a **severe fixed wrist flexion deformity in a non-functional limb**, **wrist arthrodesis** provides a durable, well-positioned wrist; a **proximal row carpectomy** can be added to shorten the skeleton and allow correction without over-tensioning the neurovascular structures/skin. Tendon transfers require a supple joint and useful control, so they are inappropriate here.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: The spastic shoulder in cerebral palsy typically rests in which position, and which muscles are usually released to improve it?

options.text: Internal rotation and adduction; release/lengthening of pectoralis major and subscapularis (± latissimus/teres major)
External rotation and abduction; release of teres minor
Flexion and elevation; release of deltoid
Neutral; no muscles require release

questions.explanation: The spastic shoulder sits in **internal rotation and adduction**, which can make the axilla inaccessible (hygiene/skin problems). Treatment lengthens/releases the offending internal rotators/adductors — chiefly **pectoralis major and subscapularis** (via a deltopectoral approach), sometimes extending to **latissimus dorsi and teres major** — to open the axilla and improve positioning. A derotation humeral osteotomy is an option for fixed bony deformity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A patient with severe spastic quadriplegia has such marked shoulder external-rotation posturing that he cannot pass through a doorway. This underscores which principle of upper-limb reconstruction in CP?

options.text: Proximal stability/position is prerequisite to distal function, and abnormal posture at any level (even excessive external rotation) can impair daily activities
The shoulder is never a surgical target in CP
Only the hand determines function
External rotation is always beneficial

questions.explanation: Although internal rotation is the common shoulder deformity, **excessive external rotation** can also be disabling (e.g., inability to pass through a doorway), illustrating that **the whole limb must be assessed and balanced** — proximal malposition undermines distal hand use. Reconstruction proceeds with attention to shoulder → elbow → forearm → wrist → digits as an integrated plan.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Videotaped/observational functional analysis is recommended in the preoperative assessment of CP because:

options.text: It reveals dynamic muscle firing and joint positioning during real tasks and has been shown to change the surgical plan in a large proportion (>70%) of cases
It measures bone density
It replaces the need for a physical examination
It is only useful postoperatively

questions.explanation: Because CP is a **movement disorder**, static exam under-captures dynamic patterns. **Video/observational analysis during functional tasks** (± dynamic EMG) exposes which muscles fire abnormally and how joints posture in use — information that **altered the surgical plan in over 70% of cases** in one review. It complements standardized tests (SHUEE, AHA, Jebsen-Taylor) in planning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Dynamic fine-needle EMG during motion analysis is particularly valuable in CP surgical planning because it helps the surgeon:

options.text: Distinguish phasic, spastic, dystonic, or flaccid firing patterns and thereby judge whether a muscle is a suitable transfer donor
Measure passive range of motion
Assess bone alignment
Grade sensation

questions.explanation: A candidate donor muscle must fire appropriately (ideally **phasic, under voluntary control**). Dynamic EMG differentiates **phasic vs continuously spastic vs dystonic vs flaccid** activity, so the surgeon can **avoid transferring a muscle with unpredictable/continuous spastic firing** — which would produce an uncontrollable transfer — and select muscles likely to function in their new role.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Multiple simultaneous procedures are commonly performed in a single anesthetic for the CP upper limb because:

options.text: It minimizes the total number of operations/anesthetics a child must undergo while addressing the interdependent multi-joint deformity
Combined procedures always have fewer complications than staged ones
It guarantees a normal limb
Insurance mandates it

questions.explanation: CP deformities are **multi-level and interdependent** (shoulder position affects hand use, wrist affects digits). Performing **several balanced procedures at once** treats the whole chain and **reduces the number of anesthetics/recoveries** for the child, with later 'fine-tuning' only if growth changes the balance. The plan must still be individualized to voluntary control and goals.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A child with spastic CP has a swan-neck posture of the fingers (PIP hyperextension) during attempted extension. What is the usual mechanism, and a reasonable surgical approach?

options.text: Intrinsic (interosseous) spasticity/imbalance drives PIP hyperextension; options include FDS tenodesis/central-slip tenotomy or intrinsic rebalancing to restrain PIP extension
FDP rupture; treat with DIP fusion
Extensor tendon laceration; treat with primary repair
It is unrelated to spasticity and needs no treatment

questions.explanation: Spastic **intrinsic imbalance** hyperextends the PIP (swan-neck), which can lock extension and impair grasp. Surgical options restrain PIP hyperextension — e.g., **FDS tenodesis** to the proximal phalanx or **spiral oblique retinacular reconstruction**, and addressing intrinsic tightness. Correcting the wrist/finger balance overall is part of the plan, since swan-necking often coexists with wrist-flexion deformity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A common and important complication of tendon transfer/lengthening for spastic deformity, particularly if tensioning is aggressive, is:

options.text: Overcorrection into the opposite deformity (e.g., a wrist transferred into fixed extension, or a thumb MCP into hyperextension)
Immediate return of normal cortical control
Malignant transformation of the transferred muscle
Permanent cure with no recurrence

questions.explanation: **Overcorrection** is a recognized pitfall — over-tensioning an FCU-to-ECRB can leave a wrist stuck in extension (worse than the original flexion), and aggressive thumb rebalancing can cause MCP hyperextension. Because spastic tone and growth continue, surgeons **err toward slightly under-correcting active transfers** and plan for possible later adjustment. Recurrence with growth is also possible.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Which feature most distinguishes traumatic brain injury (TBI) from cerebral palsy when planning upper-limb surgery?

options.text: TBI is an acquired injury to a previously normal mature brain that may undergo substantial spontaneous recovery, mandating a period of observation before reconstruction
TBI never causes spasticity
TBI deformities are always fixed from the outset
TBI cannot be treated with tendon transfers

questions.explanation: **TBI is acquired in a formerly normal brain**, so — unlike the static CP lesion — it can **recover for many months**. Management therefore emphasizes **preventing contracture (splinting, casting, botulinum, nerve blocks) while awaiting a neurologic plateau**, with definitive reconstruction deferred (often ~1–1.5 years). TBI patients may also show more **rigidity/mixed tone** and are prone to **heterotopic ossification** around joints.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A patient recovering from severe TBI develops progressive loss of elbow motion with a hard end-feel and periarticular calcification on radiographs. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Heterotopic ossification
Simple myostatic contracture of the biceps
Septic arthritis
Charcot arthropathy

questions.explanation: **Heterotopic ossification (HO)** is common after TBI (and spinal cord injury), producing periarticular bone that mechanically blocks motion — the elbow is a frequent site. It is distinguished from soft-tissue spastic contracture by a **hard end-feel and radiographic ossification**. Management involves therapy to maintain motion, and surgical excision once the HO matures (guided by activity markers/imaging), addressing spasticity concurrently.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Nonoperative management of the spastic upper limb while awaiting surgery (or in non-surgical candidates) includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.text: Early resistance strengthening of the spastic muscles to overpower the deformity
Splinting and serial casting to prevent/reduce contracture
Occupational therapy focused on function and positioning
Botulinum toxin to reduce dynamic tone

questions.explanation: Nonoperative care centers on **maintaining passive motion and preventing contracture** — splinting, serial casting, therapy, and tone reduction with **botulinum toxin** (or oral agents/intrathecal baclofen for global tone). **Strengthening a spastic muscle** is counterproductive; it would reinforce the deforming force. Therapy instead promotes balanced function and positioning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Which statement about the FCU-to-ECRB (Green) transfer's effect on forearm rotation is correct?

options.text: Removing the FCU (a wrist flexor with an ulnar/pronating deforming influence) and routing it dorsally can also improve forearm supination posture
It worsens pronation deformity
It has no effect on forearm rotation
It causes fixed supination contracture in all patients

questions.explanation: Beyond correcting wrist flexion/ulnar deviation, transferring the **FCU dorsally to the ECRB** removes a deforming flexor and can **improve the supination posture** of the forearm, complementing pronator release/rerouting. This multi-benefit is part of why the Green transfer is a workhorse in the functional spastic hand.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: The Volkmann test (passively extending the fingers with the wrist in varying positions) is used in the spastic hand to:

options.text: Detect extrinsic finger-flexor (FDP/FDS) tightness and distinguish it from intrinsic tightness or joint contracture
Grade stereognosis
Measure wrist extensor strength
Assess median nerve compression

questions.explanation: By comparing finger extension achievable with the **wrist flexed vs extended**, the **Volkmann test** reveals **extrinsic flexor tightness**: if the fingers extend with the wrist flexed but not extended, the long flexors are the limiting structure (a tenodesis effect). This distinguishes extrinsic tightness from intrinsic tightness (Bunnell intrinsic-tightness test) or fixed joint contracture, guiding which structures to lengthen.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Selective (or hyperselective) neurectomy in the spastic upper limb works by:

options.text: Partially dividing motor branches to a spastic muscle to reduce its tone while preserving some function
Completely transecting a mixed nerve to anesthetize the limb
Grafting a new nerve into the muscle
Fusing the joint the muscle crosses

questions.explanation: **Selective neurectomy** divides a portion of the **motor branches** to an overactive muscle (e.g., musculocutaneous to biceps/brachialis, or fascicles to pronator/FCU), **reducing spastic tone while retaining useful strength**. 'Hyperselective' techniques target specific intramuscular branches for finer control. It is one of the four toolbox categories and can be combined with lengthening/transfer.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: When counseling about goals, the distinction between a 'functional' and a 'hygienic/positional' operation in CP is that:

options.text: Functional procedures aim to improve active use (requiring voluntary control and sensation); hygienic procedures aim to improve position/care in hands without useful active function
Hygienic procedures always restore active grasp
Functional procedures are only for non-ambulatory patients
There is no meaningful difference between them

questions.explanation: **Functional surgery** (e.g., FCU-to-ECRB, thumb rebalancing) targets **active use** and requires voluntary control, adequate sensation/stereognosis, and cognition. **Hygienic/positional surgery** (e.g., STP transfer, flexor-pronator slide, contracture release) targets **easier care, skin hygiene, and positioning** in a hand without useful active function. Clarifying which goal applies aligns expectations and procedure choice.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with hemiplegic CP is referred for possible hand surgery. Regarding timing of functional tendon transfers in children, which is most accurate?

options.text: Functional transfers are usually deferred until the child is old enough (commonly ~6+ years) for a reliable voluntary motor/sensory exam and therapy participation
Transfers should be done in infancy to prevent any deformity
Surgery is contraindicated until skeletal maturity
Age has no bearing on candidacy

questions.explanation: Reliable assessment of **voluntary control, stereognosis, and cooperation with rehabilitation** is needed to justify a functional transfer, which is usually feasible around **6 years or older**. Earlier intervention is generally limited to tone management (splinting, botulinum) and, when necessary, contracture release. Waiting for a dependable exam avoids operating on a hand whose functional potential is not yet definable.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: For global lower-limb and trunk spasticity in CP, which neurosurgical/pharmacologic tone-reducing options are used (as adjuncts to upper-limb care)?

options.text: Selective dorsal rhizotomy and intrathecal baclofen
Peripheral nerve grafting
Free functioning muscle transfer
Distraction osteogenesis

questions.explanation: **Selective dorsal rhizotomy** (dividing selected dorsal rootlets) and **intrathecal baclofen** reduce global spasticity and are used chiefly for **lower-limb/trunk tone in ambulatory or severely affected children**. They complement targeted upper-limb procedures but do not replace tendon balancing for specific hand deformities.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: In the spastic hand, the reason digital 'opening' (active MCP/IP extension) sits LOWEST on the reconstruction ladder is that:

options.text: Wrist flexion passively opens the digits (tenodesis) which is often adequate, and true synchronous active digital extension is hard to achieve surgically
Finger opening is unimportant for any activity
It is the easiest function to restore surgically
It requires no extrinsic or intrinsic function

questions.explanation: Active digital extension needs coordinated **extrinsic (EDC/EIP/EDM) and intrinsic (interossei/lumbricals for IP extension)** function, which is difficult to reconstruct in a spastic hand. Moreover, **wrist flexion already opens the fingers passively** enough to acquire objects, so 'opening' is prioritized last after wrist extension, pinch, and grasp.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Why does restoring wrist extension improve grip strength beyond simply repositioning the hand?

options.text: It places the finger flexors on a more favorable portion of the length-tension (Blix) curve, increasing active grip force
It shortens the finger flexors permanently
It denervates the finger extensors
It has no biomechanical effect on the flexors

questions.explanation: With the wrist flexed, the extrinsic finger flexors are slackened and generate less force; **extending the wrist tensions them onto the optimal part of the length-tension (Blix) curve**, so active grip is stronger. This biomechanical gain — plus the tenodesis effect — is why wrist extension is the cornerstone of functional reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A spastic thumb-in-palm deformity with a tight extrinsic flexor (the thumb IP cannot be passively extended when the wrist and MCP are stabilized) requires which additional step at surgery?

options.text: Flexor pollicis longus lengthening (fractional or Z-plasty)
FPL tenodesis to the metacarpal
EPL tenotomy
CMC arthrodesis

questions.explanation: If the **FPL is tight** (extrinsic contribution to the thumb-in-palm, House Type IV), releasing the adductor/first web and augmenting extension will not fully correct the thumb unless the **FPL is lengthened**. Fractional or Z-plasty lengthening of the FPL restores passive IP extension while preserving some active flexion for pinch.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Fractional lengthening of a spastic muscle-tendon unit is characterized by which technical feature?

options.text: One or two transverse cuts across the tendon within the muscle-tendon junction, followed by stretching — no tendon suturing required
Complete transection of the muscle (myotomy)
Z-lengthening with end-to-end suture repair
Detaching the muscle origin and letting it slide

questions.explanation: **Fractional lengthening** incises the **tendinous portion within the muscle-tendon junction** (leaving muscle intact on both sides) and then stretches the joint, lengthening the unit **without suturing**. It suits muscles with a **broad MTJ** (e.g., brachialis, wrist flexors) but cannot provide large lengthening or work on muscles with short MTJs (e.g., biceps), where Z-plasty is used instead.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Which combination best exemplifies addressing the interdependent 'chain' of a functional spastic hemiplegic hand in a single setting?

options.text: Elbow flexor lengthening + pronator teres rerouting + FCU-to-ECRB transfer + thumb-in-palm release with MCP stabilization
Isolated wrist arthrodesis only
Botulinum toxin injection to a single muscle only
Shoulder fusion alone

questions.explanation: A functional hemiplegic limb is commonly balanced across levels in one operation: **relieve elbow flexion, correct forearm pronation (PT rerouting for active supination), reposition the wrist (FCU-to-ECRB), and open/stabilize the thumb**. Treating the whole chain — rather than one joint — yields the best composite function and reduces the number of anesthetics.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Which statement about the Modified Ashworth Scale is correct?

options.text: It grades resistance to passive movement from 0 (no increase in tone) to 4 (rigid in flexion/extension), but is not velocity-quantified
It specifically measures the difference between slow and fast stretch angles
It grades voluntary strength
It is a sensory test

questions.explanation: The **Modified Ashworth Scale** rates **passive-movement resistance/tone** on an ordinal scale (**0** = no increase … **1/1+** = slight catch … up to **4** = rigid). It is quick and widely used but does **not quantify velocity dependence** — that is the role of the **Tardieu** scale (R1 vs R2). Both help characterize spasticity and monitor treatment.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: A spastic hand has good voluntary wrist extension but the fingers cannot actively extend even when the wrist is stabilized in neutral. Before or with a wrist-balancing procedure, what should be considered?

options.text: Adding a procedure to improve finger extension (e.g., FCU-to-EDC transfer or flexor lengthening) so the hand can both grasp and release
Nothing further — finger extension is unnecessary
Immediate wrist fusion
Opponensplasty

questions.explanation: A hand that grasps but cannot **release** is poorly functional. If active finger extension is absent with the wrist stabilized, the surgeon should **augment digital extension** (e.g., route the FCU to the EDC instead of the ECRB, and/or lengthen tight flexors) so the reconstructed hand can open as well as close. This is a key planning decision when correcting wrist flexion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Which outcome measure in CP uses an individualized, semi-structured interview to set patient/parent-identified goals and defines a change of ≥2 points as meaningful?

options.text: Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM)
Modified Ashworth Scale
GMFCS
Jebsen-Taylor Hand Function Test

questions.explanation: The **COPM** is an **individualized, goal-based** patient-reported measure: through a semi-structured interview the child/parent identify important activities, rate performance/satisfaction (0–10), and reassess after treatment, with **≥2-point change considered meaningful**. It (with Goal Attainment Scaling) captures whether *the patient's own goals* were met — essential for judging success in this heterogeneous population.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Which patient is the POOREST candidate for a functional (active-use) tendon transfer in the spastic upper limb?

options.text: A child with athetoid movements, absent stereognosis, and poor voluntary control
A cooperative child with spastic hemiplegia, intact stereognosis, and voluntary grasp/release
A teenager with spastic hemiplegia and a supple, well-controlled wrist
A motivated adolescent with good cognition and phasic muscle firing on EMG

questions.explanation: Functional transfers demand **voluntary control, useful sensation (stereognosis), predictable (phasic) muscle firing, and cognitive/motivational engagement**. A child with **athetosis (unpredictable tone), absent stereognosis, and poor voluntary control** meets none of these and is best served by tone management or hygienic procedures — a functional transfer would likely be uncontrolled and the hand neglected.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: Distinguishing a DYNAMIC deformity from a FIXED (myostatic) contracture in the spastic limb is critical because:

options.text: A dynamic deformity is passively correctable and may respond to tone reduction/tendon rebalancing, whereas a fixed contracture requires lengthening/release to regain passive motion
Fixed contractures resolve spontaneously with growth
Dynamic deformities always require arthrodesis
There is no treatment difference between them

questions.explanation: A **dynamic** deformity is fully **passively correctable** (the posture is driven by active spastic tone, not shortened tissue) and can improve with **botulinum toxin, therapy, and tendon transfers/rebalancing**. A **fixed myostatic contracture** has lost passive motion and needs **lengthening or release** first — no transfer moves a joint that cannot be passively positioned. Examining passive versus active range (and Tardieu R1/R2) makes this distinction and drives the operative plan.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 32 (Cerebral Palsy & TBI)

questions.stem: The International Classification for Surgery of the Hand in Tetraplegia (ICSHT) groups patients primarily on the basis of:

options.text: The number/identity of grade ≥4 muscles remaining below the elbow, plus a sensory (O/Cu) designation
The ASIA impairment grade alone
Shoulder and elbow function only
The vertebral level of the fracture on imaging

questions.explanation: The **ICSHT** is a surgical roadmap for the **forearm and hand only** (it excludes the shoulder and considers elbow-extension reconstruction separately). Patients are grouped by the **most distal working (grade ≥4) muscle below the elbow** — each ascending group *adds* one muscle (BR → ECRL → ECRB → PT → FCR → EDC → EPL → digital flexors → all but intrinsics). A **sensory prefix (O or Cu)** is appended. It guides which donors are available for transfer.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: In the ICSHT, the sensory designation precedes the motor group (e.g., 'O2' or 'Cu2'). A patient is designated 'Cu' rather than 'O' when:

options.text: Two-point discrimination in the thumb and index is ≤10 mm (adequate cutaneous afferent)
Vision is the only afferent available
Two-point discrimination exceeds 10 mm
The patient has any elbow flexion

questions.explanation: The Moberg sensory designation: **'Cu'** (adequate cutaneous sensibility) requires **two-point discrimination ≤10 mm in the thumb and index**, meaning the patient can rely on feel to control pinch. **'O'** (ocular) means 2PD >10 mm, so the patient must **watch the hand** (visual feedback) to use it. This distinction affects how aggressively active prehension is reconstructed and how the patient is trained.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: An ICSHT Group 0 patient (≥C5 level) has which muscles available below the elbow, and what are the functional implications?

options.text: No muscles below the elbow — only elbow flexion and supination; hand reconstruction options are very limited and often begin with restoring wrist extension via BR transfer and/or elbow extension
Brachioradialis and ECRL are available
All wrist extensors are available
Finger flexors are available for grasp

questions.explanation: **Group 0** has **no functioning muscle below the elbow** (only biceps/brachialis for elbow flexion and supinator). Reconstruction is limited; priorities are typically **elbow extension** (deltoid/biceps to triceps) and, where a suitable donor exists, restoring **wrist extension** — as the number of distal donors is the main constraint, higher groups permit progressively more (pinch, grasp).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: The first muscle 'added' as one ascends from ICSHT Group 0 to Group 1 is the brachioradialis. Why is the BR such a valuable transfer donor in tetraplegia?

options.text: In most groups the biceps/brachialis still flex the elbow, so the BR is expendable and can be transferred without losing elbow flexion
The BR provides its own sensation to the hand
The BR requires no mobilization to gain excursion
The BR is the only wrist flexor

questions.explanation: The **BR (Group 1, C5)** is the workhorse donor because **elbow flexion is preserved by biceps/brachialis**, making the BR expendable, and it has useful strength. A technical caveat: the BR has **extensive fascial attachments** and must be **widely mobilized proximally** so its whole excursion transfers — otherwise the transfer is weak. It is commonly used for wrist extension (BR→ECRB) or key pinch (BR→FPL).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: The clinical difference between ICSHT Group 2 and Group 3 is the addition of the ECRB (strong wrist extension). At the bedside, how is this distinction made?

options.text: By palpating the wrist extensors during resisted extension (Bean sign) — a group 3 patient fires both ECRL and ECRB with grade 4–5 strength; the bulbous ECRL belly is palpable separate from the flat ECRB
By checking finger flexion strength
By testing thumb opposition
By MRI of the forearm

questions.explanation: **Group 2 (C6)** adds the **ECRL** (wrist extension present but the ECRL may then be needed elsewhere), whereas **Group 3 (C7)** also has the **ECRB** giving *strong* wrist extension, which frees the ECRL as a transfer donor. The **Bean sign** — palpating the bulbous ECRL and the flatter ECRB during resisted wrist extension — helps confirm both are firing (group 3). This matters because a group 3 patient can 'spend' the ECRL for grasp while the ECRB keeps the wrist extended.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: In the tetraplegic hand, which movement sits at the TOP of the reconstruction ladder (highest priority to establish)?

options.text: Wrist extension — it drives tenodesis grasp and lateral pinch and optimizes flexor length-tension
Synchronous digital opening
Intrinsic (interosseous) function
Forearm pronation

questions.explanation: As in the spastic hand, **wrist extension is fundamental**: extending the wrist closes the fingers (tenodesis grasp) and adducts the thumb to the index (tenodesis lateral pinch), and tensions the flexors on the Blix curve for stronger grip. The ladder descends: **lateral pinch → grasp → digital opening** (lowest, since wrist flexion opens the digits passively and active synchronous opening is hard to reconstruct).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A C6 tetraplegic (ICSHT ~2) lacks active wrist extension. Which transfer restores it, and why is wrist extension the logical first hand-reconstruction step?

options.text: Brachioradialis to ECRB; wrist extension enables a tenodesis (automatic) grasp and pinch
Biceps to ECRB; to preserve elbow flexion
Pronator teres to FDP; to restore grasp directly
Deltoid to triceps; to power the wrist

questions.explanation: **BR-to-ECRB** restores active wrist extension when the ECRL/ECRB are insufficient.
