Establishing wrist extension first is logical because it creates the **tenodesis mechanism** on which subsequent pinch/grasp reconstruction relies, and it aligns the flexors for a stronger eventual grip.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Restoring active elbow EXTENSION (triceps function) is a high priority in tetraplegia even though the ICSHT is a hand/forearm scheme. Why?

options.text: It enables overhead reach, wheelchair propulsion, pressure relief/transfers, and stabilizes the arm in space so pinch/grasp can be used effectively
It is required for elbow flexion
It restores hand sensation
It prevents shoulder dislocation

questions.explanation: Most cervical SCI patients retain elbow flexion (biceps/brachialis, C5–6) but **lack triceps (C7)**. Restoring **elbow extension** dramatically improves independence — **reaching overhead, propelling a manual wheelchair, weight-shifting for pressure relief, and transfers** — and it **stabilizes the limb** so a reconstructed pinch/grasp can be positioned and used. It is usually addressed early (before or with pinch/grasp).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A C6 tetraplegic with strong biceps/brachialis undergoes a biceps-to-triceps transfer for elbow extension. What is the key prerequisite and main risk?

options.text: The brachialis (and/or supinator) must maintain elbow flexion after biceps is transferred; the main risk is a loss of elbow-flexion strength or an extension weakness if healing/tensioning is imperfect
The triceps must already be grade 4
It requires sacrificing wrist extension
It provides no benefit over remaining flexed

questions.explanation: **Biceps-to-triceps** reroutes the biceps posteriorly to power extension; it works because **brachialis (and supinator) preserve elbow flexion**. Advantages over deltoid-to-triceps include a strong, direct line of pull without an interposition graft. Risks include some **loss of flexion strength/supination** and, if over- or under-tensioned, an extension lag or flexion contracture — so careful tensioning (elbow near full extension) and staged rehab are essential.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: The classic posterior deltoid-to-triceps transfer (Moberg) for elbow extension characteristically requires:

options.text: An interposition tendon graft (or long tendon extension) to bridge the deltoid to the triceps/olecranon, with a prolonged protected rehabilitation
No graft, because the deltoid reaches the olecranon directly
Sacrifice of the anterior deltoid
Immediate unrestricted elbow flexion postoperatively

questions.explanation: The **posterior deltoid** does not reach the olecranon, so a **tendon graft/extension (e.g., tibialis, toe extensors, or a strip)** bridges the gap to the triceps mechanism. Because the construct has multiple junctures and modest excursion, rehabilitation is **slow and carefully protected** (gradual increase in elbow flexion) to avoid stretching out the repair. It preserves the biceps for flexion (an advantage over biceps-to-triceps).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A wrist-driven flexor-hinge (tenodesis) orthosis is often trialed before surgery in tetraplegia. What principle does it demonstrate?

options.text: Synergistic tenodesis — active wrist extension automatically flexes the fingers/thumb for pinch, and wrist flexion opens them
It powers the fingers with an external motor independent of the wrist
It provides sensation to the hand
It replaces the need for wrist extension

questions.explanation: The **wrist-driven flexor-hinge splint** mechanically links wrist extension to finger flexion, previewing the **tenodesis prehension** that reconstruction aims to create surgically. A patient who benefits from and accepts the splint is a good candidate for tenodesis/transfer-based pinch and grasp; it also builds the motor pattern used postoperatively.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: For a lower-group tetraplegic (ICSHT 1–2, active wrist extension present but few forearm donors), the Moberg procedure restores lateral (key) pinch by:

options.text: A passive 'tenodesis' key pinch — FPL tenodesis to the volar radius plus thumb CMC/IP stabilization, so wrist extension drives the thumb against the index
An active BR-to-FPL transfer
Free functioning gracilis transfer
Median nerve grafting

questions.explanation: The **Moberg key-pinch** is a **passive/tenodesis** reconstruction for patients lacking a spare active donor: the **FPL is tenodesed to the volar radius** so that wrist extension tightens it and pulls the thumb against the index (lateral pinch), with **CMC positioning/stabilization and IP stabilization** to prevent collapse. Higher-group patients with a spare donor (e.g., BR) instead get an **active BR-to-FPL** transfer.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: During key-pinch reconstruction, a 'split FPL to EPL' tenodesis (Mohammed) is often added. What complication does it prevent?

options.text: Excessive thumb IP joint flexion (Froment-type collapse) during pinch, by balancing the FPL pull across the IP joint
MCP joint dislocation
Wrist flexion contracture
Loss of forearm supination

questions.explanation: When the FPL powers key pinch, unopposed flexion can **buckle the thumb IP joint into hyperflexion** (a Froment-like collapse), giving pulp-to-side rather than tip pinch. **Splitting the FPL and tenodesing a slip to the EPL (or an IP stabilization/tenodesis)** balances the IP joint so pinch occurs at the pad with a stable thumb. Thumb CMC fusion in a pinch position further optimizes the posture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: In a group 4 tetraplegic (BR and ECRL both available as donors), the classic combination to restore active prehension is:

options.text: BR to FPL (key pinch) and ECRL to FDP (finger flexion/grasp), often with CMC fusion and EPL/EDC tenodesis for opening
BR to FDP and ECRL to FPL
ECRL to triceps and BR to EDC
PT to FPL and FCR to FDP

questions.explanation: A **group 4** patient has wrist extension (ECRB) preserved, freeing the **BR and ECRL**. The **BR → FPL** (lower excursion needed, for pinch) and **ECRL → FDP** (synergistic, greater excursion, for grasp) is the standard active reconstruction, augmented by **CMC fusion** for a stable pinch post and **EPL/EDC tenodesis** to open the digits for object acquisition. Intrinsic reconstruction can be staged later.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Why is the ECRL preferentially transferred to the FDP (rather than the reverse pairing with BR) when both are available?

options.text: The ECRL has greater excursion (synergistic with grasp) matching the long profundus travel, while the BR's shorter excursion suits the FPL
The ECRL cannot reach the thumb
The BR is too strong for the FDP
The ECRL is the only wrist flexor

questions.explanation: Donor–recipient matching by **excursion/amplitude** is key: the **ECRL** provides the larger excursion needed to flex the long **FDP** tendons (grasp), and its action is **synergistic** (wrist extension normally accompanies grip). The **BR's** relatively shorter effective excursion (even after mobilization) is better matched to the **FPL** for key pinch.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Thumb carpometacarpal (CMC) arthrodesis is frequently combined with key-pinch reconstruction in tetraplegia because:

options.text: It fixes the thumb metacarpal in a stable adduction/opposition position so pinch force is directed usefully against the index rather than dissipated at an unstable joint
It restores CMC motion
It lengthens the FPL
It is required to power elbow extension

questions.explanation: A lax, unstable **CMC** joint lets the thumb wander so that pinch force is wasted. **CMC fusion in a pinch-optimized position** provides a stable post against which the FPL-driven thumb can generate effective lateral pinch. It is a common adjunct to both Moberg (passive) and active pinch reconstructions.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Regarding TIMING of reconstructive surgery after cervical spinal cord injury, which is most accurate?

options.text: Wait until neurologic recovery plateaus (commonly ~1 year), the spine is stable, and the patient is medically/psychologically ready — because spontaneous recovery can occur, especially in the first months
Operate within the first 2 weeks to prevent contracture
Only operate after 10 years
Timing is irrelevant to outcome

questions.explanation: Neurologic recovery — including conversion of some initially grade-0 muscles — continues for months, so **definitive reconstruction is deferred until the exam is stable (~1 year)**, the **spine is stable** (confirmed on flexion/extension films), and the patient is medically fit and **psychologically ready** with realistic goals. (Exception: certain **nerve transfers** are done earlier, before distal muscle degeneration — see below.) Contracture is prevented meanwhile with therapy/splinting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Nerve transfers (e.g., a brachialis motor branch to the anterior interosseous nerve) are increasingly used in tetraplegia. Compared with tendon transfers, a critical timing and feasibility requirement for nerve transfer is:

options.text: It must be done relatively early (before the denervated target muscle degenerates) and requires an intact lower motor neuron/reflex arc to the recipient muscle
It can be done at any time regardless of muscle degeneration
It requires a completely flail limb with no reflexes
It provides immediate full strength on the operating table

questions.explanation: A nerve transfer reinnervates a muscle, so the **target's lower motor neuron/reflex arc must be intact** and the transfer performed **before irreversible muscle degeneration** (generally within ~6–12 months) — unlike **tendon transfers, which can be done at any time** (they use an already-innervated donor). Nerve transfers can restore, e.g., finger/thumb flexion (branch→AIN) or extension (supinator→PIN) and may reach muscles hard to power by tendon transfer. Strength develops over months as reinnervation matures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Whether a paralyzed forearm muscle in tetraplegia can be reinnervated by a nerve transfer depends on the injury pattern at that spinal segment. Which situation permits nerve transfer to that muscle?

options.text: Upper-motor-neuron pattern — the muscle's anterior horn cell/peripheral nerve (lower motor neuron) is intact but lacks supraspinal control
Lower-motor-neuron destruction of that segment with a degenerated muscle
Complete transection of the peripheral nerve to that muscle
Any pattern, as innervation is irrelevant

questions.explanation: Cervical SCI can damage the **cord segment (lower motor neuron, at the level of injury)** and/or leave **infralesional muscles with intact LMN but no supraspinal control (upper-motor-neuron pattern)**. Only muscles whose **LMN is intact** can be usefully **reinnervated by a nerve transfer** (and can also be driven by FES). Muscles whose anterior horn cells were destroyed are denervated and degenerate — better served by tendon transfer or tenodesis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A functional neuromuscular stimulation (FES) neuroprosthesis restores grasp in selected tetraplegics by:

options.text: Electrically stimulating infralesional paralyzed muscles that retain intact reflex arcs, controlled by a voluntary signal from above the injury
Regrowing severed spinal cord axons
Replacing tendons with synthetic material
Stimulating muscles whose lower motor neurons are destroyed

questions.explanation: The **FES neuroprosthesis** (e.g., Freehand system) stimulates **infralesional muscles that are paralyzed but have intact LMN/reflex arcs**, producing graded contraction; the patient controls it with a **volitional signal from a supralesional site** (e.g., contralateral shoulder). It is an option when standard transfers/orthoses cannot provide useful prehension. Muscles with destroyed LMNs cannot be electrically driven.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A patient with tetraplegia rests the thumb in full supination with no tenodesis pinch on passive wrist extension. What does this imply for pinch reconstruction?

options.text: Skeletal stabilization (CMC fusion in a key-pinch position) is needed, because tendon procedures alone cannot create pinch without a stable, properly positioned thumb
The patient needs no surgery
A simple FPL tenodesis will suffice without repositioning
Nerve grafting is the only option

questions.explanation: Successful prehension requires **passive mobility and a usable tenodesis vector**. A thumb fixed in **supination with no tenodesis pinch** will not pinch usefully from tendon work alone — it must be **repositioned and stabilized (CMC arthrodesis in adduction/opposition)** so subsequent FPL tenodesis/transfer directs force against the index. Assessing passive posture/tenodesis preoperatively prevents predictable failures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: The ASIA Impairment Scale grade 'A' denotes:

options.text: A complete injury — no motor or sensory function preserved in the lowest sacral segments (S4–S5)
Normal motor and sensory function
Incomplete injury with preserved motor function below the level
Isolated sensory sparing only

questions.explanation: **ASIA A = complete** (no sensory/motor function in S4–S5). **B** = sensory but not motor incomplete; **C/D** = motor incomplete (most key muscles below the level < or ≥ grade 3, respectively); **E** = normal. The ASIA grade complements — but does not replace — the **ICSHT**, which specifically guides forearm/hand surgical planning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A prerequisite of the tetraplegic hand for successful tendon-transfer/tenodesis reconstruction is:

options.text: Supple, passively mobile joints with a demonstrable tenodesis effect
Fixed contractures to provide stability
Absent tenodesis effect
Grade 5 intrinsic muscles

questions.explanation: Reconstruction depends on a **supple hand with a working tenodesis mechanism** — passively flexing/extending the wrist should tension the digital flexors/extensors. **Fixed contractures** must be released first, and a hand with no tenodesis potential needs **skeletal stabilization** (e.g., CMC fusion) before tendon procedures can create prehension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Before proceeding with upper-limb reconstruction in a tetraplegic patient, which imaging is specifically obtained to confirm readiness for surgery?

options.text: Flexion and extension lateral cervical radiographs to confirm spinal stability
Whole-body PET scan
Upper-limb angiography
Bone density scan

questions.explanation: **Dynamic (flexion/extension) lateral cervical spine radiographs** confirm the fusion/spine is **stable** before positioning the neck for prolonged upper-limb surgery and rehabilitation. Advanced imaging of the limb is not routinely required — planning is largely clinical (manual muscle testing, sensibility, tenodesis, passive motion).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Approximately what fraction of muscles graded 0 at one month after cervical SCI may recover some function, underscoring why early reconstruction is avoided?

options.text: About one-third
Essentially none
About 90%
All of them

questions.explanation: Roughly **one-third of muscles classified grade 0 at one month can regain some function** over subsequent months. This capacity for spontaneous recovery is a major reason to **defer irreversible tendon reconstruction until the neurologic picture stabilizes (~1 year)** — operating too early risks sacrificing a donor that would have recovered, or reconstructing around a level that will change.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: When both elbow-extension and hand (pinch/grasp) reconstructions are planned in the same limb, the usual sequencing is:

options.text: Address elbow extension first (or protect it), because postoperative rehab of a distal transfer must not disrupt a healing triceps reconstruction — and stable elbow control aids hand use
Always do the hand first and ignore the elbow
Do both plus the shoulder in one stage regardless of rehab conflicts
Never reconstruct the elbow in tetraplegia

questions.explanation: Because a **triceps (elbow-extension) reconstruction requires protected, staged elbow motion**, it is typically **done first (or carefully sequenced)** so that later hand-transfer rehabilitation — which involves wrist/forearm and elbow positioning — does not stress the healing elbow. A stable, extendable elbow also lets the reconstructed hand be positioned in space for use. Surgery is generally staged and often one limb at a time.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: In restoring active finger extension/opening for object acquisition in tetraplegia, why is a simple extrinsic transfer often insufficient, and what adjunct is used?

options.text: Extrinsics extend the MCP but not the IP joints; limiting MCP hyperextension (e.g., Zancolli FDS tenodesis / House intrinsic tenodesis / a lumbrical bar) is needed for IP extension
Extrinsic transfers reliably extend all joints, so no adjunct is needed
Only nerve transfer can produce any MCP extension
A wrist fusion restores finger opening

questions.explanation: Extrinsic extensors (**EDC/EIP/EDM**) extend the **MCP** joints; **IP extension is intrinsic** (interossei/lumbricals). To get the extrinsic system to also extend the IPs, MCP hyperextension must be **restrained** — e.g., **Zancolli FDS tenodesis, House intrinsic tenodesis, or a therapist-made lumbrical bar**. Full active synchronous opening is difficult, which is why 'opening' sits lowest on the ladder (wrist flexion opens the hand passively).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A drawback of the Zancolli FDS tenodesis (looping FDS to limit MCP hyperextension) reported in tetraplegia is:

options.text: It can restrict FDP excursion and may attenuate/stretch over time
It always causes tendon rupture
It eliminates all wrist motion
It denervates the intrinsics

questions.explanation: The **Zancolli FDS tenodesis** can **limit FDP (grasp) excursion** and tends to **attenuate over time**, reducing its corrective effect. The **House intrinsic tenodesis** is an alternative but is technically demanding (graft tensioning is difficult). A simpler **lumbrical bar orthosis** is sometimes preferred to block MCP hyperextension without a surgical juncture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: In a high (ICSHT 0–1) tetraplegic where no forearm donor exists for active grasp, an option to give automatic finger flexion is:

options.text: FDP flexor tenodesis to the radius (passive wrist-extension–driven grasp), possibly combined with an FES system or nerve transfer where feasible
ECRL-to-FDP transfer
BR-to-FPL and ECRL-to-FDP
No option exists

questions.explanation: With **no spare active donor** (high groups), grasp can still be provided **passively by tenodesing the FDP to the radius**, so wrist extension flexes the fingers (and wrist flexion releases). Where a suitable LMN-intact target exists, a **nerve transfer** (e.g., to AIN) or an **FES neuroprosthesis** can restore more active flexion. Reconstruction is inherently more limited than in lower groups.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: The most common and functionally important prehension pattern targeted in tetraplegia reconstruction is:

options.text: Lateral (key) pinch
Fine tip-to-tip precision pinch
Full power grasp with intrinsic balancing
Hook grip only

questions.explanation: **Lateral (key) pinch** — thumb pad against the radial index — is used for the majority of daily tasks (holding utensils, turning a key, managing catheters), and is more attainable and durable than fine precision pinch. Reconstruction therefore prioritizes a **strong, stable key pinch** (via Moberg tenodesis or active BR-to-FPL with CMC fusion) before power grasp and opening.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: In ICSHT terms, a patient who has all forearm/hand muscles working EXCEPT the intrinsics (able to roll the digits fully into the palm) is classified as:

options.text: Group 9
Group 2
Group 5
Group 0

questions.explanation: **Group 9 (lacks only intrinsics)** is the highest ICSHT group — the patient achieves **complete digital roll-up** but lacks intrinsic (interossei/lumbrical) balance, so reconstruction focuses on **intrinsic substitution/claw correction** rather than restoring extrinsic power. **Group X** denotes exceptions that don't fit the ordered scheme.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Why must the brachioradialis be extensively mobilized proximally before it is used as a transfer in tetraplegia?

options.text: Its dense fascial attachments otherwise limit excursion, making the transfer weak; freeing it maximizes amplitude
To identify and preserve its sensory branch to the hand
To convert it into a wrist flexor
Because it is normally paralyzed and must be reinnervated

questions.explanation: The **BR has broad fascial adhesions along the forearm**; without extensive proximal release its effective **excursion/amplitude is poor**, and the transfer under-performs. Thorough mobilization (up toward its innervation, which must be preserved) is a key technical step to make BR→FPL or BR→ECRB effective.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: The primary goal that distinguishes elbow-extension reconstruction from hand reconstruction in a wheelchair-dependent tetraplegic is that elbow extension specifically enables:

options.text: Weight-shifting for pressure relief, transfers, and overhead reach — key for independence and skin protection
Fine pinch for writing
Forearm pronation for typing
Wrist tenodesis grasp

questions.explanation: Active **elbow extension** lets a patient **push up to relieve ischial pressure (preventing pressure sores), perform transfers, propel a manual wheelchair, and reach overhead** — high-impact independence gains distinct from the prehension goals of hand surgery. This is why restoring the triceps is a major, often first, reconstructive target.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A C5-6 SCI patient has developed a fixed supination deformity of the forearm from unopposed biceps with paralyzed pronators. A described treatment is:

options.text: Biceps rerouting (Zancolli) to convert the biceps into a pronator, ± release of the interosseous membrane for fixed deformity
Triceps lengthening
Wrist arthrodesis
FPL tenodesis

questions.explanation: In high SCI, **unopposed biceps** (with paralyzed pronator teres/quadratus) can drive a **fixed supination deformity** that impairs hand placement. **Zancolli biceps rerouting** redirects the biceps tendon around the radius so it acts as a **pronator**; a longstanding fixed deformity may also require **interosseous membrane release** to regain passive rotation before rebalancing.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Which statement about using the pronator teres as a transfer donor in a group 4 tetraplegic is correct?

options.text: It is available but harvesting it can reduce pronation power and impair manual wheelchair propulsion, so it is used cautiously
It is never available in group 4
Its harvest has no functional cost
It is the preferred donor for key pinch over the BR

questions.explanation: A **group 4** patient has a working **pronator teres**, which *can* be transferred, but doing so **weakens forearm pronation** — a movement important for **wheelchair propulsion and hand placement** in tetraplegia. Surgeons therefore weigh this cost and often prefer the **BR and ECRL** as donors, reserving the PT unless its loss is acceptable.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A key advantage of biceps-to-triceps over posterior deltoid-to-triceps for restoring elbow extension is:

options.text: A stronger, more direct transfer that usually needs no interposition graft and permits a somewhat faster rehabilitation
It preserves the biceps for elbow flexion
It requires a long tendon graft
It restores hand sensation

questions.explanation: **Biceps-to-triceps** provides a **strong, direct line of pull generally without a graft**, and rehabilitation can be less protracted than the graft-dependent deltoid-to-triceps. Its trade-off is **relying on brachialis/supinator to preserve elbow flexion** (and some loss of supination). **Deltoid-to-triceps** preserves the biceps but needs a graft and slow rehab — the choice depends on the patient's musculature and goals.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: The ICSHT explicitly does NOT classify which region, requiring separate consideration?

options.text: The shoulder (and the decision for elbow-extension transfer is considered separately)
The wrist
The thumb
The fingers

questions.explanation: The ICSHT is a **forearm-and-hand** scheme; it **excludes the shoulder**, and suitability for **elbow-extension reconstruction (deltoid- or biceps-to-triceps) is assessed separately**. This is why a full tetraplegia plan combines the ICSHT hand grouping with independent evaluation of shoulder function and elbow extension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: For an 'O' (ocular) designation tetraplegic hand (2PD >10 mm) after prehension reconstruction, rehabilitation must emphasize:

options.text: Visual monitoring of the hand during grasp/pinch, since cutaneous feedback is inadequate to modulate force
Blindfolded training to build stereognosis
No feedback is needed
Reliance on proprioception alone

questions.explanation: An **'O' hand lacks adequate cutaneous sensibility (2PD >10 mm)**, so the patient cannot feel to grade pinch force and must **use vision to guide and monitor** grasp/pinch. This influences training and realistic expectations; a **'Cu'** hand (2PD ≤10 mm) can rely on feel and generally achieves more automatic use.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Which best summarizes the overall surgical strategy in tetraplegia?

options.text: Match what the patient HAS (available grade ≥4 donors) with what the patient NEEDS (per the reconstruction ladder), using transfers, tenodeses, and selective arthrodeses
Apply the same single transfer to every patient regardless of level
Restore intrinsic function before wrist extension
Avoid all arthrodeses

questions.explanation: Planning is individualized: catalog the **available donors (ICSHT group)**, define the **needs by the reconstruction ladder (elbow extension → wrist extension → key pinch → grasp → opening)**, and combine **tendon transfers, tenodeses, and targeted arthrodeses (e.g., CMC fusion)** — increasingly supplemented by **nerve transfers/FES** — to build durable, useful function.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A group 2 (C6) tetraplegic has active wrist extension via the ECRL but no ECRB. If the ECRL is transferred away for grasp, what problem can arise, and how is it avoided?

options.text: Loss of active wrist extension — so wrist extension must be secured first (e.g., BR-to-ECRB) before spending the ECRL, or the ECRL is not used as the donor
Loss of elbow flexion — avoided by sparing the biceps
Loss of sensation — avoided by nerve graft
No problem occurs

questions.explanation: In **group 2**, the ECRL is the *only* strong wrist extensor (no ECRB), so transferring it for grasp would **abolish active wrist extension** and the tenodesis mechanism. Wrist extension must be **preserved or reconstructed first** (e.g., **BR-to-ECRB**) before the ECRL can be spent — or a different donor plan is used. This contrasts with **group 3**, where the ECRB keeps the wrist extended and frees the ECRL.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Postoperative rehabilitation after tendon transfers in tetraplegia differs from able-bodied transfers chiefly in that:

options.text: It must account for the patient's overall function (transfers, wheelchair use, pressure relief) and protect the reconstruction while preserving independence, often with staged, one-limb-at-a-time surgery
No immobilization is ever used
Immediate unrestricted use is encouraged
Rehabilitation is unnecessary

questions.explanation: Because tetraplegic patients depend on their arms for **transfers, weight-shifts, and mobility**, rehabilitation must **protect the healing transfer while preserving essential independence** — hence surgery is frequently **staged and done one limb at a time** so the other arm remains usable. Motor re-education (learning the new action of a transferred donor) and careful progression are central to a good outcome.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A described nerve transfer to restore finger/thumb FLEXION (grasp) in appropriate tetraplegic patients uses which donor and recipient?

options.text: A brachialis motor branch transferred to the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN)
The musculocutaneous nerve to the radial nerve
The ulnar nerve to the median nerve
The suprascapular nerve to the AIN

questions.explanation: A **brachialis branch (from the musculocutaneous nerve) to the AIN** can reinnervate **FPL and FDP (index/long)** to restore active flexion/pinch, provided the target muscles' LMN is intact and the transfer is done before degeneration. Analogously, a **supinator branch to the PIN** can restore finger/thumb extension. These expand options beyond classic tendon transfers, particularly when done early.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Which finding would make a tetraplegic patient a POOR candidate for an active-transfer key pinch, favoring instead a passive Moberg-type or skeletal approach?

options.text: No expendable grade ≥4 forearm donor available (e.g., low ICSHT group with wrist extension but nothing to spare)
Two or more spare grade ≥4 donors below the elbow
Excellent cutaneous sensibility
Supple, mobile joints with good tenodesis

questions.explanation: An **active** transfer needs an **expendable strong donor**. In **low ICSHT groups (e.g., 1–2)** with few donors, there may be nothing to spare for an active pinch without sacrificing another needed function — so a **passive (tenodesis) Moberg key pinch with CMC/IP stabilization** is chosen. Higher groups (3–4+) with spare BR/ECRL permit **active** BR-to-FPL pinch and ECRL-to-FDP grasp.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Segmental innervation (Zancolli) explains why, after a cervical SCI, the pattern of weakness is predictable. Which principle is correct?

options.text: Motor nuclei cephalad to the injury remain functional; those at and caudal to the level become nonfunctional, producing a level-based deficit
Weakness is random and unrelated to the injury level
Muscles caudal to the injury are always spared
The deficit mirrors a peripheral nerve distribution

questions.explanation: Anterior horn cells are arranged in **longitudinal columns by segment**, so a cord injury spares **muscles innervated above the level** and impairs **those at/below it** — a **predictable, level-based pattern** distinct from peripheral nerve or plexus injuries. This segmental logic underlies the ICSHT ordering (each ascending group adds the muscle of the next caudal segment).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: The deltoid and biceps are innervated at a HIGHER cervical level than the triceps. What is the clinical corollary in tetraplegia?

options.text: Many patients retain elbow flexion and deltoid function but lack triceps, making elbow-extension reconstruction (deltoid/biceps to triceps) commonly needed
Patients lose elbow flexion before triceps
The triceps is always the first muscle to recover
Deltoid and triceps share the same segment

questions.explanation: Because **deltoid and biceps are C5–6 (higher) and triceps is C7 (lower)**, a mid-cervical injury typically **preserves shoulder abduction and elbow flexion but abolishes elbow extension**. Hence the frequent need to reconstruct the **triceps** — transferring the **posterior deltoid or biceps** — to regain elbow extension for reach, transfers, and pressure relief.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST appropriate step when planning tetraplegia hand reconstruction?

options.text: Transferring the sole remaining wrist extensor away for grasp without first securing wrist extension
Confirming spinal stability with flexion/extension films
Documenting the ICSHT group and O/Cu sensibility
Ensuring supple joints and a working tenodesis before transfer

questions.explanation: Spending the **only wrist extensor** (e.g., the ECRL in a group 2 patient) for grasp **abolishes the tenodesis mechanism** and is a planning error — wrist extension must be secured first. The other three are sound prerequisites: **confirm spine stability, classify the patient (ICSHT/sensibility), and verify supple joints with tenodesis** before committing to transfers.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: The overall aim of upper-limb surgery in tetraplegia is best described as:

options.text: Restoring key functional milestones (elbow extension, wrist extension, key pinch, grasp) to improve independence in daily activities — not restoring a normal hand
Achieving a fully normal, sensate hand
Cosmetic improvement only
Reversing the spinal cord injury

questions.explanation: Reconstruction aims to gain **specific, high-value functions** — elbow extension, wrist extension, lateral pinch, and grasp — that substantially improve **independence and quality of life** (feeding, hygiene, transfers, device use). It cannot restore normal control or sensation, so **shared, realistic goals** and appropriate patient selection are central to success.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Classic two-stage grasp-and-release reconstruction in tetraplegia (e.g., for C6–C7 patients) typically sequences the stages as:

options.text: First stage restores the extensor/opening side (and passive positioning), second stage restores the flexor/grasp side — so a balanced open-and-close hand results
Both flexors and extensors are reconstructed in a single tendon juncture
The intrinsic muscles are reconstructed before any extrinsic function
Only the flexor side is ever addressed

questions.explanation: Restoring a hand that both **opens and closes** usually requires staging: one stage establishes **digital extension/opening (and thumb positioning)** and a later stage restores **active flexion/grasp**, allowing tensions to be set and healed independently. Staging (and often doing one limb at a time) reduces the risk of an imbalanced hand and protects each set of junctures during rehabilitation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A recognized late complication of a passive FPL-tenodesis (Moberg) key pinch is:

options.text: Attenuation/stretching of the tenodesis over time with loss of pinch force, sometimes requiring revision or conversion to an active transfer
Permanent improvement in strength with time
Spontaneous restoration of intrinsic function
Development of normal cutaneous sensation

questions.explanation: **Tenodesis constructs are passive and can stretch/attenuate** over months to years, weakening the key pinch; **thumb IP collapse** and **CMC malposition** are other failure modes. When a spare active donor exists, an **active BR-to-FPL transfer** is more durable. Careful CMC/IP stabilization and appropriate tensioning at surgery reduce attenuation-related failure.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: Compared with tendon transfer, a distinct ADVANTAGE of nerve transfer in appropriately selected tetraplegic patients is that it:

options.text: Reinnervates the native muscle (preserving its length-tension relationship and potentially restoring several muscles) without sacrificing a working donor tendon
Produces immediate maximal strength
Works even when the target muscle's lower motor neuron is destroyed
Requires no intact donor nerve

questions.explanation: Nerve transfer **reinnervates the patient's own muscle in situ**, keeping its natural excursion/length-tension and sometimes restoring **multiple muscles from one coaptation**, without spending a working tendon donor. Its trade-offs are a **months-long delay** while axons regenerate and the strict requirements of an **intact recipient LMN** and **early timing** before muscle degeneration — otherwise a tendon transfer/tenodesis is preferable.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 33 (Tetraplegia)

questions.stem: A 24-year-old motorcyclist has a flail, insensate arm after a high-speed crash. This complete C5–T1 (pan-plexus) pattern accounts for what proportion of supraclavicular brachial plexus injuries?

options.text: About 50–75%
About 5%
About 10%
Under 1%

questions.explanation: **Pan-plexus (C5–T1) injuries make up roughly 50–75% of supraclavicular brachial plexus injuries** and typically present as a **completely flail, insensate limb**. Even in a 'complete' picture, the pattern is often mixed — some elements (especially C5) are postganglionic ruptures while others are preganglionic avulsions — which matters greatly for reconstruction because avulsed roots cannot be grafted.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: The single most common mechanism of traumatic brachial plexus injury is:

options.text: Traction/stretch
Sharp laceration
Gunshot
Iatrogenic surgical injury

questions.explanation: **Traction (stretch)** — classically high-energy motorcycle/vehicle trauma — causes the majority of traumatic plexus injuries, producing a spectrum from neurapraxia to rupture and root avulsion within the same patient. Roughly **two-thirds are supraclavicular**. Gunshot injuries are usually in continuity (often observed), while sharp lacerations transect and need early exploration.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A fundamental distinction in brachial plexus injury is preganglionic (avulsion) versus postganglionic (rupture/stretch). Why is this distinction so critical for management?

options.text: A preganglionic (root avulsion) lesion cannot be repaired/grafted, so reconstruction must rely on nerve transfers from outside sources; postganglionic ruptures can be grafted
Preganglionic injuries always recover spontaneously
Postganglionic injuries can never be repaired
The distinction has no bearing on surgical planning

questions.explanation: In a **preganglionic (avulsion)** injury the root is torn from the cord — there is **no proximal stump to graft**, so reconstruction depends on **nerve transfers (neurotization)** using intact donors (spinal accessory, intercostals, contralateral C7, etc.). A **postganglionic rupture** leaves a proximal stump that can be **repaired or grafted**. Determining which levels are pre- vs postganglionic drives the entire operative plan.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which anatomic fact explains why the LOWER roots (C8–T1) are more likely to AVULSE while the UPPER roots (C5–C6) tend to rupture distal to the foramen?

options.text: The C5–C6 roots have stronger supporting/anchoring connective tissue at the foramen than the weakly anchored C8–T1 roots
The lower roots are thicker and more resistant
The upper roots lack dorsal root ganglia
The lower roots exit higher in the neck

questions.explanation: The **C5–C6 roots are anchored by robust supporting tissue** at the transverse processes/foramina, so under traction they tend to **rupture extraforaminally (postganglionic)**. The **C8–T1 roots are weakly anchored**, so they more readily **avulse from the cord (preganglionic)**. This anatomic gradient underlies the clinical patterns and the frequent finding of Horner syndrome with lower-root avulsion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A patient with a lower-plexus traction injury has ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the affected side. What does this Horner syndrome indicate?

options.text: Preganglionic avulsion of the C8 and/or T1 roots (interruption of sympathetic outflow near the T1 ganglion)
An isolated postganglionic upper-trunk rupture
A good prognosis for spontaneous recovery
Injury limited to the suprascapular nerve

questions.explanation: **Horner syndrome** (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, ± enophthalmos) strongly correlates with **avulsion of the lower roots (C8/T1)** — the sympathetic fibers to the head exit near T1, so a lower-root avulsion interrupts them. It signals a **severe, preganglionic** injury with poor spontaneous-recovery prognosis and mandates a transfer-based reconstruction plan.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which physical-examination or imaging finding suggests a PREGANGLIONIC (root avulsion) injury?

options.text: Winged scapula (serratus anterior/long thoracic loss) and rhomboid weakness (dorsal scapular nerve), plus a pseudomeningocele on imaging
Tenderness/Tinel over the supraclavicular fossa
An advancing distal Tinel sign
Preserved sweating in the affected dermatomes

questions.explanation: Because the **dorsal scapular (rhomboids) and long thoracic (serratus anterior) nerves arise very proximally (at the root level)**, their loss (rhomboid weakness, **winged scapula**) implies a **very proximal/preganglionic** injury. A **pseudomeningocele** on CT-myelography/MRI, a **positive histamine (triple-response) test**, and **absent neck Tinel/tenderness** likewise favor avulsion. Conversely, supraclavicular tenderness/Tinel and loss of sweating favor a postganglionic lesion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old has weak shoulder abduction/external rotation and weak elbow flexion/supination after a fall, but normal wrist, finger, and elbow-extension function. Sensory loss is over the lateral arm/forearm and thumb. Which pattern is this?

options.text: C5–C6 (upper trunk) — Erb/Erb-Duchenne palsy
C8–T1 — Klumpke palsy
Pan-plexus (C5–T1)
Posterior cord injury

questions.explanation: The **C5–C6 (upper trunk)** pattern — **Erb-Duchenne palsy** — impairs the suprascapular, axillary, and musculocutaneous territories: **shoulder abduction/ER (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, deltoid), elbow flexion (biceps/brachialis/BR), and supination**, with C5–C6 sensory loss. Hand and elbow extension are spared. It accounts for ~15% of injuries and is a prime target for nerve transfers (e.g., spinal accessory→suprascapular, Oberlin).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: The 'Erb-plus' pattern refers to which injury?

options.text: C5–C7 — an upper-trunk (C5–C6) pattern plus C7/middle-trunk involvement adding variable wrist/finger extensor weakness
An isolated C7 lesion
C8–T1 with hand intrinsic loss
A pure posterior cord lesion

questions.explanation: **C5–C7 ('Erb-plus')** combines the Erb (C5–C6) deficits with **C7/middle-trunk involvement**, adding **variable elbow/wrist/finger extensor weakness** (and sometimes FDP), plus thumb/index/middle sensory changes. It occurs in ~20–35% of patients and can occasionally mimic a pure C5–C6 pattern depending on the C7 contribution.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A patient has intact shoulder and elbow function but weak hand intrinsics and finger flexors with sensory loss over the ulnar forearm/hand and a Horner sign. Which pattern is this?

options.text: C8–T1 — Klumpke (Dejerine-Klumpke) palsy
C5–C6 — Erb palsy
Posterior cord injury
Isolated suprascapular nerve palsy

questions.explanation: The **C8–T1 (lower-plexus)** pattern — **Klumpke palsy** — impairs the **hand intrinsics and long finger flexors** with **ulnar-sided sensory loss** and a frequent **Horner sign** (lower-root avulsion). Isolated traumatic C8–T1 lesions are uncommon (~10% or less) because the lower roots tend to avulse in more severe, extensive injuries. Distant intrinsic targets recover poorly, so reconstruction is challenging.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: For a brachial plexus stretch injury being observed for spontaneous recovery, surgery is generally indicated if no recovery appears within approximately what interval?

options.text: About 3 months (with many advocating exploration by ~3–6 months)
2 years
2 weeks
Recovery time is irrelevant; always observe indefinitely

questions.explanation: For **closed traction/stretch injuries**, an initial period of observation (serial exams, EMG) is reasonable, but **absence of recovery by ~3 months** (and generally by 3–6 months) is an indication for exploration/reconstruction, because delay risks irreversible motor-endplate degeneration — especially for distal targets. **Preganglionic signs** (Horner, winged scapula, pseudomeningoceles) prompt **earlier** surgery, and **sharp lacerations** are explored acutely/subacutely.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A patient sustains a sharp knife laceration to the supraclavicular fossa with an immediate complete C5–C6 deficit. What is the appropriate timing of surgery?

options.text: Early (acute/subacute) exploration and repair, since a sharp transection will not recover spontaneously
Observe 6 months before deciding
Observe 2 years for spontaneous recovery
Never explore penetrating plexus injuries

questions.explanation: **Sharp lacerations transect the plexus and will not recover**, so — like sharp peripheral nerve cuts — they warrant **acute or subacute exploration and direct repair (or graft)**, ideally before retraction/fibrosis. This contrasts with **gunshot** injuries (usually in continuity → mostly observed) and **closed traction** injuries (observe then explore by ~3 months if no recovery).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Most gunshot-associated brachial plexus injuries are managed initially by:

options.text: Observation, because the plexal elements are usually in continuity with potential for spontaneous recovery
Immediate exploration and grafting in all cases
Primary amputation
Immediate root reimplantation

questions.explanation: In most **gunshot** injuries the nerves are **in continuity** (damaged by shock/cavitation rather than transected), so **initial observation** is appropriate, with exploration reserved for failure of recovery (more likely with high-velocity rounds) or an associated **vascular injury/expanding pseudoaneurysm** compressing the plexus. Low-velocity direct impact occasionally transects elements.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: On CT-myelography of a plexus injury, a pseudomeningocele at a given level indicates:

options.text: Root avulsion at that level (a dural tear allows contrast/CSF to pool), i.e., a preganglionic injury
A postganglionic rupture that can be grafted
Normal anatomy
A recovering neurapraxia

questions.explanation: A **pseudomeningocele** forms when root avulsion tears the dural sleeve, letting CSF/contrast collect — a marker of **preganglionic avulsion**. However, it is **not 100% reliable**: avulsion can occur without a meningocele, and a meningocele can occasionally exist with a partially intact root, so imaging is correlated with the exam and intraoperative findings (and SSEP/NAP testing).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Electrodiagnostic testing helps localize plexus lesions. Preserved sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) in an ANESTHETIC dermatome indicate:

options.text: A preganglionic (avulsion) lesion — the dorsal root ganglion cell body remains connected to its peripheral axon despite loss of central (cord) connection
A postganglionic rupture
Normal, intact sensory pathways centrally
Complete peripheral nerve transection

questions.explanation: In a **preganglionic avulsion**, the injury is proximal to the **dorsal root ganglion (DRG)**, so the DRG and its **peripheral sensory axon remain intact → SNAPs are preserved** even though the patient is clinically anesthetic (the central connection to the cord is lost). In a **postganglionic** lesion the peripheral axon degenerates and **SNAPs are absent**. This SNAP paradox is a key localizing tool, alongside needle EMG of proximal muscles.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Denervation changes on needle EMG (fibrillations, positive sharp waves) generally take how long to develop, meaning EMG is best delayed after acute injury?

options.text: About 3–4 weeks
24 hours
6 months
They appear immediately

questions.explanation: Because Wallerian degeneration and the establishment of the denervation EMG pattern take **~3–4 weeks**, baseline electrodiagnostics are typically obtained around then. Needle EMG of **proximal muscles (rhomboids, serratus, paraspinals)** is especially useful for localizing preganglionic injury, and serial studies help detect early reinnervation (nascent potentials).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which associated injury rate is correct for high-energy traumatic brachial plexus injury?

options.text: ~75% have associated head/thoracic/skeletal injuries, and ~20% have associated vascular injury
Fewer than 5% have any associated injury
100% have vascular injury
Associated injuries never affect prognosis

questions.explanation: About **75%** of traumatic plexus injuries have associated **head injury, thoracic trauma, or fractures/dislocations**, and roughly **20% have vascular injury**. These raise concern for a more severe lesion, can secondarily compress/damage the plexus (hematoma, pseudoaneurysm), and influence timing and reconstructive options — so a full trauma workup and vascular assessment are mandatory.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: In reconstruction priorities for a pan-plexus injury, which function is generally restored FIRST/most reliably?

options.text: Elbow flexion
Intrinsic hand function
Finger extension
Wrist flexion

questions.explanation: The reconstructive hierarchy prioritizes **elbow flexion first** (most valuable, most achievable), then **shoulder stability/abduction and external rotation**, then **hand sensibility and, when possible, prehension**. **Intrinsic/hand-intrinsic recovery is least attainable** because of the long regeneration distance to distal targets — a key reason lower-plexus/hand outcomes are limited and free functioning muscle transfer is sometimes used.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: The Oberlin transfer restores elbow flexion in an upper-plexus injury by transferring:

options.text: One or two expendable ulnar nerve fascicles (to FCU) to the biceps motor branch of the musculocutaneous nerve
The whole median nerve to the musculocutaneous nerve
The spinal accessory nerve to the biceps branch
Intercostal nerves to the median nerve

questions.explanation: The **Oberlin transfer** coapts a **redundant ulnar-nerve fascicle (one that innervates FCU)** to the **biceps motor branch** of the musculocutaneous nerve, restoring elbow flexion with negligible ulnar donor deficit (a 'double fascicular' or Mackinnon modification adds a median fascicle to the brachialis branch). It requires an **intact, functioning lower plexus/ulnar nerve** — hence it is used in C5–C6(±C7) injuries, not pan-plexus lesions.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: To restore shoulder abduction and external rotation in an upper-trunk injury, the classic distal nerve-transfer pair is:

options.text: Spinal accessory nerve → suprascapular nerve, plus a radial (triceps branch) → axillary nerve transfer
Intercostal → musculocutaneous nerve
Phrenic → median nerve
Contralateral C7 → suprascapular nerve

questions.explanation: Shoulder reanimation classically uses the **spinal accessory nerve → suprascapular nerve** (supraspinatus/infraspinatus for abduction + external rotation) combined with a **radial-to-axillary (triceps branch to anterior axillary) transfer** for the deltoid/teres minor. Preserving part of the spinal accessory to the trapezius (using the distal branch) maintains scapular function. This dual transfer improves both abduction and the critical external-rotation component.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which donor is commonly used to neurotize the musculocutaneous nerve for elbow flexion specifically in a PAN-plexus injury (where intraplexal donors like the ulnar nerve are unavailable)?

options.text: Intercostal nerves (typically 2–3) or the spinal accessory nerve
An ulnar nerve fascicle (Oberlin)
The median nerve
The suprascapular nerve

questions.explanation: In a **pan-plexus** injury the whole limb is denervated, so **extraplexal donors** are required: **intercostal nerves (2–3, direct to the musculocutaneous)** or the **spinal accessory** are used for elbow flexion, and **contralateral C7** may be recruited for additional targets. The **Oberlin** (ulnar fascicle) transfer is impossible here because the ulnar nerve is not functioning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: The contralateral C7 (cC7) transfer is a strategy in severe/pan-plexus injuries. What is its rationale and main trade-off?

options.text: The healthy opposite C7 supplies abundant axons (with tolerable donor deficit due to overlap), but requires a long graft/staged reinnervation and carries transient contralateral deficits
It provides immediate full recovery with no donor cost
It is only used for isolated suprascapular palsy
It permanently paralyzes the donor limb

questions.explanation: The **contralateral C7** carries a large number of axons, and because of overlapping innervation the **donor limb usually tolerates its loss with only transient deficits**. It is reserved for **severe multi-root avulsions/pan-plexus** injuries needing a high-axon-count source (often routed via a vascularized ulnar nerve graft to a distal target). Downsides are the **long regeneration distance/staging** and temporary contralateral weakness/numbness.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Why does a very proximal injury with distal targets (e.g., attempting to reinnervate hand intrinsics after a lower-root lesion) carry a poor prognosis even with technically successful nerve surgery?

options.text: The long regeneration distance means motor endplates degenerate irreversibly before axons arrive (~1 mm/day is too slow to beat the ~18-month window)
Intrinsic muscles cannot be reinnervated by any axon
Sensory recovery prevents motor recovery
Proximal injuries regenerate faster than distal ones

questions.explanation: Axons regenerate at ~**1 mm/day**, so reaching **distal hand intrinsics** from a proximal repair may take longer than the **~18-month window** before endplates degenerate and muscle becomes irreversibly fibrotic. This is why **proximal-injury/distal-target reconstructions fail**, hand recovery lags shoulder/elbow, and strategies like **distal nerve transfers (short distance) or free functioning muscle transfer** are preferred for the hand.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A free functioning muscle transfer (e.g., gracilis) in late or pan-plexus reconstruction is typically used to restore:

options.text: Elbow flexion (and sometimes finger flexion), powered by a nerve donor such as intercostals or spinal accessory
Shoulder external rotation only
Sensation to the hand
Wrist extension exclusively

questions.explanation: A **free functioning muscle transfer (usually gracilis)** provides new contractile tissue when native muscles are irrecoverable or the patient presents late (beyond the reinnervation window). It is commonly neurotized by **intercostal or spinal accessory nerves** to restore **elbow flexion** (and can be staged to add **finger flexion**), a mainstay for **pan-plexus salvage**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: The distal spinal accessory nerve (to trapezius) is a favored transfer donor. Why is it examined carefully before use, and how is it harvested?

options.text: It can be injured in the same trauma; the DISTAL branch is taken to preserve upper trapezius function
It provides sensory axons only
It must be taken entirely, sacrificing all trapezius function
It is never at risk in plexus trauma

questions.explanation: The **spinal accessory (CN XI)** is a robust donor (commonly to the suprascapular nerve), but it can be **concomitantly injured** in the trauma, so its function is verified preoperatively. Harvesting the **distal portion** preserves the proximal branches to the **upper trapezius**, limiting scapular/shoulder donor morbidity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which finding on exam would argue AGAINST a preganglionic C5 injury and instead favor a graftable postganglionic rupture at that level?

options.text: Tenderness/positive Tinel in the supraclavicular fossa and intact rhomboid/serratus function
Winged scapula
Horner syndrome
A pseudomeningocele at C5

questions.explanation: **Supraclavicular tenderness/Tinel** (a neuroma at a ruptured stump) and **preserved very-proximal muscles (rhomboids via dorsal scapular, serratus via long thoracic)** indicate the lesion is **distal to the root (postganglionic)** and therefore **graftable**. Winged scapula, Horner sign, and pseudomeningoceles all point toward **preganglionic avulsion** (not graftable → transfer needed).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Loss of function of the latissimus dorsi (thoracodorsal nerve) in a plexus injury localizes the lesion to at least which level?

options.text: The posterior cord (or more proximal)
The medial cord only
A terminal branch distal to the cords
The lateral cord only

questions.explanation: The **thoracodorsal nerve (latissimus dorsi) arises from the posterior cord**, so latissimus weakness implies a lesion **at the posterior cord or proximal to it**. Similarly, pectoralis (clavicular head → lateral pectoral/lateral cord; sternal head → medial pectoral/medial cord) involvement localizes to those cords. Mapping such cord-level branches refines the level diagnosis intraoperatively and preoperatively.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: During plexus exploration, intraoperative nerve action potential (NAP) recording across a neuroma-in-continuity shows a conducting response. What does this indicate and imply for treatment?

options.text: Axonal regeneration is crossing the lesion (favorable) → neurolysis alone rather than resection/grafting
The nerve is avulsed and must be transferred
The lesion is neurotmetic and must be resected
NAP results are irrelevant to decision-making

questions.explanation: A **conducting NAP across a neuroma-in-continuity** indicates that a critical mass of axons has regenerated through the lesion — a **favorable finding** that supports **neurolysis alone** (leaving the nerve in continuity). **Absence of a NAP** suggests the regeneration is inadequate, favoring **resection and grafting (or transfer)**. Intraoperative NAP testing thus guides the resect-vs-preserve decision.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A postganglionic C5–C6 rupture with viable proximal and distal stumps and a 4-cm gap is best reconstructed by:

options.text: Interposition nerve grafting (e.g., sural cable grafts) across the gap
Contralateral C7 transfer
Direct tension-heavy end-to-end suture
Observation for another year

questions.explanation: A **graftable postganglionic rupture** with viable stumps is reconstructed with **interposition (sural) cable grafts**, since a tension-free direct repair is usually impossible across a gap and tension impairs regeneration. **Nerve transfers** are reserved for **avulsions** (no proximal stump) or to augment/shorten reinnervation to key targets; here a graftable stump exists, so grafting (± adjunctive distal transfers) is appropriate.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about the prognosis of upper- (C5–C6) versus lower- (C8–T1) plexus reconstruction is correct?

options.text: Upper-plexus reconstruction (shoulder/elbow) generally yields better functional results than lower-plexus (hand) reconstruction
Lower-plexus hand reconstruction reliably restores intrinsic function
Both have equal, excellent outcomes
Upper-plexus injuries cannot be reconstructed

questions.explanation: **Upper-plexus** targets (shoulder abduction/ER, elbow flexion) are **closer to the injury and more reliably reinnervated**, giving better outcomes. **Lower-plexus/hand** function (intrinsics, fine motor) recovers poorly due to the **long regeneration distance and endplate degeneration**, so realistic goals for the hand are limited (protective sensation, gross grasp) and salvage may require FFMT or later tendon procedures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A patient with a complete pan-plexus avulsion has intractable, severe burning pain in the anesthetic limb ('deafferentation pain'). Which intervention specifically targets this pain?

options.text: Dorsal root entry zone (DREZ) lesioning
Peripheral nerve grafting of the avulsed roots
Free functioning muscle transfer
Wrist arthrodesis

questions.explanation: **Deafferentation pain** after root avulsion arises from hyperactive dorsal horn neurons; **DREZ (dorsal root entry zone) lesioning** ablates this abnormal activity and can relieve otherwise intractable avulsion pain. Since avulsed roots **cannot be grafted**, pain management (medications, DREZ) is an important, separate goal from motor reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Roughly what proportion of brachial plexus traction injuries are located in the SUPRACLAVICULAR region (roots/trunks)?

options.text: About two-thirds
About one-tenth
Essentially none
All of them

questions.explanation: Approximately **two-thirds of traction injuries are supraclavicular** (roots, spinal nerves, trunks), and about **one-third are retro-/infraclavicular** (divisions, cords, terminal branches). Some patients have **double-level** injuries. Knowing the likely zone directs the surgical approach and the search for graftable stumps versus avulsions.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: An infraclavicular injury with a scapular/clavicular fracture most commonly injures which structure, producing combined deltoid and radial-distribution weakness?

options.text: The posterior cord (axillary + radial nerves)
The medial cord
The upper trunk
The dorsal scapular nerve

questions.explanation: Infraclavicular/retroclavicular injuries (often with **clavicle/scapula fracture or shoulder dislocation**) frequently involve the **posterior cord**, giving combined **axillary (deltoid/teres minor) and radial (triceps, wrist/finger extensors)** deficits. Isolated **axillary** or **suprascapular** nerve injuries also occur in this region. Recognizing the cord-level pattern guides targeted grafting/transfer.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Preoperative and perioperative therapy in brachial plexus injury emphasizes which key measure to protect future reconstructive options?

options.text: Maintaining full passive range of motion of all joints (preventing contracture) while awaiting recovery or surgery
Complete immobilization of the limb
Early heavy resistance strengthening
Avoiding all movement to protect the nerves

questions.explanation: A supple limb with **full passive joint motion** is essential — a stiff shoulder or elbow will undermine any successful reinnervation or transfer. Therapists teach **passive ROM (and active where possible)** from early on, and psychological/pain support is integrated. Contracture prevention is as important to the ultimate outcome as the nerve surgery itself.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: The dorsal scapular nerve (rhomboids) and long thoracic nerve (serratus anterior) are important examination targets because they:

options.text: Arise very proximally at the root level, so their loss signals a proximal/preganglionic injury
Are the last nerves to be injured in any plexus lesion
Provide the main sensory supply to the hand
Are unaffected by root avulsion

questions.explanation: Both branch off **at the root level** (dorsal scapular from C5; long thoracic from C5–C7), so weakness of **rhomboids or serratus anterior (winged scapula)** indicates a **very proximal (preganglionic) injury** — an important localizing sign that lowers the expectation for spontaneous recovery and shifts planning toward transfers.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A double fascicular (Oberlin-Mackinnon) transfer for elbow flexion differs from the classic single Oberlin by:

options.text: Adding a median-nerve fascicle to the brachialis branch (plus the ulnar fascicle to the biceps branch), reinnervating both elbow flexors
Using intercostal nerves instead of the ulnar nerve
Transferring the entire ulnar nerve
Requiring a sural nerve graft

questions.explanation: The **double fascicular transfer** neurotizes **both** elbow flexors: a redundant **ulnar fascicle → biceps branch** and a redundant **median fascicle → brachialis branch**. Reinnervating both muscles improves strength/reliability over the single Oberlin. It still requires **intact, functioning median and ulnar nerves**, so it applies to upper-plexus (not pan-plexus) injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Compared with proximal grafting for an upper-trunk injury, distal nerve transfers (e.g., Oberlin, SAN→SSN) offer which advantage?

options.text: Coaptation close to the target shortens the reinnervation distance/time and avoids operating in the scarred zone of injury, with a single suture line
They require no functioning donor
They restore sensation better than grafts
They can reinnervate avulsed roots directly

questions.explanation: **Distal nerve transfers** place the coaptation **near the target muscle**, so axons reach endplates faster (beating the degeneration window), use a **pure motor donor to a motor target**, and **avoid dissecting the scarred injury zone** — with a single juncture. Their requirement is an **expendable functioning donor**, which is why they suit partial (upper-trunk) injuries and augment or replace proximal grafting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: In a C5–C6 injury, which functions are typically PRESERVED, confirming the lower plexus is intact?

options.text: Wrist/finger flexion and hand intrinsic function, and elbow extension
Shoulder abduction and external rotation
Elbow flexion and forearm supination
Deltoid and biceps function

questions.explanation: An Erb (C5–C6) injury spares the **C7–T1-innervated functions**: **elbow extension (triceps), wrist and finger flexion, and hand intrinsics** are intact, while shoulder abduction/ER and elbow flexion/supination are lost. The **intact lower plexus** is precisely what enables donors like an **ulnar fascicle (Oberlin)** for reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about scapulothoracic dissociation in the setting of a plexus injury is correct?

options.text: It is a severe, often high-energy injury frequently associated with vascular disruption and a poor-prognosis (often complete/avulsion) plexus lesion
It indicates a mild, self-limited plexus stretch
It never involves vascular injury
It predicts excellent spontaneous recovery

questions.explanation: **Scapulothoracic dissociation** (lateral displacement of the scapula with muscle/ligament disruption) reflects **extreme energy** and commonly accompanies **major vascular injury (subclavian/axillary)** and a **severe, often complete/avulsion plexus lesion** with a poor prognosis. Its presence should heighten suspicion for preganglionic injury and mandates urgent vascular assessment.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A patient examined 8 months after a plexus stretch injury has an advancing distal Tinel sign along the course of a trunk. What does this suggest?

options.text: A recovering (regenerating) postganglionic lesion — continued observation may be appropriate
A preganglionic avulsion requiring immediate transfer
Complete neurotmesis with no recovery
A vascular injury

questions.explanation: An **advancing Tinel sign** marks the leading edge of regenerating sensory axons progressing distally — evidence of a **recovering postganglionic lesion**. This favors **continued observation** with serial exams/EMG rather than surgery. A **static** Tinel at the injury site or **absent** neck Tinel (with avulsion signs) points the other way, toward intervention.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which combination of findings would most strongly indicate EARLY surgery rather than prolonged observation in a closed traction injury?

options.text: Multiple preganglionic signs (Horner, winged scapula, pseudomeningoceles, preserved SNAPs in anesthetic dermatomes)
An advancing Tinel and early biceps flicker at 6 weeks
Low-energy mechanism with partial deficit improving weekly
Normal EMG at 4 weeks

questions.explanation: **Preganglionic markers** (Horner sign, rhomboid/serratus loss with winged scapula, pseudomeningoceles, preserved SNAPs despite anesthesia) indicate **root avulsion** — no spontaneous recovery and no graftable stump — so **earlier surgery (transfers)** is warranted before endplate degeneration. Signs of **ongoing recovery** (advancing Tinel, returning function) argue for **observation**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: The phrenic nerve is sometimes considered a transfer donor in plexus reconstruction. What is the principal concern limiting its use?

options.text: Loss of ipsilateral diaphragm function / reduced pulmonary capacity, especially risky with concomitant chest trauma
It provides only sensory axons
It cannot reach any plexus target
It is never injured in trauma

questions.explanation: Harvesting the **phrenic nerve** sacrifices **ipsilateral diaphragm function**, reducing pulmonary reserve — hazardous in patients with **thoracic trauma, rib fractures, or marginal respiratory status**, and generally avoided in children. Its function should be confirmed (fluoroscopy) and its use weighed carefully; many centers prefer spinal accessory/intercostal donors to avoid respiratory compromise.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Why is a coordinated multidisciplinary team (neurology, nerve surgeons, physiatry/pain, therapy, ± psychology) emphasized in traumatic brachial plexus care?

options.text: These are complex injuries requiring integrated diagnosis, staged reconstruction, pain and contracture management, and long rehabilitation — no single evaluation dictates management
Because surgery is never indicated
To avoid the need for imaging
Because the injury always recovers spontaneously

questions.explanation: Traumatic plexus injuries demand **integrated care**: localization needs history/exam/EMG/imaging together; reconstruction is often **staged** and individualized; **deafferentation pain** and **contracture prevention** require physiatry and therapy; and psychosocial impact is major. A **multidisciplinary team** best addresses the short- and long-term needs, since **no single finding** determines the plan.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A patient with a C5–C6 avulsion (preganglionic, both roots) needs elbow flexion and shoulder function. Which reconstructive plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Nerve transfers: spinal accessory→suprascapular and radial(triceps)→axillary for the shoulder, plus Oberlin (ulnar fascicle)→biceps branch for elbow flexion
Sural cable grafting from the avulsed C5/C6 stumps
Observation for 18 months
Contralateral C7 transfer as the sole procedure

questions.explanation: Because the roots are **avulsed (no graftable stump)** but the **lower plexus is intact**, reconstruction relies on **intra- and extraplexal nerve transfers**: **SAN→suprascapular** and **triceps branch→axillary** restore shoulder abduction/ER, and the **Oberlin ulnar-fascicle→biceps branch** restores elbow flexion. Grafting is impossible from avulsed roots, and observation wastes the reinnervation window.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about the timing goal 'reinnervate before ~12–18 months' in plexus surgery is correct?

options.text: Motor reconstruction should aim to reach denervated muscle before end-stage endplate degeneration (~18 months), which is why definitive surgery is not deferred indefinitely
Muscle can be reinnervated with full recovery even after several years
Sensory targets have the same strict deadline as motor targets
Timing does not affect motor outcome

questions.explanation: Denervated muscle degenerates irreversibly by roughly **18 months**, so reconstruction is planned to **reinnervate motor targets before that window closes** — balancing this against allowing spontaneous recovery to declare (~3 months for stretch). **Sensory** reconstruction is less time-critical than motor. Late presentation past the window shifts strategy to **FFMT or tendon transfers**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: In late-presenting or failed plexus reconstruction, secondary shoulder procedures may include:

options.text: Shoulder (glenohumeral) arthrodesis to provide a stable, positioned shoulder driven by scapular motion
Total wrist fusion
DREZ lesioning
Sural nerve grafting of the axillary nerve

questions.explanation: When shoulder reanimation fails or the patient presents late, **glenohumeral arthrodesis** gives a **stable, well-positioned shoulder** that the patient moves via the (intact) scapulothoracic muscles — useful for positioning the hand. It is a **secondary/salvage** reconstruction, distinct from the primary nerve procedures, and requires functioning periscapular muscles (e.g., trapezius, serratus).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which finding best distinguishes a C7 (middle trunk) contribution deficit within a C5–C7 injury?

options.text: Weakness of elbow/wrist/finger EXTENSORS (radial-innervated, C7-predominant) with variable FDP weakness
Loss of hand intrinsics only
Isolated deltoid paralysis
Pure sensory loss over the small finger

questions.explanation: The **C7/middle trunk** contributes heavily to the **extensor group (triceps, wrist and finger extensors)** and variably to **FDP**, so its involvement in an Erb-plus (C5–C7) pattern adds **extensor weakness** to the shoulder/elbow-flexion deficits. Because C7 contribution overlaps with C8, isolated C7 loss is often incomplete — one reason cC7 can be harvested with tolerable donor deficit.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: A patient with brachial plexus injury and an expanding supraclavicular mass, bruit, and progressive neurologic worsening most likely has:

options.text: A vascular injury (pseudoaneurysm/AV fistula/hematoma) compressing the plexus — requiring vascular intervention
A recovering neurapraxia
Normal postinjury swelling needing no action
A benign lipoma

questions.explanation: **Progressive** deficit with an **expanding mass and bruit/thrill** signals a **vascular complication (pseudoaneurysm, AV fistula, or hematoma)** compressing the plexus — an indication for **urgent vascular imaging and intervention**, often concurrent with nerve surgery. About 20% of these injuries have associated vascular trauma, so vascular assessment (palpation/Doppler, angiography) is routine.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST accurate statement about traumatic brachial plexus injury?
