options.text: Avulsed (preganglionic) roots can be directly grafted from the proximal stump
Most injuries are traction-type and supraclavicular
Horner syndrome suggests lower-root avulsion
Elbow flexion is a top reconstructive priority

questions.explanation: The false statement is that **avulsed roots can be grafted** — a **preganglionic avulsion has no proximal stump**, so grafting is impossible and reconstruction requires **nerve transfers**. The others are correct: traction is the dominant, mostly supraclavicular mechanism; Horner sign indicates lower-root avulsion; and elbow flexion is a leading reconstructive priority.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: An intact histamine 'triple response' (wheal, flare, and axon-reflex vasodilation) elicited in an anesthetic dermatome supports which diagnosis?

options.text: Preganglionic injury — the peripheral sensory axon and its dorsal root ganglion cell remain intact despite loss of the central connection
Postganglionic rupture with degenerated peripheral axon
Normal, uninjured nerve
A purely motor injury

questions.explanation: The **axon-reflex (flare) of the triple response depends on an intact peripheral sensory axon connected to its DRG cell body**. If the flare is **preserved in a clinically anesthetic area**, the lesion is **proximal to the DRG (preganglionic)** — the same principle that preserves SNAPs in avulsions. A **postganglionic** lesion degenerates the peripheral axon, abolishing the flare.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: In pan-plexus reconstruction, restoring protective SENSATION to the hand (median distribution) is important and may be achieved by:

options.text: Transferring a donor (e.g., intercostal sensory branches or, in some plans, contralateral C7) to the median/lateral cord sensory component
Grafting the avulsed T1 root directly
Wrist arthrodesis
It is impossible to restore any hand sensation

questions.explanation: Even when motor recovery of the hand is limited, **restoring protective sensation** (especially the **median/volar radial hand**) reduces neglect and injury. This can be pursued with **sensory neurotization** — e.g., intercostal sensory branches or a contralateral C7 component to the median sensory fibers. Sensory reconstruction is less time-critical than motor and is a recognized goal in pan-plexus planning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 34 (Traumatic Brachial Plexus Injury)

questions.stem: During which window of gestation do the great majority of congenital upper-limb malformations arise?

options.text: Weeks 4–8 (embryogenesis), when the limb forms rapidly and is most vulnerable
Weeks 20–24
The third trimester
After birth

questions.explanation: The upper limb bud appears at **~day 26** and all limb structures are present by the **end of week 8**; fingers are fully separate by ~day 52–53. Because this **4–8-week embryonic period** involves rapid, fragile patterning, it is when **most malformations occur**. After 8 weeks the fetal period is mainly growth/differentiation, so insults then cause deformations rather than malformations.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: The apical ectodermal ridge (AER) controls which axis of limb development, and via which signaling molecule?

options.text: Proximodistal outgrowth, via fibroblast growth factors (FGFs)
Anteroposterior (radioulnar), via sonic hedgehog
Dorsoventral, via Wnt/Lmx-1
Left-right asymmetry, via nodal

questions.explanation: The **AER** is a thickened ectodermal ridge at the limb-bud tip that drives **proximodistal outgrowth (shoulder → arm → forearm → hand)** through **fibroblast growth factors (FGFs)**. Experimentally, **removing the AER truncates the limb**, and applying FGF rescues outgrowth. Clinically, AER failure corresponds to **transverse deficiencies**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: A newborn has a short below-elbow transverse deficiency with tiny digital 'nubbins.' Which signaling center's failure classically explains this, and what is the inheritance/recurrence risk?

options.text: AER (FGF) failure; transverse deficiencies are usually sporadic and non-inheritable, so recurrence risk is low
ZPA (SHH) failure; autosomal dominant with high recurrence
Wnt failure; X-linked
HOX duplication; autosomal recessive

questions.explanation: A **transverse deficiency** reflects **failure of AER/FGF-driven proximodistal outgrowth** (often attributed to local ischemia/hemorrhage rather than physical AER loss). These are typically **sporadic and not heritable**, so parents can be reassured about a **low recurrence risk** — an important counseling point (concern for teratogens rises only if multiple limbs are affected).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: The zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) patterns which axis, and through which morphogen?

options.text: Anteroposterior (radioulnar/preaxial-postaxial) axis, via sonic hedgehog (SHH)
Proximodistal axis, via FGF
Dorsoventral axis, via Wnt
Left-right axis, via BMP

questions.explanation: The **ZPA** lies at the **posterior (ulnar) margin** of the limb bud and establishes the **anteroposterior (radioulnar) axis** via **sonic hedgehog (SHH)**. SHH is highest posteriorly (ulnar) and lowest anteriorly (radial), setting digit identity. Ectopic anterior SHH/ZPA produces a **mirror (ulnar) duplication**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Transplanting an extra ZPA (or ectopic SHH) to the anterior limb bud experimentally produces which anomaly, mirroring a human malformation?

options.text: Mirror-hand (ulnar dimelia) — a duplicated, mirror-image posterior/ulnar structure
A transverse amputation
Dorsal-ventral reversal of the nail
Complete syndactyly of all digits

questions.explanation: An ectopic anterior **ZPA/SHH source** creates a second posterior organizing signal, yielding a **mirror-image duplication of ulnar structures — 'mirror hand' (ulnar dimelia)**, often with multiple fingers, no thumb, and a duplicated ulna. The degree of duplication is **dose-dependent**. This links the ZPA/SHH pathway directly to a recognizable clinical entity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: The Wnt signaling pathway (with the transcription factor Lmx-1) establishes which axis, and its disruption is associated with which syndrome?

options.text: Dorsoventral axis; nail-patella syndrome (abnormal nail/pulp arrangement)
Proximodistal axis; thalidomide embryopathy
Anteroposterior axis; mirror hand
Left-right axis; situs inversus

questions.explanation: The **Wnt pathway (via Lmx-1)** specifies the **dorsoventral axis** — dorsal (nail) versus ventral (pulp) identity. Its disruption is exemplified by **nail-patella syndrome**, with dorsal-structure abnormalities such as **hypoplastic/dysplastic nails** (and dorsalized features). Loss of any one of the three interdependent centers (AER, ZPA, Wnt) compromises the whole patterning system.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Fingers initially form as a webbed hand plate; their separation depends on:

options.text: Programmed cell death (apoptosis) causing interdigital necrosis, driven by bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs)
FGF-driven proliferation of interdigital tissue
SHH gradient reversal
Mechanical tearing during movement

questions.explanation: Digit separation requires **interdigital apoptosis (programmed cell death)** around day ~44, triggered by **BMPs**. **Failure of interdigital apoptosis produces syndactyly.** BMP antagonism blocks this necrosis (e.g., bats retain webbing), and altered FGF signaling (as in Apert syndrome) can negate BMP-mediated apoptosis, causing syndactyly.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: A child has bilateral complex syndactyly with a characteristic facies (midface hypoplasia, craniosynostosis). This is Apert syndrome. What is the molecular basis and inheritance?

options.text: FGFR2 gain-of-function mutation (altered fibroblast growth factor receptor signaling) inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
SHH loss of function, autosomal recessive
Lmx-1 deletion, X-linked
Complete absence of the AER, sporadic only

questions.explanation: **Apert syndrome** results from **FGFR (fibroblast growth factor receptor, FGFR2) gain-of-function mutations** that **negate BMP-mediated interdigital apoptosis**, producing severe complex syndactyly ('mitten/spade hand') plus acrocephalosyndactyly features. It is **autosomal dominant** and can be transmitted to offspring — relevant to genetic counseling.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: In the developing limb bud, the LATERAL PLATE mesoderm gives rise to which tissues?

options.text: Bone, cartilage, and tendon
Muscle, nerve, and blood vessels
Skin and nail
The apical ectodermal ridge

questions.explanation: The limb bud is mesoderm growing into overlying ectoderm. **Lateral plate mesoderm → skeletal connective tissue (bone, cartilage, tendon)**, whereas **somatic (paraxial/myotome-derived) mesoderm migrates in to form muscle, nerve, and vascular elements**. This dual origin explains how skeletal and myoneurovascular anomalies can occur together or independently.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: The somatic (somitic) mesoderm migrating into the limb bud forms which elements?

options.text: Muscle, nerve, and vascular tissue
Bone and cartilage
Tendon and ligament
The overlying ectoderm and AER

questions.explanation: **Somatic mesoderm (myogenic precursors, plus ingrowing neural and vascular cells)** forms the **muscle, nerve, and blood vessels** of the limb, migrating into a scaffold provided by lateral-plate-derived skeleton/tendon. Understanding these origins clarifies why, for example, a skeletal deficiency and its associated muscles/nerves may both be abnormal.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: By approximately which day of gestation are the fingers entirely separate?

options.text: Day ~52–53 (about week 7–8)
Day ~26
Day ~120
At birth

questions.explanation: Finger rays appear webbed around day ~41, **interdigital apoptosis** proceeds through day ~44, and the **fingers are fully separated by day ~52–53**. Insults during this narrow window (e.g., disrupted apoptosis) produce **syndactyly**. Complete embryogenesis of the limb is finished by the end of week 8.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which statement about the interdependence of the three limb signaling centers is correct?

options.text: AER, ZPA, and Wnt centers cross-talk and are interdependent, so loss of one compromises the entire patterning system
Each center acts in complete isolation
Only the AER is required; the others are redundant
The ZPA controls all three axes alone

questions.explanation: The **AER (proximodistal/FGF), ZPA (anteroposterior/SHH), and Wnt (dorsoventral/Lmx-1)** centers are **mutually dependent with extensive cross-talk** — for example, FGF and SHH maintain each other in a feedback loop. **Disruption of one center degrades the whole system**, which is why complex, multi-axis malformations occur.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: The modern Oberg-Manske-Tonkin (OMT) classification of congenital hand anomalies organizes conditions primarily into which top-level categories?

options.text: Malformations, deformations, and dysplasias (with malformations further grouped by affected axis/plate and syndromic status)
Failure of formation, failure of differentiation, duplication, overgrowth, undergrowth, constriction band, and generalized (Swanson/IFSSH only)
Radial, central, and ulnar only
Genetic and non-genetic only

questions.explanation: The **OMT classification** (adopted by the IFSSH) sorts anomalies into **malformations, deformations, and dysplasias (including tumors)**. **Malformations** are further subdivided by the **axis affected (proximodistal, radioulnar/anteroposterior, dorsoventral)** and whether the whole limb or hand plate is involved, plus syndromic associations. It is **mechanistically/genetically grounded**, superseding the older descriptive Swanson/IFSSH scheme.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: In the OMT scheme, a congenital constriction band (amniotic band) sequence is best categorized as a:

options.text: Deformation (an extrinsic mechanical disruption of an initially normally formed limb)
Malformation of the anteroposterior axis
Dysplasia
Failure of AER signaling

questions.explanation: **Constriction band syndrome** results from **extrinsic amniotic bands mechanically disrupting an already-formed limb**, so it is a **deformation/disruption**, not a primary patterning malformation. This distinction matters for counseling (sporadic, non-heritable, low recurrence) and for understanding the variable, often asymmetric pattern of amputations, lymphedema, and acrosyndactyly.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: A child with a hypoplastic/absent thumb and radius is found to have an atrial septal defect. This Holt-Oram syndrome is caused by mutation in which gene?

options.text: TBX5
FGFR2
GLI3
Lmx-1

questions.explanation: **Holt-Oram ('heart-hand') syndrome** — radial ray deficiency (thumb/radial hypoplasia) with **cardiac septal defects/conduction anomalies** — is due to **TBX5** mutation, a transcription factor essential to both limb and heart development. It is **autosomal dominant**. Recognizing a radial-ray anomaly should prompt evaluation for associated cardiac (and other VACTERL) anomalies.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: A neonate with bilateral radial longitudinal deficiency and thrombocytopenia most likely has which syndrome?

options.text: TAR syndrome (thrombocytopenia–absent radius) — notably the THUMB is present
Fanconi anemia with pancytopenia and absent thumbs
Holt-Oram with cardiac defect
Apert syndrome

questions.explanation: **TAR syndrome** pairs **absent radii with thrombocytopenia**, and characteristically **the thumbs are PRESENT** — a key discriminator from other radial-ray syndromes. In contrast, **Fanconi anemia** (a DNA-repair/chromosomal-instability disorder, diagnosed by the DEB/chromosomal-breakage test) causes radial-ray defects with **absent/hypoplastic thumbs** and progressive **pancytopenia**. Distinguishing them is vital because Fanconi carries malignancy/marrow-failure risk.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: A child with radial ray deficiency has a positive diepoxybutane (DEB) chromosomal-breakage test. What is the diagnosis and its significance?

options.text: Fanconi anemia — a DNA-repair disorder with progressive marrow failure and cancer risk; early diagnosis (before pancytopenia) is critical
TAR syndrome — benign, no systemic risk
Holt-Oram syndrome — cardiac only
Amniotic band syndrome

questions.explanation: A positive **DEB (diepoxybutane) / mitomycin chromosomal-breakage test** diagnoses **Fanconi anemia**, an autosomal recessive **DNA-repair defect** presenting with radial-ray anomalies (often absent thumbs) and later **aplastic anemia and leukemia/solid-tumor risk**. Because hand findings can precede hematologic failure, **screening children with radial deficiency** allows life-saving early treatment (e.g., transplant).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Radial polydactyly and triphalangeal thumb are frequently linked to dysregulation of which pathway?

options.text: SHH signaling (e.g., mutations in its limb enhancer, the ZRS), producing anterior/preaxial ectopic activity
FGF from the AER
Wnt/Lmx-1 dorsoventral signaling
BMP-only signaling

questions.explanation: Ectopic **anterior SHH activity** — classically via mutations in the **ZRS (zone of polarizing activity regulatory sequence, the SHH limb enhancer)** — produces **preaxial (radial) polydactyly and triphalangeal thumb**. This reflects the ZPA/SHH pathway's role in anteroposterior patterning; abnormal anterior SHH mimics an ectopic ZPA. GLI3 (a downstream SHH mediator) mutations cause other polydactylies (e.g., Greig syndrome).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which statement about teratogens and limb anomalies is most accurate?

options.text: Only a small minority of limb malformations are attributable to teratogens; multi-limb involvement raises suspicion for a teratogenic/systemic insult
Most limb anomalies are caused by teratogens
Teratogens never affect the limb
Thalidomide affects only the lower limb

questions.explanation: **Most limb anomalies are sporadic or inherited; few are teratogenic.** The classic teratogen **thalidomide** causes symmetric proximal (phocomelia-type) limb defects. **Bilateral/multi-limb involvement** should raise concern for a **teratogen or a systemic/genetic cause**, whereas an isolated unilateral transverse deficiency is usually a sporadic vascular event.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Proper joint modeling of the developing limb requires which factor in addition to chondrogen condensation and cavitation?

options.text: Fetal motion (movement shapes the articular surfaces)
Complete absence of movement
Ossification before cavitation
Loss of the AER

questions.explanation: Joints form as **interzone condensations cavitate**, but the ultimate **articular surface shape requires fetal MOTION** — immobility impairs joint modeling. This is why conditions with reduced intrauterine movement (e.g., **arthrogryposis**) produce stiff, poorly modeled joints, linking embryology to a clinically important deformity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: On what day does the human upper limb bud first appear, and how large is the embryo then?

options.text: About day 26, when the embryo is ~4 mm (crown-rump), roughly the size of a grain of rice
About day 52, at ~24 mm
About day 90, at ~40 mm
At the moment of fertilization

questions.explanation: The **upper limb bud appears at ~day 26** (embryo ~**4 mm**), *before* the lower limb bud, reflecting the cranial-to-caudal developmental gradient. It grows rapidly, with fingers separate by ~day 52–53 and limb embryogenesis complete by week 8. Knowing this timeline helps date the likely insult for a given anomaly.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: The upper limb develops slightly AHEAD of the lower limb. What is the clinical corollary of this cranial-to-caudal gradient?

options.text: A single-timepoint insult may affect the upper and lower limbs at different developmental stages, producing differing severities
The lower limb always forms first
Upper and lower limbs are always affected identically
The gradient has no clinical relevance

questions.explanation: Because the **upper limb bud leads the lower limb** by a few days, an insult at a given moment strikes each limb at a **different developmental stage**, so the **pattern/severity can differ between upper and lower limbs**. This helps explain asymmetric multi-limb involvement and aids in estimating the timing of a teratogenic exposure.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Ectopic implantation of a second apical ectodermal ridge in an experimental limb bud produces:

options.text: An additional (supernumerary) limb outgrowth
Limb truncation
Dorsoventral reversal
Mirror-image ulnar duplication

questions.explanation: Because the **AER drives proximodistal outgrowth**, an **ectopic AER induces an extra limb outgrowth**, whereas **removing the AER truncates the limb** (transverse deficiency). By contrast, manipulating the **ZPA/SHH** alters anteroposterior identity (mirror duplication), and **Wnt/Lmx-1** alters dorsoventral identity — a useful framework for predicting the phenotype of each center's disruption.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Congenital limb anomalies rank where among birth malformations in frequency?

options.text: Second only to congenital heart disease
The single most common of all
Extremely rare (under 1 in 100,000)
Less common than neural tube defects

questions.explanation: Congenital anomalies affect **1–3% of newborns**, ~**10%** of whom have upper-limb involvement, making **limb anomalies second only to congenital heart disease** in birth-malformation frequency. Their incidence has been relatively stable, and the hand surgeon plays a central role in diagnosis, counseling, and coordinating multidisciplinary/genetic evaluation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: HOX genes contribute to limb patterning primarily by:

options.text: Providing positional/segmental identity along the proximodistal (and anteroposterior) axes, coordinating which structures form where
Serving as the AER's secreted FGF
Encoding the dorsoventral morphogen
Triggering interdigital apoptosis directly

questions.explanation: **HOX genes** are master transcription factors that confer **positional identity** along the limb axes, integrating signals from the AER/ZPA/Wnt centers to specify which skeletal elements form at each level. Mutations produce segmentation/identity defects (e.g., **HOXD13** in synpolydactyly). They act upstream/parallel to the morphogen gradients rather than as the secreted signals themselves.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which anomaly is the direct developmental consequence of FAILED interdigital apoptosis?

options.text: Syndactyly
Transverse deficiency
Mirror hand
Radial club hand

questions.explanation: **Syndactyly** arises when **interdigital apoptosis fails**, so the fingers remain webbed. It can be simple/complex, complete/incomplete, and appears in syndromes (e.g., **Apert**, via FGFR-mediated suppression of BMP-driven apoptosis). Transverse deficiency (AER), mirror hand (ZPA/SHH), and radial club hand (radial-ray malformation) have distinct mechanisms.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: A child has central longitudinal deficiency ('cleft/split hand'). Which category and axis best describes its developmental basis in the OMT framework?

options.text: A malformation affecting the hand plate along the proximodistal/anteroposterior axis (abnormal central ray formation/apoptosis)
A pure dorsoventral (Wnt) malformation
A deformation from amniotic bands
A dysplasia (tumor)

questions.explanation: **Cleft (split) hand** is a **malformation of the hand plate** involving abnormal **central ray formation** (dysregulated apoptosis/AER-SHH interplay along the anteroposterior/proximodistal axes). In OMT it is classed among malformations of the hand plate; typical (central) cleft hand is often familial (e.g., associated with **SHFM** loci) and may be syndromic, whereas 'atypical cleft' overlaps with symbrachydactyly (a different, sporadic mechanism).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which best distinguishes a MALFORMATION from a DEFORMATION in congenital limb differences?

options.text: A malformation is an intrinsic error of the developmental process; a deformation is an extrinsic mechanical alteration of a normally forming part
Malformations occur only after birth
Deformations are always genetic
There is no meaningful difference

questions.explanation: A **malformation** stems from an **intrinsic defect in the developmental program** (e.g., failed signaling → radial deficiency, syndactyly), whereas a **deformation** is an **extrinsic mechanical distortion of an initially normal structure** (e.g., amniotic constriction band, some positional deformities). **Dysplasia** (the third OMT category) is abnormal tissue organization/growth (e.g., macrodactyly, tumors).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Macrodactyly and other overgrowth conditions fall into which OMT category?

options.text: Dysplasia (abnormal tissue growth/organization)
Malformation of the proximodistal axis
Deformation
Failure of interdigital apoptosis

questions.explanation: **Overgrowth (e.g., macrodactyly, often PIK3CA-related) and tumors** are classified as **dysplasias** in the OMT scheme — abnormalities of **tissue growth/organization** rather than of the initial patterning (malformation) or extrinsic disruption (deformation). This mechanistic grouping helps predict associations and guide workup.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Why is genetic counseling emphasized when evaluating a child with a congenital hand anomaly?

options.text: Because inheritance/recurrence risk and syndromic associations vary greatly by diagnosis, and parents often carry guilt needing accurate information
Because all limb anomalies are autosomal dominant
Because counseling changes the surgical technique
Because recurrence risk is always 50%

questions.explanation: Recurrence risk ranges from essentially **sporadic/non-heritable (transverse deficiency, constriction band)** to **autosomal dominant (Apert, Holt-Oram)** to **recessive (Fanconi)**, and many anomalies signal **systemic syndromes** requiring screening (cardiac, hematologic, renal). The surgeon must provide **accurate genotype-phenotype information**, relieve unwarranted parental guilt, and arrange appropriate genetic/systemic evaluation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: A feedback loop critical to sustaining limb outgrowth couples which two signaling molecules?

options.text: FGF (from the AER) and SHH (from the ZPA) mutually maintain each other
BMP and Lmx-1
Wnt and nodal
FGF and TBX5 only

questions.explanation: A well-described **positive feedback loop** couples **AER-derived FGF and ZPA-derived SHH** (via intermediaries such as Gremlin/BMP antagonism): SHH maintains AER-FGF, which in turn sustains SHH, keeping the limb bud growing and patterned. This explains the **interdependence** of the centers and why disrupting one axis distorts the others.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: The dorsoventral axis determines the difference between the nail-bearing dorsal surface and the pulp/palmar surface. Which molecule specifies the DORSAL identity?

options.text: Lmx-1 (downstream of dorsal ectoderm Wnt7a signaling)
Sonic hedgehog
En-1 (which specifies ventral)
FGF8

questions.explanation: **Dorsal identity** is specified by **Wnt7a → Lmx-1** in the dorsal mesenchyme, while **En-1** restricts ventral identity. Disrupting this pathway produces **dorsoventral abnormalities** (e.g., nail-patella syndrome, abnormal nail/pulp arrangement, or dorsal/ventral dimelia). This axis completes the three-dimensional framework alongside AER (proximodistal) and ZPA (anteroposterior).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which anomaly-mechanism pairing is INCORRECT?

options.text: Transverse deficiency ← failure of the ZPA/sonic hedgehog
Syndactyly ← failure of interdigital apoptosis (BMP)
Mirror hand ← ectopic ZPA/sonic hedgehog activity
Transverse deficiency ← failure of AER/FGF

questions.explanation: The incorrect pairing is **transverse deficiency ← ZPA/SHH**; transverse deficiencies arise from **AER/FGF failure (proximodistal outgrowth)**. Correct pairings: **syndactyly ← failed BMP-driven interdigital apoptosis**, and **mirror hand ← ectopic ZPA/SHH (anteroposterior duplication)**. Matching each phenotype to its center/morphogen is a favorite exam theme.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: After 8 weeks' gestation (the fetal period), insults to the limb generally cause:

options.text: Deformations/disruptions of already-formed structures rather than primary malformations of patterning
New failures of AER/ZPA/Wnt patterning
No abnormalities at all
Only chromosomal breakage

questions.explanation: By **8 weeks** all limb elements exist; the fetal period involves **growth, differentiation, and enlargement**. Insults then tend to produce **deformations/disruptions of formed parts** (e.g., amniotic bands, growth disturbances) rather than the **patterning malformations** that require the fragile 4–8-week window. This underpins the malformation-vs-deformation distinction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: A child has radial-ray deficiency with bilateral eye-movement abnormality (Duane anomaly) and hearing loss. Which gene is implicated (Okihiro/acro-renal-ocular spectrum)?

options.text: SALL4
TBX5
GLI3
FGFR2

questions.explanation: **SALL4** mutations cause **Duane-radial ray syndrome (Okihiro syndrome)** — radial-ray defects with **Duane eye anomaly** (and variable renal/ear findings). Along with **TBX5 (Holt-Oram)**, it exemplifies how a **radial-ray anomaly is a red flag for a systemic syndrome**, mandating cardiac, renal, ophthalmologic, and hematologic screening.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which cluster of associated anomalies should be screened for whenever a radial longitudinal deficiency is found?

options.text: VACTERL-type associations (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, limb) plus hematologic (Fanconi) workup
Only dental anomalies
Isolated hair abnormalities
No screening is needed

questions.explanation: **Radial-ray deficiency** is frequently syndromic, so evaluation includes screening for **VACTERL** components and specific syndromes — **Holt-Oram (TBX5, cardiac)**, **TAR (thrombocytopenia)**, **Fanconi anemia (DEB test)**, and **Okihiro/SALL4**. Detecting these has major implications (cardiac surgery, marrow-failure surveillance), so the hand finding triggers a broad systemic and genetic workup.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which statement about the AER and fibroblast growth factors is supported by experimental embryology?

options.text: Applying FGF to a limb bud whose AER has been removed can rescue continued proximodistal outgrowth
FGF from the AER specifies dorsal nail identity
FGF causes mirror-image ulnar duplication
FGF has no role in limb outgrowth

questions.explanation: **FGF is the AER's key secreted signal for outgrowth**: removing the AER truncates the limb, but **exogenous FGF can substitute and rescue outgrowth**, and FGF-deficient mice show transverse limb defects. This confirms FGF as the proximodistal morphogen — mechanistically distinct from SHH (anteroposterior) and Wnt/Lmx-1 (dorsoventral).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Ossification in the developing hand begins in which structures first, based on the developmental timeline?

options.text: The long bones (humerus, radius, then ulna) around weeks 7–8, well before the carpals
The carpal bones before the metacarpals
The distal phalanges before any long bone
All bones ossify simultaneously at birth

questions.explanation: Endochondral **ossification begins in the long bones (humerus, then radius, then ulna) around weeks 7–8**, whereas the **carpals ossify much later (mostly postnatally)** — which is why a neonatal wrist radiograph shows no carpal ossific nuclei. This timeline underlies age estimation from ossification and explains imaging findings in congenital wrist anomalies.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Symbrachydactyly (short, webbed/absent digits, often with a unilateral sporadic pattern) is thought to arise from:

options.text: A subclavian/limb-bud vascular disruption affecting AER function, and is generally sporadic/non-heritable
An autosomal dominant SHH duplication
Failure of the Wnt dorsoventral pathway
A chromosomal breakage disorder

questions.explanation: **Symbrachydactyly** is attributed to a **vascular disruption (e.g., subclavian artery supply disruption sequence) impairing AER/limb-bud growth**, producing short/absent digits, often with skin nubbins — typically **unilateral and sporadic (low recurrence)**. It overlaps clinically with 'atypical cleft hand,' and distinguishing it from the heritable typical cleft hand matters for counseling.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which developing nerve reaches and innervates the trapezius during limb-region embryogenesis, per the developmental milestones?

options.text: The (spinal) accessory nerve
The long thoracic nerve
The suprascapular nerve
The musculocutaneous nerve

questions.explanation: Developmental timelines note **trapezius innervation by the accessory nerve** around week 7, as the brachial plexus and its branches (radial, median, ulnar to the elbow) are established. This early neural patterning parallels the skeletal chondrification sequence and underlies the predictable adult innervation used in nerve-injury localization.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct axis-to-signaling-center-to-anomaly triad?

options.text: Anteroposterior — ZPA/SHH — mirror hand (ulnar dimelia)
Proximodistal — Wnt/Lmx-1 — nail-patella syndrome
Dorsoventral — AER/FGF — transverse deficiency
Anteroposterior — AER/FGF — syndactyly

questions.explanation: The correct triad: **anteroposterior axis → ZPA/SHH → mirror hand (ulnar dimelia)**. The others are scrambled: proximodistal is **AER/FGF (transverse deficiency)**, and dorsoventral is **Wnt/Lmx-1 (nail-patella syndrome)**. Committing these three triads to memory (axis–center–morphogen–anomaly) covers a large share of embryology exam questions.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: A key reason to understand embryology as a hand surgeon (per the chapter) is that it:

options.text: Enables mechanistic classification (OMT), informs genotype-phenotype counseling, and predicts syndromic associations
Determines the anesthetic technique
Replaces the need for physical examination
Is purely academic with no clinical relevance

questions.explanation: Embryologic understanding lets the surgeon **classify anomalies by mechanism (OMT), counsel families on inheritance/recurrence, anticipate syndromic associations (cardiac, hematologic, renal), and communicate accurately** — directly improving clinical care. The chapter stresses the surgeon's role at the interface of clinical care and genetics.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Polydactyly with a broad/duplicated great toe, hypertelorism, and macrocephaly (Greig cephalopolysyndactyly) is caused by mutation in which SHH-pathway gene?

options.text: GLI3
TBX5
SALL4
Lmx-1

questions.explanation: **GLI3** (a downstream transcriptional mediator of SHH signaling) mutations cause **Greig cephalopolysyndactyly** (pre- and postaxial polydactyly, syndactyly, craniofacial features); GLI3 truncations also cause **Pallister-Hall syndrome**. This reflects how perturbing the **SHH/GLI (anteroposterior) pathway** produces polydactyly, complementing ZRS-mediated preaxial polydactyly.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which statement about the timing of muscle versus bone differentiation in the limb is supported by the developmental milestones?

options.text: Early muscle masses appear as mesenchymal skeletal condensations chondrify (~weeks 6–7), with muscles becoming individually distinguishable by ~week 7–8
Muscles form completely before any skeletal condensation
Muscles do not form until after birth
Bone and muscle never develop concurrently

questions.explanation: The milestones show **early muscle masses arising around the time of humeral/radioulnar chondrification (~weeks 6–7)**, with **major muscles distinguishable by ~week 7 and all muscles by ~week 8** as the skeleton chondrifies/ossifies. Skeletal (lateral plate) and myogenic (somatic) development proceed **concurrently and interdependently**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: The finding that BMP both promotes chondro-/osteogenesis AND triggers interdigital apoptosis illustrates which developmental principle?

options.text: The same signaling molecule can have context-dependent (pleiotropic) effects in different tissues/locations
BMP acts identically everywhere
Apoptosis and bone formation never share signals
BMP is only relevant after birth

questions.explanation: **BMPs are pleiotropic**: in the cartilage anlagen they promote **chondrogenesis/osteogenesis**, while in the **interdigital mesenchyme they trigger apoptosis** to separate digits. This context-dependence — and its antagonism (e.g., by Gremlin, or FGFR-driven suppression in Apert) — explains how a single pathway can control both skeletal formation and digit separation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which counseling statement is most appropriate for the parents of a child with an isolated unilateral transverse forearm deficiency?

options.text: It is almost always a sporadic vascular/AER event with low recurrence risk, and is not due to anything the mother did
It is autosomal dominant with 50% recurrence
It was certainly caused by a medication
It indicates a high risk of leukemia

questions.explanation: An **isolated unilateral transverse deficiency** is typically a **sporadic, non-heritable event** (attributed to local AER ischemia/hemorrhage), with a **low recurrence risk** and **no maternal fault** — an important reassurance given parental guilt. Concern for teratogens/syndromes rises mainly with **bilateral or multi-limb** involvement, which would prompt further genetic evaluation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: The teratogen thalidomide classically produces which limb phenotype, reflecting an insult during early limb-bud formation?

options.text: Phocomelia — severe proximal deficiency with the hand attached near the trunk, often symmetric and multi-limb
Isolated unilateral small-finger polydactyly
Simple syndactyly of one web only
Dorsoventral nail reversal

questions.explanation: **Thalidomide** disrupts early limb-bud vascular/AER development, producing **phocomelia** (intercalary proximal deficiency with a hand/foot attached close to the trunk), typically **symmetric and affecting multiple limbs** because all buds are exposed simultaneously. Multi-limb, symmetric deficiencies should raise suspicion for a **teratogenic or systemic** cause rather than a sporadic vascular event.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Constriction (amniotic) band sequence can cause fingertips to fuse distally while remaining separated proximally ('acrosyndactyly') with sinus tracts. Why does this differ mechanistically from Apert syndactyly?

options.text: It is an extrinsic deformation/disruption of already-formed, separated digits — not a primary failure of interdigital apoptosis
Both are caused by FGFR mutations
It results from ZPA duplication
It is inherited autosomal dominantly like Apert

questions.explanation: In **acrosyndactyly** from **amniotic bands**, digits initially **separate normally**, then bands secondarily **fuse the tips** (with proximal fenestrations/sinuses) — an **extrinsic deformation/disruption**. **Apert syndactyly** is a **primary malformation** from **FGFR-mediated failure of interdigital apoptosis**. The distinction (sporadic band vs heritable syndrome) shapes counseling and reconstructive planning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Typical (central) cleft hand and symbrachydactyly-type ('atypical cleft') differ importantly in that:

options.text: Typical cleft hand is often bilateral, familial, and may involve the feet; symbrachydactyly is usually unilateral, sporadic, and non-heritable
Both are always inherited autosomal recessively
Symbrachydactyly is bilateral and always familial
There is no clinical or genetic difference

questions.explanation: **Typical/central cleft hand** tends to be **bilateral, familial (e.g., SHFM loci), and associated with foot clefts**, whereas **symbrachydactyly ('atypical cleft')** is generally **unilateral, sporadic (vascular-disruption based), and non-heritable**. Correctly separating them changes **recurrence-risk counseling** and the reconstructive approach — a classic pediatric-hand distinction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: Which triad of interdependent signaling centers must all function for normal three-dimensional limb patterning?

options.text: AER (proximodistal), ZPA (anteroposterior), and Wnt/Lmx-1 (dorsoventral)
Notochord, somite, and neural crest
BMP, nodal, and lefty
TBX5, SALL4, and GLI3 only

questions.explanation: Normal limb form requires the coordinated action of the **AER (FGF, proximodistal outgrowth), the ZPA (SHH, anteroposterior/radioulnar identity), and the Wnt/Lmx-1 dorsoventral center** — three interdependent organizers with extensive cross-talk. Disrupting any one degrades the whole system, and each maps to characteristic anomalies (transverse deficiency, mirror hand, and dorsoventral/nail-patella defects, respectively).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 35 (Embryology)

questions.stem: A 4-month-old has webbing between the ring and small fingers extending the full length of the web, with fused nails. How is this syndactyly classified, and what is 'synonychia'?

options.text: Complete syndactyly; synonychia is the associated fusion of the adjacent nail plates
Incomplete syndactyly; synonychia is a bony bridge
Complicated syndactyly; synonychia is joint fusion
Simple incomplete syndactyly; synonychia is skin only

questions.explanation: Syndactyly is graded by **extent** (incomplete = web does not reach the fingertips; **complete** = union to the tips) and by **tissue** (simple = skin only; complex = shared bone, usually the distal phalangeal tufts; complicated = disorganized/aberrant bone). **Complete** syndactyly reaching the tips often fuses the nails — **synonychia**. Correct classification guides timing and technique.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: The developmental basis of syndactyly is:

options.text: Failure of interdigital mesenchymal apoptosis (normally proceeding distal-to-proximal around gestational days 47–54)
Duplication of the ZPA/sonic hedgehog signal
Failure of AER/FGF outgrowth
An extrinsic amniotic band

questions.explanation: Syndactyly results from **failure of programmed cell death (apoptosis) in the interdigital mesenchyme**, which normally separates the digits **distal-to-proximal (~days 47–54)**. The overlying skin/subcutaneous tissue is normal but the interdigital fascia is thickened. (Amniotic-band **acrosyndactyly** is a different, extrinsic mechanism affecting already-separated digits.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which syndactyly should be separated EARLY (around 3–6 months) rather than deferred to 18–24 months?

options.text: Border-digit or size-mismatched webs (thumb-index or ring-small), because the shorter/slower-growing digit tethers its neighbor into flexion and rotation
Index-long (second) web with similar growth rates
Long-ring (third) web with equal-length digits
Any simple incomplete syndactyly

questions.explanation: Webs between **digits of unequal length/growth rate — the thumb-index (first) and ring-small (fourth) commissures** — are released **early (~3–6 months)** because the shorter digit **tethers the longer one, producing progressive flexion contracture and rotational deformity**. Webs between **similar-length digits (index-long, long-ring)** can wait until **~18–24 months**, when the hand has doubled in size and surgery is more reliable.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Why should only ONE web space be separated per operation when releasing a multi-digit syndactyly?

options.text: Releasing both sides of a digit simultaneously risks compromising its blood supply, causing flap/digit necrosis
To save operative time
Because insurance limits it
To avoid using skin grafts

questions.explanation: Each finger's perfusion depends on its two proper digital arteries; **operating on both borders of the same digit at once can devascularize it**. Therefore in multi-digit syndactyly, **only one web (one side of a given finger) is separated per stage**, protecting perfusion — the release of adjacent webs is staged months apart.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which incision principle is essential in syndactyly separation to prevent secondary flexion contractures?

options.text: Use interdigitating zigzag (dorsal-to-volar mirrored) flaps and avoid straight longitudinal incisions
Use straight longitudinal incisions along each digit
Excise all dorsal skin and graft circumferentially
Make transverse incisions across each joint crease

questions.explanation: **Longitudinal scars contract and cause flexion deformity**, so separation uses **interdigitating zigzag flaps** that place scars in the mid-lateral line and break up the scar vector. Dorsal and volar triangular flaps interdigitate to resurface the sides of the digits, minimizing linear contracture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Regarding commissure (web) reconstruction in syndactyly, which principle reduces 'web creep'?

options.text: Resurface the commissure with a well-vascularized local flap (e.g., dorsal rectangular flap) rather than placing a skin graft at the web base
Always place a split-thickness skin graft in the web
Leave the commissure open to granulate
Use a longitudinal scar down the web

questions.explanation: A skin graft at the **base of the web contracts and migrates distally over time ('web creep')**, narrowing the commissure. Resurfacing the commissure with a **local flap (classically a dorsal proximally-based flap)** provides supple, vascularized skin that resists contracture. Grafts, when needed, are placed on the **sides of the digits (full-thickness)**, not in the web itself.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: When skin grafting is required to cover the sides of digits after syndactyly release, which graft is preferred and from where?

options.text: Full-thickness skin graft, e.g., from the volar wrist or medial arm (avoiding the hair-bearing groin)
Split-thickness graft from the thigh
Groin full-thickness graft as first choice
No graft is ever needed

questions.explanation: **Full-thickness grafts** (better color/texture match, less secondary contracture than split-thickness) are used, ideally from the **volar wrist or medial arm**. The **groin** provides ample skin but frequently develops **hair growth and hyperpigmentation** (~70%), so it is less ideal for the hand. Graftless techniques recruit local flaps to minimize graft need.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: During first-web (thumb-index) syndactyly release, you find the common digital artery bifurcates distally, limiting web deepening. What is an accepted maneuver?

options.text: Ligate one proper digital artery (e.g., the radial proper artery of the index) after confirming the digit remains perfused on clamping/tourniquet release
Ligate both proper digital arteries to the index
Abandon the separation
Divide the digital nerves to gain length

questions.explanation: When a **distal arterial bifurcation** tethers the commissure, one **proper digital artery can be ligated** to allow the web to be deepened — but only after **confirming the digit stays perfused** once the vessel is clamped and the tourniquet released (relying on the contralateral proper artery). Nerves are separated by intraneural dissection, not divided.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A child has bilateral symmetric complex syndactyly ('mitten hand') with midface hypoplasia and craniosynostosis. This Apert hand is treated with the general goal of:

options.text: Staged separations to create a functional (not necessarily five-fingered) hand, releasing border webs first and the first web early
A single operation separating all webs at once
Observation only
Amputation of all central digits

questions.explanation: The **Apert hand (FGFR2)** has severe complex/complicated syndactyly and thumb involvement. Treatment is **staged** (respecting perfusion — one side of a digit per stage), prioritizing an **early first-web release and thumb positioning** and border digits, aiming for a **functional hand with adequate first web and separated border digits** rather than a cosmetically normal five-finger hand.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A child has a unilateral short hand with symbrachydactyly and, on chest exam, absence of the sternal head of the pectoralis major. Which syndrome is this?

options.text: Poland syndrome
Apert syndrome
Holt-Oram syndrome
Nail-patella syndrome

questions.explanation: **Poland syndrome** combines **unilateral absence of the sternocostal head of pectoralis major** (± breast/chest wall hypoplasia) with **ipsilateral hand hypoplasia/symbrachydactyly** (short, webbed/absent digits). It is sporadic (attributed to a subclavian artery supply disruption sequence in utero) and unilateral — distinguishing it from the bilateral, heritable Apert hand.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which web space is most commonly involved in isolated syndactyly?

options.text: The third web (long-ring)
The first web (thumb-index)
The fourth web (ring-small)
The second web (index-long)

questions.explanation: Isolated syndactyly most often affects the **third (long-ring) web**, followed by the fourth, second, and (least commonly) first. It is more frequent in **males**, is **bilateral in ~50%**, and often shows **autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance**. The commonly affected long-ring web involves similar-length digits, so it is typically released later (18–24 months).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A newborn of African descent has a well-formed extra digit on the ULNAR side of the small finger with its own nail, articulating with a duplicated metacarpal head. What is the diagnosis and management?

options.text: Postaxial (ulnar) polydactyly, type A (well-formed) — formal surgical excision with reconstruction of collateral ligament/attachments
Preaxial polydactyly — Wassel excision
Type B (rudimentary) — office suture ligation
Central polydactyly — ray amputation

questions.explanation: **Postaxial (ulnar) polydactyly** is common and often familial (autosomal dominant) in patients of African descent. **Type A** duplicates are **well-formed and articulated**, requiring **formal surgical excision** with reattachment of the ulnar collateral ligament and abductor digiti minimi to preserve small-finger stability. **Type B** are rudimentary/pedunculated skin tags.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A rudimentary, pedunculated (type B) postaxial polydactyly digit hangs by a narrow skin stalk. Regarding suture ligation in the nursery, which is correct?

options.text: It is simple but can leave a residual bump or a tender neuroma; surgical excision gives a cleaner result and avoids these
It restores full function of a well-formed digit
It is contraindicated in all cases
It is used for well-formed type A duplicates

questions.explanation: **Suture ligation** of a narrow-stalked **type B** postaxial digit is quick and common, but can leave a **residual nubbin or a painful neuroma** at the base. Many surgeons therefore prefer **elective surgical excision** (including the neurovascular stalk) for a cleaner, symptom-free result. Type B has no functional bone/joint to preserve; type A requires formal reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Central polydactyly (extra ring/long/index components) differs from ulnar polydactyly in that it:

options.text: Is frequently hidden within a syndactyly ('polysyndactyly'), is often complex/complicated, and is more difficult to reconstruct — commonly autosomal dominant and associated with cleft hand (SHFM)
Is always a simple skin tag amenable to office ligation
Never requires surgery
Only occurs in isolation without syndactyly

questions.explanation: **Central polydactyly** usually involves the **long or ring ray**, is frequently **concealed within a syndactyly (polysyndactyly)**, and tends to be **complex/complicated with shared bones/joints**, making reconstruction challenging (tendon/ligament balancing, joint reconstruction, or ray resection). It is often **autosomal dominant** and shares loci with **split-hand/foot malformation (SHFM)/cleft hand**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A hand has multiple fingers, no thumb, and a duplicated ulna with an absent radius (mirror hand / ulnar dimelia). This reflects abnormality of which developmental signal?

options.text: Excess/ectopic ZPA (sonic hedgehog) activity duplicating posterior (ulnar) structures
Loss of AER/FGF outgrowth
Wnt/Lmx-1 dorsoventral failure
Failure of interdigital apoptosis

questions.explanation: **Mirror hand (ulnar dimelia)** — polydactyly with a **duplicated ulna, absent radius and thumb** — arises from **excess/ectopic ZPA/sonic-hedgehog** signaling, creating a mirror-image posterior duplication. Management is complex, typically **thumb reconstruction (pollicization of an ulnar-border digit)**, excising surplus digits, and addressing forearm/elbow anatomy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A 9-year-old has a painless, progressive flexion contracture of the small-finger PIP joint that worsened at puberty, with no history of trauma. What is the diagnosis and first-line management?

options.text: Camptodactyly; first-line is stretching/splinting and therapy, reserving surgery for refractory functional cases
Boutonnière deformity; central slip repair
Dupuytren contracture; fasciectomy
Trigger finger; A1 pulley release

questions.explanation: **Camptodactyly** is a non-traumatic **PIP flexion contracture, usually of the small finger**, with two peaks (infancy and adolescence, the latter often progressing at the pubertal growth spurt). It stems from imbalance of the flexor/extensor/intrinsic apparatus (anomalous lumbrical/FDS insertions, tight retinacular structures). **First-line is prolonged splinting/therapy**; surgery has **unpredictable results** and is reserved for severe, functionally limiting contractures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Camptodactyly is commonly attributed to abnormalities of which structures?

options.text: Anomalous lumbrical and/or flexor digitorum superficialis insertions with imbalance across the PIP
The A1 pulley and flexor tendon nodule
A delta (longitudinally bracketed) phalanx
The extensor central slip rupture

questions.explanation: Multiple structural anomalies are implicated in **camptodactyly**, most often **aberrant lumbrical origins/insertions and abnormal FDS** producing a **flexion imbalance at the PIP**, sometimes with tight skin/fascia and volar plate contracture. Because the pathology is variable, nonoperative therapy is emphasized and surgery is individualized (release ± tendon rebalancing).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A child has radial angulation of the small finger at the DIP/middle-phalanx level. Radiographs show a trapezoidal middle phalanx. What is this, and a common association?

options.text: Clinodactyly (often from a triangular/'delta' phalanx or C-shaped bracketed epiphysis); commonly associated with Down syndrome
Camptodactyly; associated with arthrogryposis
Kirner deformity; associated with Apert
Boutonnière; associated with rheumatoid arthritis

questions.explanation: **Clinodactyly** is **radioulnar (coronal-plane) angulation**, most often of the **small finger** due to a **trapezoidal/triangular middle phalanx** or a **longitudinally bracketed ('delta') epiphysis** (a C-shaped physis tethering one side). Mild forms are common and often familial; more pronounced clinodactyly is associated with **Down syndrome** and various syndromes. Severe/progressive cases are corrected by **osteotomy (± physiolysis of the bracket)**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A 'longitudinally bracketed epiphysis' (delta phalanx) causes progressive angular deformity because:

options.text: A C-shaped physis extends along one side of the bone, tethering longitudinal growth on that side while the other side grows normally
The entire physis is absent, so the bone cannot grow
The tendon insertions are abnormal
There is a duplicated diaphysis

questions.explanation: In a **delta phalanx**, the epiphysis forms a **C-shaped bracket wrapping around one side of the short tubular bone**, so growth is **tethered on the bracketed side** while the opposite side grows normally, producing progressive **angulation (clinodactyly)** and a triangular/trapezoidal bone. Treatment may combine **physiolysis/bracket resection (with fat interposition)** in young children or **corrective osteotomy** in older ones.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A palmar and radial curving of the distal phalanx of the small finger appearing in later childhood, often bilateral, is:

options.text: Kirner deformity
Clinodactyly
Camptodactyly
Mallet finger

questions.explanation: **Kirner deformity** is a **palmar-radial curvature of the small-finger distal phalanx**, typically appearing around ages 8–12, more common in girls, and often bilateral. It is usually a cosmetic issue managed with observation/splinting; surgery (osteotomy) is rarely needed. It is distinct from clinodactyly (middle-phalanx coronal angulation) and camptodactyly (PIP flexion).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A 1-year-old has a unilateral hand with short fingers, shallow webs, and small nail remnants ('nubbins'), sporadic and non-familial. What is the diagnosis and its presumed mechanism?

options.text: Symbrachydactyly, thought to arise from an in-utero vascular (subclavian) disruption affecting the limb bud
Typical cleft hand, autosomal dominant
Apert syndrome, FGFR2
Macrodactyly, PIK3CA

questions.explanation: **Symbrachydactyly** presents as **short digits with shallow webs and rudimentary nail 'nubbins'**, usually **unilateral and sporadic**, attributed to a **vascular (subclavian artery supply) disruption** of the developing limb (the same mechanism as Poland syndrome). Severity ranges from short fingers to oligodactyly/monodactyly to a transverse-like peromelic hand. Reconstruction may use **nonvascularized toe phalanx transfer, microvascular toe transfer, or distraction**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which reconstructive option is used to restore a missing/short digit in symbrachydactyly in a young child, taking advantage of growth potential?

options.text: Nonvascularized toe phalanx transfer (ideally before ~18 months to retain growth) or microvascular toe-to-hand transfer
Ray amputation of remaining digits
Wrist arthrodesis
Syndactyly creation

questions.explanation: In symbrachydactyly, a **nonvascularized toe phalanx transfer** placed into the digital sleeve can grow if done **early (before ~1–1.5 years, while the transferred physis remains viable)**, and **microvascular toe-to-hand transfer** can create a functional digit/thumb. **Distraction lengthening** and **on-top plasty** are additional options. Reconstruction is individualized to the number and quality of existing parts.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A child has marked enlargement of the index finger involving bone and soft tissue, with the overgrowth conforming to the median nerve territory. What is the diagnosis and a frequently implicated genetic driver?

options.text: Macrodactyly (often lipofibromatous, nerve-territory-oriented), frequently PIK3CA-related
Camptodactyly; FGFR2
Clinodactyly; TBX5
Symbrachydactyly; SALL4

questions.explanation: **Macrodactyly** is a **dysplastic overgrowth** of a digit involving all tissues, classically following a **peripheral nerve territory (median > ulnar)** with **lipofibromatous** infiltration of the nerve. It is frequently driven by **somatic PIK3CA (PI3K-AKT pathway) mutations** (the overgrowth spectrum). It may be **static or progressive**, guiding treatment.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which distinction most influences the surgical strategy for macrodactyly?

options.text: Static versus progressive growth — progressive forms need growth-arresting measures (epiphysiodesis) and may ultimately require debulking or ray amputation
Simple versus complex
Incomplete versus complete
Type A versus type B

questions.explanation: **Static** macrodactyly grows proportionally with the child, whereas **progressive** macrodactyly enlarges disproportionately. Progressive disease warrants **epiphysiodesis (to halt length once the digit matches the parent's same finger)**, staged **soft-tissue debulking**, and sometimes **ray amputation** for grotesque/nonfunctional digits. Nerve stripping/decompression addresses associated nerve compression. Matching intervention to the growth pattern is key.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: An 18-month-old cannot actively extend the thumb IP joint, which is held flexed; a firm nodule (Notta's node) is palpable at the thumb MCP flexion crease. What is the diagnosis and typical course?

options.text: Pediatric trigger thumb — often acquired, and a substantial proportion resolve spontaneously; A1 pulley release if it persists or is fixed
Congenital clasped thumb requiring immediate tendon transfer
Camptodactyly of the thumb
Radial polydactyly

questions.explanation: **Pediatric trigger thumb** presents as a **fixed or triggering flexed IP joint** with **Notta's node** (a thickening of the FPL at the A1 pulley). It is now considered largely **acquired** (not truly congenital), and a meaningful fraction **resolve spontaneously**, so observation ± splinting is reasonable initially; **A1 pulley release** is performed for persistent (beyond ~1–3 years) or fixed cases. It differs from congenital clasped thumb (extensor deficiency).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Pediatric trigger FINGER (as opposed to trigger thumb) differs importantly in that:

options.text: It often has anomalous flexor anatomy (e.g., FDS decussation abnormalities) and A1 release alone may be insufficient, so exploration to address the FDS/A3 may be needed
It always resolves with A1 release alone, like adults
It never requires surgery
It is identical to trigger thumb

questions.explanation: **Pediatric trigger finger** is less common and more complex than trigger thumb: it frequently involves **anomalous flexor tendon anatomy (abnormal FDS decussation, proximal FDS, or nodules)**, so **A1 pulley release alone may not resolve triggering**. Surgery often requires **exploration with possible FDS slip resection or A3 release**, and results are less uniformly successful than trigger thumb.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A newborn has circumferential grooves around several digits with distal swelling (lymphedema) and tip fusion. Which condition, and what is the urgent concern?

options.text: Constriction (amniotic) band syndrome; urgent release is needed if a band causes vascular/lymphatic compromise distal to the ring
Complex syndactyly; no urgency
Macrodactyly; observe
Symbrachydactyly; observe

questions.explanation: **Constriction band (amniotic band) syndrome** produces **circumferential grooves, distal lymphedema, acrosyndactyly, and amputations**. A band causing **progressive vascular or lymphatic compromise is a surgical urgency** (release the constricting ring). Otherwise, elective **staged circumferential release with Z-plasties** (to avoid full-circumference devascularization in one stage) corrects the groove; acrosyndactyly is separated as needed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Why is complete circumferential release of a deep constriction band traditionally staged (or done carefully in one stage) rather than a simple full-circle excision?

options.text: Releasing the entire circumference at once risks devascularizing the distal part; staged (or meticulous single-stage) Z-plasty release preserves perfusion
Because the band is malignant
To allow the band to recur intentionally
Because grafts are always required

questions.explanation: A deep band may tether the only remaining vascular/lymphatic channels; a **single full-circumference excision could compromise distal perfusion**. Traditionally the release is **staged (half the circumference at a time)**, though many now perform a **careful single-stage circumferential release with multiple Z-plasties**, preserving perfusion and correcting the groove/lymphedema with local flaps.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which statement about the inheritance/epidemiology of isolated syndactyly is correct?

options.text: It is more common in males, bilateral in about half, and frequently autosomal dominant with variable penetrance
It is more common in females and always unilateral
It is always X-linked recessive
It is never inherited

questions.explanation: Isolated syndactyly shows a **male predominance**, is **bilateral in ~50%**, and commonly follows an **autosomal dominant pattern with variable penetrance/expressivity**. Syndromic syndactyly (Apert, Poland, oculodentodigital dysplasia, etc.) has its own genetics. Family history and examination for syndromic features guide counseling.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: In complex syndactyly with shared nail and distal phalanx, a key reconstructive challenge at the fingertip is:

options.text: Reconstructing the paronychial folds / nail borders (e.g., with pulp or local flaps) after dividing the shared nail and distal phalanx
Avoiding any incision at the fingertip
Leaving the nail fused permanently
Using a single straight longitudinal incision through the nail

questions.explanation: When a **synonychia/shared distal phalanx** is divided, each digit lacks a lateral **nail fold (paronychium)**, risking a widened nail and poor tip contour. Reconstruction recreates the **lateral nail folds** using pulp/local flaps (e.g., Buck-Gramcko pulp flaps), and the shared distal phalanx is split with careful bone/soft-tissue management to give each tip an acceptable nail and contour.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST appropriate action in syndactyly surgery?

options.text: Placing a skin graft in the depth of the reconstructed web to save operative time
Using a local flap to resurface the commissure
Using interdigitating zigzag flaps along the digits
Separating only one web per stage in multi-digit cases

questions.explanation: **Grafting the web depth is the least appropriate** — it predisposes to **contracture and web creep**; the commissure should be resurfaced with a **vascularized local flap**. The other options are sound: **zigzag flaps** prevent linear contracture, and **one web per stage** protects digital perfusion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A relative contraindication to aggressively separating a complex/complicated syndactyly is:

options.text: When separation would leave the digits unstable or less functional than the joined state
The presence of any webbing
Bilateral involvement
A family history

questions.explanation: If dividing a **complex/complicated** fusion (shared joints/bones) would render the digits **unstable or less functional than when conjoined**, separation may be **inadvisable** — function is prioritized over a normal digit count. This judgment (function over appearance) is central to planning, especially in severe Apert-type or complicated syndactyly.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A child with camptodactyly is most likely to benefit from surgery when:

options.text: There is a fixed, functionally limiting contracture that has failed a diligent course of splinting/therapy, with a definable correctable structural cause
The contracture is mild and non-progressive
The child is an infant with a supple, splint-responsive contracture
Surgery is always first-line

questions.explanation: Because **surgical outcomes in camptodactyly are unpredictable** and can worsen stiffness, operation is reserved for **fixed, functionally significant contractures refractory to prolonged splinting/therapy**, ideally with a **correctable structural lesion** (e.g., anomalous lumbrical/FDS to release or transfer). Mild, supple, or non-progressive cases are managed nonoperatively.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which associated systemic condition is classically linked with clinodactyly (and with a single transverse palmar crease)?

options.text: Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
Marfan syndrome
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Achondroplasia

questions.explanation: **Down syndrome** is classically associated with **fifth-finger clinodactyly** (from a short/trapezoidal middle phalanx) along with a **single transverse palmar (simian) crease** and other features. While mild clinodactyly is common and often benign/familial, its presence with dysmorphic features should prompt evaluation for a syndrome.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: When correcting a significant delta-phalanx clinodactyly in a young child, an option that both realigns the digit and can restore longitudinal growth is:

options.text: Physiolysis (resection of the bracketed epiphysis) with fat interposition to release the tether
Immediate ray amputation
Epiphysiodesis of the entire physis
Tendon transfer

questions.explanation: In a young child, **physiolysis** — resecting the abnormal **C-shaped bracket portion of the epiphysis and interposing fat** — releases the growth tether so the previously constrained side can grow, gradually improving alignment. In older children with less growth remaining, a **closing/opening-wedge osteotomy** directly corrects the angulation. The approach depends on the child's age and remaining growth.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: In macrodactyly, why might epiphysiodesis be timed to when the affected digit matches the length of the SAME finger on the unaffected/parent hand?

options.text: To halt further length growth once the digit reaches an appropriate mature length, avoiding a digit that is too long
To make the digit continue growing indefinitely
Because epiphysiodesis reduces girth
To convert static into progressive growth

questions.explanation: **Epiphysiodesis controls LENGTH** (not girth). Timing it to when the macrodactylous digit reaches the **length of the corresponding normal finger (often referenced to a parent's finger)** stops further elongation at an appropriate size. **Debulking** addresses soft-tissue girth separately, and severe cases may need **ray resection**. Length and girth are managed by different interventions.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which statement about postaxial (ulnar) polydactyly incidence is correct?

options.text: It is far more common in people of African descent (often familial/AD) and there frequently presents as a rudimentary type B; in White populations it is rarer and more often type A or syndromic
It is exclusively seen in White populations
It is never inherited
It is always associated with a syndrome regardless of population

questions.explanation: **Postaxial polydactyly is common and usually isolated/familial (autosomal dominant) in individuals of African descent**, frequently as a **type B skin tag**. In populations of European descent it is **less common and more likely well-formed (type A) or syndromic**, so a lower threshold for **syndrome screening** applies in the latter group.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: After excising a well-formed (type A) postaxial extra small finger, which step is essential for small-finger stability?

options.text: Reattaching the ulnar collateral ligament and the abductor digiti minimi to the retained small finger
Fusing the small-finger MCP joint
Leaving the collateral ligament detached
Transferring the FDS

questions.explanation: Excision of a **type A** ulnar duplicate removes the outermost digit, so the **ulnar collateral ligament and abductor digiti minimi** must be **reattached to the retained small finger** to prevent instability/deviation and preserve small-finger abduction. Simply amputating without reconstructing these ulnar-border stabilizers leads to a deviated, unstable digit.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A common late complication after syndactyly release, presenting as gradual distal migration/narrowing of the reconstructed web, is:

options.text: Web creep
Boutonnière deformity
Trigger finger
Mallet finger

questions.explanation: **Web creep** is the **gradual distal advancement and narrowing of the commissure** after syndactyly surgery, from scar contracture — especially when a **graft was placed in the web** or a linear scar crosses it. It can require revision. Prevention relies on **local flap commissure reconstruction, avoiding grafts in the web, and zigzag scars**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Regarding defatting of digits during syndactyly separation, which is correct?

options.text: Judicious defatting (preserving the dorsal veins) aids skin closure, but overaggressive defatting yields an excessively thin finger as the child loses fat with age
Aggressive removal of all digital fat is ideal
The dorsal venous system should be excised with the fat
Defatting is never done

questions.explanation: Removing some interdigital/digital fat (while **preserving the dorsal venous drainage**) reduces bulk and helps the skin flaps close over the separated digits. However, children **lose subcutaneous fat as they grow**, so **over-defatting produces a conspicuously thin finger** — hence a measured approach.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A preoperative torsional (rotational) malalignment of a digit within a syndactyly should be:

options.text: Addressed at the time of separation, because it will persist otherwise
Ignored, as it corrects spontaneously after release
Treated only years later if symptomatic
Managed by amputation

questions.explanation: **Rotational/coronal malalignment does not correct itself after simple web release** — it must be **addressed during separation** (e.g., osteotomy or soft-tissue rebalancing) to give a straight, well-aligned digit. Recognizing this preoperatively prevents a persistent deformity despite a technically successful web reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A neonate has an extra thumb. Which classification is used, and where is thumb (radial) polydactyly covered relative to ulnar polydactyly?

options.text: The Wassel (Wassel-Flatt) classification is used for radial/thumb polydactyly; it is generally discussed with thumb deformities separately from ulnar polydactyly
The Wassel classification is used for ulnar polydactyly
Radial polydactyly uses the type A/B skin-tag scheme
There is no classification for thumb duplication

questions.explanation: **Radial (preaxial) polydactyly — thumb duplication — is classified by the Wassel (Wassel-Flatt) system (types I–VII by the most proximal level of duplication; type IV, at the metacarpophalangeal level, is the most common)** and is addressed with thumb reconstruction (combining the best parts, the Bilhaut-Cloquet for some, ligament/tendon rebalancing). Ulnar (postaxial) polydactyly uses the type A/B distinction. Thumb duplication is generally covered with **thumb deformities**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: The overall guiding aim when planning reconstruction of pediatric hand malformations is best summarized as:

options.text: Maximize function (grasp, pinch, prehension) and acceptable appearance, timed to growth, while counseling families realistically
Always achieve a normal five-fingered, normal-appearing hand
Delay all surgery until skeletal maturity
Prioritize appearance over function in every case
