questions.explanation: Pediatric hand reconstruction prioritizes **durable function and a socially acceptable appearance**, **timed to the child's growth** (early for tethering/border problems; later when size aids surgery), individualized to the anomaly, with **realistic family counseling**. A perfectly 'normal' hand is often not attainable, so **function-first** goals guide decisions (e.g., not separating a fusion that would destabilize the digits).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which feature favors surgical (A1 pulley) release of a pediatric trigger thumb rather than continued observation?

options.text: A persistent fixed IP flexion deformity that has not resolved after adequate time (and/or a trial of stretching/splinting) in an older child
Presentation at a few months of age with intermittent triggering
Any palpable Notta's node regardless of function
A supple thumb that fully extends

questions.explanation: Because many pediatric trigger thumbs **resolve spontaneously**, initial **observation ± splinting** is reasonable, especially in younger children. **A1 pulley release** is indicated for a **persistent fixed IP flexion contracture** (or continued locking) beyond the expected resolution window (commonly by ~2–3 years), to prevent a lasting flexion deformity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Acrosyndactyly (distal digital fusion with proximal fenestrations) is most characteristic of which condition?

options.text: Constriction (amniotic) band syndrome
Apert syndrome
Poland syndrome
Isolated simple syndactyly

questions.explanation: **Acrosyndactyly** — fusion of the **fingertips with proximal sinus tracts/fenestrations between the digits** — is characteristic of **constriction band syndrome**, where bands secondarily fuse already-separated digit tips. This contrasts with **primary malformation syndactyly** (Apert, isolated), which fuses digits from the base without proximal fenestrations.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: In a hand with complete simple syndactyly of the long-ring web in an otherwise normal child, the optimal timing of separation is generally:

options.text: Around 18–24 months, once the hand has roughly doubled in size
Within the first month of life
At 3–6 months, because it is a border digit
After skeletal maturity

questions.explanation: The **long-ring (third) web joins similar-length digits with no significant tethering**, so early surgery is not required; separation around **18–24 months** — when the hand is larger and anesthesia/handling are safer — gives **more reliable results**. Only **border/mismatched webs** (thumb-index, ring-small) or size-mismatched digits are released early (3–6 months).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which statement about macrodactyly and nerve involvement is correct?

options.text: The enlarged nerve (lipofibromatous infiltration) can cause compressive neuropathy (e.g., carpal tunnel), which may require decompression in addition to debulking
The nerve is always normal in macrodactyly
Nerve involvement excludes the diagnosis
The ulnar nerve territory is affected far more often than the median

questions.explanation: Macrodactyly (nerve-territory-oriented type) features a grossly **enlarged, lipofibromatous nerve** — most often in the **median** distribution — which can produce **compressive neuropathy (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome)**. Management may therefore combine **nerve decompression** with soft-tissue **debulking** and length control (epiphysiodesis), tailored to symptoms and growth pattern.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which is the best initial management for most cases of mild, flexible camptodactyly detected in infancy?

options.text: A prolonged program of passive stretching and static/dynamic PIP extension splinting
Immediate flexor tenotomy
PIP arthrodesis
Amputation

questions.explanation: Most **mild/flexible camptodactyly** responds to (and is best started with) **prolonged passive stretching and PIP extension splinting**, which can correct or prevent progression of the contracture. Surgery is deferred because operative results are inconsistent; it is reserved for **fixed, functionally limiting** contractures that fail conservative care.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: A child has complete complex syndactyly of all four webs, a broad flat digital mass, and severe first-web involvement (Apert 'spade/rosebud' hand). The FIRST reconstructive priority is usually:

options.text: Releasing/creating a functional first web and freeing the thumb to enable pinch
Separating the central mass in a single operation
Cosmetic nail reconstruction
Ray amputation of the long finger

questions.explanation: In the severe Apert hand, **thumb function (pinch) drives independence**, so an **early first-web release and thumb repositioning** is prioritized, followed by **staged** separation of the remaining/border webs (respecting perfusion). Aiming for a **functional first web and separated border digits** takes precedence over restoring a normal five-finger appearance.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: The classic Cronin/skin-graft technique versus modern 'graftless' syndactyly techniques differ in that graftless methods:

options.text: Recruit local dorsal/volar flaps to resurface the digits and web without a skin graft, potentially reducing web creep and donor morbidity
Always require a groin skin graft
Separate all webs in one stage regardless of perfusion
Use only longitudinal incisions

questions.explanation: **Graftless techniques** design **local flaps** (dorsal and volar) to cover the separated digital surfaces and reconstruct the commissure **without a skin graft**, avoiding graft-related **web creep, pigmentation, and donor morbidity**. They are suited to less skin-deficient cases; larger deficits may still need a **full-thickness graft** on the digit sides. The commissure is best flap-reconstructed regardless of method.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: Which pairing of pediatric digital deformity and its defining plane/level of deformity is correct?

options.text: Camptodactyly = PIP flexion (sagittal plane); clinodactyly = coronal (radioulnar) angulation, usually at the small-finger middle phalanx
Camptodactyly = coronal angulation; clinodactyly = PIP flexion
Both are pure rotational deformities
Both occur only at the DIP joint

questions.explanation: **Camptodactyly** is a **flexion (sagittal-plane) contracture of the PIP**, whereas **clinodactyly** is **coronal-plane (radioulnar) angulation**, classically of the **small finger at the middle phalanx** (often a delta phalanx). **Kirner** is palmar-radial curving of the small-finger distal phalanx. Correctly localizing the plane and level guides diagnosis and treatment.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 36 (Deformities of the Hand & Fingers)

questions.stem: The modified Blauth classification of thumb hypoplasia is central to planning. What is the single most important distinction it hinges on for deciding RECONSTRUCTION versus POLLICIZATION?

options.text: The stability of the carpometacarpal (CMC/basal) joint — stable (type IIIA) is reconstructed, unstable (type IIIB) is pollicized
The presence of a thumbnail
The width of the first web space
Whether the thumb has a flexor pollicis longus

questions.explanation: The pivotal issue is **CMC (basal joint) stability**. A **type IIIA** thumb has a **stable CMC** worth **reconstructing** to give a prehensile thumb; a **type IIIB** thumb has an **unstable/absent CMC** — reconstruction fails ('a house without a foundation'), so it is treated by **thumb ablation and index pollicization**. Types IV (floating) and V (absent) are also pollicized. This IIIA/IIIB split is the crux of the treatment paradigm.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has a small thumb with absent thenar muscles, a narrow first web, and ulnar collateral ligament laxity, but intact extrinsic tendons and a stable CMC joint. What is the Blauth type and its treatment?

options.text: Type II — opponensplasty, first web release, and UCL reconstruction
Type I — no treatment
Type IIIB — pollicization
Type V — pollicization

questions.explanation: **Type II** hypoplasia has **absent thenar (intrinsic) muscles, a narrow/tight first web, and MCP (UCL) instability**, with **normal extrinsics and a stable CMC**. Reconstruction addresses all three: **opponensplasty** (e.g., ring FDS or abductor digiti minimi/Huber) for opposition, **first-web release** (e.g., four-flap Z-plasty), and **UCL reconstruction** for pinch stability.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: How does Blauth type III thumb hypoplasia differ from type II?

options.text: Type III adds extrinsic muscle/tendon abnormalities (deficient EPL/EPB or FPL) and skeletal deficiency, on top of the type II findings
Type III has a normal first web
Type III has no thenar deficiency
Type III always has a completely absent metacarpal

questions.explanation: **Type III** includes all **type II** features (absent thenar muscles, tight first web, UCL laxity) **plus extrinsic tendon/muscle deficiencies (EPL/EPB/FPL) and skeletal deficiency**. Assessing active MCP/IP motion reveals the extrinsic deficits. Type III is then subdivided by **CMC stability into IIIA (reconstruct) and IIIB (pollicize)**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A 1-year-old has a thumb attached to the hand only by a narrow skin bridge containing a single neurovascular pedicle; it is floppy and ignored. What is this, and its management?

options.text: Type IV hypoplasia (pouce flottant / floating thumb) — ablation and index pollicization
Type II — opponensplasty
Type I — observation
Type IIIA — extrinsic tendon reconstruction

questions.explanation: A **pouce flottant (floating thumb) is type IV** — a rudimentary thumb on a narrow skin/neurovascular bridge, functionally useless and ignored. Treatment is **thumb ablation with index pollicization**. **Type V** is complete absence (±small nubbin), likewise treated by pollicization when the index is suitable.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Type I thumb hypoplasia (minor generalized hypoplasia) is generally managed by:

options.text: Observation — functional impairment is negligible and no surgery is warranted
Pollicization
Opponensplasty and UCL reconstruction
First web release

questions.explanation: **Type I** is a **mildly small but otherwise functional thumb** with all components present; **no surgery is needed**. Surgery begins to be indicated at **type II/IIIA** (reconstruction) and shifts to **pollicization** at **IIIB, IV, and V**. Matching the intervention to the Blauth type is the essence of the paradigm.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Why are plain radiographs often UNRELIABLE for judging CMC-joint stability (IIIA vs IIIB) in a young child, and what helps instead?

options.text: The metacarpal base and trapezium do not ossify until ~6 years, so cartilage is invisible on x-ray; MRI/ultrasound and serial clinical exams are more reliable
Radiographs overestimate instability
The CMC is fully ossified at birth
X-rays cannot show the thumb at all

questions.explanation: The **first metacarpal base and trapezium remain cartilaginous until ~6 years**, so plain films cannot show the joint architecture (a metacarpal 'tapering to a point' suggests a deficient base, but milder cases look normal). **MRI or ultrasound** visualize the cartilage, and **serial clinical examination** is equally reliable — a child who **ignores the thumb, pronates the index, and uses scissor pinch** effectively has an unstable (IIIB) thumb.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Clinical signs that a hypoplastic thumb is functionally being ignored (favoring pollicization over reconstruction) include:

options.text: The child performs scissor (side-to-side) pinch between index and long fingers, the index finger pronates, and the index-long web widens
Strong tip pinch using the thumb
Normal opposition to the small finger
A stable, actively used thumb MCP joint

questions.explanation: An unstable/unusable thumb is **neglected**: the child develops **scissor pinch between the index and long fingers**, the **index pronates** toward the working position, and the **long-index web widens** — the hand is 'preparing' the index to act as a thumb. These adaptive signs support **thumb ablation and index pollicization**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A useful maxim in managing thumb hypoplasia — that guides ablating a small but present thumb in favor of pollicization — is:

options.text: 'Function trumps form' — a pollicized index outperforms a reconstructed but small/unstable thumb
'Always preserve five digits'
'Never remove a congenital part'
'Appearance is more important than pinch'

questions.explanation: The principle **'function trumps form'** justifies **ablating an unstable/too-small thumb and pollicizing the index**, which yields better prehension than a reconstructed thumb built on a poor foundation. Because cultural expectations may favor five digits, this requires careful counseling (often parent-to-parent), but the functional result is superior.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Why is attempting basal-joint (CMC) reconstruction (e.g., free metatarsophalangeal transfer) in a type IIIB thumb discouraged?

options.text: Such reconstructions give inferior outcomes to pollicization and can jeopardize the future option of a successful pollicization
It is technically impossible
It always causes malignancy
Pollicization is contraindicated afterward for anatomic reasons only

questions.explanation: Attempts to build a stable CMC (nonvascularized or free vascularized MTP joint transfer) in a **type IIIB** thumb have yielded **inferior function compared with index pollicization** and may **compromise the tissues needed for a later pollicization**. Hence the recommendation to proceed directly to **ablation + pollicization** rather than a doomed basal-joint reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A child with radial longitudinal deficiency and thumb hypoplasia must be screened for systemic syndromes. Which test is critical to obtain, and why?

options.text: Chromosomal breakage (DEB/mitomycin) test for Fanconi anemia — marrow failure can be fatal and appears after birth, so early detection is lifesaving
Only an echocardiogram is needed
No screening is required for isolated thumb hypoplasia
A random glucose level

questions.explanation: Thumb/radial hypoplasia is a red flag for syndromes: **Holt-Oram (TBX5, cardiac septal defects), VACTERL, TAR (thrombocytopenia–absent radius, thumbs present), and Fanconi anemia**. **Fanconi anemia** (autosomal recessive DNA-repair defect) causes **progressive aplastic anemia/leukemia not present at birth**, so a **DEB chromosomal-breakage test** should be sent — early diagnosis enables potentially lifesaving treatment. Cardiac and renal evaluations are also arranged.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: During index pollicization, which is the correct disposition of the index metacarpal?

options.text: The metacarpal is shortened/recessed and its head is stabilized to become the new 'trapezium' (basal joint) of the thumb
The entire metacarpal is preserved at full length
The metacarpal is lengthened with a graft
The metacarpal head is discarded

questions.explanation: In **pollicization**, the **index metacarpal is largely resected/recessed**, and the **metacarpal HEAD is rotated and fixed to function as the new trapezium (thumb basal joint)** — hyperextending it to prevent later MCP hyperextension. This shortens the ray to thumb length and creates a stable CMC-equivalent, the foundation the type IIIB thumb lacked.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: In pollicization, the index finger is rotated and positioned into approximately what orientation to act as an opposable thumb?

options.text: Pronated (~120–160°) and abducted/extended at the new basal joint, so its pulp opposes the other digits
Supinated 90°
Left in the plane of the other fingers
Fully flexed into the palm

questions.explanation: The index is **rotated (pronated ~120–160°) and placed in palmar abduction/extension** at its new basal joint so the pulp faces the other fingertips for opposition/pinch. Correct **rotation and position** are essential — the digit must confront the other fingers, not lie parallel to them. The metacarpal head is set in hyperextension to avoid recurrent hyperextension.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: During pollicization, the intrinsic muscles of the index are rebalanced to reproduce thumb muscles. Which reassignment is correct?

options.text: First dorsal interosseous → abductor pollicis brevis (abductor), and first palmar interosseous → adductor pollicis
Both interossei become the extensor pollicis longus
The lumbrical becomes the flexor pollicis longus
No muscle rebalancing is performed

questions.explanation: The index intrinsics are repurposed: the **first dorsal interosseous becomes the abductor pollicis brevis** and the **first palmar interosseous becomes the adductor pollicis**, recreating balanced thumb abduction/adduction. The extrinsic tendons are also rerouted (e.g., **EDC → APL**, **EIP → EPL**) so the pollicized digit extends/abducts like a thumb. This muscle rebalancing is what makes a pollicized index truly thumb-like.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A prerequisite for a successful index pollicization is:

options.text: A supple, mobile index finger — 'a stiff index becomes a stiff thumb'
A completely normal thumb
An absent index finger
Skeletal maturity of the hand

questions.explanation: The pollicized digit can only be as good as the index it is built from — **a stiff index will become a stiff, poorly functional thumb**. So the index must be **supple and mobile with reasonable joints** to justify pollicization. If the index is unsuitable, alternative reconstructions (e.g., microvascular toe transfer) may be considered.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Thumb hypoplasia occurring within an ULNAR longitudinal deficiency is treated:

options.text: The same way as in radial deficiency — by the Blauth classification, with pollicization for severe (IV/V/IIIB) hypoplasia
Never surgically
Only by CMC fusion
Differently, always avoiding pollicization

questions.explanation: Although thumb hypoplasia is classically associated with **radial** deficiency, it also occurs with **ulnar** deficiency, and the **treatment is the same** — guided by the Blauth type, with **pollicization** for marked hypoplasia (with minor technical/skin-design modifications). The management is dictated by the thumb's own deficiency grade, not by which side of the forearm is deficient.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: For opposition (opponensplasty) in a type II/IIIA hypoplastic thumb, a commonly used donor is:

options.text: Ring-finger flexor digitorum superficialis (routed around an FCU pulley), or the abductor digiti minimi (Huber transfer)
Flexor pollicis longus
Extensor carpi ulnaris
Pronator teres

questions.explanation: Because the thenar intrinsics are absent, opposition is restored with an **opponensplasty** — typically the **ring FDS** passed around a distally based **FCU pulley** to reproduce the abduction–opposition vector (with a slip often used to reconstruct the UCL), or a **Huber (abductor digiti minimi) transfer**, which also adds thenar bulk. These are combined with **first-web release**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A tight, narrow first web space in thumb hypoplasia is typically released with:

options.text: A four-flap (or two-flap) Z-plasty to deepen and resurface the web with local tissue
A skin graft placed in the depth of the web
A longitudinal incision left to granulate
CMC arthrodesis

questions.explanation: The tight first web is deepened with a **four-flap (or two-flap) Z-plasty**, recruiting **local skin** to widen the commissure without a graft (grafts in the web contract and narrow it). Severe web deficiency may require a **dorsal rotation/transposition flap**. Adequate first-web width is essential for thumb abduction and grasp of large objects.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A newborn has a duplicated thumb. Which classification describes it, and which type is most common?

options.text: Wassel classification (I–VII by the most proximal duplicated level); Wassel type IV (metacarpophalangeal-level duplication) is most common
Blauth classification; type II most common
The A/B skin-tag scheme; type B most common
ICSHT groups; group 2 most common

questions.explanation: **Radial (preaxial) polydactyly** is classified by **Wassel (I–VII)** according to the **most proximal level of duplication**; **type IV (duplication at the MCP level, i.e., two proximal phalanges on one metacarpal) is the most common**. Reconstruction combines the best elements, reconstructs the collateral ligaments/thenar insertions, and aligns the retained thumb (Bilhaut-Cloquet is reserved for selected symmetric duplications).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: In reconstructing a Wassel IV thumb duplication (usually retaining the ulnar thumb), which steps are essential?

options.text: Excise the (usually radial) less-developed thumb, reconstruct the radial collateral ligament, reattach the thenar/APB and adductor as needed, and correct any angular (zigzag) deformity
Simply amputate the smaller thumb with no ligament or tendon reconstruction
Always perform a Bilhaut-Cloquet combination
Fuse the IP and MCP joints

questions.explanation: The **ulnar thumb is usually retained** (it carries the ulnar collateral ligament and adductor). After **ablating the radial duplicate**, the **radial collateral ligament and abductor pollicis brevis are reconstructed/reattached** to the retained thumb, **tendons are centralized**, and any **angular ('zigzag') malalignment is corrected (osteotomy)**. Neglecting ligament/tendon rebalancing leads to instability and recurrent deformity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: The Bilhaut-Cloquet procedure for thumb duplication is best reserved for:

options.text: Symmetric duplications where each thumb is too small alone — combining central portions of both to make one adequately sized thumb (accepting a risk of nail ridging and joint stiffness)
All Wassel duplications routinely
A clearly dominant thumb with a tiny radial remnant
Ulnar polydactyly

questions.explanation: **Bilhaut-Cloquet** fuses the central halves of two **symmetric, individually inadequate** thumbs into one larger thumb. It provides bulk but risks **nail deformity (ridge), physeal/joint stiffness, and a wide nail**, so it is used selectively. When one thumb is clearly dominant, simple ablation of the smaller with ligament/tendon reconstruction is preferred.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: An infant holds the thumb flexed and adducted into the palm and cannot actively extend the MCP joint; passive extension is possible. What is the likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?

options.text: Congenital clasped thumb (often deficient EPB/EPL); first-line is prolonged extension splinting
Trigger thumb; A1 release immediately
Thumb hypoplasia type IV; pollicization
Arthrogrypotic wrist; osteotomy

questions.explanation: **Congenital clasped thumb** is a **supple thumb held flexed/adducted from deficient extensor (EPB ± EPL) function** (± thumb-in-palm intrinsic tightness). Because passive extension is preserved, **first-line is a prolonged trial of extension splinting**, which corrects many cases. Persistent, supple cases with a passively correctable thumb may need **tendon transfer for extension (e.g., EIP)**, with first-web release and MCP stabilization as indicated. Fixed/complex forms (part of arthrogryposis/windblown hand) are more involved.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: For a persistent supple congenital clasped thumb with an absent extensor pollicis brevis that fails splinting, a common reconstructive step is:

options.text: Tendon transfer to restore thumb extension (e.g., extensor indicis proprius to the thumb extensor), ± first-web release and MCP stabilization
A1 pulley release
Thumb amputation
CMC arthrodesis in a child

questions.explanation: When splinting fails and the extensor mechanism is deficient, a **tendon transfer (commonly EIP) restores active thumb extension**; associated **first-web contracture is released** and an unstable MCP is **stabilized**. This addresses the underlying extensor deficiency rather than the flexor-side pathology of trigger thumb (A1 release).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A triphalangeal thumb (an extra phalanx making the thumb finger-like) is often associated with:

options.text: Preaxial (radial) polydactyly and SHH/ZRS-pathway dysregulation; some familial forms are autosomal dominant
Failure of the AER (transverse deficiency)
Ulnar dimelia only
Fanconi anemia exclusively

questions.explanation: A **triphalangeal thumb** has an extra (often delta-shaped) middle phalanx, giving a longer, finger-like, non-opposable thumb frequently **associated with preaxial polydactyly and ZRS/SHH dysregulation** (some pedigrees autosomal dominant). Treatment reduces the extra phalanx and reconstructs a shorter, opposable thumb (resect the extra phalanx/delta phalanx, correct alignment, and address any web/rotation issues).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which associated malformation cluster should specifically prompt cardiology evaluation in a child with thumb/radial hypoplasia?

options.text: Holt-Oram syndrome (TBX5) — commonly atrial/ventricular septal defects and conduction anomalies
Poland syndrome — cardiac defects are the rule
Camptodactyly — always has cardiac disease
Isolated clinodactyly — needs echocardiography

questions.explanation: **Holt-Oram ('heart-hand') syndrome (TBX5)** pairs radial-ray/thumb anomalies with **cardiac septal defects and conduction disturbances**, so an **echocardiogram/ECG** is warranted. Together with **Fanconi (DEB test)**, **TAR (platelets)**, and **VACTERL (vertebral/renal/anal/TE)** screening, this reflects the systemic workup triggered by a thumb/radial anomaly.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which statement about the timing of index pollicization is most accurate?

options.text: It is typically performed in early childhood (often ~1–3 years) to allow cortical adaptation and incorporation of the new thumb into hand use
It must be delayed until skeletal maturity
It should be done in the first week of life
Timing has no effect on cortical adaptation

questions.explanation: **Pollicization is generally done in early childhood (commonly around 1–3 years)** so the developing brain readily **remaps the index as a thumb**, and the child grows up using it naturally. Very early surgery is limited by small size/anesthetic risk, but early-childhood timing optimizes **cortical plasticity and functional incorporation**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: After pollicization, which complication is specifically guarded against by fixing the transposed metacarpal head in hyperextension?

options.text: Hyperextension deformity of the new thumb's basal (MCP-turned-CMC) joint
Flexion contracture of the IP joint
Nail ridging
First web contracture

questions.explanation: The index **MCP joint becomes the new basal joint** and is prone to **hyperextension**; setting the **metacarpal head in hyperextension (so the joint's resting posture ends up neutral/slightly flexed)** counteracts this tendency and prevents a hyperextension deformity that would impair pinch. Correct rotation, shortening, and muscle balancing further ensure a stable, opposable thumb.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a type IIIA from a type IIIB thumb on examination when imaging is equivocal?

options.text: A IIIA thumb is actively used with a stable base for pinch, whereas a IIIB thumb is ignored with an unstable/absent basal joint on stress and repeat exams
IIIA has no thenar muscles; IIIB has normal thenar muscles
IIIA lacks a nail; IIIB has a nail
IIIB has a wider first web than IIIA

questions.explanation: Both IIIA and IIIB share type III extrinsic/skeletal deficits; the discriminator is **CMC stability and usage**. A **IIIA** thumb has a **stable base and is incorporated into pinch (reconstruct)**; a **IIIB** thumb has an **unstable/deficient base and is neglected** (index pronation, scissor pinch, widened long-index web) — favoring **pollicization**. Serial clinical assessment is as reliable as imaging for this call.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: The abductor digiti minimi (Huber) opponensplasty is particularly useful in thumb hypoplasia because it:

options.text: Restores opposition AND adds soft-tissue bulk to the deficient thenar eminence
Reconstructs the CMC joint
Provides thumb extension
Requires sacrificing the small finger

questions.explanation: In hypoplasia the **thenar eminence is flat/absent**, so the **Huber (ADM) transfer** is attractive: rotating the abductor digiti minimi on its pedicle across the palm restores **opposition** while **augmenting thenar bulk** (cosmetic and functional benefit). It is an alternative to the ring-FDS opponensplasty, chosen by surgeon preference and anatomy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which statement about counseling families toward thumb ablation and pollicization is emphasized?

options.text: It requires a prolonged, empathetic conversation (sometimes parent-to-parent) because removing a present thumb is counterintuitive, though function is superior
It requires no discussion since it is routine
Cultural preferences never influence the decision
Parents universally accept ablation immediately

questions.explanation: Recommending **removal of an existing (if unusable) thumb** is emotionally difficult for families, so it demands **thorough, empathetic counseling** — often facilitated by **connecting parents with others who have made the same choice**. While 'function trumps form,' respecting **cultural values** (some families require five digits) may occasionally lead to nonoperative retention of the unstable thumb.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: In a type II hypoplastic thumb, failure to reconstruct the ulnar collateral ligament will most likely result in:

options.text: An unstable MCP joint with poor, painful pinch (the thumb collapses into valgus during pinch)
Loss of thumb extension
A trigger thumb
Web creep

questions.explanation: The **UCL provides the stability needed for lateral/tip pinch**; leaving it incompetent yields an **MCP that collapses into valgus under load**, giving weak, painful pinch. Thus type II reconstruction bundles **UCL reconstruction** with opponensplasty and first-web release — often using a slip of the FDS opponensplasty to stabilize the joint.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which thumb-duplication scenario would make simple ablation of one thumb (without ligament reconstruction) most likely to fail?

options.text: Removing the ulnar thumb (with its UCL and adductor) and retaining the radial thumb without reconstructing the ulnar-sided stabilizers
Removing a tiny radial floating remnant from a dominant ulnar thumb after reconstructing the RCL
A well-reconstructed Wassel IV retaining the ulnar thumb
Any case where tendons are rebalanced

questions.explanation: The **ulnar thumb typically carries the ulnar collateral ligament and adductor insertion**, so **removing it without reconstructing those ulnar-sided stabilizers on the retained radial thumb** produces an unstable thumb with poor pinch and progressive deformity. Successful duplication surgery always **reconstructs the collateral ligaments and rebalances tendons/intrinsics**, not just amputates the extra part.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A hand therapist's role in thumb hypoplasia management is best described as:

options.text: Essential for evaluation, family support/decision-making, and (especially) postoperative rehabilitation that directly affects the surgical result
Limited to fitting a splint preoperatively
Unnecessary if surgery is planned
Only relevant for type I thumbs

questions.explanation: Although little **nonoperative** treatment applies to hypoplasia, an experienced **hand therapist is invaluable** — assessing function, **supporting families through the difficult decision-making**, and then serving as a **primary rehabilitation provider** whose work strongly influences the outcome of opponensplasty, UCL reconstruction, or pollicization.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: The extrinsic tendon abnormality in type III hypoplasia may include an anomalous FDS-to-EPL interconnection ('pollex abductus'). Its significance is:

options.text: It tethers the thumb (an aberrant connection between flexor and extensor systems) and must be recognized/released during reconstruction
It strengthens the thumb and should be preserved
It has no effect on surgery
It only occurs in ulnar polydactyly

questions.explanation: **Pollex abductus** is an anomalous fibrous/tendinous connection linking the **flexor (FPL/FDS) and extensor (EPL)** systems, tethering the thumb and contributing to deformity in hypoplasia and radial polydactyly. It must be **identified and released** during reconstruction to free thumb motion; failure to address it leaves a tethered, malaligned thumb.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which is the correct overall treatment map by Blauth type?

options.text: I = observe; II & IIIA = reconstruct (opponensplasty, first-web release, UCL ± extrinsic reconstruction); IIIB, IV, V = ablation + pollicization
I = pollicize; II = observe; III = amputate
All types = pollicization
All types = observation

questions.explanation: The Blauth treatment map: **Type I — observation**; **Type II and IIIA — reconstruction** (opponensplasty, first-web release, UCL reconstruction, plus extrinsic tendon reconstruction in IIIA); **Types IIIB, IV, and V — thumb ablation with index pollicization** (when the index is suitable). The **stable-vs-unstable CMC (IIIA vs IIIB)** boundary is the decisive point.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: In a child with bilateral thumb hypoplasia requiring pollicization, a reasonable approach is:

options.text: Stage the pollicizations (one hand at a time), individualized to the index quality on each side and the child's development
Pollicize both hands simultaneously in the neonatal period regardless of size
Never operate on bilateral cases
Perform CMC fusions bilaterally instead

questions.explanation: Bilateral cases are generally **staged (one hand at a time)** so the child retains a functioning hand during recovery and each side is timed to the **suitability of its index finger** and the child's growth. Each pollicization is individualized; simultaneous bilateral surgery is avoided to preserve function and manage rehabilitation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that a small but present thumb with a stable CMC should still be ablated in favor of pollicization?

options.text: The thumb is simply too small/scrawny to ever provide useful pinch despite the stable base
The thumb has a normal-sized, well-used pulp
The first web is already wide
The extrinsic tendons are all present

questions.explanation: Standard pollicization indications can be **expanded to a stable-CMC thumb that is nonetheless too small to be useful** — reconstruction would still leave an inadequate thumb, so **ablation + pollicization of the robust index** yields better function. This decision, like all pollicization counseling, requires careful family discussion around 'function trumps form.'
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which statement about extensor tendon rerouting in pollicization is correct?

options.text: The extensor digitorum communis to the index is shortened/rerouted to act as an abductor pollicis longus, and the extensor indicis proprius to act as an extensor pollicis longus
All extensor tendons are excised
The flexor tendons are transferred to become extensors
No tendon adjustment is needed

questions.explanation: To make the pollicized index behave like a thumb, the **extrinsic extensors are re-tasked: the EDC (index) is shortened to serve as the APL** (radial abduction of the new thumb) and the **EIP as the EPL** (thumb extension). Combined with the intrinsic reassignments (first dorsal interosseous → APB; first palmar interosseous → adductor), this reproduces balanced thumb motion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A thumb that is triphalangeal, long, and lies in the plane of the fingers (non-opposable) is functionally problematic because:

options.text: It behaves like a finger rather than an opposable thumb, impairing pinch/grasp; reconstruction aims to shorten it and restore opposition
It has excessive opposition
It is always painful
It cannot be operated on

questions.explanation: A **triphalangeal thumb** is longer and often in the finger plane, so it acts as a **fifth finger without true opposition**, degrading pinch. Reconstruction **removes the extra (often delta) phalanx to shorten it, corrects alignment, and re-establishes an opposable posture** (± first-web and rotational adjustments), converting a finger-like digit into a functional thumb.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: The most reliable single determinant of whether a hypoplastic thumb should be reconstructed or pollicized is:

options.text: The status (stability) of the carpometacarpal joint
The size of the nail
The presence of a Notta's node
The child's age at presentation

questions.explanation: Everything in the Blauth paradigm turns on the **CMC (basal joint)**: **stable → reconstruct (types II/IIIA); unstable/absent → pollicize (IIIB/IV/V)**. A stable base is the 'foundation' required for a reconstructed thumb to work; without it, reconstruction fails and index pollicization is the superior option.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST appropriate management pairing?

options.text: Type IIIB thumb → basal-joint reconstruction to preserve five digits
Type I thumb → observation
Type II thumb → opponensplasty, first-web release, UCL reconstruction
Type IV (floating) thumb → index pollicization

questions.explanation: The least appropriate is **reconstructing a type IIIB basal joint** to keep five digits — these attempts function poorly and can **compromise a later pollicization**; IIIB is best treated by **ablation + pollicization** ('function trumps form'). The other pairings are correct (observe type I; reconstruct type II; pollicize type IV).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Radial (preaxial) polydactyly is generally which pattern of occurrence, in contrast to postaxial polydactyly?

options.text: Usually unilateral and often sporadic (whereas postaxial is frequently bilateral and familial/AD, especially in patients of African descent)
Always bilateral and X-linked
Identical epidemiology to postaxial polydactyly
Never requires surgery

questions.explanation: **Radial/thumb (preaxial) polydactyly** is typically **unilateral and often sporadic** (Wassel-classified, more common in some Asian populations), whereas **postaxial (ulnar) polydactyly** is frequently **bilateral and autosomal dominant**, especially common in people of African descent. Recognizing the pattern aids counseling and syndrome screening (e.g., triphalangeal/preaxial forms with SHH-pathway conditions).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: In pollicization, adequate SHORTENING of the ray is important because failure to shorten enough results in:

options.text: A new thumb that is too long, impairing opposition and pinch
A thumb that is too short to reach the fingers
Immediate vascular necrosis
Loss of sensation

questions.explanation: The pollicized digit must be **thumb-length** (roughly reaching the proximal-to-mid index-turned-long finger), which requires **resecting most of the index metacarpal**. Insufficient shortening leaves an **overly long 'thumb' that opposes poorly**. Proper length, rotation, position, and muscle balance together determine a good functional result.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has a stable-CMC hypoplastic thumb with absent FPL and EPL but a reconstructable base (type IIIA). Beyond opponensplasty/first-web/UCL work, reconstruction also requires:

options.text: Reconstruction of extrinsic thumb extension and flexion (tendon transfers) to power the MCP/IP joints
Pollicization
Only observation
CMC arthrodesis

questions.explanation: Because **type IIIA adds extrinsic deficiencies (absent EPL/FPL)**, reconstruction must **restore extrinsic thumb flexion and extension** (e.g., tendon transfers to power the IP/MCP) in addition to the type II components (opponensplasty, first-web release, UCL reconstruction). The **stable CMC** makes this worthwhile — distinguishing IIIA (reconstruct) from IIIB (pollicize).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which statement about the goal of thumb reconstruction/pollicization is most accurate?

options.text: To provide a stable, mobile, opposable post of adequate length for pinch and grasp — prioritizing function
To reproduce a perfectly normal-appearing thumb regardless of function
To maximize thumb length above all
To fuse the joints for stability

questions.explanation: The overriding aim is a **stable, mobile, opposable thumb of appropriate length** that enables **pinch and grasp** — function first. Whether via reconstruction (types II/IIIA) or pollicization (IIIB/IV/V), the surgeon balances **stability (CMC/UCL), motion (opposition/extension), position (first web), and length** to optimize hand function.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A congenital clasped thumb that is part of a broader picture (multiple flexed digits, ulnar deviation — 'windblown hand'/distal arthrogryposis) differs from simple clasped thumb in that:

options.text: It is more complex and rigid, often with fixed contractures and skin deficiency, and typically requires surgical release/reconstruction rather than splinting alone
It always resolves with a few weeks of splinting
It never involves the first web
It is identical to a simple supple clasped thumb

questions.explanation: The **complex clasped thumb** (as in **windblown hand/distal arthrogryposis**) features **rigid contractures, MCP ulnar deviation, first-web and skin deficiency, and collateral/capsular tightness**, so **splinting alone is insufficient**; management involves **soft-tissue release, first-web reconstruction, extensor reconstruction/tendon transfer, and MCP stabilization**. This contrasts with the **simple, supple clasped thumb** that often corrects with prolonged extension splinting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: The single most important structure to protect during index pollicization to keep the transferred digit alive is:

options.text: The neurovascular bundles — the index is transposed on its intact digital arteries and nerves (with one common vessel often ligated after confirming perfusion)
The A1 pulley
The extensor retinaculum
The trapezium

questions.explanation: Pollicization transposes the index as an **island on its neurovascular pedicles**, so meticulous **preservation of the digital arteries and nerves** is essential to viability. As in syndactyly release, the artery to the adjacent web may be **ligated only after confirming the index remains perfused**. Injury to the pedicle risks digit loss — the feared catastrophic complication.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A duplicated thumb often shows a 'zigzag' collapse deformity. What causes it, and how is it corrected?

options.text: Angular malalignment at the MCP/IP with eccentric tendon pull; correction requires osteotomy and centralization/rebalancing of the extrinsic tendons
Excess length; correct by lengthening
A1 pulley stenosis; correct by release
It cannot be corrected

questions.explanation: The retained thumb after duplication surgery may deviate in a **'zigzag' (angulation at one joint compensated at the next)** from **skeletal malalignment and eccentric/insertion-abnormal extrinsic tendons**. Durable correction requires **corrective osteotomy plus centralizing and rebalancing the FPL/EPL tendons** (and releasing any pollex abductus), not merely removing the extra part.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which best differentiates a pediatric trigger thumb from a congenital clasped thumb?

options.text: Trigger thumb has a fixed/locking FLEXED IP with a Notta's node (flexor-side); clasped thumb is a flexed/adducted thumb from EXTENSOR deficiency, passively correctable
They are the same condition
Trigger thumb is due to absent EPB
Clasped thumb has a Notta's node at the A1 pulley

questions.explanation: **Trigger thumb** is a **flexor-side** problem — the FPL catches at the A1 pulley (**Notta's node**), locking the **IP in flexion** — treated by **A1 release** if persistent. **Clasped thumb** is an **extensor-side** deficiency (weak/absent EPB±EPL) holding the thumb **flexed and adducted but passively correctable**, treated first by **extension splinting** (then tendon transfer if needed). Recognizing flexor vs extensor pathology directs the operation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Adequate first-web width after thumb reconstruction is functionally important because it allows:

options.text: Palmar abduction of the thumb to grasp large objects and to position the thumb for opposition
Increased grip strength of the small finger
Wrist extension
Elbow flexion

questions.explanation: A wide, supple **first web** lets the thumb **abduct away from the palm** to span and grasp large objects and to reach an opposing position for pinch. A tight web tethers the thumb into adduction, so **first-web release (Z-plasty/flap)** is a routine component of hypoplasia and clasped-thumb reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: Which imaging or exam approach best resolves an equivocal CMC-stability question in a 2-year-old with thumb hypoplasia?

options.text: MRI/ultrasound of the cartilaginous base, or simply repeated clinical examination for thumb use over time
A single plain radiograph is definitive
CT with 3D reconstruction is mandatory in all
Bone scan

questions.explanation: Because the base/trapezium are **cartilaginous until ~6 years**, plain films are unreliable; **MRI or ultrasound** can image the cartilage, and **serial clinical examination** (does the child incorporate the thumb, or ignore it with index pronation/scissor pinch?) is equally reliable for the **IIIA vs IIIB** determination that drives reconstruct-vs-pollicize.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 37 (Deformities of the Thumb)

questions.stem: A newborn has a hand radially deviated ('radial club hand') with a hypoplastic thumb. Which classification (Bayne/James) grades radial longitudinal deficiency, and on what is it based?

options.text: The modified Bayne/James classification, graded by the degree of distal-then-proximal radius deficiency (types N, 0, I–IV)
The Wassel classification, based on thumb duplication level
The ICSHT classification
The Blauth classification of the radius

questions.explanation: **Radial longitudinal deficiency (RLD)** is graded by the **modified Bayne/James** scheme: **N** = isolated thumb hypoplasia (normal radius), **0** = deficient carpus with a normal-length radius, **I** = short distal radius, **II** = hypoplastic radius (deficient proximal and distal physes), **III** = partial absence of the radius, **IV** = total absence of the radius. Thumb hypoplasia (Blauth) is graded separately and frequently coexists.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: In radial longitudinal deficiency, which neurovascular structure is characteristically the most PROMINENT on the radial side of the wrist (and must be protected at surgery)?

options.text: The median nerve (always present, often lying superficially on the radial wrist)
The radial artery (which is typically robust)
The radial nerve below the elbow
The ulnar artery, displaced radially

questions.explanation: In RLD the **radial artery is usually absent** and the **radial nerve is generally absent below the elbow**, whereas the **median nerve is always present and frequently the most prominent radial-wrist structure** (it supplies the radial sensation). It can be mistaken for a tendon and is at risk during centralization — protecting it is essential.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which finding is a CONTRAINDICATION to centralization/radialization of a radially deficient wrist?

options.text: A fixed elbow extension contracture — the child needs the radial wrist deviation to bring the hand to the mouth/face
Coexisting thumb hypoplasia
Bilateral involvement
A stable, mobile elbow

questions.explanation: If the **elbow cannot flex (fixed extension contracture)**, the **radially deviated wrist is the only way the child reaches the mouth/face**; straightening the wrist would eliminate that function. Therefore a **stiff extended elbow contraindicates centralization**. Elbow flexion must be preserved/present for wrist realignment to be beneficial.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: What is the recommended initial (nonoperative) management for the radially deviated wrist in RLD, before considering centralization?

options.text: Serial casting/splinting (± soft-tissue distraction with an external fixator) to stretch the taut radial structures
Immediate bony resection of the carpus
No treatment until skeletal maturity
Primary wrist arthrodesis in infancy

questions.explanation: The tight **radial soft tissues are first stretched** with **serial casting/splinting**, and for rigid or older (type III/IV) deformities a **gradual soft-tissue distraction (external fixator)** is applied. This lengthens the radial structures so the wrist can be centralized with **less (or no) bony resection**, reducing recurrence and physeal injury.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: For centralization of a radially deficient wrist, the best results are generally obtained when:

options.text: It is performed before ~1 year of age and aberrant radial wrist extensors can be transferred to help hold the correction
It is deferred until after puberty
The ulnar physis is deliberately shaved
No tendon transfers are used

questions.explanation: Centralization outcomes are best when done **before ~1 year** (provided anesthesia is safe given syndromic issues) and when **aberrant radial wrist extensors (e.g., an FCU/ECU transfer to the ulnar side) are transferred to maintain the corrected position**, countering the strong tendency to recur. Preliminary stretching and preserving the ulnar physis further improve results.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: 'Radialization' (Buck-Gramcko) differs from classic centralization in that it:

options.text: Positions the carpus on the ulna in slight overcorrection and relies on tendon transfers/balancing (avoiding carpal resection or shaving the ulna) to reduce recurrence and physeal damage
Resects more of the carpus than centralization
Fuses the wrist in infancy
Shaves the distal ulnar physis for a notch

questions.explanation: **Radialization** places the carpus so the ulna supports the second metacarpal/radial side (slight overcorrection) and emphasizes **soft-tissue balancing (transferring radial wrist extensors ulnarly)** rather than carving a notch in the carpus or shaving the distal ulna. Avoiding **iatrogenic ulnar physeal injury and carpal resection** aims to lower **recurrent deformity, stiffness, and growth arrest** compared with aggressive centralization.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: A child with RLD undergoes DEB (diepoxybutane) chromosomal-breakage testing. Which associated syndrome is being screened for, and why is it critical?

options.text: Fanconi anemia — a DNA-repair disorder causing progressive pancytopenia/leukemia that appears after birth, so early detection is lifesaving
Holt-Oram — cardiac only
VACTERL — no systemic risk
TAR — benign

questions.explanation: RLD is frequently syndromic; the **DEB (or mitomycin) chromosomal-breakage test screens for Fanconi anemia**, an **autosomal recessive DNA-repair defect** whose **aplastic anemia/leukemia is not present at birth** but develops later. Because hand findings can precede marrow failure, screening allows early, potentially **lifesaving** intervention (e.g., transplant). Other associations include Holt-Oram (TBX5, cardiac), TAR (platelets), and VACTERL.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which syndrome associated with radial deficiency is characterized by absent radii with the THUMBS PRESENT?

options.text: TAR syndrome (thrombocytopenia–absent radius)
Holt-Oram syndrome
Fanconi anemia
VACTERL association

questions.explanation: **TAR syndrome** is distinctive because the **thumbs are present** despite **absent radii**, alongside **thrombocytopenia** (which often improves after infancy). This contrasts with Fanconi and Holt-Oram, in which the **thumbs are typically absent/hypoplastic**. The 'present thumb' is a key exam clue that points to TAR.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: The VACTERL association linked with radial deficiency includes anomalies of which systems?

options.text: Vertebral, Anal, Cardiac, Tracheo-Esophageal, Renal, and Limb
Only cardiac and renal
Only craniofacial
Only hematologic

questions.explanation: **VACTERL** = **V**ertebral, **A**nal atresia, **C**ardiac, **T**racheo-**E**sophageal fistula, **R**enal, and **L**imb anomalies. A radial-ray defect should prompt a systematic search for these (spine films, echocardiogram, renal ultrasound, etc.). It is typically **sporadic**, unlike autosomal dominant Holt-Oram or recessive Fanconi.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: In unilateral type III/IV radial deficiency, the affected forearm is often about how long compared with the normal side, and how is length addressed?

options.text: Roughly half as long; ulnar lengthening by distraction osteogenesis (often repeated) can improve length, usually after centralization
Full length; no lengthening ever needed
Slightly longer; requires shortening
Length cannot be changed surgically

questions.explanation: In severe unilateral RLD the forearm is often **~50% of normal length**. **Ulnar lengthening by distraction osteogenesis** can add length (typically after the wrist is centralized), but lengthening may **retard ulnar growth**, so **repeated lengthenings** are often needed through growth. Microvascular epiphyseal transfer (Vilkki) is an alternative for type IV in selected centers.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which statement about the ulnar physis during centralization surgery is correct?

options.text: Iatrogenic damage to the distal ulnar physis must be avoided, as it causes forearm growth impairment; many surgeons therefore avoid resecting the carpus/shaving the ulna
The ulnar physis should be excised to seat the carpus
The distal ulnar physis contributes little to forearm growth
Physeal injury improves long-term outcome

questions.explanation: The **distal ulnar physis provides most forearm longitudinal growth** in RLD (the radius being deficient), so **iatrogenic injury causes further shortening/deformity**. Concern about physeal damage, wrist stiffness, and recurrence has driven many surgeons toward **radialization/soft-tissue balancing that avoids carpal resection and ulnar shaving**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: A recognized long-term problem after centralization for RLD is:

options.text: Recurrence of radial deviation (and/or wrist stiffness) — durable correction is difficult without adequate tendon balancing and growth
Excessive forearm overgrowth
Permanent full wrist motion
Spontaneous regeneration of the radius

questions.explanation: **Recurrent radial deviation** is common because the deforming radial forces and growth tendencies persist; **wrist stiffness** and **forearm growth impairment** also occur, especially after aggressive bony procedures. Maintaining correction depends on **tendon transfers to balance the wrist**, prolonged splinting, and accepting that revision may be needed — one reason soft-tissue-sparing techniques are favored.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: A newborn has a hand deviated toward the ULNAR side, a small/absent small-finger side of the hand, and a stiff elbow. Which deficiency is this, and how does its elbow issue differ from RLD?

options.text: Ulnar longitudinal deficiency; the elbow (radiohumeral/proximal) is often the main problem (instability/synostosis), whereas RLD's key issue is the wrist
Radial longitudinal deficiency; identical elbow issues
Madelung deformity
Congenital pseudarthrosis

questions.explanation: **Ulnar longitudinal deficiency (ULD)** affects the **ulnar/postaxial side** (small/ring rays, ulna) and, importantly, the **ELBOW** — with radiohumeral instability, dislocation, or **synostosis** — is frequently the dominant functional problem, unlike RLD where the **wrist** dominates. ULD is graded by a Bayne-type scheme (I–IV) and is more often associated with **musculoskeletal (not visceral) syndromes**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Compared with radial deficiency, ulnar longitudinal deficiency is:

options.text: Rarer, more often unilateral, and typically associated with musculoskeletal syndromes rather than visceral/hematologic ones
More common than radial deficiency
Strongly associated with Fanconi anemia and cardiac defects
Always bilateral

questions.explanation: **ULD is much rarer than RLD**, usually **unilateral**, and its associations are predominantly **musculoskeletal** (e.g., proximal focal femoral deficiency, fibular deficiency, phocomelia) rather than the **visceral/hematologic syndromes (VACTERL, Fanconi, Holt-Oram, TAR)** tied to radial deficiency. This changes the systemic workup.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: The most FUNCTIONALLY important consideration in many ulnar longitudinal deficiency cases is:

options.text: Elbow function/stability and the position of the hand for use, rather than the forearm/wrist itself
Restoring a normal-length ulna
Thumb duplication correction
Carpal coalition release

questions.explanation: Because ULD prominently affects the **elbow (instability, synostosis, limited motion)**, management focuses on **optimizing elbow function and hand position** for activities — e.g., addressing a fixed pronation/position, releasing tethering, or accepting a stable functional posture — often more than on lengthening the deficient ulna. First-web/thumb and syndactyly issues are also common and addressed as needed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: A child cannot supinate or pronate the forearm, which is fixed in pronation; radiographs show the proximal radius and ulna fused. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Congenital proximal radioulnar synostosis
Madelung deformity
Radial head dislocation alone
Distal radioulnar synostosis from trauma

questions.explanation: **Congenital proximal radioulnar synostosis** is a bony (or fibrous) union of the proximal radius and ulna causing **fixed forearm rotation (usually pronation)** with absent pro-/supination; the radial head is often dislocated. It may be bilateral and is sometimes associated with chromosomal anomalies. Compensation comes from the shoulder/wrist, so many mild cases are functional.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: When is surgery considered for congenital proximal radioulnar synostosis, and what is the usual procedure?

options.text: When the fixed pronation is severe/functionally disabling (especially bilateral) — a derotational osteotomy to reposition the forearm in a more functional degree of rotation (attempting to restore rotation is usually unsuccessful)
Always, to restore full pronation-supination by resecting the synostosis
Never, regardless of severity
Only by wrist fusion

questions.explanation: Most patients compensate and need no surgery. When **fixed pronation is severe and disabling (particularly bilateral cases where neither hand can supinate)**, a **derotational osteotomy** repositions the forearm to a **more functional fixed rotation** (e.g., near neutral). Attempts to **excise the synostosis and restore rotation typically fail (re-fusion/loss of motion)**, so realignment — not motion restoration — is the goal.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: An adolescent girl has bilateral wrists with a prominent distal ulna, volar-ulnar tilt of the distal radius, and a 'V-shaped' proximal carpal alignment on x-ray. What is the deformity and its classic tethering structure?

options.text: Madelung deformity, tethered by an abnormal volar radiolunate ligament (Vickers ligament) with volar-ulnar distal radial physeal growth arrest
Radial club hand, tethered by radial soft tissues
Kienböck disease
Scaphoid nonunion

questions.explanation: **Madelung deformity** results from **growth impairment of the volar-ulnar distal radial physis**, tethered by an abnormal **volar radiolunate (Vickers) ligament**. The radius tilts **volar and ulnar**, the ulna appears dorsally prominent, and the carpus wedges into a **triangular/V configuration** (lunate at the apex). It is more common in **adolescent girls** and often bilateral.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Madelung deformity is classically associated with which genetic condition?

options.text: Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis / SHOX gene (short-stature homeobox) haploinsufficiency
Neurofibromatosis type 1
TBX5 (Holt-Oram)
FGFR2 (Apert)

questions.explanation: **Madelung deformity** is associated with **SHOX gene abnormalities**, as in **Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis** (mesomelic short stature with Madelung), and homozygous SHOX loss causes **Langer mesomelic dysplasia**. This is why bilateral Madelung with short stature warrants **SHOX/genetic evaluation**. (Congenital forearm pseudarthrosis, by contrast, is linked to NF1.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: In a symptomatic, growing child with Madelung deformity, a key surgical option that addresses the cause is:

options.text: Release of the Vickers ligament and a physiolysis/dome or radial osteotomy (± ulnar shortening) to correct alignment and relieve the tether
Proximal row carpectomy
Wrist arthrodesis in a young child
Radial head excision

questions.explanation: In a **growing** child, releasing the tethering **Vickers ligament** (with physiolysis of the abnormal physis) and performing a **radial (dome/opening-wedge) osteotomy ± ulnar shortening** corrects the volar-ulnar tilt and can arrest progression. In the mature wrist, corrective osteotomies (± ulnar procedures like Sauvé-Kapandji for DRUJ symptoms) address deformity/pain. Many mild cases are managed nonoperatively.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: A child with a bowed forearm sustains a low-energy fracture that fails to heal, forming a pseudarthrosis, and has café-au-lait spots. Which underlying condition is most likely?

options.text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
Osteogenesis imperfecta type I
Fanconi anemia
Fibrous dysplasia (McCune-Albright)

questions.explanation: **Congenital pseudarthrosis of the forearm** (like the more common tibial form) is strongly associated with **neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)** — suggested here by **café-au-lait macules**. The dysplastic bone fails to unite/heal, and treatment (resection of abnormal bone with vascularized fibular grafting or other union strategies) is difficult with high recurrence, so NF1 should be sought and monitored.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which statement about the radial artery and nerve in radial longitudinal deficiency is correct?

options.text: The radial artery is usually absent and the radial nerve is generally absent below the elbow (the ulnar/interosseous supply predominates)
Both are normal
The radial artery is enlarged and the radial nerve is duplicated
The median nerve is absent

questions.explanation: The anomalous but **predictable** anatomy of RLD: the **radial artery is usually absent** (perfusion via the ulnar/interosseous system), the **radial nerve is generally absent below the elbow** (so wrist/finger extension relies on anomalous muscles), the **radial wrist extensors and thumb extrinsics are absent/aberrant**, and the **median nerve is always present and radially prominent**. Knowing this prevents surgical misadventure.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which skin-management maneuver facilitates centralization by redistributing tissue in RLD?

options.text: A bilobed or dorsal rotation flap that moves excess ulnar-side skin to the deficient radial side
Circumferential skin grafting
Excising all dorsal skin
Leaving the radial defect open

questions.explanation: After a radially deficient wrist is straightened, the **radial side is skin-deficient while the ulnar side has excess**; a **bilobed or dorsal rotation flap** (or ellipse excision of ulnar excess) **redistributes the redundant ulnar skin to the radial side**, closing without tension. Adequate soft-tissue release/distraction beforehand minimizes this challenge.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Preliminary soft-tissue distraction before centralization is MOST helpful in which scenario?

options.text: Older children with untreated, rigid type III/IV radial deficiency
A newborn with a supple type I deformity
Isolated thumb hypoplasia (type N)
A stable elbow with no wrist deviation

questions.explanation: Gradual **external-fixator distraction** is most valuable for **older children with rigid, untreated type III/IV** deformities, where the radial soft tissues are severely contracted. Distraction lengthens these structures so the wrist can be **centralized without extensive bony resection**, lowering recurrence and physeal-injury risk. Supple infant wrists often need only casting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: In the Bayne/James scheme, a wrist with a normal-length radius but a deficient/anomalous carpus (radial carpal bones absent) is:

options.text: Type 0 radial longitudinal deficiency
Type IV
Type N
Type II

questions.explanation: **Type 0** RLD has a **normal-length radius but a deficient carpus** (radial carpal bones hypoplastic/absent or coalitions), sometimes with radial deviation from carpal/ligamentous laxity. **Type N** is isolated thumb hypoplasia with a normal radius and carpus. Types I–IV describe progressive distal-then-total radius deficiency.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which best explains why microvascular epiphyseal transfer (Vilkki) is proposed for some type IV radial deficiencies, and its main caveat?

options.text: A vascularized growing epiphysis (from the toe/metatarsal) can support the radial wrist and continue growing — but the technique is demanding and long-term (skeletal-maturity) outcomes are uncertain
Nonvascularized bone transfer reliably grows
It restores a normal radius
It eliminates the need for any tendon balancing

questions.explanation: Because **nonvascularized bone grafts historically failed to grow**, Vilkki combined **soft-tissue distraction with microvascular transfer of a growing (vascularized) epiphysis** to buttress the radial wrist and provide ongoing growth in **type IV** deficiency. Early/midterm results are promising, but it is **technically demanding** and the **outcome at skeletal maturity remains unknown**, so it is used selectively.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: The incidence of radial longitudinal deficiency is approximately:

options.text: About 1 in 5,000–100,000 live births (commonly cited near ~1:5,000–1:30,000)
About 1 in 100
About 1 in 10
Essentially never occurs

questions.explanation: RLD is uncommon (on the order of **~1 in several thousand to tens of thousands of live births**), frequently **bilateral (~50%+)**, and often **syndromic**, which is why every case triggers a **systemic/genetic workup** (cardiac, renal, hematologic, spine). The exact figure varies by series/definition.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: When thumb hypoplasia coexists with radial deficiency, the sequencing of reconstruction is typically:

options.text: Address the wrist (centralization/radialization) first (in infancy), then perform thumb reconstruction or pollicization later
Always pollicize before touching the wrist
Never treat the thumb
Fuse the wrist before any thumb surgery in all cases

questions.explanation: The **wrist is generally realigned first (centralization/radialization around infancy)** to provide a stable, well-positioned platform, followed later by **thumb reconstruction (types II/IIIA) or pollicization (IIIB/IV/V)**. Coordinating the two (with attention to shared radial soft-tissue anatomy and anesthetic considerations) optimizes overall hand function.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST appropriate action in managing a radially deficient wrist?

options.text: Straightening the wrist by centralization in a child with a fixed elbow extension contracture
Preliminary casting/distraction to stretch radial soft tissues
Transferring aberrant radial wrist extensors to hold the correction
Screening for Fanconi anemia and cardiac/renal anomalies

questions.explanation: **Centralizing the wrist when the elbow cannot flex** removes the child's only means of reaching the face/mouth (via the radially deviated hand) — the least appropriate action. The others are correct: **stretch the soft tissues first, balance with tendon transfers, and screen for systemic syndromes**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Madelung deformity most often becomes symptomatic (pain, deformity, limited motion) at which stage, and in whom?

options.text: Late childhood/adolescence, more commonly in girls, often bilaterally
At birth, equally in boys and girls
Only after age 60
Exclusively in males

questions.explanation: Madelung deformity typically manifests during the **adolescent growth spurt (late childhood/adolescence)**, is **more common in girls**, and is frequently **bilateral**. Progressive volar-ulnar radial tilt causes **prominence of the distal ulna, cosmetic deformity, decreased extension/supination, and sometimes pain** — prompting evaluation and, when growing and symptomatic, tether release/osteotomy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Congenital proximal radioulnar synostosis most commonly fixes the forearm in which position, and why is this functionally problematic (especially bilaterally)?

options.text: Pronation — bilateral fixed pronation makes it hard to accept objects, manage hygiene, and perform supination-dependent tasks
Full supination, impairing keyboard use
Neutral, with no functional impact
Wrist flexion

questions.explanation: The forearm is usually fused in **pronation**. Unilateral cases are often well-compensated (shoulder/wrist), but **bilateral fixed pronation** severely limits tasks requiring supination (accepting change, feeding, catching, perineal care), so **derotational osteotomy toward neutral** improves function when disabling.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: A key reason attempts to RESTORE forearm rotation by resecting a congenital radioulnar synostosis usually fail is:

options.text: The synostosis tends to re-form and the surrounding musculotendinous/interosseous structures are abnormal, so motion is not durably regained
The bones cannot be cut
The radial head is normal and blocks motion
There is no blood supply to the forearm

questions.explanation: Excision of the fusion commonly leads to **re-synostosis**, and the **pronator/supinator musculature and interosseous anatomy are congenitally abnormal**, so active rotation is not restored. Because motion restoration is unreliable, the accepted strategy is a **derotational osteotomy to a functional fixed position** rather than trying to recreate pro-/supination.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which associated finding is characteristic of ULNAR (postaxial) longitudinal deficiency of the hand?

options.text: Absent/deficient ulnar (small ± ring) digits, syndactyly of remaining digits, and frequent thumb/first-web anomalies
Absent thumb with a normal small finger
A duplicated radius
Isolated Madelung deformity

questions.explanation: In **ULD** the **ulnar digits (small ± ring) are deficient/absent**, remaining digits may be **syndactylized**, and **thumb/first-web anomalies are common** (thumb hypoplasia, malrotation, or index-thumb web problems) — so hand reconstruction often targets the **thumb and web** in addition to the elbow. The radius is intact (contrast with RLD).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Serial casting for a supple radial club hand in infancy primarily aims to:

options.text: Stretch the contracted radial soft tissues and maintain/improve wrist position, easing later surgery (or maintaining correction)
Fuse the wrist
Lengthen the ulna
Correct thumb hypoplasia

questions.explanation: **Serial casting/splinting** in infancy **stretches the taut radial structures and holds the wrist in a better position**, either as definitive management for mild cases or as **preparation that reduces the soft-tissue release/bony resection needed at centralization**. It does not address the skeletal deficiency or the thumb, which are handled separately.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which statement about growth in the radially deficient forearm is correct?

options.text: Because the radius is deficient, the ULNA provides most forearm growth — so protecting the distal ulnar physis is critical
The radius provides most growth despite being deficient
Forearm growth is unaffected by physeal injury
The carpus is the main growth center

questions.explanation: With a deficient/absent radius, **the ulna (and its distal physis) supplies the bulk of forearm longitudinal growth**.
