Iatrogenic injury to the **distal ulnar physis** (as can occur with carpal resection/ulnar shaving during aggressive centralization) worsens shortening — a core rationale for **physis-sparing radialization** techniques.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: The overall goal of treating a radial club hand is best described as:

options.text: A stable, better-positioned wrist over the ulna that preserves motion and growth and improves hand function/appearance — accepting that recurrence is a risk
Restoring a normal radius
Wrist arthrodesis in infancy for all
Prioritizing appearance over function

questions.explanation: The aim is a **stable, functionally positioned wrist supported by the ulna**, with **preserved wrist motion and forearm growth** and improved hand use/appearance. Because the deforming forces persist, **recurrence and stiffness are real risks**, so techniques emphasize soft-tissue balancing and physeal preservation, with realistic family counseling and long-term follow-up.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: A bilateral radial club hand child also has short stature, a triangular facies, and later develops aplastic anemia. Which diagnosis and confirmatory test apply?

options.text: Fanconi anemia; confirmed by chromosomal breakage (DEB/mitomycin) testing
Holt-Oram; confirmed by echocardiography only
TAR; confirmed by platelet count only
Madelung; confirmed by SHOX testing

questions.explanation: Progressive **aplastic anemia with radial-ray defects** points to **Fanconi anemia**, confirmed by a **chromosomal breakage (DEB/diepoxybutane) test**. Because marrow failure/leukemia risk is high and treatable if caught early (e.g., transplant), any radial deficiency should prompt this screen. (Holt-Oram = cardiac/TBX5; TAR = platelets/thumbs present; Madelung = SHOX.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: The Vickers ligament in Madelung deformity is best described as:

options.text: An abnormal thickened volar radiolunate (radiotriquetral/short radiolunate) ligament that tethers the lunate to the volar-ulnar radius, restraining physeal growth there
A dorsal ligament that pushes the ulna forward
The transverse carpal ligament
A normal variant with no role in the deformity

questions.explanation: The **Vickers ligament** is an **anomalous, thick volar radiolunate ligament** that tethers the lunate to the **volar-ulnar corner of the distal radius**, contributing to the localized **physeal growth arrest** that produces the volar-ulnar tilt of Madelung deformity. **Releasing it (with physiolysis)** is a central corrective step in the growing wrist.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which pairing of forearm/wrist malformation and its key association is correct?

options.text: Madelung deformity — SHOX (Léri-Weill); congenital forearm pseudarthrosis — NF1
Madelung — NF1; pseudarthrosis — SHOX
Radial deficiency — SHOX; Madelung — Fanconi
Radioulnar synostosis — TBX5; Madelung — TAR

questions.explanation: Correct associations: **Madelung deformity ↔ SHOX (Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis)**, and **congenital forearm pseudarthrosis ↔ neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)**. **Radial deficiency** is associated with **VACTERL/Holt-Oram/TAR/Fanconi**. Matching malformation to syndrome/gene is a common exam theme and guides screening.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: In ulnar longitudinal deficiency with a stiff, malpositioned forearm and a functional hand, a reasonable strategy is often:

options.text: Optimize hand and thumb/web function and accept/adjust a stable forearm position, rather than pursue high-risk ulnar lengthening
Always lengthen the ulna aggressively
Amputate the hand
Fuse the wrist in infancy

questions.explanation: Because the **elbow and forearm anatomy are complex and lengthening carries risk/limited benefit**, many ULD cases are managed by **maximizing hand function (thumb reconstruction, syndactyly release, first-web deepening) and ensuring a stable, useful limb position** rather than aggressive forearm lengthening. Treatment is highly individualized to the elbow/hand deficits.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which physical-exam feature helps confirm congenital (rather than acquired) proximal radioulnar synostosis?

options.text: A fixed forearm rotation from early childhood with compensatory shoulder/wrist motion and (often) a dislocated radial head, without a trauma history
Full, painful pro-supination
Acute onset after a fall
A normal radial head with free rotation

questions.explanation: **Congenital** proximal radioulnar synostosis presents as a **long-standing fixed forearm rotation (no trauma)**, frequently with a **posteriorly dislocated/dysplastic radial head** and **compensatory shoulder/wrist maneuvers**; it may be **bilateral/familial**. Acquired synostosis follows trauma/surgery with a relevant history. Recognizing the congenital pattern guides expectations (compensation vs derotational osteotomy).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: For which degree of fixed pronation is a derotational osteotomy in radioulnar synostosis typically considered functionally beneficial to move toward?

options.text: From severe/hyperpronation toward neutral or slight pronation (a position that balances everyday tasks)
Toward full supination in all cases
Toward maximal pronation
Position does not matter

questions.explanation: Since motion cannot be restored, the osteotomy repositions the forearm to a **functionally optimal fixed rotation** — typically **neutral to slight pronation** (unilateral cases may be set near neutral; in bilateral cases the dominant side may favor slight pronation and the other slight supination) to balance tasks like feeding, hygiene, and accepting objects. The exact target is individualized to bilaterality and the child's needs.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: A radially deviated hand in RLD limits function primarily by:

options.text: Positioning the hand so grip strength and bimanual/positioning tasks are impaired, and (with a short forearm) reducing reach
Improving grip strength
Causing pain as the primary problem in infancy
Having no functional consequence

questions.explanation: The **radially deviated, unstable wrist** malpositions the hand, **weakening grip and hampering bimanual tasks and hand placement**, compounded by the **short forearm**. Realigning and stabilizing the wrist over the ulna (with preserved motion) improves the mechanical advantage and hand use — the functional rationale for centralization/radialization, provided the elbow can flex.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which combination represents the modern trend in surgical management of the radially deficient wrist?

options.text: Preliminary soft-tissue distraction + physis-sparing radialization + tendon transfers, minimizing carpal resection and ulnar shaving
Aggressive carpal resection with a deep ulnar notch and physeal shaving
Infant wrist arthrodesis for all types
Observation only, never operating

questions.explanation: Recognizing that **aggressive centralization (carpal resection, ulnar notching/shaving) causes stiffness, growth arrest, and recurrence**, the trend favors **soft-tissue distraction to ease correction, physis-sparing radialization, and tendon transfers to balance the wrist** — preserving the crucial **distal ulnar physis** and wrist motion while accepting some recurrence risk.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which statement about bilateral radial deficiency and surgical decision-making is correct?

options.text: Elbow flexion capacity is assessed on each side; a stiff extended elbow contraindicates straightening that side, and surgery is individualized/staged
Both wrists are always centralized in one operation
Bilateral cases are never treated
The elbow is irrelevant to the decision

questions.explanation: In bilateral RLD, each limb is judged separately — especially **elbow flexion**, since a **fixed extended elbow means the radial wrist deviation is needed to reach the face** (contraindicating straightening that side). Surgery is **individualized and typically staged**, integrating wrist realignment and later thumb reconstruction/pollicization with the child's systemic (syndromic) status.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: A dorsally prominent distal ulna ('reverse'/dorsal prominence) that is actually due to volar carpal translation and volar radial tilt is the hallmark of:

options.text: Madelung deformity
Radial club hand
Ulnar dimelia
Congenital radial head dislocation

questions.explanation: In **Madelung deformity**, the **distal radius tilts volar-ulnar and the carpus translates volarly**, making the **distal ulna appear dorsally prominent**. The lunate wedges into the V-shaped distal radius. This is distinct from radial club hand (radial deviation from radial deficiency) — the ulna is intact but relatively prominent because the radius is malaligned.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Before deciding to straighten a radially deficient wrist, the surgeon specifically tests whether the child can bring the hand to the mouth. Why?

options.text: If the elbow lacks flexion, the radially deviated wrist is the child's mechanism for reaching the mouth/face, so straightening it would remove that function
To assess grip strength
To measure forearm length
To evaluate the thumb

questions.explanation: Reaching the mouth is a critical function. In a child with **poor/absent elbow flexion**, the **radial deviation at the wrist substitutes** to bring the hand to the face; **centralizing (straightening) the wrist would abolish this**. Hence a stiff, extended elbow is a contraindication to wrist realignment — the deviation is functionally protective there.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Ulnar longitudinal deficiency is graded by a Bayne-type scheme. Which best captures its spectrum?

options.text: From ulnar hypoplasia (I), through partial (II) and total (III) ulnar absence, to radiohumeral synostosis (IV)
By the level of thumb duplication
By the number of grade-4 muscles below the elbow
By distal radial physeal status only

questions.explanation: A common **ULD grading (Bayne/Kummel/others)** runs from **type I (ulnar hypoplasia, both physes present)**, to **type II (partial ulnar absence — often the distal ulna, with a fibrocartilaginous anlage tethering the wrist)**, **type III (total ulnar absence)**, and **type IV (radiohumeral synostosis)** — emphasizing the **elbow** end of the spectrum. The anlage in type II can bow the radius and is sometimes excised.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: In ulnar longitudinal deficiency, the fibrocartilaginous 'anlage' (ulnar remnant) is significant because it:

options.text: Can tether the ulnar carpus and progressively bow the radius/deviate the wrist, and may be excised if it causes progressive deformity
Is a normal structure requiring no attention
Provides most of the forearm growth
Should always be lengthened

questions.explanation: The **ulnar anlage** is a non-growing **fibrocartilaginous band** replacing the deficient ulna; it can act as a **tether that progressively bows the radius and deviates the wrist ulnarly** as the child grows. When it drives **progressive deformity**, **excision of the anlage** is considered. Its recognition distinguishes ULD management from the radial-sided problems of RLD.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: Which is an appropriate NONoperative approach for a mild, asymptomatic Madelung deformity?

options.text: Observation (± activity modification/splinting for symptoms), reserving surgery for progressive deformity or pain
Immediate wrist arthrodesis
Prophylactic proximal row carpectomy
Radial head excision

questions.explanation: Many patients with **mild, asymptomatic Madelung deformity** are managed with **observation** (and symptomatic splinting/activity modification). Surgery — **Vickers ligament release/physiolysis and corrective osteotomy in the growing child, or corrective osteotomy ± ulnar procedures at maturity** — is reserved for **progressive deformity, functional limitation, or pain**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 38 (Malformations of the Wrist & Forearm)

questions.stem: A newborn has symmetric, rigid contractures of all four limbs with internally rotated shoulders, extended elbows, flexed wrists, and thumbs-in-palm, but normal sensation and (later) normal intelligence. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Amyoplasia (the classic form of arthrogryposis multiplex congenita)
Cerebral palsy
Brachial plexus birth palsy
Spinal muscular atrophy

questions.explanation: **Amyoplasia** is the classic sporadic form of arthrogryposis: **symmetric, rigid, non-progressive contractures** with the characteristic posture — **shoulders internally rotated/adducted, elbows extended, wrists flexed, thumbs-in-palm** — from absent/hypoplastic muscle replaced by fibrofatty tissue. **Sensation and intelligence are normal**, distinguishing it from CP (a brain lesion with spasticity) and from plexus palsy (unilateral, sensory involvement).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Why does the classic amyoplasia elbow rest in EXTENSION rather than flexion?

options.text: The triceps is usually preserved while the elbow flexors (biceps/brachialis) are deficient
Spasticity of the triceps overpowers the flexors
The biceps is contracted
The joint is fused in extension

questions.explanation: In amyoplasia the **elbow flexors are typically deficient while the triceps is preserved**, so the unopposed extensor holds the elbow **extended** (an elbow extension contracture). Occasionally the triceps is weak/absent (flexion contracture), and absence of **both** flexors and extensor leaves a poorly mobile elbow around ~60° flexion. This muscle-balance insight guides whether to add passive flexion (release) and/or active flexion (transfer).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Distal arthrogryposis (DA) differs from amyoplasia in that it:

options.text: Predominantly affects the distal limbs (hands/feet), is usually inherited (autosomal dominant, sarcomeric-gene mutations), and often spares proximal joints
Is always sporadic and affects mainly proximal joints
Involves spasticity from a brain lesion
Has abnormal sensation

questions.explanation: **Distal arthrogryposis** primarily involves the **hands and feet (camptodactyly, ulnar deviation, clasped thumb, clubfoot)** with relative sparing of large proximal joints, and is typically **autosomal dominant** due to mutations in **sarcomeric/contractile-apparatus genes** (e.g., TNNI2, TNNT3, TPM2, MYH3). This contrasts with **sporadic amyoplasia**, which affects proximal and distal joints symmetrically.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: A child with distal arthrogryposis has a 'whistling face' (small mouth/pursed lips), deep-set eyes, camptodactyly, and clasped thumbs. Which subtype is this?

options.text: Distal arthrogryposis type 2A (Freeman-Sheldon syndrome)
Distal arthrogryposis type 9 (Beals syndrome)
Distal arthrogryposis type 8 (Escobar syndrome)
Amyoplasia

questions.explanation: **Freeman-Sheldon syndrome (DA type 2A, 'whistling face'/craniocarpotarsal dystrophy)** features a **small pursed mouth, deep-set eyes, and hand contractures (camptodactyly, clasped/ulnar-deviated thumbs)**. **Sheldon-Hall (DA2B)** is a milder related form. Recognizing these facial/hand gestalt patterns helps subtype DA and anticipate anesthetic risks (difficult airway/malignant-hyperthermia-like reactions).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: A child has multiple pterygia (webbing across the flexor aspects of joints) with contractures. Which distal arthrogryposis subtype is this?

options.text: DA type 8 (Escobar / multiple pterygium syndrome)
DA type 2A (Freeman-Sheldon)
DA type 7 (trismus-pseudocamptodactyly)
DA type 5

questions.explanation: **Escobar syndrome (DA type 8, multiple pterygium syndrome)** is defined by **pterygia (skin webs) across joints (neck, axilla, elbow, knee, digits)** limiting extension, along with contractures and other features. The pterygia contain neurovascular structures, making correction challenging (staged release, Z-plasty, and sometimes shortening osteotomy rather than aggressive lengthening).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: A child with distal arthrogryposis has a 'crumpled' external ear and contractural arachnodactyly (long, contracted fingers). Which subtype is this?

options.text: DA type 9 (Beals syndrome / congenital contractural arachnodactyly)
DA type 2A (Freeman-Sheldon)
DA type 8 (Escobar)
Amyoplasia

questions.explanation: **Beals syndrome (DA type 9, congenital contractural arachnodactyly)** features **crumpled/abnormal ears, arachnodactyly with joint contractures**, and can resemble Marfan (it involves FBN2). Cardiac and ophthalmologic screening may be warranted. Recognizing these named DA subtypes aids counseling, systemic screening, and anesthetic planning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: The overarching goal for upper-limb reconstruction in arthrogryposis is best summarized by the maxim:

options.text: 'One hand to eat and one to wipe' (which can be the same hand) — maximizing functional independence
Restoring normal, symmetric bilateral function
Achieving full range of motion in every joint
Prioritizing appearance over function

questions.explanation: Because deficits are severe and non-normalizable, planning targets **functional independence** — famously, **'one hand to eat and one to wipe'** (feeding and perineal hygiene), which may be accomplished by the **same hand** in different positions. Self-feeding requires acquiring, gripping, and releasing food with adequate elbow/wrist/forearm positioning — the framework for choosing procedures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: When BOTH elbows are stiff and being reconstructed for active flexion in arthrogryposis, an important principle is:

options.text: Preserve/position at least one elbow to reach the perineum (extension for hygiene), so the child can perform toileting — do not flex both without considering hygiene/transfers
Flex both elbows maximally regardless of hygiene
Fuse both elbows in flexion
Never operate on bilateral cases

questions.explanation: Active elbow flexion enables **hand-to-mouth** function, but **perineal care/hygiene and transfers/crutch use need an elbow that can extend/reach behind**. So in bilateral cases the surgeon **balances the two limbs** — typically giving one elbow reliable flexion (to eat) while ensuring the other (or a position of the same limb) allows **reach to the perineum ('to wipe')**. Flexing both without this consideration can impair toileting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: For a child whose elbows lack passive flexion (cannot reach the mouth), what is the recommended early procedure and timing?

options.text: Posterior elbow release (capsulotomy ± triceps lengthening) within the first ~2 years to gain passive flexion
Active flexion tendon transfer in the neonatal period
Elbow arthrodesis in infancy
No intervention until adulthood

questions.explanation: **Passive flexion must be established first** — a **posterior elbow release (capsulotomy, triceps lengthening/tenotomy)** performed **within the first ~2 years** provides an arc (ideally ~30° extension to ≥100° flexion). **Active flexion transfers** (to power flexion) are done **later (usually ≥4 years)**, once passive motion and suitable donors are available. You cannot power motion into a joint that will not passively move.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Active elbow-flexion reconstruction (tendon/muscle transfer) in arthrogryposis is generally performed at what age, and why not earlier?

options.text: Around 4 years or older — to allow passive motion to be established, donor muscles to be assessable, and the child to participate in rehabilitation
In the neonatal period, for best plasticity
Only after skeletal maturity
Age is irrelevant

questions.explanation: **Active elbow flexion transfers are typically done at ≥4 years**, after **passive flexion is achieved (earlier releases)**, **donor availability is confirmed** (exam, MRI/CT, needle stimulation), and the child can **cooperate with rehabilitation/motor re-education**. Transferring too early risks an unpowered joint or an unassessable donor and poor motor learning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which donor is commonly used to restore ACTIVE elbow flexion in amyoplasia when the triceps is strong?

options.text: Triceps-to-biceps transfer (posterior-to-anterior), accepting loss of active extension in that elbow
Biceps-to-triceps transfer
Flexor carpi ulnaris to the biceps only
Pronator teres to the biceps

questions.explanation: When the **triceps is strong but the flexors are deficient**, a **triceps-to-biceps transfer** converts the extensor into an active flexor — powerful and reliable, but it **sacrifices active extension** in that elbow (hence the bilateral-hygiene caveat). Alternatives when the triceps is unsuitable include **bipolar pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, Steindler flexorplasty, or free functioning gracilis** transfers.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which alternative donors may power active elbow flexion when the triceps is weak/absent in arthrogryposis?

options.text: Bipolar pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, Steindler flexorplasty, or a free functioning gracilis transfer
Only the triceps
The deltoid
The supinator

questions.explanation: If the triceps cannot be used, options to restore elbow flexion include a **bipolar pectoralis major transfer**, **latissimus dorsi transfer**, **Steindler flexorplasty (proximal transfer of the flexor-pronator origin)**, or a **free functioning muscle (gracilis)** when no local donor exists. Donor availability is assessed by **exam, imaging (MRI/CT), and intraoperative needle stimulation** — many arthrogrypotic muscles are absent/hypoplastic.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Why is the arthrogrypotic forearm often only APPARENTLY pronated, and how does its position tend to change with age?

options.text: The internal-rotation shoulder contracture plus extended elbow create the illusion of pronation; most forearms are actually neutral/slightly supinated, and repeated hand-to-mouth pushing gradually increases supination over time
It is truly fixed in full pronation and worsens
It is fixed in full supination from birth
Forearm position never changes

questions.explanation: The classic 'pronation contracture' is often an **illusion created by shoulder internal rotation and elbow extension**; most forearms sit **neutral or slightly supinated**. As the child pushes the hand against surfaces to achieve hand-to-mouth, this repeated action produces **elbow flexion, forearm supination, and wrist flexion**, gradually **supinating the forearm** over time. Recognizing the true position avoids unnecessary derotation surgery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: In amyoplasia, the wrist typically rests in flexion. Which hand function is usually PRESERVED even when digital motion is poor?

options.text: Ulnar-nerve-innervated intrinsic thumb function (some thumb motion often persists)
Full finger flexion and extension
Wrist extension
Elbow flexion

questions.explanation: Hand function is variable, but **ulnar-innervated intrinsic thumb function is often preserved** even when extrinsic digital motion is limited. In amyoplasia the **wrist is flexed** (absent wrist extensors); some children extend to just short of neutral using the EDC — but at the cost of **MCP hyperextension**. Preserved intrinsics can be leveraged in reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which statement about sensation and cognition in amyoplasia is correct?

options.text: Sensation and intelligence are typically NORMAL, which supports investing in functional reconstruction
Sensation is absent, so surgery is futile
Intelligence is usually severely impaired
Both sensation and cognition are always abnormal

questions.explanation: In **amyoplasia, sensation is preserved and intelligence is normal** — the problem is **motor (absent/hypoplastic muscle and secondary contracture)**. Because these children can sense and learn to use a reconstructed limb, **functional upper-limb surgery is worthwhile** (unlike settings with dense sensory loss or profound cognitive impairment). This is a key counseling and planning point.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which is the recommended target shoulder rotation when performing a humeral rotational osteotomy in arthrogryposis?

options.text: About 15–30 degrees of internal rotation
Full external rotation
90 degrees of internal rotation
Neutral abduction with maximal internal rotation

questions.explanation: When the shoulder internal-rotation contracture prevents functional positioning, a **humeral rotational (derotation) osteotomy** repositions the arm to roughly **15–30° of internal rotation** — a posture that lets the hand reach the mouth/midline and the perineum. Children with **>90° active abduction and active external rotation past neutral rarely need shoulder surgery**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: What is the optimal passive elbow arc targeted by a posterior elbow release in arthrogryposis?

options.text: From about 30° of extension to at least 100° of flexion
Full extension only
0–20° of motion
Fixed at 90°

questions.explanation: The goal is a **functional passive arc — roughly 30° extension to ≥100° flexion** — enabling both reaching out (to a plate/table) and hand-to-mouth. Achieving this passive range early (first ~2 years) sets the stage for later **active-flexion transfers**. Over-releasing into excessive flexion at the expense of extension can compromise hygiene/reach.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: For a fixed wrist flexion contracture in amyoplasia impairing hand use, which corrective options are used?

options.text: Dorsal carpal (closing) wedge osteotomy and/or proximal row carpectomy, sometimes with an FCU-to-wrist-extensor transfer to rebalance
Volar wedge osteotomy to increase flexion
Wrist arthrodesis in infancy for all
No treatment is possible

questions.explanation: Fixed wrist flexion is corrected by **shortening/realigning the carpus** — a **dorsal closing-wedge carpal osteotomy** and/or **proximal row carpectomy** to bring the wrist to a functional (slightly extended/neutral) position — and, when a donor exists, an **FCU (or other) transfer to a wrist extensor** to maintain the correction. Position is prioritized over motion in the severely affected wrist.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: A child with amyoplasia has a thumb-in-palm deformity limiting grasp. Reconstruction typically involves:

options.text: First-web release (Z-plasty ± dorsal flap), release of the tight adductor/thenar structures, and augmentation of thumb extension/abduction (± MCP stabilization)
Thumb amputation
A1 pulley release
CMC fusion in infancy

questions.explanation: The arthrogrypotic **thumb-in-palm** is opened by **releasing the first web (Z-plasty/flap) and tight adductor/thenar/FPL structures**, and **augmenting extension/abduction** (tendon transfer if a donor exists), with **MCP stabilization** for instability — analogous to thumb-in-palm correction in spasticity. Freeing the thumb from the palm is essential to enable grasp of objects.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: How are potential donor muscles for transfer assessed preoperatively in arthrogryposis, given that many muscles are absent/hypoplastic?

options.text: Clinical exam plus MRI/CT to quantify muscle bulk, and intraoperative percutaneous needle stimulation (often during an exam under anesthesia)
Muscle biopsy of every candidate
Routine plain radiographs
No assessment is needed

questions.explanation: Because arthrogrypotic muscles are frequently **absent or hypotrophic**, donor availability is confirmed by **clinical examination, MRI/CT (to quantify pectoralis, latissimus, gracilis bulk)**, and **intraoperative needle stimulation** (commonly during an **exam under anesthesia** at the time of other procedures). **Muscle biopsy is not routinely useful** unless an alternative diagnosis is suspected.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which imaging is generally NOT routinely required to diagnose arthrogryposis?

options.text: Routine radiographs, CT, or MRI for the diagnosis itself (diagnosis is clinical); imaging is used mainly to evaluate donor muscles
Physical examination
Assessment of active/passive motion
Family history

questions.explanation: Arthrogryposis is a **clinical diagnosis** — routine radiographs, CT, and MRI are **not needed to make it**. Imaging (MRI/CT) is reserved for **quantifying donor muscles for transfers**, which is hard by exam alone. Electrodiagnostics are rarely needed except to exclude neurogenic mimics (e.g., spinal muscular atrophy), and biopsy is generally uninformative.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which condition should be considered/excluded when a neurogenic (rather than myopathic amyoplasia) cause of congenital contractures is suspected, and how?

options.text: Spinal muscular atrophy — evaluated with electrodiagnostic studies (and genetic testing) rather than the routine arthrogryposis workup
Cerebral palsy — via muscle biopsy
Fanconi anemia — via SHOX testing
Madelung deformity — via EMG

questions.explanation: When a **neurogenic** basis is suspected (e.g., progressive weakness, tongue fasciculations), **spinal muscular atrophy** and other neuromuscular disorders are considered, using **electrodiagnostic studies and genetic testing**. This matters because prognosis and management differ from classic amyoplasia. Otherwise EMG/biopsy are rarely needed in typical arthrogryposis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: In overall treatment strategy for a child with arthrogryposis, the relationship between lower-limb (ambulation) and upper-limb goals is best described as:

options.text: Upper-limb function (feeding, hygiene, independence) is as important as ambulation and should not be neglected
Ambulation is the only goal worth pursuing
Upper-limb surgery should always precede any lower-limb surgery
Upper-limb function is irrelevant if the child cannot walk

questions.explanation: Although centers historically prioritized **ambulation**, **basic upper-limb function (self-feeding, toileting, independence) is equally important** to quality of life and should be actively addressed. Care is coordinated with pediatric orthopedics (lower limb, spine) and timed around the child's multiple surgeries, integrating upper-limb reconstruction into the overall plan rather than treating it as an afterthought.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: The 'rate-limiting step' in optimizing independence (self-feeding) for a child with arthrogryposis is usually:

options.text: Finger and thumb motion (the ability to acquire, grip, and release food)
Shoulder abduction
Forearm supination alone
Wrist extension alone

questions.explanation: Even with good elbow/wrist positioning, **self-feeding fails without adequate finger and thumb motion** to **acquire, grip firmly, and release** food. Hand function is the most variable and often the **limiting factor**, so reconstruction addresses digital/thumb function alongside the more predictable proximal repositioning. The elbow and wrist must also combine enough extension (to reach the plate) and flexion (to reach the mouth).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Nonoperative management begun in infancy for arthrogrypotic contractures consists primarily of:

options.text: Passive stretching, serial casting, and splinting to improve/maintain passive motion and joint position
Early strengthening against resistance
Immobilization to prevent motion
Observation only

questions.explanation: Early care emphasizes **passive stretching, serial casting, and splinting** (often started in the nursery) to **improve and preserve passive motion and joint position**, laying the groundwork for later surgery. Because the muscles are deficient (not spastic), the aim is to keep joints supple and well-positioned rather than to strengthen weak/absent muscles.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: A Steindler flexorplasty restores elbow flexion by:

options.text: Proximally transferring the flexor-pronator (medial epicondyle) origin up the humerus so the forearm flexors also flex the elbow
Transferring the triceps anteriorly
Transferring the latissimus dorsi
Fusing the elbow in flexion

questions.explanation: The **Steindler flexorplasty** advances the **common flexor-pronator origin proximally on the humerus**, converting the forearm flexor mass into an **elbow flexor**. It requires functioning **forearm flexor muscles** (so it is unsuitable when these are deficient) and can produce a flexion/pronation posture; it is one option among triceps-to-biceps, pectoralis, latissimus, and free gracilis transfers depending on available donors.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Why must PASSIVE elbow motion be achieved before ACTIVE flexion transfer in arthrogryposis?

options.text: A tendon/muscle transfer cannot move a joint that is passively stiff — the release provides the arc the transfer will then power
Because active transfer weakens the joint capsule
Because passive motion prevents the transfer from healing
It is not necessary

questions.explanation: A transfer only **powers an existing passive arc**; it cannot overcome a **fixed contracture**. Thus the sequence is **release first (passive flexion 30–100°), then transfer** to provide active flexion. This mirrors a universal reconstructive principle — supple joints are a prerequisite for any motor transfer.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which statement about the bones in arthrogryposis is correct?

options.text: Bones are often osteopenic (from lack of muscle load), thin/small in diameter with thick cortices and a nearly absent medullary canal
Bones are enlarged with wide medullary canals
Bone quality is entirely normal
The bones are hypertrophic from overuse

questions.explanation: Reduced muscle activity/weight-bearing yields **osteopenic, thin, small-diameter bones with thickened cortices and a nearly obliterated medullary canal**. The **subcutaneous fat makes up a large proportion of limb bulk** because muscle is deficient. These features affect osteotomy/fixation technique (small, dense bones) and the feel of the limb on examination.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: A child with a fixed wrist flexion contracture uses the EDC to weakly extend the wrist toward neutral. What undesirable effect does this produce?

options.text: Concomitant MCP joint (finger) hyperextension, because the extrinsic finger extensors are being used to extend the wrist
Improved finger flexion
Thumb opposition
Elbow flexion

questions.explanation: Without wrist extensors, some children substitute the **EDC to extend the wrist**, but this simultaneously **hyperextends the MCP joints** (the EDC's finger action), impairing grasp. Reconstruction that **repositions the wrist (carpal osteotomy/PRC) and, if possible, transfers a donor to a wrist extensor** frees the EDC to do its proper job (finger extension).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which distal arthrogryposis subtype is associated with trismus (limited mouth opening) and pseudocamptodactyly (finger flexion on wrist extension)?

options.text: DA type 7 (trismus-pseudocamptodactyly / Hecht syndrome)
DA type 2A (Freeman-Sheldon)
DA type 9 (Beals)
DA type 8 (Escobar)

questions.explanation: **DA type 7 (trismus-pseudocamptodactyly, Hecht syndrome)** features **trismus (restricted jaw opening)** and **pseudocamptodactyly** — the fingers flex only when the wrist is dorsiflexed (a short-flexor/tenodesis phenomenon), correcting with wrist flexion. Recognizing the subtype is important for **anesthetic airway planning** (trismus) and for understanding the dynamic, position-dependent finger posture.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Why is building rapport and careful, play-based examination especially emphasized in children with arthrogryposis?

options.text: Many have undergone extensive prior interventions and may be wary; observing play/feeding reveals true functional capacity better than forced commands
Because the examination is unimportant
Because sensation is absent
Because they cannot cooperate at any age

questions.explanation: These children often have **extensive prior medical/surgical experiences** and may be anxious, so **trust-building and observing them play with toys, eat finger foods, or drink** yields a more accurate picture of **real-world function** (active/passive motion, resting posture) than rigid command-based testing — directly informing which functions to prioritize surgically.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: A shoulder in arthrogryposis that rarely needs surgery is characterized by:

options.text: Greater than ~90° of active abduction and active external rotation past neutral
A fixed internal rotation contracture with no abduction
Complete absence of deltoid function
A dislocated glenohumeral joint

questions.explanation: A shoulder with **>90° active abduction and active external rotation past neutral** provides functional positioning and **rarely requires intervention**. Surgery (humeral derotation osteotomy to ~15–30° IR) is reserved for a **significant internal-rotation contracture** that prevents the hand from reaching the mouth/midline and perineum.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: When both the elbow flexors AND the triceps are absent, the elbow tends to sit at ~60° and reconstruction is challenging because:

options.text: There is no strong local donor to power flexion, so a free functioning muscle transfer (or acceptance of a fixed functional position) may be needed
The triceps can simply be transferred
The Steindler flexorplasty is always ideal
No treatment is ever attempted

questions.explanation: Absence of **both** flexors and the triceps leaves **no strong local donor** for a flexion transfer, so options narrow to a **free functioning muscle transfer (gracilis)** — if a suitable innervation source and passive arc exist — or **accepting/optimizing a fixed functional elbow position**. Donor imaging/stimulation is critical to determine what, if anything, can be transferred.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which best describes the natural history of amyoplasia contractures (as opposed to a progressive neuromuscular disease)?

options.text: Non-progressive (the underlying condition does not worsen), though contractures can recur/change with growth and require staged management
Steadily progressive weakness like a degenerative disease
Complete spontaneous resolution by age 2
Fluctuating like a movement disorder

questions.explanation: **Amyoplasia is non-progressive** — the muscle deficiency is static — but **contractures can recur or evolve with growth**, so treatment is **staged over childhood** (releases early, transfers later, revisions as needed). This contrasts with **progressive** neuromuscular diseases (e.g., SMA), which must be excluded when the picture is atypical.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: For the elbow reconstruction sequence in a child needing both passive and active flexion, the correct order is:

options.text: Posterior release (early, <2 years) to gain passive flexion → later (≥4 years) active-flexion transfer
Active transfer first, then release
Simultaneous arthrodesis and transfer
Transfer in infancy, release at maturity

questions.explanation: The staged sequence is **(1) posterior elbow release early (first ~2 years)** to create a passive arc, then **(2) active-flexion transfer at ≥4 years** once passive motion, donor availability, and cooperation are established. Reversing the order would attempt to power a stiff joint or transfer before the child can rehabilitate it.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST appropriate management step in arthrogryposis upper-limb care?

options.text: Performing active elbow-flexion transfers on both elbows without preserving any elbow's ability to reach the perineum
Serial casting/splinting in infancy
Posterior elbow release before an active-flexion transfer
Assessing donor muscles with MRI and needle stimulation

questions.explanation: Flexing **both elbows without leaving one able to reach the perineum** compromises **toileting/hygiene** — the least appropriate step, violating the 'one to eat, one to wipe' principle. The others are sound: early **casting/splinting**, **release before transfer**, and **donor assessment (MRI/needle stimulation)**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which broad category does amyoplasia fall under, and roughly how symmetric is its involvement?

options.text: It is the classic 'classic arthrogryposis,' typically symmetric involvement of all four limbs
A unilateral, asymmetric condition
A purely lower-limb condition
A spastic (upper-motor-neuron) disorder

questions.explanation: **Amyoplasia** is the prototypical arthrogryposis with **symmetric involvement of all four limbs** and the characteristic posture. It is **sporadic** (low recurrence risk), whereas **distal arthrogryposis** is inherited (AD) and more distally focused. Neither is spastic — the deficit is myopathic/structural, not from a brain lesion.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: The recurrence risk counseling for the classic sporadic amyoplasia versus autosomal dominant distal arthrogryposis differs in that:

options.text: Amyoplasia is generally sporadic with low recurrence risk, whereas distal arthrogryposis carries up to ~50% recurrence per pregnancy (AD)
Both have 50% recurrence
Amyoplasia is autosomal recessive
Distal arthrogryposis is never inherited

questions.explanation: **Amyoplasia is typically sporadic** (attributed to a fetal-akinesia/vascular event) with **low recurrence risk**, so parents can be reassured. **Distal arthrogryposis** is usually **autosomal dominant**, so an affected parent has up to a **~50% chance of transmission** — important for genetic counseling and family planning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: A common thread underlying the joint contractures in arthrogryposis at the tissue level is:

options.text: Fetal akinesia — reduced intrauterine movement (from absent/weak muscle) leads to periarticular soft-tissue fibrosis and fixed contractures
Excessive fetal movement stretching the joints
Primary bone overgrowth
A demyelinating process

questions.explanation: Contractures share a final common pathway of **fetal akinesia**: whatever the cause (myopathic amyoplasia, neurogenic, connective-tissue, or extrinsic constraint), **decreased fetal movement** leads to **periarticular fibrosis, capsular tightening, and poorly modeled joint surfaces**, producing the fixed contractures. This is why maintaining/restoring motion (stretching, releases) is central to management.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: When counseling a family about realistic upper-limb goals in a severely affected child with arthrogryposis, the surgeon should emphasize:

options.text: Achievable functional milestones (independent feeding, hygiene, positioning) rather than a normal limb, with staged surgery over childhood
That a normal limb is attainable
That no surgery will ever help
That a single operation will correct everything

questions.explanation: Goals are framed around **specific, achievable functions (self-feeding, toileting, hand positioning)** — not restoration of a normal limb — via **staged procedures across childhood** (releases, osteotomies, transfers). Because sensation and cognition are usually normal, meaningful functional gains are realistic and worthwhile with appropriate expectations.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which finding on examination of an arthrogrypotic limb reflects the muscle deficiency rather than joint pathology?

options.text: Slender limbs where subcutaneous fat forms much of the bulk, with weak/absent active motion but variably preserved passive motion
Warm, swollen, tender joints
Hypertrophied muscle bellies
Normal full active motion in all joints

questions.explanation: Because muscle is **absent/hypoplastic**, the limbs are **slender with fat comprising much of the girth**, and **active motion is weak/absent** while **passive motion varies** (limited by secondary contracture). There is no inflammation. Distinguishing weak active from restricted passive motion is essential to choose between **releases (for passive limitation)** and **transfers (for absent active power)**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: In distal arthrogryposis type 1 (the 'common/typical' form), the characteristic hand/foot findings are:

options.text: Camptodactyly, clasped/ulnar-deviated thumbs, and clubfoot, generally without the facial features of the syndromic subtypes
Whistling face and deep-set eyes
Multiple pterygia
Sensorineural hearing loss

questions.explanation: **DA type 1** is the **common/typical distal arthrogryposis**, defined by **hand and foot contractures — camptodactyly, clasped/ulnar-deviated thumbs, and clubfoot (talipes)** — without the additional facial/systemic features that mark subtypes like Freeman-Sheldon (2A), Beals (9), Escobar (8), or the hearing-loss/ophthalmoplegia variants. It is autosomal dominant.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which statement about the goal position of the elbow after reconstruction, considering the whole limb for self-feeding, is correct?

options.text: The elbow and wrist together must provide enough EXTENSION to reach the plate/table and enough FLEXION to reach the mouth, with forearm/shoulder rotation orienting the hand appropriately
Maximal flexion is the only requirement
Maximal extension is the only requirement
Joint position is irrelevant to feeding

questions.explanation: Self-feeding is a **whole-limb task**: the child must **extend (elbow/wrist) to reach the food** and **flex to bring it to the mouth**, while **forearm/shoulder rotation** faces the hand first to the plate then to the mouth. Reconstruction therefore balances **extension and flexion across the elbow/wrist** rather than maximizing one — the functional rationale behind the target arcs.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which overall statement best captures the philosophy of upper-limb surgery in arthrogryposis?

options.text: Stage procedures to reposition and power joints toward specific functional tasks, respecting that muscle donors are scarce and goals are functional, not normal
Attempt to normalize every joint in a single operation
Avoid surgery entirely
Prioritize cosmetic symmetry

questions.explanation: Management is a **staged, function-directed strategy**: **reposition** joints (osteotomies), **restore passive motion** (releases), and **power** key motions (transfers, using scarce donors identified by imaging/stimulation), all aimed at concrete tasks (**feeding, hygiene, positioning**). Expectations are **functional independence, not a normal limb**, coordinated with the child's other (spine/lower-limb) needs.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Anesthetic planning is especially important in certain distal arthrogryposis subtypes because of:

options.text: Difficult airway (e.g., small mouth/trismus in Freeman-Sheldon and Hecht syndromes) and reported susceptibility to malignant-hyperthermia-like reactions
A bleeding diathesis in all subtypes
Absent pain sensation
No anesthetic concerns exist

questions.explanation: Subtypes such as **Freeman-Sheldon (small pursed mouth) and trismus-pseudocamptodactyly (limited jaw opening)** pose **difficult-airway** challenges, and some distal arthrogryposes have been associated with **malignant-hyperthermia-like/anesthetic reactions**. Since these children undergo **multiple procedures**, coordinated preoperative airway assessment and anesthetic planning are essential.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: An examination under anesthesia (EUA) during another procedure is useful in arthrogryposis mainly to:

options.text: Determine the true passive range/extent of contractures and stimulate potential donor muscles to confirm availability
Perform a muscle biopsy routinely
Obtain screening radiographs
Avoid the need for any therapy

questions.explanation: Under anesthesia the child is relaxed, so the surgeon can accurately gauge **true passive motion/contracture severity** and perform **percutaneous needle stimulation of candidate donors (pectoralis, latissimus, gracilis)** to confirm which muscles can be transferred. Since these children visit the OR several times (spine, lower limb), EUA is efficiently combined with other procedures.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: For a bilateral elbow-flexion reconstruction plan, a common approach is to:

options.text: Give one elbow reliable active flexion (to eat) while positioning/preserving the other for reach to the perineum and transfers (to wipe)
Flex both elbows to 130° and fuse them
Extend both elbows fully
Operate on neither elbow

questions.explanation: The **'one to eat, one to wipe'** principle drives bilateral planning: **one elbow is set up for dependable active flexion** (hand-to-mouth for feeding), while the **other retains extension/reach** for **perineal hygiene, transfers, and pushing up**. Balancing the two limbs avoids creating a child who can feed but cannot toilet independently.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: Which statement about camptodactyly in the context of distal arthrogryposis is correct?

options.text: It is a frequent hand finding (PIP flexion contracture) in several DA subtypes and is managed like isolated camptodactyly — therapy/splinting first, selective surgery
It is unique to amyoplasia and never seen in DA
It always requires immediate PIP fusion
It reflects a brain lesion

questions.explanation: **Camptodactyly (PIP flexion contracture)** is a hallmark hand feature across multiple **distal arthrogryposis subtypes** (types 1, 2, 4, 6, etc.). As with isolated camptodactyly, first-line care is **prolonged splinting/therapy**, with **selective surgery** for fixed, functionally limiting contractures — recognizing that results are variable and the underlying myopathy limits correction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: A free functioning gracilis transfer for elbow flexion in arthrogryposis requires which key prerequisites?

options.text: A passive elbow arc, a suitable motor nerve to power it (e.g., intercostal or a spinal accessory branch), and adequate recipient vessels
A stiff, fused elbow
An intact, strong triceps to transfer instead
No nerve source at all

questions.explanation: A **free functioning muscle (gracilis) transfer** is used when no local donor exists; it needs a **passively mobile elbow, a motor nerve to neurotize the muscle (e.g., intercostals or a spinal accessory branch), and suitable recipient vessels** for microvascular anastomosis. Strength develops over months as reinnervation matures — making passive motion and rehabilitation participation essential.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: The single most important distinction to make when deciding between a joint RELEASE and a tendon TRANSFER in an arthrogrypotic joint is:

options.text: Whether the limitation is a loss of PASSIVE motion (needs release) or a loss of ACTIVE power with adequate passive motion (needs transfer)
The child's cognitive level
The presence of a syndrome
The color of the limb

questions.explanation: **Passive vs active** is the key axis: a joint that **won't move passively needs a release/osteotomy** first, while a supple joint that **lacks active motion needs a motor (tendon/muscle) transfer**. Many arthrogrypotic joints need **both, staged in sequence (release then transfer)**. Correctly classifying the deficit at each joint drives the whole operative plan.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 39 (Arthrogryposis)

questions.stem: A term newborn does not move the right arm after a shoulder-dystocia delivery. The arm lies adducted/internally rotated at the shoulder, extended at the elbow, and pronated ('waiter's tip'), but the hand grips normally. Which pattern is this?

options.text: Upper trunk (C5–C6) — Erb's palsy
Global (C5–T1) palsy
Isolated C8–T1 (Klumpke) palsy
Posterior cord injury

questions.explanation: The **'waiter's tip' posture with preserved hand function** is the classic **upper-trunk (C5–C6) Erb's palsy** — loss of shoulder abduction/external rotation, elbow flexion, and forearm supination, with intact wrist/finger flexion and extension. It is the **most common** birth-palsy pattern and has the **best prognosis** for spontaneous recovery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which is the single most important prognostic milestone for spontaneous recovery in an infant with an upper-trunk brachial plexus birth injury?

options.text: Recovery of active biceps (elbow flexion) by about 3–4 months of age predicts a good outcome
Recovery of wrist extension by 1 week
Presence of a grasp reflex at birth
Normal shoulder abduction at 2 weeks

questions.explanation: **Return of antigravity biceps/elbow flexion by ~3–4 months** is the classic favorable prognostic sign (Gilbert), predicting a high likelihood of good spontaneous recovery. **Absence of biceps function at 3 months** is a widely used indication to consider **primary nerve reconstruction**. Serial exams every 1–3 months during infancy track this trajectory.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which perinatal factor is the classic mechanical risk factor for brachial plexus birth injury in a vertex delivery?

options.text: Shoulder dystocia (often with fetal macrosomia and maternal diabetes)
Elective cesarean section
Premature delivery of a small infant
Oligohydramnios alone

questions.explanation: **Shoulder dystocia** — impaction of the anterior shoulder behind the symphysis — is the classic mechanical cause in vertex deliveries, associated with **macrosomia, maternal diabetes, multiparity, prolonged labor, and assisted (forceps/vacuum) delivery**. Breech deliveries cause a different pattern (often C5–6 avulsion, sometimes bilateral). Cesarean section markedly reduces but does not eliminate the risk.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: The Narakas classification of brachial plexus birth injury groups I–IV. Which description is correct?

options.text: I = C5–6 (Erb); II = C5–7 (extended, waiter's tip); III = complete flail arm WITHOUT Horner; IV = flail arm WITH Horner syndrome
I = global palsy; IV = mild Erb
I = flail with Horner; IV = C5–6 only
The groups are based on birth weight

questions.explanation: **Narakas I** = **C5–6 (Erb)**, best prognosis (~90% recover); **II** = **C5–7** (adds wrist/finger extensor loss, 'waiter's tip'); **III** = **complete flail extremity WITHOUT Horner**; **IV** = **flail extremity WITH Horner syndrome** (± phrenic palsy), the worst prognosis. Ascending groups correlate with more roots involved, more avulsion, and lower spontaneous-recovery potential.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: A 4-month-old with a global birth palsy has ptosis, miosis, and a small pupil on the affected side. What does this Horner syndrome indicate?

options.text: A lower-root (C8–T1) avulsion (preganglionic) — a marker of severe injury with poor spontaneous-recovery prognosis
A mild upper-trunk stretch with good prognosis
A clavicle fracture
Normal newborn finding

questions.explanation: **Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, enophthalmos)** reflects **cervicothoracic sympathetic (T1) involvement**, indicating a **lower-root avulsion (preganglionic)** and a **poor prognosis** (Narakas IV). It should prompt earlier surgical planning, since avulsed roots cannot recover or be grafted and require **nerve transfers**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which examination/imaging finding suggests a PREGANGLIONIC (avulsion) birth injury?

options.text: Elevated hemidiaphragm (phrenic/C5), absent rhomboids (dorsal scapular/C5), winged scapula (long thoracic), Horner sign (T1), and a pseudomeningocele on imaging
An advancing Tinel over the trunk
Early biceps recovery
A clavicle fracture

questions.explanation: Nerves arising very proximally localize the lesion: **phrenic (C5) → elevated hemidiaphragm; dorsal scapular (C5) → absent rhomboids; long thoracic → winged scapula; sympathetic (T1) → Horner sign**, and **paraspinal (dorsal rami) denervation** — all imply a **preganglionic avulsion**, as does a **pseudomeningocele** on MRI/CT myelography. These predict poor spontaneous recovery and mandate transfer-based reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which birth-injury pattern carries the WORST prognosis for spontaneous recovery?

options.text: Global (C5–T1) palsy, especially with Horner syndrome (Narakas IV)
Isolated C5–6 Erb's palsy
Neurapraxia of the upper trunk
A pattern with early biceps recovery

questions.explanation: **Global (C5–T1) palsy** — a flail arm, worst with an associated **Horner syndrome (Narakas IV)** — has the **least chance of meaningful spontaneous recovery** and the strongest indication for early microsurgery. **Erb's (C5–6)** has the best prognosis (~90% recover spontaneously).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Approximately what proportion of infants with a Narakas group I (C5–6 Erb) birth palsy recover spontaneously?

options.text: About 90%
About 10%
About 50%
Essentially 0%

questions.explanation: **Roughly 90% of Narakas I (C5–6)** infants recover useful function spontaneously, which is why **watchful serial examination** (rather than early surgery) is appropriate for most upper-trunk palsies — reserving reconstruction for those who fail to show recovery (e.g., no biceps by ~3 months). Prognosis worsens with each additional root involved.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Why is the RIGHT arm more commonly affected in brachial plexus birth injury?

options.text: The common left-occiput-anterior vertex presentation places the right (anterior) shoulder behind the symphysis pubis, at risk during dystocia
The right plexus is anatomically weaker
Right-handed obstetricians pull harder
The right side has no dorsal root ganglion

questions.explanation: In the usual **left-occiput-anterior vertex presentation**, the **right shoulder is anterior and can impact behind the maternal symphysis**, so the **right upper limb is more often injured**. Breech deliveries produce a different mechanism (often bilateral C5–6 avulsions).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: A newborn's arm is immobile ('pseudoparalysis'). Which alternative diagnosis must be excluded before diagnosing a plexus injury?

options.text: A fracture (e.g., clavicle or humeral shaft) causing painful pseudoparalysis — obtain radiographs
Congenital heart disease
Neonatal jaundice
Hip dysplasia

questions.explanation: **Fracture-related pseudoparalysis** (clavicle or humerus) can mimic a plexus palsy, so **radiographs are indicated**; a clavicle fracture may also **coexist** with a plexus injury. A severely displaced humeral shaft fracture can cause an **isolated radial nerve palsy**. Other differentials include CNS/cervical cord injury, infection, and congenital limb anomalies.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: What is the standard indication and timing for considering PRIMARY microsurgical nerve reconstruction in an upper-trunk birth palsy?

options.text: Failure of biceps (elbow flexion) recovery by ~3 months (or a persistent flail arm / global palsy with avulsion signs) — reconstruction typically around 3–9 months
Immediately at birth in all cases
Only after age 5
Never — surgery is not indicated for birth palsy

questions.explanation: Most centers offer **primary nerve reconstruction when biceps function has not returned by ~3 months** in upper-trunk lesions (some use additional tests at 6–9 months, e.g., the 'cookie test' for hand-to-mouth), and **early** in **global palsies with avulsion signs (Horner)**. Surgery is generally done between **~3 and 9 months** to reinnervate before endplate degeneration while allowing spontaneous recovery to declare.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: A postganglionic RUPTURE at the upper trunk in a birth injury is best reconstructed by:

options.text: Resecting the neuroma and bridging the gap with interpositional (sural) nerve grafts (± distal nerve transfers)
Direct suture under tension
Nerve transfer only, because grafting is impossible
Observation indefinitely

questions.explanation: A **postganglionic rupture has viable proximal and distal stumps**, so reconstruction involves **neuroma resection and interpositional nerve grafting (typically sural)**, sometimes augmented with **distal nerve transfers**. In contrast, **preganglionic avulsions have no proximal stump** and require **nerve transfers** (intercostal, spinal accessory, contralateral C7).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: For a preganglionic (avulsion) birth injury, reconstruction relies on nerve transfers. Which donors are commonly used?

options.text: Intercostal nerves, a branch of the spinal accessory nerve, or contralateral C7 (and partial peripheral nerve transfers)
Direct grafting from the avulsed root
The phrenic nerve as first choice in infants
The median nerve trunk

questions.explanation: Because avulsed roots cannot be grafted, **extraplexal/partial donors** are used: **intercostal nerves, a spinal accessory branch, contralateral C7**, and **partial peripheral nerve transfers** (e.g., ulnar fascicle to biceps in older infants). The **phrenic nerve is generally avoided in infants** given respiratory concerns. Donor choice depends on which targets need reinnervation and which roots remain.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: An infant with a global palsy has an elevated right hemidiaphragm on fluoroscopy. What does this indicate, and why does it matter?

options.text: Phrenic nerve (C5) injury — it signals a very proximal (preganglionic) lesion, affects respiratory reserve, and influences donor choice (avoid the phrenic)
A normal finding requiring no action
A diaphragmatic hernia unrelated to the plexus
A sign of good prognosis

questions.explanation: An **elevated hemidiaphragm** reflects **phrenic nerve (C5) palsy**, indicating a **proximal/preganglionic injury** and a poorer prognosis; it also **reduces respiratory reserve** (important perioperatively) and makes the **phrenic unavailable/undesirable as a transfer donor**. Diaphragm status is best assessed by **dynamic fluoroscopy or ultrasound** during breathing.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: The most common long-term musculoskeletal sequela of an incompletely recovered Erb's palsy is:

options.text: An internal-rotation/adduction contracture of the shoulder with secondary glenohumeral dysplasia and posterior humeral head subluxation
A flail, insensate hand
Wrist drop
Elbow extension contracture only

questions.explanation: Muscle imbalance (weak external rotators/abductors vs relatively strong internal rotators/adductors) produces a progressive **internal-rotation/adduction contracture**, which in the growing shoulder causes **glenohumeral dysplasia and posterior subluxation/dislocation of the humeral head**. Early recognition (exam, ultrasound/MRI) allows treatment (therapy, botulinum toxin, tendon transfers, or reductions/osteotomy) before fixed deformity.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with residual Erb's palsy has weak shoulder external rotation and abduction with a supple (reducible) glenohumeral joint. A classic secondary reconstruction is:

options.text: Latissimus dorsi and teres major transfer to the rotator cuff (L'Episcopo-type) to restore external rotation/abduction, ± anterior (subscapularis/pectoralis) release
Shoulder arthrodesis
Biceps-to-triceps transfer
Wrist fusion

questions.explanation: When the joint is still **reducible**, transferring the **latissimus dorsi and teres major (internal rotators) posteriorly onto the rotator cuff (L'Episcopo/Hoffer transfer)** converts deforming internal rotators into **external rotators/abductors**, often combined with **release of the tight anterior structures (subscapularis, ± pectoralis major)**. For a fixed/dysplastic joint, a **humeral derotation osteotomy** is used instead.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: For a shoulder with an established, fixed glenohumeral deformity (non-reducible dysplasia) in birth palsy, the appropriate procedure is often:

options.text: Humeral external-rotation (derotation) osteotomy to reposition the arm functionally
Only botulinum toxin injections
Latissimus/teres major transfer alone
No treatment is possible

questions.explanation: Once the glenohumeral joint is **fixed/dysplastic and not reducible**, soft-tissue balancing cannot re-center it, so a **humeral derotation osteotomy** repositions the arm into more useful external rotation (improving hand-to-mouth/space positioning). Earlier, reducible deformity is treated with **release + tendon transfer (± glenohumeral reduction)** to prevent progression.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: During hand-to-mouth activity, a child with birth palsy abducts the shoulder markedly to compensate for weak elbow flexion/external rotation. This is called the:

options.text: Trumpet sign (hornblower's posture)
Froment's sign
Wartenberg's sign
Mallet sign

questions.explanation: The **trumpet sign** describes excessive **shoulder abduction to bring the hand to the mouth**, compensating for **weak elbow flexion and/or external rotation** (the elbow can't flex against gravity without abducting the arm). It signals a functional deficit that reconstruction (shoulder external-rotation restoration and/or elbow flexion) aims to address. The **Mallet score** grades shoulder function.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: The modified Mallet classification is used to assess:

options.text: Shoulder function (global abduction, external rotation, hand-to-neck, hand-to-spine, hand-to-mouth) in birth palsy
Sensory recovery of the hand
The degree of Horner syndrome
Elbow flexion strength only

questions.explanation: The **modified Mallet score** grades **shoulder function** across standardized positions — **active abduction, external rotation, hand-to-neck, hand-to-spine, and hand-to-mouth** — providing a reproducible measure to track recovery and outcomes of shoulder reconstruction in brachial plexus birth injury.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about the incidence and trend of brachial plexus birth injury is correct?

options.text: Roughly 0.4–1.6 per 1000 live births, and decreasing over recent decades in the US
About 1 in 10 live births and rising sharply
Essentially never occurs today
Exactly 5% of all births

questions.explanation: BPBI occurs in about **0.4–1.6 per 1000 live births**, with a **declining trend** in the US (e.g., ~1.6 in 2000 to ~0.9 per 1000 by 2012), likely reflecting obstetric-care changes. Rising maternal BMI/gestational diabetes/fetal size are countervailing risk factors, and cesarean section reduces but does not eliminate risk.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which delivery scenario is particularly associated with C5–C6 root AVULSIONS that can be bilateral?

options.text: Breech delivery
Elective cesarean at term
Precipitous vaginal delivery of a small infant
Water birth

questions.explanation: **Breech deliveries** (with difficult arm/head extraction and traction on the neck) are notably associated with **C5–C6 avulsions**, which can be **bilateral**. Vertex deliveries with shoulder dystocia more often produce **upper-trunk extraforaminal ruptures**. The mechanism influences the likelihood of avulsion (preganglionic) versus rupture (postganglionic).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Why can some postganglionic birth injuries recover spontaneously even when initial deficits are marked?

options.text: Partial (incomplete) ruptures and the redundant/plastic innervation present at birth allow reinnervation and functional recovery
Avulsed roots regrow into the cord
The dorsal root ganglion regenerates the motor neuron
Spontaneous recovery is impossible in any birth injury

questions.explanation: Many lesions are **partial ruptures**, and the neonate's plexus has **redundant innervation pathways and high plasticity**, so **postganglionic injuries frequently recover spontaneously** — the basis for initial observation. This differs from **preganglionic avulsions**, which cannot recover. Serial exams distinguish those recovering from those needing surgery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: What proportion of brachial plexus birth injuries involve the classic C5–C6 (Erb) pattern, making it the most common?

options.text: About 46% (C5–6), with C5–7 next (~29%)
About 5%
About 90%
Less than 1%

questions.explanation: The **C5–6 (Erb) pattern accounts for ~46%** and the **extended C5–7 pattern for ~29%** — together the large majority, and usually **postganglionic**. **Global (C5–T1) palsies are least common** but most severe; when the lower plexus is involved, **C8–T1 (± C7) preganglionic avulsions** are typical.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: The primary purpose of serial neurologic examinations (every 1–3 months) in an infant with birth palsy is to:

options.text: Determine the trajectory/prognosis for recovery and identify infants who need surgical intervention
Confirm the diagnosis, which is otherwise impossible
Decide on immediate amputation
Replace the need for any imaging ever

questions.explanation: Because recovery is **dynamic** over the first months, **serial exams (every 1–3 months)** track whether key functions (especially **biceps**) are returning — the crux of **prognostication and the decision to operate**. Reliable infant examination requires patience, observation of spontaneous movement, neonatal reflexes, and tactile stimulation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about cesarean section and brachial plexus birth injury is correct?

options.text: Cesarean delivery greatly reduces (but does not eliminate) the risk; injuries can even occur before/without vaginal delivery
Cesarean delivery fully prevents all birth palsies
Cesarean delivery increases the risk 100-fold
The mode of delivery has no effect

questions.explanation: **Cesarean section markedly lowers** the risk of BPBI (reported ~100-fold reduction) but **does not guarantee prevention** — reports document injuries with cesarean delivery and even **intrauterine-onset** paralysis (e.g., from an anomalous uterus/compression). Thus prevention is imperfect, underscoring the importance of optimally **treating** the sequelae.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Early physical/occupational therapy in an infant with birth palsy focuses primarily on:

options.text: Maintaining passive range of motion (preventing contractures, especially shoulder external rotation and forearm/elbow) while awaiting recovery
Aggressive strengthening of paralyzed muscles
Immobilizing the limb completely
Electrical stimulation to regrow avulsed roots

questions.explanation: Therapy centers on **passive ROM to prevent contractures** — particularly the shoulder **internal-rotation/adduction** contracture and elbow/forearm stiffness — and on incorporating the limb into use. Preserving supple joints protects future function and keeps reconstructive options open. It does not strengthen denervated muscle or reverse avulsions.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: A common secondary deformity at the ELBOW/forearm in birth palsy that impairs hand positioning is:

options.text: A supination contracture of the forearm (± radial head dislocation) and/or an elbow flexion contracture
A fixed hyperextension of the elbow with pronation lock
Wrist ankylosis in extension
Thumb duplication

questions.explanation: Muscle imbalance can produce a **forearm supination contracture (sometimes with posterior radial head dislocation)** that places the palm up and impairs function, and/or an **elbow flexion contracture**. Treatment ranges from therapy/splinting to **biceps rerouting/tendon rebalancing, osteotomy, or radial head management** depending on severity and reducibility.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which nerves, arising close to the spinal cord, are tested to help localize a preganglionic lesion in birth palsy?

options.text: Phrenic (C5, diaphragm), dorsal scapular (C5, rhomboids), long thoracic (C5–7, serratus/scapular winging), and the sympathetic chain (T1, Horner)
Median, ulnar, and radial nerves in the hand
The digital nerves
The recurrent laryngeal nerve

questions.explanation: Very proximal branches localize the lesion: **phrenic (diaphragm), dorsal scapular (rhomboids), long thoracic (serratus → winging), and the T1 sympathetic outflow (Horner)**. Their involvement implies a lesion **at/near the roots (preganglionic)**, correlating with **avulsion and poor spontaneous recovery** — key to prognosis and surgical planning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: The 'cookie test' (or a similar hand-to-mouth test) at ~9 months is used to:

options.text: Assess whether elbow flexion is strong enough to bring the hand to the mouth (with the shoulder adducted) — inadequate function supports reconstruction
Measure sensory two-point discrimination
Test the grasp reflex
Evaluate diaphragm motion

questions.explanation: The **cookie test** evaluates **antigravity elbow flexion to reach the mouth with the arm adducted (no trumpeting)** around **9 months**; failure indicates inadequate biceps function and, in the appropriate context, supports **nerve reconstruction or later secondary procedures**. It complements the 3-month biceps milestone in surgical decision-making.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: A pseudomeningocele seen on MRI/CT myelography in an infant with birth palsy indicates:

options.text: Dural/arachnoid avulsion at that level (a marker of preganglionic root avulsion)
A postganglionic rupture that is easily grafted
Normal infant anatomy
A clavicle fracture

questions.explanation: A **pseudomeningocele** forms when root avulsion tears the **dura/arachnoid**, letting CSF collect — a marker of **preganglionic avulsion**. As in adults, it is **suggestive but not perfectly reliable**, so imaging is correlated with clinical avulsion signs (Horner, diaphragm, rhomboids, winging) and intraoperative findings.
