references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST accurate statement about brachial plexus birth injury?

options.text: Global (C5–T1) palsy is the most common and has the best prognosis
Erb's (C5–6) palsy is the most common pattern
Absence of biceps recovery by ~3 months suggests the need for surgery
Horner syndrome indicates a poor prognosis

questions.explanation: The false statement is that **global palsy is the most common with the best prognosis** — in fact **global (C5–T1) palsy is the LEAST common and has the WORST prognosis**, while **Erb's (C5–6) is the most common with the best prognosis**. The other statements are correct (3-month biceps rule; Horner = poor prognosis).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Botulinum toxin is sometimes used in the birth-palsy shoulder to:

options.text: Temporarily weaken the internal rotators (e.g., subscapularis/pectoralis) to reduce muscle imbalance and aid reduction/therapy or a co-contraction
Permanently strengthen the external rotators
Regrow avulsed roots
Replace the need for any therapy

questions.explanation: **Botulinum toxin** can temporarily weaken the **overactive internal rotators/adductors** (or address biceps-triceps co-contraction), rebalancing forces to **facilitate glenohumeral reduction, splinting, and therapy** and delay/limit contracture. It is an adjunct — not a substitute for tendon transfers, releases, or definitive reconstruction when needed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: In an infant with a global palsy undergoing reconstruction, priority for reinnervation is typically given to:

options.text: Elbow flexion and shoulder stability/function, then hand function/sensation (hand recovery is least reliable)
Intrinsic hand muscles first
Wrist flexion first
Forearm pronation first

questions.explanation: As in adult plexus reconstruction, priorities are **elbow flexion and shoulder function/stability first**, then **hand function and protective sensation**. **Hand/intrinsic recovery is least reliable** owing to long regeneration distances, so realistic goals and, at times, later secondary hand procedures (tendon transfers, free muscle) are planned.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which finding at birth would MOST reassure you that an upper-trunk palsy is likely to recover spontaneously?

options.text: Early, progressive return of antigravity biceps (elbow flexion) over the first weeks to ~3 months
A Horner syndrome
An elevated hemidiaphragm
A flail arm with winged scapula

questions.explanation: **Progressive recovery of biceps/elbow flexion toward the ~3-month mark** is the strongest early indicator of a **good spontaneous outcome**. The other findings (**Horner, phrenic palsy, flail arm/winged scapula**) indicate **proximal/avulsion injury and poor prognosis**, favoring surgical reconstruction.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: A humeral shaft fracture sustained during delivery (e.g., posterior arm maneuver) can specifically mimic which isolated nerve palsy?

options.text: Radial nerve palsy (wrist/finger extension weakness)
Ulnar nerve palsy with clawing
Median nerve palsy with benediction posture
Axillary nerve palsy

questions.explanation: A **displaced humeral shaft fracture** can injure the **radial nerve**, causing an **isolated radial palsy** (wrist/finger drop) that mimics part of a plexus injury; the fracture also causes painful pseudoparalysis. Because such fractures and plexus injuries usually occur on **opposite limbs**, and radiographs clarify the picture, careful examination and imaging distinguish them.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about the overall approach to birth palsy is most accurate?

options.text: Most (upper-trunk) cases are observed with therapy and recover; a minority with avulsion signs or failed biceps recovery undergo microsurgery, and residual deformities are treated with secondary procedures
All cases require immediate microsurgery at birth
No cases ever benefit from surgery
Surgery is only cosmetic

questions.explanation: The strategy is **stratified by prognosis**: **most upper-trunk palsies recover with observation and therapy**; **primary nerve reconstruction** is reserved for **failed biceps recovery (~3 months) or severe/avulsion (global, Horner) injuries**; and **secondary procedures (releases, tendon transfers, osteotomies)** address residual shoulder/elbow/forearm deformities in later childhood. Serial examination drives each decision.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: In the Narakas classification, what additional deficit distinguishes group II from group I?

options.text: Added C7 involvement, producing loss of wrist and finger extension (the 'waiter's tip' hand) on top of the C5–6 deficits
The presence of a Horner syndrome
A completely flail arm
Loss of hand intrinsics only

questions.explanation: **Group II (C5–7)** adds **C7/middle-trunk involvement** — loss of **wrist and finger extension** — to the group I (C5–6) deficits of shoulder abduction/ER, elbow flexion, and supination, giving the classic **waiter's-tip** posture. Groups III (flail, no Horner) and IV (flail + Horner) denote progressively more severe, worse-prognosis injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Glenohumeral dysplasia in birth palsy is best detected/monitored with which imaging in an infant?

options.text: Ultrasound (or MRI) of the shoulder to assess humeral head position/subluxation and glenoid version
Plain radiographs alone, which reliably show the cartilaginous joint
Bone scan
No imaging is useful

questions.explanation: Because the infant shoulder is largely **cartilaginous**, **ultrasound (or MRI)** is preferred to assess **posterior humeral head subluxation and glenoid dysplasia/version** — plain films underestimate the deformity. Early detection allows timely intervention (therapy, botulinum, reduction, tendon transfer) before **fixed dysplasia** develops that would require osteotomy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: The overall goal of managing residual deformity in birth palsy is best summarized as:

options.text: Restoring functional shoulder positioning/motion (external rotation, abduction), elbow flexion, and forearm position to improve hand use — accepting that full normality is rarely achieved
Achieving a completely normal limb in all cases
Prioritizing appearance over function
Fusing all involved joints

questions.explanation: Secondary reconstruction aims at **functional gains** — better **shoulder external rotation/abduction, elbow flexion, and forearm/hand positioning** — via **releases, tendon transfers, and osteotomies**, guided by tools like the **Mallet score**. As with other severe congenital/neurologic hand conditions, **function is prioritized** and realistic, individualized goals are set with the family.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which pairing of birth-palsy pattern and prognosis is correct?

options.text: Erb (C5–6) — best; extended Erb (C5–7) — intermediate; global with Horner (Narakas IV) — worst
Global with Horner — best; Erb — worst
All patterns have identical prognosis
Extended Erb — best; Erb — worst

questions.explanation: Prognosis worsens with more roots and avulsion: **Erb (C5–6) has the best** spontaneous-recovery outlook (~90%), **extended Erb (C5–7) is intermediate**, and **global palsy with Horner (Narakas IV) is worst**. This gradient drives the intensity and timing of surveillance and the threshold for microsurgery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about nerve transfers versus grafting in birth palsy reconstruction is correct?

options.text: Transfers are required for avulsions (no proximal stump) and can also augment/shorten reinnervation; grafting is used for postganglionic ruptures with viable stumps
Grafting can reconstruct avulsed roots directly
Transfers can only be used in adults
Neither is ever used in infants

questions.explanation: **Avulsions (preganglionic)** lack a proximal stump, so **nerve transfers (intercostal, spinal accessory, contralateral C7, partial peripheral)** are required; **postganglionic ruptures** are bridged with **interpositional (sural) grafts** after neuroma resection, and distal transfers may be added to speed reinnervation of key targets. The choice mirrors adult plexus principles adapted to the infant.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Preserving passive external rotation of the shoulder in infancy is important because loss of it leads to:

options.text: A progressive internal-rotation contracture and secondary glenohumeral dysplasia/subluxation
A flail hand
Elbow hyperextension
Loss of grasp reflex

questions.explanation: If **passive external rotation is lost**, the unopposed internal rotators drive a **fixed internal-rotation/adduction contracture**, and in the growing shoulder this **remodels the glenohumeral joint (dysplasia, posterior subluxation)**. Therapy to maintain external rotation — and timely botulinum/surgery — prevents this cascade, protecting shoulder function.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: A 6-month-old with C5–6 palsy has recovered some elbow flexion but essentially no shoulder external rotation, and ultrasound shows early posterior subluxation. A reasonable next step is:

options.text: Anterior shoulder release (± botulinum) with tendon transfer for external rotation and glenohumeral reduction to re-center the joint before fixed dysplasia sets in
Observation for 3 more years
Immediate shoulder arthrodesis
Wrist tendon transfer

questions.explanation: Early **posterior subluxation with absent external rotation** is addressed by **releasing the tight anterior structures (± botulinum to internal rotators), reducing/re-centering the glenohumeral joint, and transferring internal rotators (latissimus/teres major) to restore external rotation** — done **before the deformity becomes fixed**. A late, fixed dysplastic joint would instead require a **derotation osteotomy**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which best explains why the hand is usually SPARED in a typical Erb's (C5–6) birth palsy?

options.text: Hand/finger flexion and extension are supplied by C7–T1, which are uninjured in an isolated upper-trunk (C5–6) lesion
The hand has no nerve supply from the plexus
C5–6 supplies only the hand
The ulnar nerve arises from C5

questions.explanation: In an **isolated C5–6 lesion**, the **C7–T1 contributions (median/ulnar/radial supply to the wrist and hand) are intact**, so **wrist and finger flexion/extension are preserved** — the hand grips normally. The deficits are proximal (shoulder ER/abduction, elbow flexion, supination). Involvement of the hand implies extension to C7 or a global injury.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which overall statement about brachial plexus birth injury outcomes is correct?

options.text: The majority (upper-trunk) recover well spontaneously, but a significant minority have permanent deficits/deformities requiring nerve and/or secondary reconstructive surgery
All infants fully recover without exception
No infant ever recovers
Outcome is unrelated to injury pattern

questions.explanation: Most **upper-trunk** palsies recover useful function spontaneously, but a **meaningful minority — especially extended, global, and avulsion (Horner) injuries — sustain permanent deficits** needing **primary nerve reconstruction and/or secondary procedures** (tendon transfers, osteotomies) for residual shoulder/elbow/forearm/hand problems. Injury pattern (and biceps-recovery timing) strongly predicts outcome.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: An infant with a persistent C5–6 palsy develops a co-contraction of biceps and triceps, so elbow flexion is weak despite biceps activity. Which adjunct can help?

options.text: Botulinum toxin to the triceps (± biceps) to reduce the co-contraction and allow effective elbow flexion and motor re-education
Elbow arthrodesis in flexion
Immediate humeral osteotomy
Wrist fusion

questions.explanation: **Biceps–triceps co-contraction** — aberrant simultaneous firing after reinnervation — can neutralize elbow flexion. **Botulinum toxin (typically to the triceps)** temporarily weakens the antagonist, letting the biceps flex the elbow and enabling **therapy/motor re-education** to establish a better firing pattern. It is a reversible adjunct while the pattern is retrained.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which statement about sensory involvement in brachial plexus birth injury is correct?

options.text: Sensory loss accompanies the motor deficit in the affected distribution and, when dense (e.g., global palsy), the child may neglect or self-mutilate the insensate hand
Sensation is always completely normal
Sensory testing is impossible and irrelevant in infants
Sensory recovery never occurs

questions.explanation: Unlike amyoplasia (normal sensation), **plexus injury impairs sensation in the affected roots**. In severe/global palsies the **insensate hand may be neglected or even self-mutilated (biting)**, which affects prognosis and care. Assessing response to tactile/painful stimuli is part of the infant exam, and protective sensation is a reconstructive goal in global injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: A partial (fascicular) ulnar-to-biceps (Oberlin) nerve transfer may be used in an older infant/child with birth palsy provided that:

options.text: The lower plexus/ulnar nerve is functioning (so a redundant ulnar fascicle can be spared) — i.e., an upper-trunk lesion with an intact hand
The ulnar nerve is also avulsed
It is a global palsy with a flail hand
The child has a Horner syndrome

questions.explanation: An **Oberlin-type ulnar-fascicle-to-biceps transfer** requires an **intact, functioning ulnar nerve** to donate a redundant fascicle — feasible in **upper-trunk (C5–6) lesions with a working hand**, not in global/lower-plexus injuries where the ulnar nerve is involved. It can restore elbow flexion with minimal donor deficit, mirroring its use in adult upper-trunk injuries.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which best describes why primary nerve surgery is generally NOT delayed much beyond ~9–12 months in a non-recovering birth palsy?

options.text: Prolonged denervation leads to motor-endplate degeneration and poorer reinnervation outcomes, so reconstruction should reach muscle before that window closes
The nerves become malignant
Anesthesia is impossible after 1 year
Spontaneous recovery accelerates after 1 year

questions.explanation: As in all nerve reconstruction, **denervated muscle degenerates over time**, so reinnervation must arrive before the **endplate/motor-unit window** closes — hence primary reconstruction for non-recovering lesions is generally performed within roughly the **first 9–12 months** (balanced against allowing spontaneous recovery to declare). Very late presentations shift toward **secondary tendon/free-muscle procedures**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST appropriate management of a newborn with an isolated C5–6 palsy and a normal hand?

options.text: Immediate nerve grafting in the first week of life
Serial examinations every 1–3 months tracking biceps recovery
Passive range-of-motion therapy to prevent contracture
Radiographs if a clavicle fracture is suspected

questions.explanation: **Immediate neonatal grafting is least appropriate** — most **C5–6 palsies recover spontaneously (~90%)**, so early observation with **serial exams (biceps by ~3 months)** and **contracture-preventing therapy** is standard, reserving surgery for those who fail to recover. Imaging for a suspected concomitant clavicle fracture is reasonable.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 40 (Brachial Plexus Birth Injury)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman reports numbness of the thumb, index, middle, and radial ring finger that wakes her at night and is relieved by shaking the hand. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve compression at the wrist)
Cubital tunnel syndrome
C6 radiculopathy
Pronator syndrome

questions.explanation: **Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS)** classically causes **median-distribution numbness (thumb, index, middle, radial ring)**, **nocturnal symptoms**, and relief with **shaking (the 'flick sign')**. It is the most common compression neuropathy. Pronator syndrome affects a similar sensory territory but adds **forearm pain, palmar (thenar) sensory involvement, and lacks night symptoms**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which provocative test has the best combination of sensitivity and specificity for carpal tunnel syndrome?

options.text: Carpal compression (Durkan) test
Tinel sign at the wrist
Phalen test
Froment sign

questions.explanation: The **Durkan carpal compression test** (direct pressure over the carpal tunnel reproducing symptoms within ~30 seconds) generally has the **best combined sensitivity/specificity** for CTS. **Phalen** (wrist flexion) and **Tinel** (percussion) are useful but individually less reliable. Froment sign is for **ulnar** (adductor pollicis) weakness, not median compression.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which systemic condition is NOT a recognized risk factor for carpal tunnel syndrome?

options.text: Hyperthyroidism
Diabetes mellitus
Hypothyroidism
Acromegaly

questions.explanation: Recognized CTS risk factors include **diabetes, HYPOthyroidism, acromegaly, obesity, pregnancy, rheumatoid arthritis, alcohol and tobacco use, and amyloidosis** — conditions that increase canal contents or nerve susceptibility. **Hyperthyroidism** is not a classic risk factor; it is **hypothyroidism** (myxedematous tissue) that predisposes to CTS.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Regarding the pathophysiology of chronic nerve compression, what is the typical sequence of changes with increasing pressure/duration?

options.text: Impaired venular flow/endoneurial edema → segmental demyelination (conduction slowing) → axonal loss (denervation)
Immediate axonal transection, then demyelination
Muscle atrophy before any sensory change
Wallerian degeneration precedes edema

questions.explanation: Compression first raises endoneurial pressure, **impairing venular then arterial flow and causing endoneurial edema** (intermittent symptoms), progressing to **segmental demyelination (conduction slowing, constant paresthesia)** and finally **axonal loss with denervation (numbness, weakness, atrophy)**. Rising pressures (~20–30 mmHg impair flow; ~50 mmHg block conduction) drive this reversible-to-irreversible continuum.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: The 'double-crush' phenomenon describes:

options.text: A proximally compressed nerve being more susceptible to a second, distal compression (impaired axoplasmic flow at two sites)
Two nerves compressed at the same site
Crushing a nerve twice during surgery
Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome

questions.explanation: The **double-crush** hypothesis (Upton & McComas) holds that **impaired axonal transport from one compression site renders the nerve more vulnerable to a second site** — e.g., cervical radiculopathy plus CTS. It explains why some patients have symptoms out of proportion to a single lesion, and why proximal disease should be sought when a distal release underperforms.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: First-line NONoperative treatment for mild-to-moderate carpal tunnel syndrome is:

options.text: Neutral-position (night) wrist splinting, ± a corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel
Immediate open release in all cases
Wrist arthrodesis
Long-term oral corticosteroids

questions.explanation: For **mild-to-moderate CTS**, **neutral wrist splinting (especially at night)** and a **carpal-tunnel corticosteroid injection** provide symptom relief and can be diagnostic/prognostic (a good response predicts a good surgical outcome). **Surgical release** is offered for persistent symptoms, thenar atrophy, or denervation on EMG. Prolonged systemic steroids are not standard.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: During open carpal tunnel release, injury to which structure most likely causes painful numbness over the base of the thenar eminence (palmar skin)?

options.text: Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
Recurrent motor branch of the median nerve
Common digital nerve to the third web
Superficial palmar arch

questions.explanation: The **palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve** arises ~5 cm proximal to the wrist crease and runs superficial to the transverse carpal ligament to supply the **thenar/central palm skin**; injuring it (incision too radial) causes **painful palmar numbness/neuroma**. The **recurrent motor branch** injury instead weakens thumb opposition (thenar palsy). Incisions are kept slightly ulnar to the thenar crease to protect it.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: The recurrent (thenar) motor branch of the median nerve most commonly arises in which configuration relative to the transverse carpal ligament?

options.text: Extraligamentous (distal to the ligament) — the most common pattern
Transligamentous (piercing the ligament) — the most common
Subligamentous only
It always arises from the ulnar side of the median nerve

questions.explanation: In the Lanz classification, the recurrent motor branch is most often **extraligamentous (arising distal to the transverse carpal ligament, ~50%)**, then **subligamentous**, then **transligamentous** (piercing the ligament — at particular risk during release). Anomalous (e.g., ulnar-origin or high-division) patterns also occur. Awareness protects thumb opposition during carpal tunnel surgery.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient has persistent numbness after a carpal tunnel release. Nerve conduction studies were only mildly abnormal preoperatively. Which possibility should be strongly considered?

options.text: A more proximal median compression (e.g., pronator syndrome) or a second site (double crush) — and/or incomplete release
The diagnosis is certainly correct and no further evaluation is needed
Cubital tunnel syndrome
Trigger thumb

questions.explanation: Persistent median symptoms after release — particularly when NCS were only mildly abnormal — should prompt consideration of **incomplete release, a more proximal compression (pronator syndrome), a second site (double crush), or an alternative diagnosis (cervical radiculopathy)**. Pronator syndrome can have relatively normal wrist NCS, so it is easily missed.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient has forearm aching, median-distribution numbness INCLUDING the thenar palm, symptoms provoked by activity (not at night), and a negative Phalen test. Which diagnosis fits best?

options.text: Pronator syndrome (proximal median compression in the forearm)
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Cubital tunnel syndrome
Radial tunnel syndrome

questions.explanation: **Pronator syndrome** is proximal median compression producing **forearm pain, activity-related (not nocturnal) symptoms, and — because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the wrist and is involved — sensory changes over the THENAR palm** (spared in CTS). **Phalen is typically negative**. Compression sites include the ligament of Struthers/supracondylar process, lacertus fibrosus, the two heads of pronator teres, and the FDS arch.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which provocative maneuver, if it reproduces symptoms, implicates the FDS arch (sublimis bridge) as the compression site in pronator syndrome?

options.text: Resisted flexion of the FDS to the long finger
Resisted pronation with the elbow extended (pronator teres)
Resisted elbow flexion/supination (lacertus fibrosus)
Wrist flexion (Phalen)

questions.explanation: Site-specific provocation in pronator syndrome: **resisted FDS long-finger flexion → the FDS (sublimis) arch**; **resisted forearm pronation (elbow extended) → pronator teres**; **resisted elbow flexion/supination → lacertus fibrosus**; and pain with **elbow hyperflexion → ligament of Struthers/supracondylar process**. These localize the offending structure preoperatively.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient cannot make a normal 'OK' sign — the thumb IP and index DIP hyperextend during pinch — but has NO sensory loss. Which diagnosis is this?

options.text: Anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome — weakness of FPL and FDP to the index (± pronator quadratus)
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Ulnar tunnel syndrome
Radial tunnel syndrome

questions.explanation: The **AIN** is a pure motor branch of the median nerve supplying **FPL, FDP to the index (± long), and pronator quadratus**. Its palsy produces **weak thumb IP and index DIP flexion** (an abnormal, 'pinched'/hyperextended OK sign) with **NO sensory deficit**. Many cases are a **neuritis (Parsonage-Turner/neuralgic amyotrophy)** and recover spontaneously, so a period of observation is warranted before considering decompression.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient with a suspected AIN palsy has no clear compressive lesion. What is a reasonable initial management, and why?

options.text: Observation for several months, because many AIN palsies are a self-limited neuritis (neuralgic amyotrophy) that recovers spontaneously
Immediate exploration and decompression in all cases
Carpal tunnel release
Tendon transfer without delay

questions.explanation: Because a large proportion of AIN palsies represent **neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner)** rather than mechanical compression, **initial observation (often 3–6+ months) with serial exams/EMG** is appropriate; many recover spontaneously. Surgical exploration/decompression is reserved for a demonstrable compressive lesion or failure to recover.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A cyclist develops numbness of the ring and small fingers and weak intrinsics after long rides ('handlebar palsy'). Where is the lesion?

options.text: Ulnar nerve at Guyon's canal (wrist)
Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel (elbow)
Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
C8 nerve root

questions.explanation: **Handlebar palsy** is **ulnar nerve compression at Guyon's canal** (hypothenar/hamate region) from sustained pressure. Unlike cubital tunnel, the **dorsal cutaneous branch (arising proximal to the wrist) is spared**, so **dorsal ulnar hand sensation is normal** — a key localizing feature. Causes include ganglia, hook-of-hamate fracture, ulnar artery pathology, and repetitive pressure.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: In Guyon's canal, the ZONE of compression predicts the deficit. A purely MOTOR deficit (weak intrinsics) with normal sensation localizes to which zone?

options.text: Zone 2 (distal to the bifurcation, involving the deep motor branch)
Zone 1 (proximal, mixed motor and sensory)
Zone 3 (involving the superficial sensory branch only)
The dorsal cutaneous branch

questions.explanation: Guyon's canal zones: **Zone 1** (proximal to bifurcation) → **mixed motor + sensory**; **Zone 2** (deep motor branch) → **pure motor (intrinsic weakness, spared sensation)**; **Zone 3** (superficial branch) → **pure sensory**. A ganglion or hook-of-hamate fracture commonly compresses the **deep motor branch (zone 2)**, giving intrinsic weakness with intact sensation — an important localizing pattern.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient has numbness of the small and ulnar-ring fingers, weak grip, and worse symptoms with elbow flexion. The DORSAL ulnar hand is ALSO numb. Where is the ulnar nerve compressed?

options.text: Cubital tunnel (at the elbow) — the dorsal cutaneous branch arises distal to it, so dorsal hand numbness implies an elbow-level lesion
Guyon's canal (wrist)
Carpal tunnel
Radial tunnel

questions.explanation: **Cubital tunnel syndrome** (ulnar nerve at the elbow) worsens with **elbow flexion** and, crucially, involves the **dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve** (which arises ~5–7 cm proximal to the wrist), so **dorsal ulnar hand sensation is affected**. In **Guyon's canal (wrist)** lesions the dorsal branch is spared. This distinction localizes the lesion clinically.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which is a recognized site of ulnar nerve compression around the elbow in cubital tunnel syndrome?

options.text: Osborne's ligament (the FCU aponeurotic arcade) — the most common site
The arcade of Frohse
The lacertus fibrosus
The transverse carpal ligament

questions.explanation: Ulnar compression at the elbow occurs at several sites, most commonly **Osborne's ligament / the aponeurotic arcade between the two FCU heads**, and also the **arcade of Struthers, medial intermuscular septum, medial epicondyle (cubital tunnel retinaculum), and the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis distally**. The **arcade of Frohse** is a RADIAL-tunnel (PIN) site; the **lacertus fibrosus** is a median (pronator) site.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: The McGowan grading of cubital tunnel syndrome: which describes Grade III?

options.text: Motor weakness WITH intrinsic muscle wasting/atrophy
Intermittent paresthesia only, no weakness
Sensory loss with mild, measurable motor weakness but no atrophy
Normal exam with only electrodiagnostic changes

questions.explanation: **McGowan I** = sensory disturbance/paresthesia without weakness; **II** = intermediate, with measurable motor weakness (± some intrinsic involvement) but no wasting; **III** = **motor weakness WITH intrinsic muscle atrophy** (severe). Higher grades correlate with poorer recovery, so earlier decompression is favored before wasting develops.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: For idiopathic cubital tunnel syndrome without gross elbow instability or bony deformity, which surgical option has outcomes comparable to transposition with less dissection?

options.text: In situ decompression (simple release of the compressive structures)
Submuscular transposition in all cases
Medial epicondylectomy in all cases
Wrist-level release

questions.explanation: For **idiopathic cubital tunnel** without subluxation or deformity, **in situ decompression** yields outcomes comparable to transposition with **less dissection and devascularization**. **Anterior transposition (subcutaneous, intramuscular, or submuscular)** is chosen when the nerve subluxates, there is prior trauma/deformity, or in revisions; **medial epicondylectomy** is an alternative that removes the epicondyle to relieve tension/subluxation.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: The 'scratch collapse test' is used to help localize:

options.text: The site of a compressive neuropathy (e.g., cubital or carpal tunnel), by eliciting a brief loss of external-rotation resistance after scratching over the compressed nerve
Rotator cuff tears
Lateral epicondylitis only
Cervical instability

questions.explanation: In the **scratch collapse test**, the examiner lightly scratches the skin over a suspected compression site while the patient resists shoulder external rotation; a transient **collapse (loss of resistance)** suggests an allodynic response over the compressed nerve, helping **localize** the lesion (described for cubital and carpal tunnel). It complements Tinel/compression tests.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient has LATERAL forearm pain reproduced by resisted middle-finger extension and resisted supination, but NO motor weakness of finger/thumb extension. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.text: Radial tunnel syndrome (compression of the PIN causing pain without motor loss)
Posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) palsy
Lateral epicondylitis alone
De Quervain tenosynovitis

questions.explanation: **Radial tunnel syndrome** is compression of the **posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) in the radial tunnel**, causing **pain (over the mobile wad/proximal-dorsal forearm) WITHOUT motor deficit**; the **middle-finger extension test** and **resisted supination** provoke pain. Tenderness is typically **3–4 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle (over the supinator)**, distinguishing it from **lateral epicondylitis** (tenderness at the epicondyle). It commonly coexists with tennis elbow.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: The most common site of PIN compression within the radial tunnel is:

options.text: The arcade of Frohse (proximal edge of the supinator)
Osborne's ligament
The lacertus fibrosus
The transverse carpal ligament

questions.explanation: Within the radial tunnel, the PIN can be compressed by fibrous bands at the radiocapitellar joint, the **recurrent radial vessels (leash of Henry)**, the medial edge of **ECRB**, and — most commonly — the **arcade of Frohse (the fibrous proximal margin of the supinator)**. The same anatomy underlies **PIN palsy** (motor loss) and **radial tunnel syndrome** (pain).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient cannot extend the fingers/thumb at the MCP joints and the wrist extends with RADIAL deviation, but sensation is normal. Which lesion, and how is it distinguished from an extensor tendon rupture?

options.text: Posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) palsy; a tenodesis test (passive wrist flexion) produces finger extension if tendons are intact (nerve problem), but not if tendons are ruptured
Radial tunnel syndrome; confirmed by MRI
Cubital tunnel syndrome; confirmed by Froment sign
Carpal tunnel syndrome; confirmed by Phalen

questions.explanation: **PIN palsy** causes loss of **finger/thumb MCP extension** with **radial-deviated wrist extension** (ECRL, radial-nerve-proper, is spared while ECU is out) and **NO sensory loss**. The **tenodesis test** differentiates it from **extensor tendon rupture**: passively flexing the wrist should extend the fingers if the tendons are intact (nerve lesion), whereas ruptured tendons will not respond.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient has numbness/paresthesia over the dorsoradial hand and thumb, worsened by wrist flexion/ulnar deviation and forearm pronation. Which nerve is compressed (Wartenberg syndrome)?

options.text: Superficial branch of the radial nerve (between the brachioradialis and ECRL tendons)
Posterior interosseous nerve
Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
Dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve

questions.explanation: **Wartenberg syndrome (cheiralgia paresthetica)** is entrapment of the **superficial radial sensory nerve** where it emerges between the **brachioradialis and ECRL tendons** in the distal forearm; forearm pronation/wrist ulnar deviation compresses it (scissoring). It causes **dorsoradial hand/thumb sensory symptoms with no motor deficit** and can mimic or coexist with **de Quervain tenosynovitis** (a positive Finkelstein may be seen in both).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A Martin-Gruber anastomosis is important to recognize on electrodiagnostic testing because it:

options.text: Is a median-to-ulnar motor communication in the forearm that can alter expected patterns of weakness and confound NCS interpretation
Is an ulnar-to-median sensory branch in the palm
Causes carpal tunnel syndrome
Is a normal variant with no clinical relevance

questions.explanation: A **Martin-Gruber anastomosis** is a **median-to-ulnar motor crossover in the forearm** (often via AIN fibers) present in ~15–20% of people. It can make **ulnar-innervated intrinsics function despite a proximal ulnar lesion**, or produce confusing NCS findings, so recognizing it prevents misinterpretation. (The **Riche-Cannieu** anastomosis is an ulnar-to-median communication in the hand.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which electrodiagnostic finding is most consistent with carpal tunnel syndrome?

options.text: Prolonged median distal sensory and motor latencies across the wrist (with relative sparing of the ulnar nerve)
Prolonged ulnar latency across the elbow
Denervation of the pronator quadratus only
Normal median studies with abnormal radial studies

questions.explanation: CTS shows **focal slowing of median conduction across the wrist** — prolonged **distal sensory latency (often the earliest change) and distal motor latency**, with reduced amplitudes in severe/axonal cases — while the **ulnar nerve is comparatively normal** (useful internal control). Comparative median-vs-ulnar or median-vs-radial sensory studies increase sensitivity in mild cases.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient with cubital tunnel syndrome holds the small finger abducted and catches it on pockets (Wartenberg SIGN). This reflects weakness of:

options.text: The third palmar interosseous (ulnar), with unopposed EDM abducting the small finger
The abductor digiti minimi
The first dorsal interosseous
The extensor carpi ulnaris

questions.explanation: The **Wartenberg SIGN** (persistent small-finger abduction) results from **weak third palmar interosseous (ulnar-innervated adductor of the small finger)** with **unopposed EDM (radial)**. It is distinct from **Wartenberg SYNDROME** (superficial radial nerve entrapment) — a classic naming pitfall. Both reflect ulnar intrinsic weakness in cubital/ulnar neuropathy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which statement about endoscopic versus open carpal tunnel release is most accurate?

options.text: Both reliably relieve symptoms; endoscopic release may allow faster early recovery but carries a small risk of transient/iatrogenic nerve injury and incomplete release
Endoscopic release cures more patients long-term
Open release cannot fully divide the transverse carpal ligament
Endoscopic release has no risk of nerve injury

questions.explanation: **Long-term symptom relief is similar** for endoscopic and open carpal tunnel release. **Endoscopic** techniques may give **quicker early recovery/less pillar pain** but carry a small risk of **transient nerve injury or incomplete ligament division** if visualization is poor. The essential surgical goal in both is **complete division of the transverse carpal ligament** while protecting the median nerve, its recurrent motor branch, and the palmar cutaneous branch.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which nerve provides sensation that, if abnormal, argues AGAINST an isolated carpal tunnel syndrome and suggests a more proximal median lesion?

options.text: The palmar cutaneous branch (thenar palm sensation) — spared in CTS, involved in proximal median lesions
The proper digital nerve to the index
The dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve
The superficial radial nerve

questions.explanation: The **palmar cutaneous branch** arises **~5 cm proximal to the wrist and passes over (not through) the carpal tunnel**, so **thenar/central palm sensation is SPARED in CTS**. **Numbness of the thenar palm** therefore points to a **proximal median lesion (pronator syndrome)** or another cause — a valuable localizing clue.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient with cubital tunnel syndrome and a nerve that visibly subluxates over the medial epicondyle with flexion is best treated by:

options.text: Anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve (subcutaneous or submuscular)
In situ decompression alone
Carpal tunnel release
Observation

questions.explanation: When the ulnar nerve **subluxates/dislocates over the medial epicondyle** with elbow flexion (a source of recurrent friction/traction), **anterior transposition** relocates it anterior to the epicondyle, eliminating the subluxation — in situ decompression alone would leave the unstable nerve to keep subluxating. Options include **subcutaneous, intramuscular, or submuscular** transposition; **medial epicondylectomy** is an alternative.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A complication specific to ANTERIOR ulnar nerve transposition (compared with in situ decompression) is:

options.text: Creating a NEW compression/kink at the proximal or distal end of the transposition if the nerve is not fully mobilized and the fascial edges released
Injury to the recurrent median motor branch
Division of the transverse carpal ligament
Radial tunnel syndrome

questions.explanation: Transposition requires **extensive mobilization**; if the nerve is inadequately freed (e.g., the **medial intermuscular septum** left intact proximally, or a tight fascial sling distally), the transposed nerve can **kink or be newly compressed at the entry/exit points** — a cause of persistent/failed cubital tunnel surgery. This risk (and greater devascularization) is why **in situ decompression** is preferred when the nerve is stable.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: The 'elbow flexion test' for cubital tunnel syndrome is performed by:

options.text: Holding the elbow in maximal flexion (± wrist extension) for ~30–60 seconds to reproduce ulnar paresthesia
Compressing the carpal tunnel
Resisting middle-finger extension
Percussing the radial tunnel

questions.explanation: The **elbow flexion test** places the elbow in **maximal flexion** (often with wrist extension) for **30–60 seconds**; reproduction of **ulnar-distribution paresthesia** supports cubital tunnel syndrome (flexion tightens the cubital tunnel and stretches the nerve). Combined with **Tinel over the cubital tunnel** and the **scratch collapse test**, it aids clinical localization.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which finding distinguishes radial tunnel syndrome from lateral epicondylitis on examination?

options.text: Maximal tenderness ~3–4 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle (over the supinator/mobile wad) rather than at the epicondyle itself
Weakness of finger extension
A positive Finkelstein test
Sensory loss over the dorsal thumb

questions.explanation: Both cause lateral elbow pain and often coexist, but **radial tunnel tenderness is more DISTAL (~3–4 cm distal to the epicondyle, over the supinator)**, whereas **lateral epicondylitis is tender right at the epicondyle/ECRB origin**. Radial tunnel has **no motor weakness** (that would be PIN palsy) and is aggravated by **resisted supination/middle-finger extension**. Distinguishing them affects treatment and surgical planning.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: In severe carpal tunnel syndrome with thenar atrophy and long-standing denervation, an adjunct sometimes added to release is:

options.text: An opponensplasty (e.g., EIP or ring-FDS transfer) to restore thumb opposition
Wrist arthrodesis
Cubital tunnel release
A1 pulley release

questions.explanation: When the **recurrent motor branch has irreversibly denervated the thenar muscles** (fixed atrophy, poor opposition) and reinnervation after release is unlikely, an **opponensplasty (EIP, ring FDS, or ADM/Huber)** can restore thumb opposition. Release still decompresses the nerve; the transfer addresses the established motor deficit.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A ganglion or hook-of-hamate fracture causing an isolated motor ulnar deficit at the wrist would be evaluated with which imaging to identify the cause?

options.text: MRI or CT of the wrist (± ultrasound) to demonstrate a mass/ganglion or hamate hook fracture in Guyon's canal
Cervical spine MRI only
Chest radiograph
No imaging is ever indicated

questions.explanation: A space-occupying cause of ulnar neuropathy at Guyon's canal (deep motor branch, zone 2) — such as a **ganglion, hook-of-hamate fracture, or ulnar artery aneurysm/thrombosis** — is identified with **MRI/CT (and ultrasound/carpal-tunnel or hook-of-hamate views)**. Finding and treating the mass/fracture is essential; simple decompression without addressing the lesion would fail.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which statement about the timing of surgery relative to muscle atrophy in compression neuropathy is correct?

options.text: Decompression before fixed muscle atrophy/denervation offers better functional recovery; established atrophy predicts incomplete recovery
Outcome is independent of pre-existing atrophy
Surgery should be delayed until atrophy is complete
Atrophy always fully reverses after release

questions.explanation: As with all nerve compression, **decompressing before irreversible axonal loss/muscle atrophy** yields better recovery; once **fixed thenar or intrinsic atrophy** is present (severe CTS; McGowan III cubital tunnel), decompression may halt progression but **recovery of strength is often incomplete**, sometimes requiring tendon transfers. This drives earlier surgery for progressive motor deficits.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which pairing of nerve, common compression site, and hallmark deficit is correct?

options.text: Median at the carpal tunnel → transverse carpal ligament → thenar (APB) weakness with median sensory loss (sparing the palm)
Ulnar at Guyon's canal → arcade of Frohse → wrist drop
Radial (PIN) at the elbow → Osborne's ligament → clawing
Median (AIN) → cubital tunnel → sensory loss over the small finger

questions.explanation: Correct: **median at the carpal tunnel (transverse carpal ligament) → APB weakness + median sensory loss with a spared palm**. The distractors scramble anatomy: **arcade of Frohse is a PIN/radial-tunnel site**, **Osborne's ligament is a cubital-tunnel (ulnar) site**, and the **AIN is purely motor (no sensory loss)**. Matching nerve-site-deficit triads is a favorite exam pattern.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which is the LEAST appropriate initial step for a patient with mild, intermittent carpal tunnel symptoms and no thenar atrophy?

options.text: Immediate endoscopic carpal tunnel release
Night-time neutral wrist splinting
Activity modification and ergonomic advice
Consideration of a corticosteroid injection

questions.explanation: For **mild, intermittent CTS without atrophy**, jumping to **surgery is least appropriate** — a trial of **splinting, activity modification, and possibly a steroid injection** is first-line and often effective. Surgery is reserved for persistent symptoms despite conservative care, or for **motor deficit/thenar atrophy or denervation on EMG**.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient develops persistent 'pillar pain' (tenderness at the thenar/hypothenar bases) after open carpal tunnel release. This is best described as:

options.text: A common, usually self-limited postoperative phenomenon (pain at the divided ligament edges/palmar arch) that typically improves over weeks to months
A sign of median nerve transection
Recurrent carpal tunnel syndrome
A deep space infection

questions.explanation: **Pillar pain** — aching/tenderness at the **thenar and hypothenar pillars** after carpal tunnel release — is a **common, usually self-limited** issue (thought to relate to altered transverse arch mechanics/soft tissue), improving over **weeks to a few months** with therapy. It is distinguished from nerve injury (which causes numbness/motor loss), recurrence, or infection (erythema, discharge).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Persistent OR recurrent carpal tunnel syndrome after prior release differs in that:

options.text: 'Persistent' means symptoms never resolved (often incomplete release or wrong diagnosis); 'recurrent' means symptoms returned after an initial symptom-free interval (often scarring/tenosynovitis)
They are the same and managed identically
Persistent CTS is always due to a new proximal lesion
Recurrent CTS never requires surgery

questions.explanation: **Persistent** CTS (no symptom-free interval) suggests **incomplete ligament division, a missed proximal/second site, or a wrong diagnosis**, whereas **recurrent** CTS (return after relief) implies **perineural scarring/fibrosis or recurrent tenosynovitis**. This distinction guides revision — confirming complete release, imaging/EDX, and adding **coverage (e.g., hypothenar fat pad or synovial flap)** for scarred recurrent cases.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which nerve compression would MOST likely be missed by standard wrist-level nerve conduction studies?

options.text: Pronator syndrome / proximal median compression (wrist NCS may be relatively normal)
Severe carpal tunnel syndrome
Severe cubital tunnel syndrome with atrophy
Complete ulnar transection at the wrist

questions.explanation: **Pronator syndrome** (and other proximal, dynamic compressions) can have **relatively normal standard NCS**, so it is easily missed if the clinician relies on electrodiagnostics alone. Diagnosis rests on the **clinical pattern (forearm pain, thenar-palm sensory change, site-specific provocation, negative Phalen)**. Severe CTS and cubital tunnel typically show clear NCS abnormalities.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient with clawing of the ring and small fingers, a positive Froment sign, and weak pinch has an ulnar neuropathy. Which additional finding would localize the lesion to the ELBOW rather than the wrist?

options.text: Weakness of the flexor carpi ulnaris and FDP to the ring/small fingers, plus dorsal ulnar hand numbness
Preserved FCU and FDP with numbness only of the volar small finger
Thenar atrophy
Wrist drop

questions.explanation: An **elbow-level (cubital tunnel) ulnar lesion** weakens the **FCU and ulnar FDP (ring/small DIP flexion)** and involves the **dorsal cutaneous branch (dorsal ulnar hand numbness)** — all arising proximal to the wrist. A **wrist (Guyon's) lesion spares FCU/FDP and the dorsal branch**. Note the **ulnar paradox**: elbow lesions may claw LESS because the ulnar FDP is also weak.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which statement about corticosteroid injection for carpal tunnel syndrome is correct?

options.text: It often provides temporary relief and a good response predicts a favorable outcome from subsequent surgical release
It is curative in the majority of cases long-term
It should be injected directly into the median nerve
A poor response guarantees surgery will fail

questions.explanation: A **carpal-tunnel steroid injection** frequently gives **temporary symptom relief**, and a **good (even if transient) response is a positive prognostic indicator for surgical release**. It is injected **into the canal (ulnar to/around, not into, the median nerve)** to avoid nerve injury. Long-term cure from injection alone is uncommon, so it is a bridge/diagnostic aid rather than definitive treatment for most.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient has painless, progressive loss of thumb and finger EXTENSION developing over days, with normal sensation and a preceding viral illness/vaccination. Which diagnosis should be considered alongside PIN compression?

options.text: Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner syndrome) affecting the PIN/radial nerve
Carpal tunnel syndrome
Dupuytren disease
Trigger finger

questions.explanation: **Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage-Turner)** can present as a seemingly isolated **PIN or AIN palsy**, often after a **viral illness, vaccination, or severe pain prodrome**, and typically **recovers spontaneously**. Recognizing it (vs mechanical PIN compression) supports a period of **observation** rather than early exploration, similar to AIN neuritis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which overall principle guides the workup of a suspected compression neuropathy?

options.text: Localize the lesion by the pattern of motor/sensory deficits and provocation tests, consider a possible second (proximal) site, and confirm with electrodiagnostics/imaging when needed
Proceed directly to surgery without examination
Treat all upper-limb numbness as carpal tunnel syndrome
Ignore proximal sources of symptoms

questions.explanation: Sound evaluation **localizes the lesion** using the **distribution of sensory/motor findings and site-specific provocation tests**, **considers double-crush/proximal contributions (cervical spine, thoracic outlet)**, and uses **NCS/EMG and imaging selectively** to confirm and grade severity. Precise localization prevents the classic errors of missing a proximal lesion or over-diagnosing carpal tunnel syndrome.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: The intracarpal-canal pressure in carpal tunnel syndrome is characteristically:

options.text: Elevated at rest and rises further with wrist flexion/extension, exceeding levels that impair epineurial blood flow
Lower than normal
Unchanged by wrist position
Only elevated during sleep due to gravity

questions.explanation: In CTS, **resting carpal-canal pressure is elevated** (often ~30 mmHg vs a few mmHg normally) and **increases markedly with wrist flexion or extension**, exceeding the ~20–30 mmHg threshold that **impairs epineurial venular flow** and contributes to symptoms — the rationale for **neutral splinting**. Sustained high pressure drives the ischemia/edema cascade of chronic compression.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which finding would prompt evaluation for a proximal/systemic cause rather than a simple entrapment in a patient with bilateral hand numbness?

options.text: Symptoms/signs outside a single nerve's distribution, neck pain, or systemic features — suggesting radiculopathy, polyneuropathy, or double crush
Classic nocturnal median paresthesia relieved by shaking
A positive Durkan test
Isolated thenar atrophy

questions.explanation: Symptoms that **cross multiple nerve territories, involve the neck, or accompany systemic features** point beyond a single entrapment — toward **cervical radiculopathy, peripheral polyneuropathy (e.g., diabetic), or a double-crush** situation — and warrant broader evaluation. Classic isolated median findings (nocturnal paresthesia, positive compression test, thenar atrophy) support a straightforward CTS diagnosis.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: A patient with cubital tunnel syndrome asks about activity modification. Which advice directly targets the pathomechanics?

options.text: Avoid prolonged/repetitive elbow flexion and direct pressure on the elbow (e.g., leaning on it); use a night splint holding the elbow near extension
Keep the elbow maximally flexed at all times
Wear a wrist splint in flexion
Avoid all shoulder motion

questions.explanation: Because **elbow flexion tightens the cubital tunnel and stretches/compresses the ulnar nerve**, conservative care advises **avoiding sustained/repetitive flexion and direct elbow pressure**, plus a **night extension splint (~30–45°)** to keep the nerve slack while sleeping. This mirrors the neutral-splint logic used for carpal tunnel and can relieve mild cases.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: During PIN decompression for radial tunnel syndrome, which structure is the principal target for release?

options.text: The arcade of Frohse and the proximal edge of the supinator (± fibrous bands, ECRB edge, and the recurrent radial vessels)
The transverse carpal ligament
Osborne's ligament
The lacertus fibrosus

questions.explanation: Radial tunnel/PIN decompression releases the **arcade of Frohse and supinator margin** (the most common compressive band), and addresses the other radial-tunnel structures — **fibrous bands at the radiocapitellar joint, the leash of Henry (recurrent radial vessels), and the medial edge of ECRB**. This is the same anatomy released for a compressive PIN palsy.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: Which best distinguishes ulnar neuropathy at the wrist (Guyon's) from a C8/T1 radiculopathy, which can also weaken hand intrinsics?

options.text: Guyon's lesions spare the FCU/ulnar FDP and dorsal ulnar sensation and cause no neck symptoms; C8/T1 radiculopathy affects a broader (root) distribution with possible neck/arm pain
Both produce identical findings and cannot be distinguished
Guyon's lesions cause thenar atrophy
C8/T1 radiculopathy spares all hand muscles

questions.explanation: A **Guyon's (wrist) ulnar lesion** is confined to the distal ulnar distribution — **intrinsics ± hypothenar/volar small-finger sensation**, sparing **FCU, ulnar FDP, and the dorsal cutaneous branch**, with **no neck symptoms**. A **C8/T1 radiculopathy** affects a **root-level distribution** (median- and ulnar-innervated C8/T1 muscles) and may include **neck/radicular arm pain** — a key double-crush/differential consideration.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Ch. 28 (Compression Neuropathies)

questions.stem: How many **dorsal extensor compartments** are there at the wrist, and which tendons occupy the **first** compartment?

images.caption: Six dorsal extensor compartments at the wrist
images.alt: Cross-section of the dorsal wrist showing six extensor compartments

options.text: Six compartments; first contains APL and EPB
Four compartments; first contains ECRL and ECRB
Six compartments; first contains EPL alone
Five compartments; first contains FCR and PL

questions.explanation: There are **six** dorsal extensor compartments. The **first** contains **abductor pollicis longus (APL)** and **extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)** — the tendons involved in **de Quervain tenosynovitis**. (Compartment 3 holds EPL, which turns around Lister's tubercle; compartment 2 holds ECRL/ECRB.)
references: Netter, Atlas of Human Anatomy — Wrist

questions.stem: A laceration over the volar aspect of the **middle phalanx** of the ring finger divides the flexor digitorum profundus. In which flexor tendon zone (Verdan classification) does this injury lie?

images.caption: Verdan flexor tendon zones I–V
images.alt: Diagram of the palmar hand showing flexor tendon zones

options.text: Zone I
Zone II
Zone III
Zone IV

questions.explanation: **Zone II** extends from the distal palmar crease (proximal edge of the A1 pulley) to the insertion of flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) on the middle phalanx. Within this fibro-osseous sheath the FDS and FDP run together, so repairs here historically had poor outcomes — Bunnell's **"no man's land."** Modern core + epitendinous suture techniques and early active motion have greatly improved results.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Flexor Tendon

questions.stem:
## Flexor pulley system

The flexor sheath is reinforced by **annular (A1–A5)** and **cruciate (C1–C3)** pulleys.

- The **A2** (over proximal phalanx) and **A4** (over middle phalanx) pulleys are the most biomechanically important — losing them causes tendon **bowstringing**.
- The **A1 pulley** at the MCP joint is the site released in **trigger finger** surgery.

Preserve A2 and A4 whenever possible during tendon repair and sheath surgery.
references: Doyle JR. Anatomy of the flexor tendon sheath and pulley system.

questions.stem: A patient reports numbness of the **thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger**, worse at night, with a positive Phalen test. Which nerve is compressed, and where?

images.caption: Carpal tunnel cross-section
images.alt: Cross-section of the carpal tunnel showing the median nerve and flexor tendons

options.text: Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
Ulnar nerve at Guyon's canal
Median nerve at the pronator teres
Radial nerve in the radial tunnel

questions.explanation: This is classic **carpal tunnel syndrome** — compression of the **median nerve** beneath the transverse carpal ligament. The tunnel contains **9 flexor tendons** (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL) plus the median nerve. The **ulnar nerve travels through Guyon's canal**, superficial to the transverse carpal ligament, and is therefore spared.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Compression Neuropathies

questions.stem: A high-energy fracture of the **mid-shaft humerus** injures the radial nerve. Select **all** deficits you would expect. *(Choose every correct option.)*

options.text: Wrist drop (loss of wrist extension)
Inability to extend the MCP joints
Loss of thumb opposition
Numbness of the dorsal first web space
Clawing of the ring and little fingers

questions.explanation: The **radial nerve** supplies the wrist and finger extensors, so injury produces **wrist drop** and loss of **MCP extension**, plus sensory loss over the **dorsal first web space**. Thumb **opposition** is a **median** (recurrent motor branch) function, and **clawing** of the ring/little fingers is an **ulnar** nerve sign — neither is caused by radial nerve injury.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Radial Nerve

questions.stem: An elderly patient falls onto an outstretched hand. Radiographs show a distal radius fracture with **dorsal angulation** of the distal fragment ("dinner-fork" deformity). What is the eponym?

images.caption: Colles fracture — dorsal angulation
images.alt: Lateral wrist radiograph schematic showing dorsal angulation of the distal radius

options.text: Colles fracture
Smith fracture
Barton fracture
Galeazzi fracture

questions.explanation: A **Colles fracture** is an extra-articular distal radius fracture with **dorsal** displacement/angulation, typically from a FOOSH in osteoporotic bone. A **Smith** fracture is the reverse (volar angulation). A **Barton** fracture is an intra-articular rim fracture with carpal subluxation; a **Galeazzi** injury is a radial shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint disruption.
references: Rockwood & Green's Fractures in Adults — Distal Radius

questions.stem: A young man has wrist pain and **anatomic snuffbox tenderness** after a fall, but initial radiographs are normal. Which statement about the likely fracture is correct?

options.text: The scaphoid is involved; the proximal pole is at risk of avascular necrosis
The lunate is involved; it never develops avascular necrosis
The triquetrum is involved; it is the most commonly fractured carpal bone
No fracture is possible if initial X-rays are normal

questions.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness signals a **scaphoid fracture** — the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Its blood supply enters **distally and runs retrograde**, so **proximal pole** fractures risk **avascular necrosis** and non-union. Initial films are often normal: immobilize and re-image (or obtain MRI/CT) rather than clear the patient. (Avascular necrosis of the **lunate** is Kienböck disease.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Carpal Fractures

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man of Northern European descent has a painless **firm cord** in the palm and a progressive **flexion contracture** of the ring finger MCP joint. The predominant cell type driving this disease is:

options.text: Myofibroblast
Osteoblast
Chondrocyte
Mast cell

questions.explanation: This is **Dupuytren disease** — a proliferative fibromatosis of the **palmar fascia** driven by **myofibroblasts** (which express α-smooth-muscle actin and generate the contractile force). It most often affects the **ring and little fingers**, causing **MCP and PIP** flexion contractures. The positive tabletop test (inability to lay the hand flat) is a common surgical threshold.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Dupuytren

questions.stem: A new mother presents with radial-sided wrist pain and a **positive Finkelstein test**. Which structure is inflamed?

options.text: The first dorsal compartment (APL and EPB)
The A1 pulley of the thumb
The extensor pollicis longus at Lister's tubercle
The triangular fibrocartilage complex

questions.explanation: **De Quervain tenosynovitis** is stenosing tenosynovitis of the **first dorsal compartment**, which contains **APL** and **EPB**. The **Finkelstein / Eichhoff** maneuver (thumb in fist, ulnar deviation) reproduces the pain. First-line care is a thumb spica splint and a corticosteroid injection into the compartment; surgical release is reserved for refractory cases (watch for a septum separating the EPB subsheath).
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Tendinopathies

questions.stem: A patient's finger painfully **catches and locks** in flexion, releasing with a snap. Palpation reveals a tender nodule at the distal palm. Surgical treatment releases which structure?

options.text: The A1 pulley
The A2 pulley
The transverse carpal ligament
The extensor retinaculum

questions.explanation: **Trigger finger** (stenosing flexor tenosynovitis) is a size mismatch between the flexor tendon and the **A1 pulley** at the MCP level. Release of the **A1 pulley** is curative. The **A2** pulley must be **preserved** to prevent bowstringing. Non-operative options include a corticosteroid injection into the sheath and splinting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Trigger Finger
